D) 4.50 is not the average of the two pKa values. Trap: Using the difference of the two pKa values, or assuming the pI is neutral pH 7, instead of averaging pKa1 and pKa2.

qs.q: Which of the following statements about pKa values is incorrect?
o: pKa values are independent of ionic strength.
The isoelectric point is the pH at which the net charge is zero.
The α‑carboxyl group has a lower pKa than the α‑amino group.
A basic amino acid has a pI greater than 7.
qs.x: Correct: A) is the incorrect statement; pKa values shift with ionic strength and temperature. Why the others are wrong: B) The pI is by definition the pH of zero net charge. C) The alpha-carboxyl (about 2.2) has a lower pKa than the alpha-amino group (about 9.5). D) A basic amino acid such as lysine has a pI above 7 (9.74). Trap: Assuming pKa is a fixed constant of a group that is unaffected by ionic strength or temperature.

qs.q: Which amino acid side chain most commonly acts as a proton shuttle in enzyme active sites near physiological pH?
qs.x: Correct: A) Histidine's imidazole pKa (about 6) lets it act as both proton donor and acceptor near physiological pH. Why the others are wrong: B) Lysine (pKa about 10.5) is almost always protonated at pH 7.4. C) Aspartate (pKa about 3.9) is almost always deprotonated at pH 7.4. D) Leucine has no ionizable side chain. Trap: Picking lysine because it is basic; its pKa of about 10.5 is far from physiological pH, so it is rarely switching protonation state there.

passages.title: Research design and data reasoning (all science sections) · passage
text: Researchers at the University of BioChem conducted a systematic titration study to determine the pKa values of the side chains of lysine and arginine across a temperature range of 4 °C to 60 °C. Using a calibrated pH electrode and a buffer system that maintained ionic strength at 0.1 M, they recorded the pH at which the first, second, and third protonation events occurred. The data were plotted as titration curves, and the inflection points were identified by the first derivative of the pH vs. added base curve. The resulting pKa values were compiled in Table 1. The experiment demonstrated that the pKa of the ε‑amino group of lysine decreased by about 0.26 pH units per 10 °C increase, whereas the guanidinium group of arginine remained essentially unchanged. These observations provide insight into how temperature influences the ionization behavior of basic amino acids and help refine models of protein folding under physiological and non‑physiological conditions.

qs.q: Which variable was manipulated by the researchers to observe changes in the pKa values?
o: Method used to locate the inflection points
qs.x: Correct: B. The study varied temperature (4 to 60 °C) and recorded the pKa values at each temperature; temperature is the independent variable. Why the others are wrong: A) pH is the response measured during each titration, not the condition imposed to test pKa changes. C) ionic strength was held at 0.1 M. D) the inflection points were located by the first-derivative method for every curve, so the method was constant. Trap: Treating a measured or held-constant quantity such as pH or ionic strength as the variable the researchers changed, instead of temperature.

qs.q: If the temperature were increased from 25 °C to 70 °C, what would most likely happen to the pKa of lysine’s ε‑amino side chain?
o: It would increase by about 1.2 pH units
It would decrease by about 1.2 pH units
qs.x: van ’t Hoff: d(pKa)/dT = −ΔH°/(2.303 R T²); for an ammonium group ΔH° ≈ +45 kJ/mol, so pKa falls by about 0.026 per K, whereas carboxylic acids (ΔH° ≈ 0) barely change. Over 45 K: ΔpKa ≈ −0.026 × 45 ≈ −1.2. Trap: Choosing C (no change) because the passage says arginine stays unchanged, even though lysine's ε-amino pKa is stated to fall about 0.26 per 10 °C.

qs.q: What is the theoretical isoelectric point (pI) of lysine based on the pKa values provided?
qs.x: Correct: B. Lysine's net charge is zero between the deprotonation of the α-ammonium (pKa2 = 8.95) and of the side-chain ammonium (pKa3 = 10.53), so pI = (8.95 + 10.53)/2 = 9.74. Why the others are wrong: A) 8.95 is only pKa2. C) 10.53 is only pKa3. D) 9.04 is arginine's pKa2 and is not a lysine value. Trap: Reporting a single pKa (8.95 or 10.53) as the pI instead of averaging the two pKa values that flank the neutral species.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage?
o: Ionic strength was held at 0.1 M while temperature was varied.
The pKa of lysine's ε-amino side chain decreases with increasing temperature.
The pKa of arginine's guanidinium group fell by about 0.26 pH units per 10 °C, like lysine's ε-amino group.
The side-chain pKa of arginine (12.48) is higher than that of lysine (10.53).
qs.x: Correct: C. The passage says the guanidinium pKa of arginine remained essentially unchanged with temperature, so a 0.26 per 10 °C fall is not supported. Why the others are wrong: A) the buffer system maintained ionic strength at 0.1 M. B) the passage reports a decrease of about 0.26 per 10 °C for lysine. D) Table 1 lists 12.48 for arginine and 10.53 for lysine. Trap: Transferring the lysine temperature dependence to arginine, although the passage says the guanidinium pKa stayed essentially unchanged.

qs.q: At pH 4.0, a protein with pI 6.0 will carry a net charge and migrate toward which electrode in an electric field?
o: No charge; it does not migrate
qs.x: Correct: A. Below its pI (pH 4 < 6) the protein has taken up protons and carries a net positive charge, so it migrates toward the negative electrode (cathode). Why the others are wrong: B) a negative charge would require pH above the pI, and negative species move toward the anode. C) the charge is positive but cations move toward the cathode, not the anode. D) the protein is neutral only at pH = pI (6.0), not at pH 4. Trap: Mixing up the electrode names: cations are attracted to the cathode (negative electrode), so a positively charged protein does not move toward the anode.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers studied the titration of eight common amino acids to determine their side‑chain pKa values and isoelectric points (pI). Each amino acid was dissolved in water at pH 1.0 and titrated with 0.1 M NaOH while continuously measuring the pH with a calibrated electrode. The titration curves were plotted, and the inflection points were used to calculate the pKa values of the side chains. The side‑chain values were then combined with the α‑COOH and α‑NH3⁺ pKa values in the table to compute the pI of each amino acid. The experiment was performed in triplicate to ensure reproducibility; the final values agreed with published literature values. The results confirmed that basic residues such as lysine and arginine have high pI values, whereas acidic residues like aspartate and glutamate have low pI values.

qs.q: Which amino acid has the highest side‑chain pKa value according to the data?
qs.x: Correct: The table lists arginine's side-chain pKa as 12.5, the highest of the eight amino acids (lysine 10.5, tyrosine 10.1, histidine 6.0). Why the others are wrong: A) Lysine's side-chain pKa is 10.5, lower than arginine's. C) Histidine's side-chain pKa is only 6.0. D) Tyrosine's side-chain pKa is 10.1. Trap: Lysine is the best-known basic residue, so students pick it without reading the table; its side-chain pKa (10.5) is lower than arginine's (12.5).

qs.q: If the researchers wanted to determine the pI of a new amino acid with an unknown side‑chain pKa, which experimental approach would be most appropriate?
o: Measure the pH of a 0.1 M solution at room temperature and record the value.
Perform a full titration curve and identify both α‑COOH and α‑NH3⁺ pKa values.
Use a spectrophotometer to detect absorption changes at 280 nm.
Calculate the pI directly from the amino acid’s molecular weight.
qs.x: Correct: A full titration curve gives the pKa of every ionizable group (alpha-COOH, alpha-NH3+ and the side chain) from its inflection points or half-equivalence points, which is what is needed to compute pI. Why the others are wrong: A) A single pH reading gives no pKa values. C) Absorbance at 280 nm reports on aromatic residues, not on ionization constants. D) Molecular weight does not determine the ionizable groups or pI. Trap: Students think a single pH reading of the solution gives the pI, but pI requires the pKa values of the groups flanking the neutral species, obtained from a titration curve.

qs.q: Using the table, calculate the isoelectric point (pI) of lysine.
qs.x: For lysine the neutral species lies between the α‑NH₃⁺ (9.0) and side-chain (10.5) pKa values: pI = (9.0 + 10.5)/2 = 9.75. Trap: Students may mistakenly average the α‑COOH pKa with the side‑chain pKa instead of the two basic pKa values.

qs.q: The pKa of an acid is expressed in which units?
qs.x: pKa = −log10 Ka is dimensionless. Trap: Because pKa depends on temperature, students assume it carries Kelvin units; but pKa is the negative log of a unitless quantity and has no units.

qs.q: Buffering capacity of an ionizable group is greatest at which pH?
o: Two pH units above its pKa
Two pH units below its pKa
At the pH where it is fully deprotonated
qs.x: By Henderson–Hasselbalch, at pH = pKa the acid and conjugate base are equal, so the solution resists added acid or base best (within about ±1 pH unit of the pKa). Trap: Students pick the fully deprotonated form (D) or a point far from the pKa, but buffering is best only where acid and conjugate base are about equal, at pH near pKa.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers investigated the acid–base properties of three common amino acids—glycine, alanine, and lysine—by performing standard titrations with 0.1 M NaOH. Each amino acid was dissolved to a final concentration of 0.1 M in deionized water, and the pH was recorded continuously with a calibrated glass electrode as NaOH was added in 0.5 mL increments. The resulting titration curves showed two distinct buffering regions for glycine and alanine (carboxyl and amino groups) and three for lysine, which also has a side-chain amino group with a third pKa of 10.53. From the curves the researchers calculated the first and second pKa values (pKa1 and pKa2) and the isoelectric point (pI) for each amino acid (for lysine, pI is the average of pKa2 and the side-chain pKa3). The data are summarized in Table 1. The experiment demonstrates how the relative strengths of the acidic and basic groups determine the pI, and it provides a practical example of the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation in action.

qs.q: Which amino acid has the highest isoelectric point (pI) according to the data?
qs.x: Correct: Lysine has the highest pI (9.74), versus 5.97 for glycine and 6.02 for alanine, because its extra basic side chain raises the pH at which the net charge is zero. Why the others are wrong: A) Glycine's pI is 5.97. B) Alanine's pI is 6.02. D) Histidine is not in the data set, so the table cannot show it has the highest pI. Trap: Choosing glycine or alanine by comparing only pKa1 values, which are nearly the same for all three, instead of reading the pI column.

qs.q: If the researchers had used 0.05 M NaOH instead of 0.1 M NaOH, what would happen to the shape of the titration curve?
o: The curve would shift to the right (more NaOH required).
The curve would shift to the left (less NaOH required).
The curve would become steeper at the equivalence points.
qs.x: Correct: Halving the NaOH concentration means twice the volume is needed to deliver the same moles of base, so the whole curve shifts to the right along the volume axis. Why the others are wrong: B) Less volume would be needed only with a more concentrated base. C) The pH values stay the same but the volume axis is stretched, so the curve is not unchanged. D) Steepness at the equivalence points is set by the amino acid's buffering, not made greater by dilute titrant. Trap: Assuming the curve is independent of titrant concentration because the pKa values, read off the pH axis, do not change.

qs.q: Using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, what is the ratio [deprotonated amino group]/[protonated amino group] for glycine at pH 8.60 (pKa2 = 9.60)?
qs.x: Correct: pH = pKa + log(base/acid), so log(ratio) = 8.60 − 9.60 = −1 and the ratio is 0.1. Why the others are wrong: B) A ratio of 1 occurs only when pH equals pKa2 (9.60). C) A ratio of 10 would need pH 10.60. D) A ratio of 0.01 would need pH 7.60. Trap: Inverting the ratio (acid over base) and answering 10, or forgetting that one pH unit below the pKa gives a tenfold, not a hundredfold, difference.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: For simple amino acids, the pI is the average of pKa1 and pKa2.
pKa values are independent of ionic strength.
The titration curve of lysine shows three buffering regions.
The pH at the half‑equivalence point of the first buffering region equals pKa1.
qs.x: Correct: pKa values shift with ionic strength and temperature, so B is the incorrect statement. Why the others are wrong: A) For an amino acid with two ionizable groups the pI is the average of the two pKa values. C) Lysine has three ionizable groups and so three buffering regions. D) At half-equivalence of the first region, acid and conjugate base are equal, so pH = pKa1. Trap: Treating pKa values as fixed constants of the molecule and overlooking the effect of ionic strength and temperature on the measured value.

qs.q: Which concept is directly linked to the information presented in this passage?
qs.x: Correct: pKa, pI and titration curves all describe acid–base equilibria of ionizable groups. Why the others are wrong: A) Protein folding is not addressed by free amino acid titration data. B) Enzyme catalysis is not studied here. D) DNA replication is unrelated. Trap: Picking a broad, familiar biochemistry topic such as protein folding or enzyme catalysis instead of the concept the titration data directly measure.

passages.title: Research design and data reasoning (all science sections) · passage
text: Researchers performed a titration experiment to determine the pKa and pI values of glycine, lysine, and aspartic acid. Each amino acid (0.1 M) was dissolved in unbuffered 0.1 M NaCl (background electrolyte). A calibrated NaOH solution (0.1 M) was added in 0.5 mL increments while the pH was recorded after each addition. The resulting titration curves were plotted as pH versus volume of NaOH added. The midpoint of each buffering region (where the pH change per added volume is minimal) was taken as the pKa of the corresponding functional group. The pI was calculated by averaging the pH values at which the net charge of the amino acid is zero. The experiment was repeated three times to assess reproducibility. The data were tabulated and used to validate Henderson–Hasselbalch calculations and to illustrate the influence of ionic strength on acid–base equilibria.

qs.q: Which variable was manipulated by the researchers during the titration?
qs.x: Correct: B) The experimenter chose how much 0.1 M NaOH to add (0.5 mL increments); pH was then recorded in response, so volume of NaOH is the manipulated (independent) variable. Why the others are wrong: A) pH is the measured response. C) Time was not varied as a treatment. D) Temperature was not manipulated. Trap: Choosing pH as the manipulated variable because it is the quantity plotted and recorded most often, when it is the measured response to the NaOH volume added.

qs.q: If the ionic strength of the solution were increased, what would most likely happen to the apparent pKa of the α‑NH₃⁺ group of glycine?
qs.x: Extended Debye–Hückel: pKa′ = pKa + A(2z − 1)√I/(1 + √I), where z is the net charge of the acid form and A ≈ 0.51 at 25 °C. At I = 0.1 M the shift is about ±0.1 pH unit per unit of (2z − 1). For α‑NH₃⁺ the acid form is the zwitterion (net 0, 2z − 1 = −1), so pKa₂′ decreases slightly with ionic strength. Trap: Believing that more salt makes the amine group more acidic or leaves it unchanged; for a zwitterionic acid form (net charge 0) added ions stabilize the charged conjugate base, lowering the apparent pKa slightly rather than raising it or leaving it unchanged.

qs.q: Using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, what is the pH when the α‑COOH group of glycine is 50 % neutralized?
qs.x: Correct: A) At 50% neutralization of the alpha-carboxyl group [A-]/[HA] = 1, so pH = pKa + log(1) = 2.34. Why the others are wrong: B) 5.97 is the pI, where the net charge is zero, not the carboxyl pKa. C) 9.60 is the pKa of the amino group. D) 7.00 is neutral pH and has no link to this group. Trap: Students may mistakenly use the pI (5.97) instead of the α‑COOH pKa.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes the units of a pKa value?
o: pKa is expressed in joules per mole (J/mol)
pKa is expressed in kilocalories per mole (kcal/mol)
pKa is expressed in moles per liter (mol/L)
qs.x: Correct: D) pKa = -log10(Ka) is a logarithm of a ratio of activities, so it is a pure number with no units. Why the others are wrong: A) J/mol would be an energy unit such as the free energy, which is related to pKa but is not pKa itself. B) kcal/mol is likewise an energy unit. C) mol/L is the unit of concentration, not of a negative logarithm. Trap: Confusing pKa with the free energy change or with Ka concentration units; taking the logarithm removes any units, so pKa is dimensionless.

qs.q: Why is the solubility of a protein usually lowest at its isoelectric point?
o: Net charge is zero, so electrostatic repulsion between molecules is minimal and aggregation is favored
The protein is fully denatured at its pI
The protein carries maximum positive charge at its pI
Water cannot hydrate a neutral protein at all
qs.x: Correct: A) At the pI the net charge is zero, so repulsion between protein molecules is minimal and aggregation and precipitation are favored. Why the others are wrong: B) The protein is not necessarily denatured at its pI. C) The net charge is zero at the pI, not maximal. D) A neutral protein still has polar surface groups and is hydrated; solubility is lowest, not absent. Trap: Thinking that zero net charge means the protein is denatured or cannot bind water at all; the pI only removes electrostatic repulsion between molecules, so aggregation is favored.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers at the University of Example conducted a titration study to determine the acid‑base properties of glycine, the simplest amino acid. In a 0.01 M glycine solution, a strong base (NaOH) was added incrementally while the pH was recorded after each addition. The experiment was performed at 25 °C, and the ionic strength was maintained at 0.1 M by adding NaCl to minimize activity coefficient effects. The resulting titration curve shows two distinct buffering regions corresponding to the carboxyl (pKa ≈ 2.34) and amino (pKa ≈ 9.60) functional groups. To aid in data interpretation, the researchers compiled a table of pH values versus the fraction of each group that is protonated or deprotonated, as well as the net charge of the glycine molecule at each pH. This table is provided below and will be referenced in the following questions.

qs.q: Which pH value corresponds to 50 % ionization of the carboxyl group of glycine?
qs.x: Correct: B) A group is 50% ionized at pH = pKa, so the carboxyl group of glycine (pKa 2.34) is half ionized at about pH 2.3. Why the others are wrong: A) at pH 2.0 only about 31% is ionized. C) at pH 3.0 about 82% is ionized. D) at pH 3.5 about 94% is ionized. Trap: Misinterpreting the midpoint of the titration curve instead of using the precise pKa.

qs.q: If the researchers increased the ionic strength of the solution to 0.5 M, what would happen to the observed pKa of the carboxyl group?
o: Not supported: the charges on both sides of the dissociation offset, so salt screening barely moves the pKa.
Not supported: the same offset applies, so the pKa does not drop.
Correct: the acid form (net +1) and the products (zwitterion plus H+, net +1) carry the same total charge, so salt affects both sides about equally.
The breadth of the transition is set by the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship, not by salt.
qs.x: For glycine's carboxyl group the acid form carries a net charge of +1 and the products (the zwitterion plus H+) also carry a total of +1. Because the charges on the two sides match, extra salt screens both sides about equally and the pKa barely moves. The best answer is no meaningful change. Trap: assuming that more salt must shift the pKa up or down.

qs.q: Using the Henderson‑Hasselbalch equation, calculate the net charge of glycine at pH 7.0.
qs.x: Correct: B) At pH 7.0 the carboxyl group (−1) is deprotonated and the amino group (+1) is protonated, so the net charge is 0. Why the others are wrong: A) −1 would require the amino group to be deprotonated, which needs a pH well above 9.6. C) +1 would require the carboxyl group to be protonated, which needs a pH below 2.34. D) +2 is impossible for glycine, whose maximum charge is +1. Trap: Applying the equation to only one group instead of both.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a molar concentration unit?
qs.x: Correct: D) mg/mL is a mass concentration, not a molar concentration. Why the others are wrong: A) µM is micromolar. B) mM is millimolar. C) mmol/L is the same unit as mM, a molar concentration. Trap: Assuming mg/mL is acceptable for molarity calculations.

qs.q: A protein with pI 9.0 is applied in pH 7.4 buffer. Which column would retain it?
o: A size-exclusion column that binds by charge
Neither; proteins never bind ion exchangers
qs.x: At pH 7.4 (< pI 9.0) the protein has a net positive charge and binds a negatively charged cation exchanger (e.g., carboxymethyl); it would be eluted with higher salt or higher pH. Trap: Choosing the anion exchanger because a pI of 9.0 sounds basic; at pH 7.4 the protein is below its pI, so it is positive and would be repelled by a positive resin.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers at the University of Chemville investigated the acid–base properties of lysine using a classical titration. A 25 mL solution of 0.1 M lysine dihydrochloride (fully protonated, net charge +2; 2.5 mmol) was titrated with 0.1 M NaOH while the pH was recorded with a calibrated electrode at 25 °C. The titration curve showed three buffering regions, corresponding to deprotonation of the α‑carboxyl group (pKa₁ = 2.18), the α‑ammonium group (pKa₂ = 8.95), and the ε‑ammonium side chain (pKa₃ = 10.53). Because each group contains 2.5 mmol of acid, each requires 25 mL of NaOH, and each pKa is found at the half‑equivalence point (12.5, 37.5 and 62.5 mL). The investigators tabulated the volume of NaOH added, the pH, and the predominant species. Table 1 gives the data.

qs.q: Which volume of NaOH added corresponds to the first pKa (α‑carboxyl) of lysine?
qs.x: A pKa is read at the half-equivalence point: half of the 25 mL needed to titrate the carboxyl group is 12.5 mL, where pH = pKa₁ = 2.18. Trap: Reading the equivalence point (25 mL) instead of the half-equivalence point.

qs.q: If the researchers added a 0.1 M phosphate buffer to the lysine solution before titration, what would be the most likely effect on the titration curve?
o: The curve would be flatter, with an added buffering plateau near pH 7
The overall slope of the curve would become steeper
The volume of NaOH required to reach the third inflection would decrease
The curve would show no change in inflection points
qs.x: Phosphate adds its own buffering region (pKa₂ ≈ 7.2) and flattens the curve; it does not change the intrinsic pKa values of lysine. Trap: Thinking an added buffer sharpens the curve or lowers the NaOH needed, when phosphate adds its own buffering near pH 7 and flattens the curve.

qs.q: Using the data, calculate the isoelectric point (pI) of lysine.
qs.x: Net charge is zero between pKa₂ (α‑NH₃⁺, 8.95) and pKa₃ (ε‑NH₃⁺, 10.53): pI = (8.95 + 10.53)/2 = 9.74, the pH at the second equivalence point (50 mL). Trap: Averaging the wrong pair of pKa values, such as pKa₁ and pKa₂ (5.57).

qs.q: Which statement is NOT supported by Table 1?
o: The pH equals pKa₁ (2.18) at the half-equivalence point of 12.5 mL.
At 37.5 mL the solution is a 1:1 mixture of the +1 and neutral forms.
The pH at 50.0 mL (9.74) lies midway between pKa₂ and pKa₃.
The pH at 25.0 mL equals pKa₁.
qs.x: Correct: At 25.0 mL the pH is 5.57, not 2.18; pKa₁ is read at the half-equivalence point (12.5 mL). Why the others are wrong: A) the table lists pH 2.18 at 12.5 mL, so it is supported. B) the table lists a +1/0 (1:1) mixture with pH 8.95 at 37.5 mL, so it is supported. C) (8.95 + 10.53)/2 = 9.74, matching the table, so it is supported. Trap: Reading the first equivalence point as the pKa, when pKa values are read at half-equivalence points and the 25.0 mL pH (5.57) lies between pKa₁ and pKa₂.

qs.q: Which species predominates at the second equivalence point (50.0 mL, pH 9.74) of the lysine titration?
qs.x: At pH 9.74, between pKa₂ (8.95) and pKa₃ (10.53), the α‑amino group has lost its proton but the ε‑amino group has not: COO⁻, α‑NH₂, ε‑NH₃⁺, net charge 0, the isoelectric species. Trap: Choosing the +1 form (the species at the first equivalence point).

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers investigated the acid–base properties of five common amino acids—glycine, alanine, glutamic acid, lysine, and histidine—using potentiometric titration. Each amino acid was dissolved in 0.01 M aqueous solution and titrated with 0.1 M NaOH while the pH was recorded at 25 °C. A glass electrode calibrated with standard buffers (pH 4.0, 7.0, 10.0) was employed to ensure accurate measurements. The resulting titration curves displayed the characteristic inflection points corresponding to the dissociation of the α‑carboxyl, side‑chain, and α‑ammonium groups. From the curves, the researchers calculated the pKa values for each functional group and derived the isoelectric point (pI) as the average of the two pKa values that bracket a net zero charge. The data are summarized in the table below. This experimental setup allows comparison of how side‑chain chemistry influences the overall charge state of the amino acid across the physiological pH range.

qs.q: Which amino acid has the highest isoelectric point (pI) based on the data presented?
qs.x: Correct: D) Lysine pI = (8.95 + 10.53)/2 = 9.74, the highest in the table because its side chain adds a second positive charge that persists to high pH. Why the others are wrong: A) Glycine has pI 5.97. B) Alanine has pI 6.01. C) Glutamic acid, with an acidic side chain, has the lowest pI (3.22). Trap: Averaging the wrong pair of pKa values for lysine; the pI is the average of the two pKa values that bracket the neutral form (8.95 and 10.53), not of the carboxyl and ammonium groups.

qs.q: At pH 9.60, what is the ratio of deprotonated (–NH₂) to protonated (–NH₃⁺) α-amino groups in a glycine solution?
qs.x: Correct: B) The α-NH₃⁺ pKa of glycine is 9.60, so at pH 9.60 log([base]/[acid]) = 0 and the ratio is 1 : 1. Why the others are wrong: A) 1 : 10 would be found at pH 8.60. C) 10 : 1 would be found at pH 10.60. D) 1 : 100 would be found at pH 7.60. Trap: Thinking the group is fully protonated or deprotonated at its pKa; at pH = pKa the group is exactly half ionized.

qs.q: Calculate the isoelectric point (pI) of glutamic acid using the pKa values provided.
qs.x: Correct: A) Glutamic acid is acidic, so its neutral form lies between the loss of the α-carboxyl proton and the side-chain proton: pI = (2.19 + 4.25)/2 = 3.22. Why the others are wrong: B) 5.00 is not the average of any bracketing pair of pKa values. C) 5.93 is (2.19 + 9.67)/2, which wrongly uses the α-NH₃⁺ pKa. D) 7.59 is the pI of histidine. Trap: Averaging the α-COOH and α-NH₃⁺ pKa values (giving about 5.9) instead of the α-COOH and side-chain pKa values for an acidic residue.

qs.q: Which of the following statements about the effect of temperature on pKa is FALSE?
o: Ammonium (–NH₃⁺) pKa values fall by roughly 0.02–0.03 per °C (ΔH° ≈ +40–50 kJ/mol).
Carboxylic acid pKa values change very little with temperature because ΔH° of ionization is near zero.
Temperature has no effect on any amino acid pKa.
The size of the temperature effect depends on the functional group.
qs.x: van ’t Hoff: d(pKa)/dT = −ΔH°/(2.303 R T²); for an ammonium group ΔH° ≈ +45 kJ/mol, so pKa falls by about 0.026 per K, whereas carboxylic acids (ΔH° ≈ 0) barely change. So temperature does change ionization constants, in a group-dependent way; the statement that it has no effect is false. Trap: Students may think temperature has no effect because they recall the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation as temperature‑independent.

qs.q: At physiological pH (7.4), which side chain in the table carries a predominantly negative charge?
qs.x: Correct: A) pH 7.4 is well above 4.25, so the glutamate carboxyl is deprotonated and negative. Why the others are wrong: B) pH 7.4 is far below 10.53, so the lysine side chain stays protonated and positive. C) With pKa 6.00 the imidazole is about 96% in its neutral (deprotonated) form at pH 7.4, not negative. D) The alanine methyl side chain has no ionizable group. Trap: Assuming any side chain with a pKa below 7.4 is negatively charged; histidine's deprotonated imidazole is neutral, so only the acidic carboxyl side chain is negative.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers investigated the acid–base properties of four amino acids—glycine, alanine, lysine, and glutamic acid—using potentiometric titration. In each experiment, the amino acid was dissolved in 0.1 M NaCl, and the pH was recorded as incremental amounts of 0.1 M HCl or NaOH were added. The titration curves revealed two pKa values for glycine and alanine (carboxyl, pKa1; α-amino, pKa2) and three for lysine and glutamic acid, which also have an ionizable side chain (pKa side). The data were plotted as pH versus volume of titrant to determine the precise pKa values. This approach allows for direct comparison of the intrinsic acidity of the side chains and the determination of each amino acid’s isoelectric point (pI). The experiment also highlights the importance of buffer selection and ionic strength on the accuracy of pKa measurements, which are critical for understanding protein folding, enzyme catalysis, and drug design.

qs.q: Which amino acid has the highest side‑chain pKa among those studied?
qs.x: Correct: C) Lysine. Its side-chain (ε-amino) pKa of 10.53 is the highest value in the side-chain column, while glutamic acid's carboxyl side chain is 4.25 and glycine and alanine have no ionizable side chain. Why the others are wrong: A) Glycine has no side-chain pKa. B) Alanine has no side-chain pKa. D) Glutamic acid's side-chain pKa (4.25) is far below lysine's. Trap: Reading the α-amino pKa column (about 9 to 10) as the side-chain value, which could make glycine or alanine look as if they have a high side-chain pKa.

qs.q: If the goal is to determine the pKa of lysine’s side‑chain amine, which pH range should the buffer system cover?
qs.x: Correct: C) 8.0 to 12.0. Lysine's side-chain pKa is about 10.5, so the titration must cover pH values on both sides of 10.5 to locate the midpoint of the transition. Why the others are wrong: A) 2.0 to 4.0 covers only the carboxyl region (pKa about 2.2). B) 4.0 to 6.0 contains no ionization of lysine. D) 12.0 to 14.0 lies entirely above the side-chain pKa, so the midpoint would be missed. Trap: Choosing a range that contains no ionizing lysine group, or one lying entirely above the pKa so the midpoint of the transition is never reached.

qs.q: Using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, what fraction of lysine’s side‑chain amine is deprotonated at pH 9.0? (pKa = 10.53)
qs.x: Correct: B) 2.9%. pH minus pKa = 9.0 - 10.53 = -1.53, so [base]/[acid] = 10^-1.53 = 0.0295 and the deprotonated fraction is 0.0295/1.0295 = 2.9%. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.29% would require a pH about 2.5 units below the pKa. C) 10.5% has no basis in the equation (it echoes the pKa digits). D) 50% occurs only when pH equals the pKa. Trap: Treating the amine as half-ionized (50%) or ignoring that pH 9.0 is 1.5 units below the pKa, so only a few percent is deprotonated.

qs.q: Which of the following quantities is dimensionless?
qs.x: pKa = −log10 Ka is dimensionless; molarity, moles and grams all carry units. Trap: Counting pKa as a quantity with units like molarity, moles or grams, even though it is the negative logarithm of Ka and therefore unitless.

qs.q: Which concept is most directly linked to the determination of the isoelectric point (pI) in this study?
qs.x: Correct: B) The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation relates pH, pKa and the ionization state of each group, so the pI follows from the pKa values on either side of the net-neutral form (for glycine, (2.34 + 9.60)/2 = 5.97). Why the others are wrong: A) Michaelis-Menten kinetics describes enzyme rates. C) Enzyme inhibition concerns catalysis, not charge balance. D) Folding thermodynamics is not needed to locate a pI. Trap: Reaching for kinetic or thermodynamic concepts because the passage mentions catalysis and folding, although the pI depends only on pKa values and charge balance.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers at the University of Metropolis used NMR spectroscopy to determine the pKa values of the side chains of four amino acids: aspartic acid, lysine, histidine, and glutamic acid. The experiment involved preparing 0.1 M solutions of each amino acid in 10 mM phosphate buffer and recording ¹H NMR chemical shifts while incrementally adjusting the pH from 1.0 to 12.0. The resulting titration curves were fitted to the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation to extract the pKa values. The data were then compared to literature values to assess the influence of ionic strength and temperature on the measurements. The study also examined how the protonation state of each side chain affects the overall charge of the amino acid at physiological pH.

qs.q: Which amino acid has the lowest side‑chain pKa among those listed?
qs.x: Correct: A) Aspartic acid's side-chain pKa (3.9) is the lowest of the four listed (3.9, 10.5, 6.0 and 4.3). Why the others are wrong: B) lysine's 10.5 is the highest. C) histidine's 6.0 is higher than 3.9. D) glutamic acid's 4.3 is slightly higher than 3.9. Trap: Confusing the side‑chain pKa with the pKa of the α‑amino or α‑carboxyl groups.

qs.q: At pH 7.0, which of the four side chains in Table 1 is predominantly in its protonated (conjugate acid) form?
qs.x: Correct: B) The lysine side-chain pKa (10.5) is far above pH 7.0, so the group is almost entirely protonated. Why the others are wrong: A) The aspartic acid side-chain pKa is 3.9, well below 7.0, so it is almost entirely deprotonated. C) The histidine side-chain pKa is 6.0, below 7.0, so about 91% is deprotonated. D) The glutamic acid side-chain pKa is 4.3, well below 7.0, so it is almost entirely deprotonated. Trap: Assuming acidic side chains such as aspartic and glutamic acid are protonated at pH 7.0 because they are called acids; at pH above the pKa the deprotonated form predominates.

qs.q: Using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, calculate the fraction of protonated side chain of lysine (pKa = 10.5) at pH 7.0.
qs.x: Correct: A) Fraction protonated = 1/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)) = 1/(1 + 10^(7 − 10.5)) = 1/(1 + 0.00032) = 0.9997. Why the others are wrong: B) 0.9999 would require a pH of about 6.5. C) 0.9995 would require a pH of about 7.2. D) 0.999 would require a pH of about 7.5. Trap: Using the wrong sign in the exponent (pKa‑pH instead of pH‑pKa) or forgetting to convert to a fraction.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by Table 1?
o: Lysine is the only side chain in the table with a pKa above 7.
The aspartic acid and glutamic acid side chains both have pKa values below 5.
At pH 7.0, the histidine side chain is predominantly protonated.
Histidine has the side-chain pKa closest to physiological pH.
qs.x: Correct: C) Histidine's side-chain pKa is 6.0, so at pH 7.0 (one unit above) the ratio of deprotonated to protonated is 10:1 and the group is mostly deprotonated. Why the others are wrong: A) The pKa values are 3.9, 6.0, 4.3 and 10.5, so only lysine exceeds 7. B) 3.9 and 4.3 are both below 5. D) At pH 7.0 histidine's pKa (6.0) is 1.0 unit away, versus 2.7 for glutamic acid and 3.1 for aspartic acid and 3.5 for lysine. Trap: Treating histidine as protonated at pH 7.0 because its pKa is near physiological pH; when pH exceeds the pKa the deprotonated form predominates.

qs.q: At pH 7.0, what is the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] for a group with pKa 6.0?
qs.x: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) ⇒ log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 7.0 − 6.0 = 1, so the ratio is 10:1 (about 91% deprotonated). Trap: Inverting the logarithm (using pKa minus pH) gives 1:10, the tempting reversed ratio; when pH is above the pKa the deprotonated form A- predominates.

passages.title: Research design and data reasoning (all science sections) · passage
text: Researchers at the Institute of Biochemistry conducted a systematic titration study to determine the acid–base dissociation constants (pKa) of a representative set of ten standard amino acids. They titrated each amino acid solution with strong base, recording the pH after each increment from pH 1.0 to 13.0 with a calibrated pH meter. The resulting titration curves displayed distinct inflection points corresponding to the ionization of the α‑carboxyl, α‑amino, and, where present, side‑chain functional groups. By applying the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation to the slope of each linear segment, the researchers extracted precise pKa values. The data were summarized in Table 1, which lists the pKa of the carboxyl, amino, and side‑chain groups for each amino acid. These values were subsequently used to calculate the isoelectric point (pI) of each residue, a key parameter in protein purification and electrophoresis. The experiment demonstrates how systematic variation of a single independent variable—pH—enables the determination of multiple dependent variables (pKa values) that define the acid–base behavior of amino acids.

qs.q: Which variable did the researchers systematically alter to determine the pKa values of the amino acids?
qs.x: Correct: B) The researchers changed the pH step by step and measured the resulting titration curve, so pH is the independent variable. Why the others are wrong: A) Temperature is not described as being varied. C) Ionic strength is not described as being varied. D) Concentration is not described as being varied; the pKa values are what is derived from the curve. Trap: Confusing the variable that is manipulated with the one that is measured.

qs.q: If the temperature were held constant but the ionic strength were raised from 0.01 M to 0.5 M, what would most likely happen to the pKa of lysine’s ε‑amino group (side chain)?
o: It would not change at all
Only the carboxyl pKa would change
qs.x: Extended Debye–Hückel: pKa′ = pKa + A(2z − 1)√I/(1 + √I), where z is the net charge of the acid form and A ≈ 0.51 at 25 °C. At I = 0.1 M the shift is about ±0.1 pH unit per unit of (2z − 1). For the ε‑NH₃⁺ ionization the acid form has net charge 0, so 2z − 1 = −1 and the apparent pKa decreases as ionic strength rises. Trap: Choosing option C (no change) or option A (increase); the ionic atmosphere lowers the apparent pKa of a group whose acid form is uncharged overall, such as the epsilon-NH3+ group here.

qs.q: Using the table, calculate the isoelectric point (pI) of lysine.
qs.x: pI = average of the α‑amino (8.95) and side-chain amino (10.53) pKa values = 9.74. Averaging all three pKa values would give a wrong answer. Trap: Averaging all pKa values or using the wrong pair of pKa values.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the determination of pI from pKa values?
o: pI is calculated as the average of the pKa values of the groups that are protonated and deprotonated at the isoelectric point.
For amino acids with multiple ionizable side chains, pI is calculated using the pKa values of the two groups that bracket the net charge of zero.
The pI of lysine is higher than that of arginine.
qs.x: Arginine's side-chain pKa (12.48) gives pI = (9.04 + 12.48)/2 ≈ 10.76, higher than lysine's 9.74, so the claim that lysine's pI is higher is incorrect. Trap: Assuming more basic groups mean a higher pI.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between the pKa values listed in the table and the pI of an amino acid?
o: pI is always equal to the lowest pKa value.
pI is always equal to the highest pKa value.
pI is the average of the pKa values of the groups that change charge around the pI.
pI is unrelated to pKa values.
qs.x: The pI is calculated as the average of the pKa values of the groups that change charge around the point where the net charge is zero. It is not simply the lowest or highest pKa. The correct statement is that pI is the average of the two pKa values that bracket zero charge. Trap: Thinking pI equals the lowest or highest pKa.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers at the University of Biochem performed a titration study on a panel of amino acids to characterize their side‑chain ionization behavior. In a 25 °C aqueous solution, they added standardized NaOH to each amino acid solution while monitoring pH with a calibrated pH electrode. The titration curves revealed distinct inflection points corresponding to the side‑chain pKa values. Glycine, lacking a functional side chain, showed only the alpha‑carboxyl (pKa ≈ 2.34) and alpha‑amino (pKa ≈ 9.60) groups. Aspartic acid displayed a side‑chain pKa of 3.65, lysine 10.53, histidine 6.00, and cysteine 8.18. Tryptophan has no ionizable side chain. The researchers calculated the isoelectric points (pI) by averaging the pKa values of the groups that change charge at the pI. The data were compiled into a concise table for comparison and used to design further experiments on protein folding and enzyme activity at varying pH levels.

qs.q: Which amino acid has the lowest side‑chain pKa value according to the study?
qs.x: Correct: A) Aspartic acid's side-chain pKa (3.65) is lower than all the others in the table. Why the others are wrong: B) lysine's side-chain pKa is 10.53. C) histidine's is 6.04. D) cysteine's is 8.18. Trap: Choosing histidine or cysteine because their side chains are best known for ionizing near neutral pH, instead of comparing the numbers in the side‑chain pKa column.

qs.q: If the temperature of the titration were increased from 25 °C to 45 °C, what would most likely happen to the pKa of lysine’s ε‑ammonium side chain?
qs.x: van ’t Hoff: d(pKa)/dT = −ΔH°/(2.303 R T²); for an ammonium group ΔH° ≈ +45 kJ/mol, so pKa falls by about 0.026 per K, whereas carboxylic acids (ΔH° ≈ 0) barely change. Over 20 K: ΔpKa ≈ −0.026 × 20 ≈ −0.5. Trap: Some students mistakenly think that increased temperature stabilizes the protonated form, leading to higher pKa.

qs.q: Calculate the isoelectric point (pI) of lysine.
qs.x: pI = (α‑NH₃⁺ pKa 8.95 + side‑chain pKa 10.53)/2 = 9.74. Trap: Students sometimes use the alpha‑carboxyl pKa instead of the side‑chain pKa, leading to an incorrect average.

qs.q: Which statement is incorrect regarding the data presented?
o: The pI of aspartic acid is 2.34.
qs.x: Correct: The table lists the pI of aspartic acid as 2.77, so the statement that it is 2.34 is incorrect (2.34 is glycine's alpha‑carboxyl pKa). Why the others are wrong: A) glycine has no ionizable side chain, as the passage states. B) the histidine side‑chain pKa is 6.00 in the table. C) the lysine side‑chain pKa is 10.53 in the table. Trap: The alpha‑carboxyl pKa (≈2.34) is often confused with the pI, creating a subtle error.

qs.q: Which amino acid side chain most commonly acts as a proton shuttle in enzyme active sites near physiological pH?
qs.x: Correct: Histidine's side chain (pKa about 6) is partly protonated and partly deprotonated near pH 7.4, so it can both donate and accept protons in general acid‑base catalysis. Why the others are wrong: B) lysine (pKa about 10.5) is almost always protonated near neutral pH. C) aspartate (pKa 3.65) is almost always deprotonated near neutral pH. D) leucine has no ionizable side chain. Trap: Picking lysine because it is the best known basic residue; its pKa near 10.5 means it is nearly always protonated at physiological pH and cannot shuttle protons efficiently.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers investigated the acid–base properties of four amino acids—glycine, alanine, lysine, and glutamic acid—by titrating each with standardized NaOH and recording the pH at each half-equivalence point. The titration curves revealed distinct pKa values corresponding to the carboxyl and amino functional groups. The table below summarizes the experimentally determined pKa values and the calculated isoelectric points (pI). The study aimed to correlate these physicochemical parameters with the solubility behavior of the amino acids in aqueous solutions at physiological pH. The authors also examined how the presence of a strong base or acid shifts the pH at which each amino acid becomes neutral, thereby affecting its precipitation tendency. This data set is commonly used in biochemistry courses to illustrate the concept of pI and to practice calculations involving Henderson–Hasselbalch and ionization fractions.

qs.q: Based on the table, which amino acid has the highest isoelectric point (pI)?
qs.x: Correct: C) Lysine's pI is 9.74, the highest in the table. Why the others are wrong: A) Glycine's pI is 5.97. B) Alanine's pI is 6.02. D) Glutamic acid's pI is 3.22, lowered by its acidic side chain. Trap: Picking glutamic acid or alanine by ignoring the side chains; the extra basic amine of lysine pushes its pI far above the neutral amino acids.

qs.q: Strong base is added to lysine at pH 7.0 and the pH rises toward lysine's pI. How does the average net charge of lysine change?
qs.x: Correct: A) At pH 7.0 the carboxyl is deprotonated and both amines are protonated, so the net charge is about +1; raising the pH to the pI of 9.74 removes the positive charge from the alpha-amino group, giving a net charge of 0. Why the others are wrong: B) At pH 7.0 lysine is not negative; the side-chain amine (pKa 10.53) is still protonated. C) The +2 form exists only below the carboxyl pKa of 2.18. D) Adding base removes protons, so positive charge cannot increase. Trap: Assuming lysine is already neutral or negative at pH 7.0; its side-chain amine stays protonated until pH is near 10.5, so the net charge is +1.

qs.q: Using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, calculate the fraction of lysine that is protonated at its amino group (NH3⁺) when the solution pH is 7.0.
qs.x: Fraction protonated = 1/(1 + 10^(pH - pKa)) = 1/(1 + 10^(7.0 - 8.95)) = 1/1.011 = 0.99. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.12 does not follow from the equation at a pH-pKa gap of about 2 units. B) 0.50 holds only when pH equals the pKa. C) 0.88 would require the pH to be only about 0.8 unit below the pKa. Trap: Assuming half-ionization (0.50) at pH 7.0; that holds only at pH = pKa (8.95), and at pH 7.0 the amine is about 99% protonated.

qs.q: Which of the following statements about the units of pKa is correct?
o: pKa is measured in moles per liter (M)
pKa is dimensionless and expressed as a logarithm of a concentration ratio
pKa is expressed in kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol)
pKa is expressed in degrees Celsius (°C)
qs.x: Correct: B) Ka is defined with activities (relative to the standard state), so it is dimensionless and pKa = -log10 Ka has no units. Why the others are wrong: A) Molarity is a concentration unit, not the unit of a logarithm. C) kJ/mol is an energy unit; pKa is related to free energy but is not itself an energy. D) Temperature units do not apply to pKa. Trap: Assuming pKa has the same units as concentration (M) or energy (kJ/mol).

qs.q: At pH 4.0, a protein with pI 6.0 will carry a net charge and migrate toward which electrode in an electric field?
o: No charge; it does not migrate
qs.x: Below its pI the protein is protonated and carries a net positive charge, so it migrates toward the negative electrode (cathode). At pH = pI it has no net charge and stops migrating (isoelectric focusing). Trap: Choosing the anode because the protein is positive; positive species migrate toward the negative cathode, and below its pI (pH 4.0 < 6.0) this protein is positive.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers studied the acid–base behavior of twenty standard amino acids by titrating solutions of each at 25 °C. Each amino acid (0.1 M) was titrated with 0.1 M HCl or NaOH while monitoring pH with a calibrated glass electrode. The pH at which the solution’s net charge was zero was recorded as the isoelectric point (pI). The titration curves revealed distinct inflection points corresponding to the ionizable groups: α‑COOH, α‑NH3⁺, and side‑chain groups (e.g., side‑chain carboxyl of Glu, side‑chain amine of Lys). The experiment also measured the pKa values for each ionizable group by determining the midpoints of the buffer regions. The resulting data are summarized in Table 1. The researchers noted that temperature variations shift the pKa of amino groups by about 0.03 pH units per °C (carboxyl groups change little), and that the presence of 0.5 M NaCl slightly compresses the titration curves due to ionic strength effects.

qs.q: Which amino acid has the highest side‑chain pKa value in the experiment?
qs.x: Correct: A) Lysine's side-chain pKa (10.5) is the highest in Table 1. Why the others are wrong: B) glutamic acid's is 4.3. C) histidine's is 6.0. D) tyrosine's is 10.1, slightly below lysine's 10.5. Trap: Assuming all side‑chain pKa values are similar; confusing the α‑COOH pKa with side‑chain pKa.

qs.q: To study the ionization of the Glu side chain near its pKa of 4.3 (Table 1), which buffer would resist pH change best at that pH?
qs.x: Correct: A) A buffer works best within about one pH unit of its pKa, and acetate (4.8) is closest to 4.3. Why the others are wrong: B) A pKa of 7.2 is almost 3 units above 4.3, so little buffering occurs. C) A pKa of 8.1 is almost 4 units away. D) A pKa of 10.4 is more than 6 units away. Trap: Choosing the buffer nearest physiological pH (phosphate or Tris) from habit instead of matching the buffer pKa to the target pH of 4.3.

qs.q: Using the pKa values in Table 1 and an α‑NH₃⁺ pKa of ≈9.0 for the free N‑terminus, calculate the pI of a dipeptide composed of Glu–Lys.
qs.x: Net charge is zero between deprotonation of the Glu side chain (pKa 4.3) and the free α‑NH₃⁺ (pKa ≈ 9.0), while the Lys side chain (10.5) is still protonated: pI = (4.3 + 9.0)/2 ≈ 6.6. Trap: Using the wrong pKa values or forgetting to average.

qs.q: Which of the following statements about the titration curves is incorrect?
o: The inflection point for the α‑COOH group occurs at a lower pH than that for the α‑NH3⁺ group.
Increasing ionic strength compresses the titration curves.
Ammonium pKa values fall by about 0.03 per °C (ΔH° ≈ +45 kJ/mol), while carboxyl pKa values change little.
The pI is independent of temperature.
qs.x: pKa values depend on temperature (van ’t Hoff: d(pKa)/dT = −ΔH°/(2.303 R T²); for an ammonium group ΔH° ≈ +45 kJ/mol, so pKa falls by about 0.026 per K, whereas carboxylic acids (ΔH° ≈ 0) barely change.) so the pI, which is calculated from pKa values, shifts with temperature too; statement D is incorrect. Trap: Assuming pI is constant; confusing pKa shift with pI stability.

qs.q: Which statement best links the pI concept to protein solubility?
o: Proteins are most soluble at their pI.
Proteins are least soluble at their pI.
Proteins become insoluble only when the pH is far from their pI.
Protein solubility is unrelated to pI.
qs.x: Correct: B) At the pI the net charge is zero, so electrostatic repulsion between molecules is minimal and aggregation is favored, giving the lowest solubility. Why the others are wrong: A) This reverses the relationship. C) Moving away from the pI increases net charge and usually raises solubility, so insolubility far from the pI is the opposite of the trend. D) Net charge, which depends on pH relative to pI, strongly affects solubility. Trap: Assuming that a protein carrying more charge is less soluble, or that solubility is unrelated to net charge; solubility is lowest where net charge is zero.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers conducted a series of acid–base titrations to determine the pKa values of the alpha‑carboxyl, alpha‑amino, and side‑chain functional groups of six amino acids (glycine, serine, lysine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid, and histidine). Each amino acid (0.1 M) was titrated with 0.1 M NaOH while the pH was recorded after each addition. The resulting titration curves displayed two buffering regions for glycine and serine and three for the other four amino acids. The lowest region (pH 1.5–4.5) corresponded mainly to carboxyl groups, while the higher regions (pH 6–11) reflected the amino and histidine or lysine side‑chain groups. The researchers plotted pH versus the volume of NaOH added and used the inflection points to calculate the pKa values. The data were compiled into a table that lists the experimentally determined pKa values for each functional group, which were then compared to literature values to assess experimental accuracy. This experiment illustrates how the intrinsic pKa values dictate the charge state of amino acids at physiological pH and how they can be experimentally determined via titration curves.

qs.q: During the titration of lysine, the researchers observed a buffering region around pH 10. Which functional group is responsible for this buffering behavior?
qs.x: Correct: The epsilon-amino side chain of lysine has a pKa of about 10.53, so it buffers around pH 10. Why the others are wrong: A) the alpha-carboxyl group buffers near pH 2. B) the alpha-amino group (pKa 8.95) buffers near pH 9, further from pH 10. D) lysine has no gamma-carboxyl side chain. Trap: Students may confuse the α‑amino group with the ε‑amino side chain because both are amino groups.

qs.q: If the researchers titrated fully deprotonated aspartate with 0.1 M HCl instead of titrating the protonated form with NaOH, what would the curve look like?
o: A mirror-image curve with the same pKa values (1.88, 3.65 and 9.60)
A curve with all pKa values shifted to lower numbers
A curve with no buffering regions
A curve showing only the pKa at 3.65
qs.x: Titrating from the other direction traces the same equilibria in reverse; pKa values are properties of the groups, not of the titrant. Trap: Students may think the titrant concentration matters more than the direction of proton addition.

qs.q: Using the pKa values from the table, calculate the isoelectric point (pI) of glutamic acid.
qs.x: Glutamic acid is acidic: pI = (pKa1 + pKaR)/2 = (2.19 + 4.25)/2 = 3.22. Trap: Students may average the wrong pair of pKa values or forget to consider the α‑amino group.

qs.q: What are the units of pKa?
qs.x: pKa = −log10 Ka is a logarithm of a dimensionless quantity, so it has no units. Trap: Students may think pKa is a pH measurement and thus use pH units.

qs.q: Buffering capacity of an ionizable group is greatest at which pH?
o: Two pH units above its pKa
Two pH units below its pKa
At the pH where it is fully deprotonated
qs.x: By Henderson–Hasselbalch, at pH = pKa the acid and conjugate base are equal, so the solution resists added acid or base best (within about ±1 pH unit of the pKa). Trap: Assuming buffering is best where the group is fully deprotonated or fully charged, when capacity requires comparable amounts of HA and A- and so peaks at the pKa.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers at the University of Midvale conducted a double‑blind, randomized controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of a novel antihypertensive agent, Hypertrol, in adults with stage 1 hypertension. Eighty participants were randomly assigned to receive either Hypertrol (n = 40) or a placebo (n = 40). Baseline systolic blood pressure (SBP) was measured after a 5‑minute seated rest period and recorded in millimeters of mercury (mmHg). After 8 weeks of daily dosing, SBP was re‑measured using the same protocol. The study aimed to determine whether Hypertrol could produce a clinically meaningful reduction in SBP compared to placebo. All participants provided informed consent, and the trial was approved by the institutional review board. The investigators collected demographic data, medication adherence, and adverse events throughout the study period. The primary outcome was the mean change in SBP from baseline to week 8. Secondary outcomes included diastolic BP change and incidence of adverse events. The results were presented in Table 1 below.

qs.q: What was the mean reduction in systolic blood pressure (SBP) for participants receiving Hypertrol after 8 weeks of treatment?
qs.x: The mean SBP in the Hypertrol group decreased from 139.2 to 123.4 mmHg. The mean reduction is 139.2 - 123.4 = 15.8 mmHg. Trap: The table lists SDs that might distract you into using them in the calculation; the correct calculation uses only the means.

qs.q: Which type of study design best describes the research described in the passage?
qs.x: The passage states that participants were randomly assigned to Hypertrol or placebo, and the study was double‑blind. This is the definition of a randomized controlled trial (RCT). Trap: The mention of a 5‑minute seated rest period might lead you to think of a cross‑sectional design, but the randomization and blinding are key RCT features.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in mean systolic blood pressure for the Hypertrol group after 8 weeks?
qs.x: Percent reduction = [(139.2 - 123.4)/139.2] × 100 = 15.8/139.2 × 100 ≈ 11.4%. Trap: Options B-D overestimate the reduction; the percent must be computed from the reported means, dividing by the baseline mean.

qs.q: Which of the following conclusions is NOT supported by Table 1?
o: The Hypertrol group mean SBP fell by about 16 mmHg.
The placebo group mean SBP fell by about 1.8 mmHg.
The mean fall in SBP was larger with Hypertrol than with placebo.
Hypertrol lowered SBP in every individual participant.
qs.x: Correct: D) The table reports only group means and SDs, so nothing can be said about every individual participant. Why the others are wrong: A) 139.2 − 123.4 = 15.8 mmHg; supported. B) 138.5 − 136.7 = 1.8 mmHg; supported. C) 15.8 mmHg versus 1.8 mmHg; supported. Trap: Treating a fall in a group mean as proof that every individual responded; the table gives only means and SDs.

qs.q: What is the placebo‑adjusted mean reduction in SBP for the Hypertrol group (mean change in Hypertrol minus mean change in placebo)?
qs.x: Correct: Hypertrol change = 139.2 − 123.4 = 15.8 mmHg; placebo change = 138.5 − 136.7 = 1.8 mmHg; difference = 15.8 − 1.8 = 14.0 mmHg. Why the others are wrong: A) 15.8 mmHg is the Hypertrol change alone and ignores the placebo change. B) 1.8 mmHg is the placebo change alone. D) 17.6 mmHg adds the two changes instead of subtracting. Trap: Reporting the raw Hypertrol reduction (15.8 mmHg) without subtracting the change seen with placebo.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of three different dietary supplements on the recovery time of athletes after a standardized high-intensity exercise protocol. The study recruited 90 healthy adults aged 20–35, randomly assigning 30 participants to each of three groups: Group A received Supplement X, Group B received Supplement Y, and Group C received a placebo. All participants performed the same treadmill run until volitional fatigue, after which their recovery time was measured as the duration required to return to baseline heart rate and perceived exertion. Blood samples were taken pre- and post-exercise to assess markers of muscle damage (creatine kinase, CK) and inflammation (C-reactive protein, CRP). The table below summarizes the mean recovery times (in minutes) and the mean changes in CK and CRP levels for each group. The researchers hypothesized that Supplement X would reduce recovery time and inflammatory markers more effectively than Supplement Y or placebo.

qs.q: According to the table, which group had the smallest post-exercise rise in C-reactive protein (CRP)?
o: All groups had the same reduction
qs.x: The table shows ΔCRP (post-exercise increase) of 1.8 mg/L for Group A, 2.5 mg/L for Group B, and 3.9 mg/L for Group C. Group A had the smallest rise, i.e. the least exercise-induced inflammation. Trap: Reading a higher ΔCRP as a better outcome; a larger post-exercise rise reflects more inflammation.

qs.q: Which experimental design element best controls for individual differences in baseline fitness levels?
o: Random assignment of participants to groups
Measuring baseline CK and CRP levels
Providing all participants with identical nutrition plans
qs.x: Random assignment distributes individual differences such as baseline fitness evenly across groups, reducing bias. The other options address protocol standardization, baseline marker assessment, or nutrition but do not directly control for fitness variability. Trap: Confusing protocol standardization (B) with randomization as the primary control for individual differences.

qs.q: If the total post-exercise rise in CK across all participants in Group A is 1,356 U/L, what is the average rise per participant?
qs.x: Average rise per participant = total rise ÷ number of participants = 1,356 ÷ 30 = 45.2 U/L, which matches the table’s ΔCK value for Group A. Trap: Using the wrong denominator or averaging across groups, which produces a value that does not equal 1,356 divided by the 30 participants in Group A (45.2 U/L).

qs.q: Which of the following statements is a common misinterpretation of the study’s findings?
o: Supplement X had the shortest mean recovery time.
The placebo group had the longest recovery time.
All supplements reduced CK levels equally.
CRP levels increased after exercise in all groups.
qs.x: ΔCK values (post-exercise rises) were 45.2, 58.9 and 72.4 U/L for Groups A, B and C, so the supplements did not blunt the CK rise equally; Supplement X blunted it most. Saying all supplements had equal effects is a misinterpretation. Trap: Assuming equal effectiveness across supplements because every group showed some CK change.

qs.q: If the three groups were compared with three separate pairwise t-tests each at α = 0.05 (assume independent tests), what is the approximate probability of at least one false-positive result?
qs.x: Familywise error = 1 - (1 - 0.05)^3 = 1 - 0.857 = 14.3%. This inflation of type I error is why ANOVA with post hoc correction is used for three or more groups. Trap: Option B (9.8%) is the value for two tests; option A ignores multiple comparisons.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers at the Greenhouse Institute investigated how varying light intensity influences the rate of photosynthesis in spinach (Spinacia oleracea) leaves. To quantify this relationship, they exposed detached leaf discs to four controlled light levels: 100, 250, 500, and 750 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, each for a 30‑minute interval. Discs were assigned to light levels at random. Oxygen evolution, measured via a Clark electrode, served as a proxy for photosynthetic activity. The experiment was replicated thrice to ensure statistical reliability. Table 1 summarizes the mean oxygen production rates (µmol O₂ m⁻² s⁻¹, per unit leaf area) along with standard deviations and sample sizes for each light intensity. The data reveal a saturating (hyperbolic) trend, with a steep increase from 100 to 250 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, followed by a plateau approaching saturation near 500 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. Notably, the mean rate at 750 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ was only 0.7 units above the 500 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ rate, suggesting a saturation point. These findings align with the light‑response curve model, indicating that spinach photosynthesis is limited by light intensity up to a threshold beyond which other factors, such as enzyme capacity, become rate‑determining.

qs.q: What is the mean oxygen production rate at 250 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹?
qs.x: Correct: B) The 250 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ row of Table 1 gives 18.3 µmol O₂ m⁻² s⁻¹. Why the others are wrong: A) 12.5 is not listed; the neighboring rows are 8.2 and 18.3. C) 24.7 is not listed; the 500 row is 25.4. D) 30.1 is not listed and exceeds every value in the table (the maximum is 26.1). Trap: Reading the wrong row of the table, for example choosing the 500 or 750 value, instead of the mean listed for the 250 level.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the experimental design used in this study?
qs.x: The researchers applied each light intensity to leaf discs in a completely randomized manner, with no blocking factors or multiple factors being varied simultaneously. Trap: Confusing the presence of replication with a randomized block design.

qs.q: If the standard deviation at 500 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ is 1.8 µmol O₂ m⁻² s⁻¹, what is the coefficient of variation (CV) expressed as a percentage?
qs.x: Correct: B) CV = SD/mean × 100 = 1.8/25.4 × 100 = 7.1%. Why the others are wrong: A) 5% would need an SD of about 1.3. C) 15% would need an SD of about 3.8. D) 20% would need an SD of about 5.1, or dividing 1.8 by a much smaller mean such as 8.2 (which gives about 22%). Trap: Dividing the SD by the wrong group's mean (for example 1.8/8.2, about 22%) or forgetting to divide by the mean at all.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: Photosynthesis rate increases linearly with light intensity up to 750 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
Photosynthesis saturates near 500 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
The mean rate at 750 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ was numerically higher than at 500 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
Light intensity of 100 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ yields the lowest oxygen production rate.
qs.x: Correct: A) The data show a saturating increase, not a linear one: +10.1 from 100 to 250, +7.1 from 250 to 500 (a smaller gain over a wider interval), and only +0.7 from 500 to 750. Why the others are wrong: B) The rate nearly stops rising after 500, which supports saturation. C) 26.1 is higher than 25.4, so the statement is supported. D) 8.2 is the smallest mean in the table, so it is supported. Trap: Assuming a gradual increase implies linearity.

qs.q: At 750 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ the mean O₂ production (26.1) was only slightly higher than at 500 (25.4). Which interpretation is best supported by the data and passage?
o: Light capture is still the limiting factor at 750, so the rate would rise in proportion to light if the discs were measured longer.
Beyond about 500 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, extra light cannot be used because a step other than light capture (such as enzyme capacity) limits the rate.
Photosynthesis was already saturated at 100 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, so the rate cannot increase with light.
The 750 treatment caused photoinhibition, so O₂ production fell well below the 500 value.
qs.x: Correct: B. The rate rose steeply from 100 to 250 (8.2 to 18.3) but changed by only 0.7 between 500 and 750, and the passage states that beyond a threshold other factors such as enzyme capacity become rate-determining. Why the others are wrong: A) If light capture were still limiting, the rate would keep rising with light, but the 500 to 750 increase is only 0.7 units (about 3%). C) The rate more than doubled from 100 to 250, so the discs were not saturated at 100. D) The 750 mean (26.1) is higher than the 500 mean (25.4), not lower, so no fall in O₂ production occurred. Trap: Assuming that more light always means more photosynthesis, so a flat rate must reflect damage or measurement artifact.

passages.title: Research design and data reasoning (all science sections) · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of varying doses of a novel drug on plasma concentration in healthy volunteers. Thirty participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups: a control group receiving a placebo, a low‑dose group receiving 10 mg, and a high‑dose group receiving 30 mg. Blood samples were collected 2 hours post‑dose and analyzed for drug concentration (µg/mL). The study aimed to assess dose‑dependent pharmacokinetics while balancing participant characteristics across groups through randomization. The results are summarized in Table 1 below. The researchers plan to use these findings to inform dose‑finding studies in patients with the target disease.

qs.q: Which experimental condition shows the greatest increase in mean plasma concentration relative to the control group?
qs.x: The high‑dose group has a mean concentration of 12.3 µg/mL, which is higher than the control mean of 5.2 µg/mL, representing the largest absolute increase among the groups. Trap: Choosing the Control group because it is listed first, or Low Dose because it is the first increase, instead of the largest mean.

qs.q: Which experimental design best controls for inter‑individual variability in this study?
qs.x: A crossover design allows each participant to receive multiple treatments in a randomized order, thereby controlling for inter‑individual differences by using participants as their own controls. Trap: Picking randomized controlled trial because the study was randomized, but only a crossover design uses each person as their own control.

qs.q: Calculate the percent increase in mean plasma concentration from the control group to the high‑dose group.
qs.x: Percent increase = (12.3 - 5.2)/5.2 x 100 = 136.5%. Trap: Dividing the difference by the high-dose mean (7.1/12.3 = 58%) or reporting the ratio (237%) instead of dividing by the control mean.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the study design?
o: The standard deviation indicates variability within each group.
The mean concentration can be influenced by outliers.
A sample size of 10 is adequate to assume normality.
All data points contribute equally to the mean.
qs.x: A sample size of 10 is generally considered small; it may not reliably satisfy the central limit theorem for normality, especially with potential outliers. Trap: Assuming n = 10 per group is enough to treat the data as normal, which a small sample cannot guarantee.

qs.q: The high-dose mean (12.3 µg/mL) exceeds the control mean (5.2 µg/mL) with n = 10 per group. What is needed to judge whether this 7.1 µg/mL difference is larger than expected by chance?
o: A statistical test comparing the two means that uses the group SDs and sample sizes
The range of the control group alone
The ratio of the doses (30 mg : 10 mg)
qs.x: Correct: A) Whether a difference in means exceeds chance variation depends on the spread (SD) and sample size, which is what a hypothesis test for two means uses. Why the others are wrong: B) the control range ignores the high-dose group and the sample size. C) the dose ratio says nothing about sampling variability. D) a percent increase gives the size of the difference, not whether it exceeds chance. Trap: Treating a large percent increase as proof of a real difference without considering variability and sample size.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel dietary supplement on fasting glucose levels in adults with prediabetes. A randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial enrolled 120 participants who were assigned to either the supplement (n = 60) or placebo (n = 60) for 12 weeks. Fasting glucose was measured at baseline and at week 12. The supplement group showed a mean reduction of 4.2 mg/dL (SD 3.1) while the placebo group had a mean reduction of 1.8 mg/dL (SD 2.9). The investigators reported a statistically significant difference between groups (p < 0.01). A secondary outcome was the change in HbA1c, which decreased by 0.3% in the supplement group versus 0.1% in the placebo group. Adverse events were mild and comparable between groups. The authors concluded that the supplement may modestly improve glycemic control in prediabetic adults, but further studies are needed to confirm long‑term benefits and safety.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the primary outcome of this study?
o: The supplement increased fasting glucose levels by 4.2 mg/dL.
The supplement decreased fasting glucose by 4.2 mg/dL from baseline, which was 2.4 mg/dL more than placebo.
The supplement had no effect on fasting glucose levels.
The supplement decreased fasting glucose levels by 1.8 mg/dL compared to placebo.
qs.x: The supplement group’s mean reduction was 4.2 mg/dL versus 1.8 mg/dL in placebo, a between-group difference of 2.4 mg/dL. Trap: Option D uses the placebo reduction as if it were the treatment effect; the effect relative to placebo is 4.2 − 1.8 = 2.4 mg/dL.

qs.q: Which experimental design element best ensures that the observed effect is attributable to the supplement?
o: Random assignment to supplement or placebo.
qs.x: Random assignment balances known and unknown confounders between groups, attributing differences to the intervention. Trap: Option A is tempting because blinding reduces bias, but it does not alone control for confounding variables.

qs.q: Calculate the absolute risk reduction (ARR) for fasting glucose improvement if 30% of the supplement group improved versus 15% of the placebo group.
qs.x: ARR = 30% – 15% = 15% = 0.15. Trap: Option B (0.30) is only the supplement group's improvement rate; ARR requires subtracting the placebo rate (0.30 - 0.15).

qs.q: Which of the following statements is a common misinterpretation of the study’s findings?
o: The supplement causes a clinically significant reduction in fasting glucose.
The supplement's effect on fasting glucose is statistically significant.
The 2.4 mg/dL net difference is modest in absolute terms, and long-term benefit is not established.
The supplement's safety profile appears acceptable based on mild adverse events.
qs.x: Correct: A) The passage reports a statistically significant difference and only a modest net reduction (2.4 mg/dL beyond placebo) with no clinical threshold, so calling it clinically significant is an overstatement. Why the others are wrong: B) The authors report p < 0.01. C) The authors themselves call the improvement modest and say further studies are needed. D) Adverse events were mild and comparable between groups. Trap: Treating the p < 0.01 result as proof of clinical significance, when statistical significance does not show that a 2.4 mg/dL net change matters clinically.

qs.q: Which design feature of this trial most limits conclusions about long-term benefit and safety?
o: Random assignment to supplement or placebo
qs.x: Correct: A) Outcomes were measured only at baseline and week 12, so durable benefit and long-term safety cannot be judged; the authors say further studies are needed. Why the others are wrong: B) Randomization strengthens causal inference and does not limit duration. C) A placebo comparator improves the comparison. D) Blinding reduces bias and says nothing about follow-up length. Trap: Picking randomization or blinding as the limitation because they are familiar design terms, when they strengthen internal validity rather than limit follow-up.

passages.title: Research design and data reasoning (all science sections) · passage
text: Researchers investigated the pharmacokinetics of a novel combination therapy using Drug A and Drug B in a randomized, double-blind, crossover study involving 30 healthy volunteers. Each participant received a single oral dose of Drug A (50 mg) and Drug B (25 mg) separately, with a 7‑day washout period between administrations. Blood samples were collected at baseline and at 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, and 24 hours post‑dose. The primary endpoints were plasma concentration of each drug and a composite patient response score derived from a standardized symptom questionnaire administered at each sampling time. Table 1 summarizes the mean concentrations and response scores at each sampling time. The investigators hypothesized that co‑administration would result in a synergistic reduction in symptom severity without altering the pharmacokinetic profiles of either drug. Secondary analyses included assessment of inter‑individual variability and correlation between drug levels and response scores. The study was approved by the institutional review board, and all volunteers provided written informed consent.

qs.q: Which time point had the highest combined plasma concentration of Drug A and Drug B?
qs.x: The combined concentration at 0.5 hours is 5.2 + 2.5 = 7.7 mg/L, which is higher than any other time point. Trap: Assuming the highest response score corresponds to the highest concentration.

qs.q: The investigators hypothesized that co-administration would act synergistically. Which comparison would best isolate what Drug B adds to the response produced by Drug A?
o: Placebo compared with Drug B alone
Combination compared with Drug A alone
Drug A alone compared with Drug B alone
qs.x: Correct: B) The two arms differ only by the presence of Drug B, so any difference in response is attributable to Drug B. Why the others are wrong: A) This shows Drug B's own effect against placebo, not what it adds to Drug A. C) This shows the effect of the combination as a whole, not Drug B's contribution. D) This compares two different drugs and cannot isolate the contribution of Drug B. Trap: Choosing Drug B alone versus placebo (A), which measures Drug B's stand-alone effect rather than its added effect on top of Drug A.

qs.q: Calculate the average patient response score from 0.5h to 4h.
qs.x: Average = (8.0 + 7.5 + 6.8 + 5.4) / 4 = 27.7 / 4 = 6.925 ≈ 6.9. Trap: Picking 7.5, the response score at 1 hour, or otherwise failing to average all four time points (8.0, 7.5, 6.8, 5.4).

qs.q: Which statement is NOT supported by Table 1?
o: Drug A concentration fell below 1 mg/L by 12 hours.
Drug B concentration at 4 hours was lower than at 2 hours.
The response score declined as plasma concentrations declined.
Drug B concentration exceeded Drug A concentration at every time point.
qs.x: Drug A concentration is higher than Drug B at every time point (e.g., 5.2 vs 2.5 mg/L at 0.5 h), so D is false. A (0.5 mg/L at 12 h), B (1.2 vs 1.8 mg/L), and C are supported. Trap: Option A may seem borderline, but Drug A is 1.1 mg/L at 8 h and 0.5 mg/L at 12 h, so it is below 1 mg/L by 12 hours.

qs.q: By approximately what percentage did the response score fall between 0.5 h and 24 h in Table 1?
qs.x: Correct: B) (8.0 - 2.5)/8.0 = 5.5/8.0 = 68.75%, about 69%. Why the others are wrong: A) 31% is the final score as a fraction of the starting score (2.5/8.0), not the decrease. C) 98% is the fall in Drug A concentration (5.2 to 0.1 mg/L), not the response score. D) 220% divides the drop by the final score instead of the starting score.
