passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers studied the impact of extra sleep on memory recall in a sample of 30 adults. Participants were randomly assigned to either a control group (no sleep extension) or an intervention group (allowed an extra 2 hours of sleep the night before the recall test). Each participant studied a standardized word list and completed a recall test 24 hours later, after the intervening night of sleep. The study recorded the hours each participant slept on the night before the test, as well as their recall score (number of words correctly recalled). The data suggest that participants in the intervention group performed better on average, but variability within groups was notable. The researchers aimed to determine whether increased sleep hours directly improve recall performance, while controlling for baseline sleep habits and age. The findings could inform workplace policies on shift scheduling and academic recommendations for students. The accompanying table lists data for five of the participants.

qs.q: Based on the data presented, what is the mean recall score for participants in the control group?
qs.x: The control group consists of participants P01, P02, and P05 with recall scores 18, 20, and 22. The mean is (18 + 20 + 22) / 3 = 20. Trap: Taking the lowest control score (18, P01) or a single participant's score instead of averaging all three control scores (18, 20 and 22), which gives 20.

qs.q: Which experimental design element best controls for potential confounding variables such as baseline sleep habits and age?
o: Blinding participants to the study hypothesis
Giving all participants the same word list
Increasing the sample size to 100 participants
qs.x: Correct: A) Random assignment distributes baseline sleep habits, age and other characteristics evenly across groups on average. Why the others are wrong: B) Blinding reduces expectation effects but does not balance baseline characteristics. C) Using the same word list standardizes the task, not the participants' baseline traits. D) A larger sample increases power but does not by itself remove confounding in a nonrandomized comparison. Trap: Choosing blinding because it is a familiar bias-reducing feature, although it does not balance baseline sleep habits or age between groups.

qs.q: Calculate the difference in mean recall scores between the intervention and control participants shown in the table.
qs.x: Correct: D) Control mean = (18 + 20 + 22)/3 = 20; intervention mean = (28 + 26)/2 = 27; difference = 27 − 20 = 7.0 points. Why the others are wrong: A) 4.0 is the difference between one intervention participant (26) and one control participant (22), not between group means. B) 5.5 does not equal the difference between the two group means. C) 6.0 is the difference between participant P03 (28) and P05 (22), not between group means. Trap: Comparing single participants rather than group means (for example 28 - 22 = 6.0 or 26 - 22 = 4.0) instead of 27 - 20 = 7.0.

qs.q: Which statement is an overinterpretation of this study's design and findings?
o: The intervention group scored higher on average than the control group in the sample shown.
Random assignment guarantees that no confounding variables were present.
Recall was tested 24 hours after the word list was studied.
Participants' recall scores varied within each group.
qs.x: Correct: B) Randomization balances confounders on average but cannot guarantee that none exist in a sample of 30. Why the others are wrong: A) The intervention participants shown averaged 27 versus 20 for controls, so this is descriptive. C) The passage states recall was tested 24 hours after the list was studied. D) Scores ranged 18–22 in controls and 26–28 in the intervention group, so they varied. Trap: Treating random assignment as eliminating all confounding, when it only balances confounders on average and a sample of 30 can still differ by chance.

qs.q: In the five participants shown, how many more hours of sleep did the intervention group average than the control group?
qs.x: Correct: Control mean = (6.5 + 7 + 7.5)/3 = 7.0 h; intervention mean = (8.5 + 8)/2 = 8.25 h; difference = 1.25 h. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.75 does not follow from the table means. C) 1.5 does not follow from the table means. D) 2 hours is the planned extension, not the difference in the recorded sleep hours. Trap: Using the planned 2-hour extension instead of the recorded sleep hours, which differ by only 1.25 h between the groups shown.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel antihypertensive drug on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in adults aged 40–65 with untreated hypertension. The randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial enrolled 100 participants, 50 receiving the drug and 50 receiving placebo. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups (mean SBP about 150 mmHg in each). After 12 weeks, mean SBP decreased by 12 mmHg in the drug group and by 4 mmHg in the placebo group. The study also recorded adverse events, with 6 participants in the drug group reporting mild headaches versus 2 in the placebo group. The authors concluded that the drug significantly lowers SBP with a tolerable safety profile.

qs.q: Based on the table, what is the absolute difference in headache incidence between the drug and placebo groups (drug minus placebo)?
qs.x: Headache incidence is 6/50 = 12% in the drug group and 2/50 = 4% in the placebo group. Absolute difference = 12% - 4% = 8 percentage points (an absolute risk increase with the drug). Trap: Subtracting the raw counts (6 - 2 = 4) instead of the percentages, or reporting a relative rather than absolute difference.

qs.q: Which study design best describes this investigation?
qs.x: Participants were randomly assigned to drug or placebo, and both groups were followed prospectively for 12 weeks, fitting the definition of a randomized controlled trial. Trap: Choosing cohort study because participants were followed forward for 12 weeks, overlooking that the investigators randomly assigned the drug or placebo.

qs.q: What is the relative risk (RR) of headache in the drug group compared to placebo?
qs.x: RR = incidence in drug group / incidence in placebo group = (6/50)/(2/50) = 0.12/0.04 = 3.00. The drug group has the higher headache incidence, so RR > 1. Trap: Inverting the ratio (placebo/drug = 0.33).

qs.q: Which of the following would be a misinterpretation of the study's headache data?
o: The drug group had a higher absolute number of headaches.
The relative risk of headache is less than 1.
The difference in headache frequency did not reach p < 0.05.
Headache events occurred in both groups.
qs.x: Correct: Headache incidence was 12% with drug vs 4% with placebo, so RR = 3.0, which is greater than 1, not less than 1. Why the others are wrong: A) 6 headaches in the drug group vs 2 in placebo is correct. C) the table gives p = 0.27 for headaches, which is above 0.05. D) the table lists 6 and 2 events, so both groups had headaches. Trap: Assuming a drug with an effective BP result must also carry the lower headache risk.

qs.q: Using the headache data (12% with drug, 4% with placebo), what is the approximate number needed to harm (NNH) for headache?
qs.x: NNH = 1/absolute risk increase = 1/(0.12 - 0.04) = 1/0.08 = 12.5, about 13 patients treated for one additional headache. Trap: Using the absolute difference in percentage points (8) or the raw count difference (4) instead of its reciprocal.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of varying doses of a novel antihypertensive drug on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in a randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial. One hundred and twenty adults with stage‑1 hypertension were assigned to one of four groups: placebo (n = 30), low dose (5 mg, n = 30), medium dose (10 mg, n = 30), or high dose (20 mg, n = 30). After 12 weeks of daily dosing, the mean change in SBP from baseline was measured. The results are summarized in Table 1. The investigators reported a dose‑response pattern, with the high‑dose group showing the greatest reduction in SBP. No serious adverse events were observed. The study concluded that the largest reductions occurred at higher doses.

qs.q: Which treatment group had the highest mean reduction in systolic blood pressure?
qs.x: The table shows the mean change in SBP for each group. The high‑dose group had the largest mean reduction (–14.2 mmHg), indicating the greatest effect. Trap: The medium‑dose group also shows a substantial reduction, but it is not the highest.

qs.q: Which design feature best ensures that the groups did not differ systematically in baseline characteristics, measured or unmeasured?
qs.x: Correct: A) Random assignment balances both known and unknown participant characteristics across groups on average. Why the others are wrong: B) a 12-week follow-up sets the timing of measurement but does not balance groups. C) measuring only SBP defines the outcome and does not balance groups. D) a placebo group controls for expectation effects but does not by itself balance baseline characteristics. Trap: Choosing the placebo group because it is the most visible control, although balancing baseline characteristics is the job of random assignment.

qs.q: Calculate the effect size (Cohen’s d) for the difference between the high‑dose and placebo groups. (Use pooled SD).
qs.x: Pooled SD = √[(4.5² + 5.2²)/2] ≈ 4.86 (equal n). Mean difference = 14.2 − 2.1 = 12.1. Cohen's d = 12.1/4.86 ≈ 2.49. Trap: Using only the high-dose SD (5.2) gives 2.33, an underestimate.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage and Table 1?
o: The mean SBP reduction increased with each higher dose.
The drug's long-term safety was established by this 12-week trial.
The high-dose group had the largest mean reduction.
qs.x: Correct: B) A 12-week trial with no long-term follow-up cannot establish long-term safety. Why the others are wrong: A) the mean changes were −2.1, −5.3, −9.7 and −14.2 mmHg. C) −14.2 mmHg was the largest mean change. D) the passage gives n = 30 for each of the four groups. Trap: Accepting 'safe' as shown after a 12-week trial with no serious events, which says nothing about long-term safety.

qs.q: Two drugs show the same maximal effect, but drug 1 reaches half-maximal effect at a lower dose than drug 2. Which statement describes drug 1 relative to drug 2?
o: It is more potent (lower EC50; curve shifted left).
qs.x: Potency is the dose needed to produce a given effect and is reflected by EC50/ED50; a lower EC50 shifts the dose-response curve left. Efficacy is the maximal effect (Emax), which is equal here. Half-life and LD50 are not determined by this curve. Trap: Confusing potency (position of the curve) with efficacy (height of the curve).

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of a novel antihypertensive agent, Hypotensol, on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in adults with stage 1 hypertension. In a randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial, 120 participants were assigned to either Hypotensol (n = 60) or placebo (n = 60) and followed for 12 weeks. Baseline characteristics were similar between groups (mean age 52 ± 9 years; mean baseline SBP 148 ± 8 mmHg). After 12 weeks, the Hypotensol group exhibited a mean SBP reduction of 12.4 mmHg (SD 5.2), whereas the placebo group showed a reduction of 3.1 mmHg (SD 4.7). The difference between groups was statistically significant (p < 0.001). Adverse events were mild and comparable across groups. These findings suggest that Hypotensol effectively lowers SBP in this population, with a favorable safety profile.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the main finding of the study?
o: A significant increase in diastolic blood pressure in the Hypotensol group
A statistically significant greater reduction in systolic blood pressure in the Hypotensol group compared to placebo
No difference in systolic blood pressure reduction between the two groups
A higher incidence of adverse events in the placebo group
qs.x: Correct: Hypotensol lowered SBP by 12.4 mmHg versus 3.1 mmHg for placebo, a significant difference (p < 0.001). Why the others are wrong: A) diastolic pressure is not reported to have increased, and SBP fell. C) the groups differed (12.4 versus 3.1 mmHg). D) adverse events were mild and comparable across groups, not more frequent in placebo. Trap: Option A misinterprets the direction of blood pressure change; option C ignores the reported statistical significance; option D incorrectly attributes adverse events.

qs.q: Which aspect of the study design best ensures that the observed effect is attributable to Hypotensol?
o: The use of a 12‑week follow‑up period
Random assignment to treatment and placebo groups
Reporting of mean baseline SBP values
qs.x: Random assignment minimizes selection bias and balances known and unknown confounders, allowing attribution of differences to the intervention. The double‑blind design and placebo control further reduce bias, but randomization is the key element for causal inference. Trap: Option A describes duration, not design; option C is descriptive; option D omits blinding of investigators, which is also important.

qs.q: What is the absolute risk reduction (ARR) in systolic blood pressure reduction of ≥10 mmHg between the Hypotensol and placebo groups, assuming 40% of the Hypotensol group and 15% of the placebo group achieved this threshold?
qs.x: ARR = proportion in treatment group achieving ≥10 mmHg reduction – proportion in placebo group achieving ≥10 mmHg reduction = 0.40 – 0.15 = 0.25. Trap: Option B (0.15) is just the placebo group's response rate; ARR requires subtracting it from the treatment rate (0.40 - 0.15 = 0.25).

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: Hypotensol lowered SBP more than placebo (12.4 versus 3.1 mmHg).
Hypotensol lowered SBP by about 9 mmHg more than placebo.
Adverse events were more common in the Hypotensol group.
Baseline SBP values were similar between groups.
qs.x: Correct: C) The passage says adverse events were mild and comparable across groups, so more events with Hypotensol is not supported. Why the others are wrong: A) The reductions are 12.4 and 3.1 mmHg. B) 12.4 - 3.1 = 9.3 mmHg. D) The passage states that baseline characteristics, including SBP, were similar. Trap: Assuming a new drug must cause more adverse events, ignoring that the passage says they were mild and comparable between groups.

qs.q: What is the approximate Cohen's d for the between-group difference in SBP reduction (pooled SD of the two groups)?
qs.x: Correct: A) The difference is 12.4 - 3.1 = 9.3 mmHg; pooled SD = sqrt((5.2^2 + 4.7^2)/2) = 4.96; d = 9.3/4.96 = 1.88. Why the others are wrong: B) 0.94 divides by the sum of the two SDs (9.9). C) 0.38 divides by the pooled variance (24.6) instead of the SD. D) 2.38 uses the Hypotensol reduction (12.4) instead of the between-group difference. Trap: Using the raw Hypotensol reduction (12.4 mmHg) or the summed SDs instead of the between-group difference over the pooled SD.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of caffeine on reaction time in a controlled laboratory setting. Sixty healthy adults were randomly assigned to one of four groups: placebo, 50 mg caffeine, 100 mg caffeine, or 200 mg caffeine. After ingestion, participants completed a computerized simple reaction time task. The mean reaction times (ms) and standard deviations (SD) were recorded. The results suggest a dose–response relationship, with higher caffeine doses associated with faster reaction times. These findings contribute to the understanding of how stimulants influence cognitive performance and have implications for occupational safety and athletic performance.

qs.q: Which condition had the lowest mean reaction time?
qs.x: The table shows the mean reaction times for each group. The 200 mg caffeine group had the lowest mean (250 ms), indicating the fastest responses. Trap: Picking the placebo or a middle dose by ignoring that a lower mean RT means faster responding.

qs.q: Which feature of the design described in the passage best supports attributing differences in reaction time to caffeine dose?
o: Random assignment to four groups, including a placebo group
Use of a computerized reaction time task
Reporting a standard deviation for each group
qs.x: Correct: A) Random assignment makes the groups comparable at the start, and the placebo group provides a baseline, so differences can be attributed to caffeine. Why the others are wrong: B) A computerized task standardizes measurement but does not address confounding. C) Reporting SDs describes spread, not cause. D) The unit of measurement has no bearing on causal inference. Trap: Crediting the measurement details (computerized task, milliseconds, SDs) with causal inference, when it is random assignment with a placebo group that handles confounding.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in mean reaction time from placebo to 100 mg caffeine?
qs.x: Percent reduction = (320–260)/320 × 100 % = 60/320 × 100 % ≈ 18.8 %. Option B is correct. Trap: Using the 50 mg group (280 ms) instead of 100 mg gives 12.5%; the 100 mg group is 260 ms, 60 ms below placebo (320 ms).

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?
o: Higher caffeine doses are associated with faster reaction times.
The 200 mg caffeine group had the fastest mean reaction time.
Standard deviation increases with increasing caffeine dose.
Placebo participants had the slowest reaction times.
qs.x: The standard deviations fall from 15 ms (placebo) to 12, 10, and 9 ms as dose rises, so the statement that SD increases with dose is not supported. The other statements agree with the table. Trap: Assuming that faster mean times must come with larger variability.

qs.q: Which description of the dose–response pattern is supported by the table?
o: Successive dose increases produced progressively smaller decreases in mean reaction time (40, 20, then 10 ms).
Each dose increase produced the same decrease in mean reaction time.
The step from 100 mg to 200 mg produced the largest decrease in mean reaction time.
The 200 mg group was more than 100 ms faster than the placebo group.
qs.x: Correct: A) Mean RT fell 40 ms (placebo to 50 mg), 20 ms (50 to 100 mg) and 10 ms (100 to 200 mg). Why the others are wrong: B) The decreases were 40, 20 and 10 ms, not equal. C) The 100 to 200 mg step gave the smallest decrease (10 ms). D) 320 - 250 = 70 ms, not more than 100 ms. Trap: Assuming that doubling the dose keeps producing equal or larger gains; the decreases shrink (40, 20, 10 ms) as the dose rises.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers at the University of Health Sciences conducted a randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of a novel antihypertensive agent, Hypertensol, in adults with stage 1 hypertension. A total of 200 participants were assigned to one of four groups: placebo (n = 50), 10 mg (n = 50), 20 mg (n = 50), or 40 mg (n = 50). Baseline systolic blood pressure (SBP) was measured after a 5‑minute seated rest. After 4 weeks of daily dosing, SBP was reassessed under identical conditions. The investigators recorded mean SBP values and calculated mean reductions for each group. The study aimed to determine dose‑response relationships and to identify the optimal dose that maximizes blood pressure lowering while minimizing adverse effects. The data are summarized in Table 1 below. The researchers also collected safety data, but the primary outcome was the mean change in SBP.

qs.q: Which dosage group achieved the greatest mean reduction in systolic blood pressure after 4 weeks?
qs.x: The mean reduction for the 40 mg group was 29 mmHg, which is the largest among all groups. The placebo group had only a 2 mmHg reduction, and the 10 mg and 20 mg groups had 15 mmHg and 12 mmHg reductions, respectively. Trap: The option that lists the 10 mg group (B) might be tempting because it shows a substantial reduction, but it is not the greatest.

qs.q: Which study design best controls for the placebo effect in this trial?
qs.x: A randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial is specifically designed to minimize bias and placebo effects by randomly assigning participants to treatment or placebo groups and blinding both participants and investigators. Trap: A crossover design (A) might seem appropriate, but it was not used in this study and can introduce carry‑over effects.

qs.q: What is the mean reduction in systolic blood pressure for the 20 mg group?
qs.x: The table lists the mean reduction for the 20 mg group as 12 mmHg (148 mmHg baseline minus 136 mmHg after 4 weeks). Trap: Option C (15 mmHg) reflects the reduction for the 10 mg group, which is a common misreading.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented in Table 1?
o: The 40 mg group experienced the largest mean reduction in SBP.
The placebo group showed a statistically significant reduction in SBP.
The 10 mg group had a greater mean reduction than the 20 mg group.
The 40 mg dose produced a greater mean SBP reduction than each lower dose.
qs.x: The table shows a mean reduction of only 2 mmHg for placebo, and no p-values are given, so a statistically significant placebo reduction is not supported. The other statements are directly supported (note 10 mg gave 15 mmHg vs 12 mmHg for 20 mg, so the response is not monotonic across all doses). Trap: Option C might look wrong because higher dose is expected to give more reduction, but 15 > 12 mmHg is what the table shows; the unsupported claim is the placebo significance.

qs.q: Which pharmacological concept is most closely linked to the dose‑response relationship observed in this study?
qs.x: Correct: B. Pharmacodynamics describes the relationship between drug dose and the size of the effect on the body, here the SBP reduction at each dose. Why the others are wrong: A) pharmacokinetics concerns absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion, not effect size. C) therapeutic index compares toxic and effective doses, and the table has no toxicity data. D) drug metabolism is one pharmacokinetic process and is not measured here. Trap: Option A (pharmacokinetics) deals with drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion, not the observed effect magnitude.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers investigated the impact of visual complexity on reaction time in a simple target detection task. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three display conditions: (1) minimal visual clutter, (2) moderate clutter, and (3) high clutter. Each participant completed 60 trials, and mean reaction times were recorded. The study aimed to quantify how increasing visual complexity affects cognitive processing speed. The results are summarized in Table 1. The researchers also collected subjective workload ratings using the NASA-TLX scale, but these data are not shown here. The findings are intended to inform interface design guidelines for high‑stakes environments such as air traffic control and surgical navigation systems.

qs.q: Which display condition produced the fastest mean reaction time?
qs.x: The table shows the mean reaction time for each condition. Minimal clutter has the lowest mean (350 ms), indicating the fastest responses. Trap: Assuming that a higher standard deviation indicates faster processing.

qs.q: For a follow-up study of the effect of color contrast on reaction time, which comparison isolates color contrast as the only difference between conditions?
o: Minimal clutter with low contrast versus minimal clutter with high contrast
Minimal clutter with low contrast versus high clutter with high contrast
Moderate clutter with low contrast versus high clutter with low contrast
Minimal clutter with high contrast versus moderate clutter with high contrast
qs.x: Correct: Only color contrast differs between the two minimal-clutter conditions, so any difference in reaction time can be attributed to contrast. Why the others are wrong: B) clutter and contrast both differ, so their effects are confounded. C) only clutter differs, which tests clutter rather than contrast. D) only clutter differs again (minimal versus moderate), with contrast held constant. Trap: Choosing a pair that differs in clutter as well as contrast, so the two factors are confounded.

qs.q: What percent increase in mean reaction time occurs when moving from the minimal clutter condition to the moderate clutter condition?
qs.x: Increase = (410 − 350) / 350 = 60 / 350 ≈ 17.1%, option B. Trap: Calculating the increase as a decrease because the mean reaction time is higher.

qs.q: If one display condition also used a smaller target than the others, which variable would confound the effect of clutter on reaction time?
o: The number of trials per participant, which is 60 in every condition
The mean reaction time recorded for each condition
Target size, because it would differ between conditions and independently affect reaction time
The standard deviation of reaction times in each condition
qs.x: Correct: A confounding variable changes along with the independent variable and also affects the outcome; target size differing between conditions would do both. Why the others are wrong: A) Trial number is constant across conditions, so it cannot account for differences between them. B) Mean reaction time is the outcome being measured, not a confound. D) The SD is a summary of the outcome data, not a manipulated or uncontrolled cause. Trap: Calling any measured or listed quantity a confound, even if it is constant or is the outcome itself.

qs.q: How do the findings of this study relate to the broader principle of cognitive load theory?
o: They suggest that extraneous visual load consumes working-memory resources, raising total cognitive load and slowing processing.
They show that extraneous visual load decreases germane cognitive load, improving learning.
They suggest that intrinsic cognitive load is unaffected by visual clutter.
They indicate that germane cognitive load is the primary driver of reaction time.
qs.x: Cognitive load theory posits that extraneous load (e.g., visual clutter) consumes working memory resources, thereby increasing overall cognitive load and reducing processing speed. Trap: Confusing extraneous load with intrinsic load.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel dietary supplement on resting metabolic rate (RMR) in adults aged 25‑45. In a double‑blind, randomized controlled trial, 120 participants were assigned to either the supplement group (n=60) or placebo group (n=60). Baseline RMR was measured using indirect calorimetry after an overnight fast. After 12 weeks of daily supplementation, RMR was reassessed. The supplement group exhibited a mean increase of 120 kcal/day (SD 35) relative to baseline, whereas the placebo group showed a mean increase of 45 kcal/day (SD 30). Secondary outcomes included changes in body composition and lipid profile. No adverse events were reported. The authors concluded that the supplement significantly enhances RMR compared to placebo, potentially aiding weight management strategies.

qs.q: Which group experienced the larger mean increase in resting metabolic rate after 12 weeks?
o: Both groups experienced the same increase
qs.x: The supplement group’s mean ΔRMR was 120 kcal/day, whereas the placebo group’s mean ΔRMR was 45 kcal/day, making the supplement group’s increase larger. Trap: A common mistake is to misinterpret the baseline values; the increase is calculated from the difference between baseline and week‑12, not from the absolute baseline values.

qs.q: What type of study design was used in this research?
qs.x: The passage explicitly states that participants were randomly assigned to supplement or placebo groups in a double‑blind fashion, which defines a randomized controlled trial. Trap: Students sometimes confuse the term "randomized" with a simple observational cohort; the key is the controlled assignment and blinding.

qs.q: What is the percent increase in RMR for the supplement group relative to baseline?
qs.x: Percent increase = (ΔRMR / Baseline) × 100 = (120 / 1500) × 100 = 8%. Trap: A common error is using the week‑12 value (1620) as the numerator instead of the change (120).

qs.q: Which of the following statements is FALSE?
o: The supplement increased RMR by 120 kcal/day.
The placebo increased RMR by 45 kcal/day.
qs.x: The data show an increase in RMR for both groups; there is no evidence of a decrease in the supplement group. Trap: Students sometimes misread the word "decreased" as "decreased relative to placebo"; the statement is simply false.

qs.q: Which clinical application is most directly supported by the study’s findings?
qs.x: An increase in resting metabolic rate can contribute to greater energy expenditure, which is a key component of weight management strategies. Trap: Students may incorrectly link metabolic rate changes to cardiovascular or respiratory conditions; the primary implication is for weight control.

text: Researchers investigated the effect of a novel antihypertensive agent, Hypto, on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in adults with stage 1 hypertension. After 4 weeks of daily dosing, SBP was reassessed using the same protocol. The Hypto group exhibited a mean SBP of 140 mmHg at 4 weeks, compared with 150 mmHg at baseline, whereas the placebo group’s mean SBP rose from 140 mmHg to 145 mmHg. The mean change in SBP for Hypto was a reduction of 10 mmHg, while the placebo group experienced a mean increase of 5 mmHg. These results suggest Hypto may effectively lower SBP in this population, though the study’s short duration limits conclusions about long‑term efficacy and safety.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the change in systolic blood pressure in the Hypto group?
qs.x: The mean SBP in the Hypto group decreased from 150 mmHg to 140 mmHg, a reduction of 10 mmHg. Trap: Option A appears plausible but indicates the opposite direction of change.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the experimental design used in this study?
qs.x: Participants were randomly assigned to receive either Hypto or placebo, characteristic of a randomized controlled trial. Trap: Option B describes a prospective observational study, which was not used here.

qs.q: What is the mean change in systolic blood pressure for the placebo group?
qs.x: The placebo group’s mean SBP increased from 140 mmHg to 145 mmHg, a mean change of +5 mmHg. Trap: Option D suggests a decrease, which is incorrect for the placebo group.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?
o: Hypto reduced systolic blood pressure by 10 mmHg
The placebo group had a slight increase in blood pressure
The study had 50 participants per group
Hypto produced a greater reduction than placebo
qs.x: The study included 40 participants in each group, not 50. Trap: Option A is supported by the data but is a distractor because the question asks for the unsupported statement.

qs.q: What is the placebo-adjusted mean change in SBP attributable to Hypto at 4 weeks?
qs.x: Hypto changed SBP by -10 mmHg; placebo changed it by +5 mmHg. The placebo-adjusted effect = -10 - (+5) = -15 mmHg. Trap: Reporting the raw -10 mmHg ignores that placebo SBP rose by 5 mmHg.

text: Researchers investigated the impact of caffeine on short‑term memory recall in healthy adults. One hundred and twenty participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a placebo group, a low‑dose caffeine group (50 mg), a medium‑dose caffeine group (150 mg), and a high‑dose caffeine group (300 mg). After a 30‑minute absorption period, all participants completed a standardized word‑list recall test. The researchers measured the percentage of words correctly recalled for each group. The study aimed to determine whether increasing caffeine dosage improves recall performance and whether there is a dose‑response relationship. The findings were summarized in Table 1 below, which lists the mean recall percentages and standard deviations for each dosage condition. The authors concluded that moderate caffeine intake enhances memory recall relative to placebo, but excessive intake does not yield additional benefits.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, which caffeine dosage group achieved the highest mean recall percentage?
qs.x: The medium‑dose group (150 mg) reported a mean recall of 82.3 %, which is higher than the other groups. Trap: Students often assume that the highest dose yields the best performance, overlooking the slight decline at 300 mg.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of randomly assigning the 120 participants to the four dosage groups?
o: To make it likely that pre-existing differences in memory ability are spread evenly across the groups
To ensure every participant has exactly the same baseline recall ability
To make sure participants know which dose they received
To increase the recall percentage of the caffeine groups
qs.x: Correct: Random assignment spreads pre-existing differences (such as memory ability) across groups by chance, reducing systematic bias. Why the others are wrong: B) randomization balances groups on average; it does not make individuals identical. C) randomization has no role in telling participants their dose. D) assignment method does not change recall in any group. Trap: Assuming randomization guarantees identical groups, when it only balances them on average by chance.

qs.q: What is the percent increase in mean recall from the low‑dose to the high‑dose group?
qs.x: Percent increase = (80.7 - 75.1)/75.1 x 100 = 7.5%. Trap: 5.6 is the absolute difference in percentage points, not the percent increase.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by Table 1?
o: Mean recall rose from placebo through the 150 mg dose.
The 300 mg group recalled a higher percentage than the 50 mg group.
The 300 mg group had the highest mean recall of all four groups.
The 150 mg group had the smallest SD.
qs.x: Correct: The 300 mg mean (80.7%) is below the 150 mg mean (82.3%), so the high-dose group did not have the highest recall. Why the others are wrong: A) 68.4, 75.1 and 82.3% rise at each step. B) 80.7% is greater than 75.1%. D) SD of 4.5 is smaller than 5.2, 4.8 and 5.0. Trap: Assuming the highest dose must give the best recall, overlooking the small decline from 82.3% to 80.7%.

qs.q: Which interpretation of the 150 mg versus 300 mg results in Table 1 is best supported?
o: The 300 mg group recalled 1.6 percentage points less than the 150 mg group, so doubling the dose gave no added recall benefit.
The 300 mg group recalled less than the placebo group, so the high dose impaired memory.
The 300 mg group recalled exactly the same percentage as the 150 mg group.
The decline at 300 mg proves caffeine at that dose is toxic.
qs.x: Correct: A) 82.3 - 80.7 = 1.6 points lower at 300 mg, while both caffeine groups remain above placebo (68.4), so no additional benefit appeared. Why the others are wrong: B) 80.7% is well above the placebo 68.4%. C) The means are 82.3% and 80.7%, not equal. D) Toxicity was not measured in the study. Trap: Reading the small decline from 82.3% to 80.7% as harm; the 300 mg group still recalled about 12 points more than placebo, so the data show no added benefit rather than impairment.

text: Researchers studied the effect of caffeine on cognitive performance in a controlled experiment. One hundred twenty healthy adults were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: no caffeine (Placebo), 50 mg caffeine, 100 mg caffeine, and 150 mg caffeine. Each participant completed a series of reaction‑time tasks while their responses were recorded. The mean response times (in milliseconds), standard deviations, and sample sizes for each condition are summarized in Table 1 below. The study aimed to determine whether increasing caffeine dosage would produce a dose‑dependent improvement in reaction time and to assess any potential plateau or adverse effects at higher doses.

qs.q: Which condition had the fastest average response time?
qs.x: The mean response time for the 100 mg caffeine condition (395 ms) is lower than all other conditions, indicating the fastest average reaction time. Trap: The 150 mg caffeine condition has a mean of 400 ms, which is only slightly slower than the 100 mg condition and could mislead students into choosing it.

qs.q: Which experimental design best controls for placebo effect in this study?
qs.x: A double‑blind randomized controlled trial ensures that neither participants nor researchers know which dose is administered, thereby minimizing expectancy and observer bias. Trap: Single‑blind designs still allow researchers to know the dose, which can influence data collection and interpretation.

qs.q: What percent improvement in mean response time does the 100 mg caffeine condition represent over the placebo condition?
qs.x: Improvement = (450 ms – 395 ms) / 450 ms × 100 ≈ 12.2%, which rounds to 12%. Trap: Choosing 8% from the 50 mg condition (40 ms of 450 ms is about 8.9%) instead of the 100 mg condition (55 ms of 450 ms).

qs.q: Which statement is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: Higher doses always produce faster times.
The 100 mg condition had a lower mean response time than the placebo.
The 150 mg condition had a lower mean response time than the placebo.
qs.x: Means were 450, 410, 395 and 400 ms. Higher doses do not always produce faster times because 150 mg (400 ms) was slower than 100 mg (395 ms). The other statements are supported. Trap: Assuming a higher dose always gives faster times, ignoring that 150 mg (400 ms) was slower than 100 mg (395 ms).

qs.q: The findings of this study most closely illustrate which of the following concepts?
qs.x: The data show a clear relationship between caffeine dose and reaction time up to a point, demonstrating a dose‑response effect. Trap: The placebo effect might be mistaken because there is a control group, but the key finding is the systematic change with dose.

text: Researchers investigated how varying light intensity affects photosynthetic performance in spinach (Spinacia oleracea) leaves. Spinach leaf discs were exposed to four controlled light regimes: 200, 400, 600, and 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, using a calibrated LED light source. For each intensity, oxygen evolution (µmol O₂ m⁻² s⁻¹), stomatal conductance (mol m⁻² s⁻¹), and chlorophyll fluorescence (ΦPSII) were measured after a 10‑minute acclimation period. The data are summarized in Table 1. The results show a near-linear increase in oxygen evolution from 200 to 600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, with only a small further rise at 800. Stomatal conductance rises modestly across the range, while ΦPSII remains relatively stable, suggesting efficient photochemistry at higher light levels. These findings support the hypothesis that spinach photosynthesis is light‑limited up to ~600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, after which additional light does not markedly enhance electron transport.

qs.q: Which light intensity resulted in the highest oxygen evolution rate?
qs.x: The table shows the oxygen evolution rate increases with light intensity, reaching 36.8 µmol O₂ m⁻² s⁻¹ at 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, the highest value among the four intensities. Trap: Students often assume the plateau occurs at 600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹; however, the data indicate a slight further increase at 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.

qs.q: Design an experiment to test how temperature influences the same photosynthetic parameters measured in the passage. Specify the key variables, controls, and the method you would use to isolate temperature effects.
o: Use a single temperature and vary light intensity while keeping all other conditions constant.

Maintain constant light intensity and vary temperature across a range of 10 °C to 40 °C, using a temperature‑controlled growth chamber and measuring O₂ evolution, stomatal conductance, and ΦPSII at each temperature.
Randomly assign leaves to different temperatures without replication to save time.
Use a greenhouse with natural temperature fluctuations and record photosynthetic rates at random times.
qs.x: Correct: B holds light constant while varying only temperature across a range, in a controlled chamber, and measures all three parameters at each temperature, isolating the temperature effect. Why the others are wrong: A) it varies light intensity at one temperature, so it does not test temperature. C) without replication, chance variation cannot be separated from a temperature effect. D) natural temperature fluctuations in a greenhouse leave light and other conditions uncontrolled. Trap: Choosing an option that varies light or leaves other conditions uncontrolled or unreplicated, instead of varying only temperature with light held constant.

qs.q: Calculate the percent increase in oxygen evolution rate when light intensity increases from 200 to 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
qs.x: Percent increase = (36.8 − 12.3) / 12.3 × 100 = 24.5 / 12.3 × 100 ≈ 199.2%. Trap: Dividing by the final value (36.8) or reporting only part of the increase, when the denominator must be the 200 µmol baseline value of 12.3.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is false regarding the data presented?
o: Oxygen evolution increases with light intensity up to 600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
Stomatal conductance shows a modest increase across all light intensities.
ΦPSII decreases significantly at the highest light intensity.
The data suggest a light‑limited photosynthesis up to ~600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
qs.x: The table shows ΦPSII remains stable (~0.68–0.71) across all intensities; it does not decrease significantly at 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. Trap: Option C is a trap because students may assume photoinhibition at high light, but the data contradict this.

qs.q: Between which two adjacent light intensities did oxygen evolution increase the least?
o: The increase was the same in all three intervals
qs.x: Correct: The increases are 11.4 (12.3 to 23.7), 11.4 (23.7 to 35.1) and only 1.7 µmol O₂ m⁻² s⁻¹ (35.1 to 36.8), so the 600 to 800 interval is smallest. Why the others are wrong: A) 200 to 400 gave 11.4. B) 400 to 600 also gave 11.4. D) the third interval is far smaller than the first two. Trap: Assuming oxygen evolution keeps rising by the same amount per step, when the gain collapses from 11.4 to 1.7 above 600 µmol photons.

text: Researchers investigated the impact of three different cognitive training protocols on reaction time in a sample of 120 adults aged 20‑35. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group that received no training, a group that practiced a working‑memory task (Treatment A), a group that engaged in a visuospatial task (Treatment B), and a group that received a combined working‑memory and visuospatial training (Combined). Each training program consisted of 30 minutes per day for 10 consecutive days. Reaction times were measured before and after the training period using a computerized simple‑reaction‑time task. The pre‑training mean reaction times (in milliseconds) were 350 ± 25 for the control group, 345 ± 30 for Treatment A, 342 ± 28 for Treatment B, and 340 ± 27 for Combined. Post‑training means were 320 ± 20 for control, 310 ± 22 for Treatment A, 305 ± 23 for Treatment B, and 300 ± 18 for Combined. Descriptively, each training group showed a larger mean pre-to-post decrease than the control group, and the combined group showed the largest decrease; no inferential statistical tests were reported. However, the variability in the data indicates that individual differences may moderate the effectiveness of each protocol.

qs.q: Which group had the lowest mean reaction time after training?
qs.x: The combined training group had the lowest post‑training mean reaction time of 300 ms, lower than the other groups. Trap: Treating a higher reaction time as better performance and choosing the slowest group (Control, 320 ms) instead of the lowest post-training mean.

qs.q: If you want to test whether Treatment A improves reaction time over Control, what experimental design is most appropriate?
o: Randomized controlled trial with pre‑ and post‑measurements
qs.x: A randomized controlled trial with pre‑ and post‑measurements allows comparison of the change in reaction time between the two groups while controlling for confounders. Trap: Students may incorrectly select observational designs; the key is that the study must be randomized and controlled.

qs.q: Calculate the percent reduction in mean reaction time from pre-training to post-training for Treatment A.
qs.x: Percent reduction = (345 – 310) / 345 × 100 = 10.1%, using the pre-training mean as the baseline. Trap: 3.1% is the post-training difference between Control and Treatment A relative to Control post (10/320), which is not a pre-to-post change in Treatment A.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a valid interpretation of the data?
o: The Combined group showed the largest mean pre-to-post decrease in reaction time.
Treatment A had the lowest pre‑training mean.
Each training group showed a larger mean pre-to-post decrease than the control group.
qs.x: Correct: C) Treatment A's pre-training mean (345 ms) was higher than both Treatment B (342 ms) and Combined (340 ms); Combined had the lowest. Why the others are wrong: A) Combined fell 40 ms (340 to 300), more than Treatment A (35), Treatment B (37) or Control (30). B) The passage notes that the variability suggests individual differences may moderate effectiveness. D) Decreases of 35, 37 and 40 ms all exceed the control decrease of 30 ms. Trap: Students often focus on post‑training results and overlook pre‑training comparisons.

qs.q: Compared with the control group's pre-to-post change, how many additional milliseconds of reduction in mean reaction time did the Combined group show?
qs.x: Correct: A) Control fell 350 - 320 = 30 ms; Combined fell 340 - 300 = 40 ms; the difference is 10 ms. Why the others are wrong: B) 20 ms is the difference between the post-training means (320 - 300), which ignores that the groups started at different baselines. C) 30 ms is the control group's own change. D) 40 ms is the Combined group's own change, not its excess over control. Trap: Reporting the Combined group's total change without subtracting the improvement that also occurred in controls.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of a novel antihypertensive agent, Hypotensol, in adults with stage 1 hypertension. A total of 200 participants were randomly assigned to receive either Hypotensol (n = 100) or a placebo (n = 100) for 12 weeks. Systolic blood pressure (SBP) was measured at baseline and at weeks 4, 8, and 12. The study aimed to determine whether Hypotensol could produce a clinically meaningful reduction in SBP compared to placebo. The investigators also recorded adverse events and adherence rates. The primary endpoint was the mean change in SBP from baseline to week 12. Secondary endpoints included the proportion of patients achieving target SBP < 140 mmHg and the incidence of serious adverse events. The trial was double‑blinded, and all participants provided informed consent. The data presented in Table 1 summarize the mean SBP and standard deviation for each group at each time point. These results will inform clinicians about the potential benefits and safety profile of Hypotensol in a real‑world setting.

qs.q: What does the table primarily illustrate regarding the treatment groups over time?
o: The placebo group consistently had lower SBP than the Hypotensol group.
Hypotensol produced a greater reduction in mean SBP compared to placebo.
Both groups experienced identical changes in SBP over the 12 weeks.
The standard deviations increased over time for both groups.
qs.x: The table shows a progressive decline in mean SBP for the Hypotensol group, reaching 130.1 mmHg at week 12, whereas the placebo group remains above 140 mmHg. This indicates a greater reduction in SBP with Hypotensol. Trap: Option A incorrectly states that the placebo group had lower SBP.

qs.q: Which of the following study designs would best allow the researchers to attribute changes in SBP to Hypotensol?
o: A cross‑sectional survey of hypertensive patients using Hypotensol.
A randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial with parallel groups.
A case‑control study comparing patients who achieved target SBP to those who did not.
A cohort study following patients who choose to take Hypotensol versus those who do not.
qs.x: Randomization and blinding control for confounding variables and bias, providing the strongest evidence that observed differences are due to the intervention. Trap: Option D suggests a cohort design, which is more prone to selection bias.

qs.q: Calculate the percent reduction in mean SBP from baseline to week 12 for the Hypotensol group.
qs.x: Percent reduction = [(148.2 - 130.1)/148.2] x 100 = 18.1/148.2 x 100 = 12.2%. Trap: Using the placebo mean or the week-12 value as the denominator gives a different (incorrect) percentage.

qs.q: Which statement is a potential trap when interpreting the study results?
o: The double‑blind design reduces observer bias.
A statistically significant difference in SBP implies clinical significance.
Adverse events were monitored throughout the trial.
The study included a 12‑week follow‑up period.
qs.x: Statistical significance does not automatically equate to clinical relevance; the magnitude of change and patient outcomes must also be considered. Trap: Assuming that a statistically significant 11 mmHg difference between groups automatically means a clinically meaningful benefit for patients.

qs.q: Which statistical test is most appropriate for comparing the primary endpoint (mean change in SBP from baseline to week 12) between the two treatment groups?
qs.x: The primary endpoint is a continuous variable (mean change in SBP) compared between two independent groups, so a two-sample t-test is appropriate. Chi-square and McNemar tests analyze categorical outcomes, and the log-rank test compares time-to-event data. Trap: Choosing a categorical-outcome test (chi-square) because the secondary endpoint (proportion reaching target SBP) is dichotomous.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers investigated the impact of two novel cognitive training programs on working memory performance in adults aged 18-35. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups: a control group that received no training, Intervention A that used a visuospatial task, and Intervention B that used a verbal task. Baseline working memory was assessed using the Digit Span Forward and Backward tests. After a 4-week training period, post-intervention scores were re-evaluated. The study aimed to determine whether task modality influences the magnitude of working memory improvement and to assess the durability of training effects over a 3-month follow-up. Results were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA, and effect sizes were reported as Cohen’s d. The authors discussed potential neural mechanisms underlying observed gains and suggested implications for educational and occupational settings.

qs.q: Which group demonstrated the greatest absolute improvement in working memory scores?
o: Both Intervention A and B equally
qs.x: Intervention A improved from 12.2 to 15.8, a gain of 3.6 points, which is larger than the 1.7-point gain in Intervention B and the 0.4-point gain in Control. Trap: Assuming both interventions helped equally because both improved over control, ignoring the 3.6-point gain for A versus 1.7 for B.

qs.q: Which experimental design feature best controls for confounding variables in this study?
o: Assessing working memory with Digit Span tests
Reporting effect sizes as Cohen’s d
qs.x: Random assignment ensures that participant characteristics are evenly distributed across groups, minimizing confounding effects. Trap: Choosing the training length or the test choice, which are design features but do not balance participant characteristics across groups the way random assignment does.

qs.q: Calculate the percent improvement for Intervention A.
qs.x: Percent improvement = (15.8 − 12.2)/12.2 × 100 = 29.5%. Trap: Option B divides by the post-test score (3.6/15.8 = 22.8%); the baseline is the correct denominator.

qs.q: Which statement is NOT supported by the passage and Table 1?
o: Intervention A's post-test mean was higher than Intervention B's.
The control group's mean score changed by less than 1 point.
Intervention B's mean score rose from pre-test to post-test.
The training gains were still present at the 3-month follow-up.
qs.x: Correct: D) The passage says the study aimed to assess durability over 3 months, but Table 1 reports only pre- and post-test scores; no follow-up data are given. Why the others are wrong: A) 15.8 is greater than 14.1. B) The control mean went from 12.3 to 12.7, a change of 0.4. C) Intervention B went from 12.4 to 14.1. Trap: Assuming that the stated aim of assessing 3-month durability means follow-up results were reported.

qs.q: In Baddeley's working memory model, which component is most directly engaged by Intervention B's verbal task and by the Digit Span tests?
qs.x: Rehearsing digits and verbal material relies on the phonological loop, whereas Intervention A's visuospatial task taxes the visuospatial sketchpad. Trap: Option B is the component trained by Intervention A, not by the verbal task.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of caffeine on working memory performance in college students. Forty‑eight participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups: a placebo group (0 mg caffeine), a low‑dose group (50 mg caffeine), and a high‑dose group (200 mg caffeine). After ingestion, participants completed a 30‑minute n‑back task while their reaction times (RTs) and accuracy were recorded. The mean RTs (in milliseconds) and standard deviations (SD) for each group are presented in Table 1. The researchers hypothesized that moderate caffeine would improve working memory, reflected by faster RTs and higher accuracy, while excessive caffeine might produce a U‑shaped performance curve. Additionally, the study collected subjective alertness ratings on a 7‑point Likert scale. The results showed a statistically significant difference in RTs among the groups (p < 0.01). The low‑dose group had the fastest mean RT, whereas the high‑dose group had the slowest. Accuracy rates followed a similar pattern, with the low‑dose group achieving the highest percentage correct. The authors concluded that a moderate caffeine dose optimizes working‑memory performance, supporting the inverted‑U hypothesis of arousal and cognition.

qs.q: Which group had the fastest mean reaction time?
qs.x: The low‑dose group’s mean RT was 350 ms, faster than the placebo (400 ms) and high‑dose (420 ms) groups. Trap: Choosing placebo or high-dose because more caffeine is assumed to mean faster responding; the low-dose group at 350 ms was fastest.

qs.q: Which design choice would let each participant serve as their own control for individual caffeine tolerance?
qs.x: Correct: B) In a crossover design every participant receives each dose, so tolerance is held constant within a person. Why the others are wrong: A) Random assignment balances tolerance only on average between groups, not within each person. C) A larger sample reduces random error but does not control tolerance. D) Using only male participants restricts the sample and does not remove individual differences in tolerance. Trap: Choosing random assignment (option A), which balances tolerance only on average across groups rather than within each individual.

qs.q: What is the percent improvement in mean RT from placebo to low‑dose?
qs.x: Improvement = (400–350)/400 × 100 % = 12.5 %. Trap: Choosing 10% or 20% by using the wrong base; percent improvement uses the placebo mean (400 ms) as the denominator: 50/400 = 12.5%.

qs.q: Which statement is contradicted by Table 1?
o: Low-dose caffeine produced a faster mean reaction time than placebo.
High-dose caffeine produced the fastest mean reaction time.
Performance was best at the low dose and worse at the high dose than at the placebo (an inverted-U pattern).
The low-dose group had the fastest mean reaction time.
qs.x: Correct: B) The high-dose mean RT (420 ms) was the slowest, not the fastest. Why the others are wrong: A) Low-dose RT was 350 ms versus 400 ms for placebo. C) Low dose was best (350 ms) and high dose worst (420 ms), an inverted-U pattern in performance. D) 350 ms is the fastest of the three means. Trap: Reading the high dose as best because more caffeine is assumed to give more alertness; its mean RT of 420 ms was the slowest.

qs.q: Which broader psychological theory is supported by the study’s results?
qs.x: The inverted‑U pattern of performance with moderate caffeine aligns with the Yerkes‑Dodson law of arousal and optimal performance. Trap: Choosing classical conditioning or another unrelated theory because caffeine is a stimulus; an inverted-U of performance against arousal is the Yerkes-Dodson pattern.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers at the University of Health Sciences conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effect of a novel antihypertensive drug, Hypertenso, on systolic blood pressure (SBP). A total of 120 participants with stage‑1 hypertension were enrolled and randomly assigned to either the treatment group (Hypertenso) or a placebo control group. Baseline SBP was measured after a 5‑minute seated rest, and follow‑up measurements were taken at 4 weeks. The study aimed to determine whether Hypertenso could produce a clinically meaningful reduction in SBP compared to placebo. In addition to SBP, researchers recorded heart rate, serum potassium, and patient-reported side effects. The investigators hypothesized that the drug would lower SBP by at least 8 mmHg more than placebo, a threshold considered clinically significant for reducing cardiovascular risk. The trial was double‑blind, and adherence was monitored via pill counts and electronic medication event monitoring systems. Results were analyzed using intention‑to‑treat principles and a two‑sided alpha of 0.05. The findings are summarized in Table 1 below, which presents mean SBP values and mean reductions for both groups.

qs.q: What was the mean reduction in systolic blood pressure for participants in the treatment group?
qs.x: The table shows the treatment group’s baseline SBP as 140 mmHg and week‑4 SBP as 132 mmHg, yielding a mean reduction of 8 mmHg. Trap: Option A (5 mmHg) might be chosen if a reader mistakenly subtracts the control group’s reduction from the treatment group’s reduction.

qs.q: Which statement best describes the study’s design?
qs.x: Participants were randomly assigned to treatment or placebo, the study was double‑blind, and outcomes were measured prospectively—hallmarks of a randomized controlled trial. Trap: Option B (observational cohort) might be chosen if a reader focuses on the fact that participants were followed over time.

qs.q: If the treatment group had 30 participants with a mean baseline SBP of 140 mmHg and a mean week‑4 SBP of 128 mmHg, what is the mean reduction?
qs.x: Mean reduction = 140 - 128 = 12 mmHg. Trap: Option A (10 mmHg) results from misreading one of the values.

qs.q: In this randomized trial, why is age unlikely to be a major confounder of the drug-SBP relationship?
o: Random assignment tends to balance age across the treatment and placebo groups
Age has no effect on systolic blood pressure
Both groups were measured after a 5-minute seated rest
Intention-to-treat analysis removes the effect of age
qs.x: Correct: Randomization distributes participant characteristics such as age, BMI and smoking similarly between arms, so they are unlikely to be systematically linked to treatment. Why the others are wrong: B) Age is a known influence on SBP; the point is that it is balanced, not irrelevant. C) The seated rest standardizes measurement conditions but does not balance participant characteristics. D) Intention-to-treat keeps participants in their assigned groups to preserve randomization; it does not adjust for age. Trap: Believing a confounder must be absent from the study rather than balanced across groups by randomization.

qs.q: Which statement best links the study’s findings to clinical practice?
o: Hypertenso lowered SBP more than placebo (a net difference of about 6 mmHg), but this is below the prespecified 8 mmHg threshold, so clinical benefit is not established.
Hypertenso is ineffective for lowering SBP.
Hypertenso increases the risk of hyperkalemia.
No conclusion can be drawn from the data.
qs.x: Treatment reduced SBP by 8 mmHg and placebo by 2 mmHg, a net effect of 6 mmHg, which is below the 8 mmHg threshold the investigators set for clinical significance. Options B, C, and D are not supported by the data. Trap: Comparing the raw 8 mmHg reduction to the threshold ignores the placebo response.

text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel dietary supplement on exercise performance in healthy adults.
