passages.title: Structure, growth, physiology, and genetics of prokaryotes and viruses · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of a novel probiotic supplement on gut microbiota composition and inflammatory markers in adults with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). The study enrolled 120 participants randomized to probiotic or placebo for 12 weeks. Stool samples were collected at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks and analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing to quantify relative abundance of key bacterial taxa. Serum C‑reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin‑6 (IL‑6) levels were measured at the same time points. Table 1 summarizes the primary outcomes for the probiotic group versus placebo at week 12. The probiotic group showed a 25 % increase in Bifidobacterium spp. relative abundance, a 15 % reduction in Proteobacteria, and a 30 % decrease in serum CRP compared to baseline. In contrast, the placebo group exhibited no significant changes. The authors concluded that the probiotic supplementation may modulate gut microbiota and reduce systemic inflammation in IBS patients.

qs.q: Which bacterial group decreased in relative abundance in the probiotic group by week 12?
qs.x: Correct: B) The passage reports a 15% reduction in Proteobacteria, and the table shows 25.5% versus 29.8% in placebo. Why the others are wrong: A) Bifidobacterium increased by 25%. C) No Firmicutes data are reported. D) No Actinobacteria data are reported. Trap: Choosing Bifidobacterium because it is the first taxon named in the table; it rose in the probiotic group rather than fell.

qs.q: Which statement best describes the comparison used in this study?
o: Crossover in which every participant received both treatments
qs.x: Correct: A) Participants were randomized to probiotic or placebo, a randomized placebo-controlled comparison. Why the others are wrong: B) A placebo group was included. C) Each participant received one treatment for 12 weeks, not both. D) The placebo group is a control group. Trap: Assuming a crossover design because both probiotic and placebo appear in the study; each participant received only one of them.

qs.q: At week 12, by what percent was mean CRP lower in the probiotic group than in the placebo group?
qs.x: Correct: B) (4.9 - 3.5)/4.9 x 100 = 28.6%. Why the others are wrong: A) 1.4 is the absolute difference in mg/L, not a percent. C) 30% is the within-group fall from baseline given in the passage, not the comparison with placebo. D) 40% divides 1.4 by the probiotic value (3.5) instead of the placebo reference. Trap: Using the passage figure of 30% (change from baseline) or dividing by the probiotic value, instead of dividing the 1.4 mg/L difference by the placebo CRP of 4.9.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?
qs.x: Correct: D) The passage lists IL-6 only as something that was measured and reports no IL-6 result, so a claim that the probiotic increased IL-6 is unsupported. Why the others are wrong: A) Bifidobacterium rose 25% (12.5% vs 10.2% placebo). B) Proteobacteria fell 15% (25.5% vs 29.8%). C) CRP fell 30% (3.5 vs 4.9 mg/L placebo). Trap: Assuming that because IL-6 was measured it must have changed; the results report no IL-6 values, so a claimed rise is unsupported.

qs.q: Which interpretation of the placebo-row p-value of 0.45 in Table 1 is best supported?
o: No statistically significant change was detected in the placebo group
There is a 45% probability that the null hypothesis is true
The result proves that the probiotic has no effect
qs.x: Correct: A) A p-value of 0.45 is above the usual 0.05 cutoff, so no significant change was detected in the placebo group. Why the others are wrong: B) A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. C) The p-value is not a percent change. D) The placebo row says nothing about the probiotic, which had p < 0.01. Trap: Reading the p-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true, or as a percent change, instead of as evidence about whether a change was detected.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of light wavelength on the photosynthetic rate of the freshwater alga *Chlorella vulgaris*. Cultures were grown under monochromatic LEDs at 450 nm (blue), 550 nm (green), 650 nm (red), and 700 nm (far-red), all at the same photon flux. Photosynthetic rates were measured as CO₂ uptake, and chlorophyll‑a concentrations were quantified spectrophotometrically. The results are summarized in Table 1.
Table 1. Photosynthetic rate (µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹) and chlorophyll‑a content (µg mL⁻¹) for *C. vulgaris* under different wavelengths.
The authors concluded that photosynthetic rate was highest at 650 nm, coinciding with the highest chlorophyll‑a concentration, and lowest in the green region, where chlorophyll absorbs least.

qs.q: Which wavelength produced the highest photosynthetic rate in *C. vulgaris* according to Table 1?
qs.x: Correct: The rate is 24.9 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹ at 650 nm, higher than at 450 nm (21.6), 550 nm (9.2), and 700 nm (12.4). Why the others are wrong: A) 21.6 is below 24.9. B) 9.2 is the lowest rate in the table. D) 12.4 is well below 24.9. Trap: Choosing 450 nm because blue light is also strongly absorbed by chlorophyll, although the table shows a lower rate there.

qs.q: Which of the following must be kept the same across all four LED treatments so that differences in photosynthetic rate can be attributed to wavelength?
qs.x: Correct: If photon flux differed among treatments, rate differences could reflect the amount of light rather than its wavelength, so it must be held constant. Why the others are wrong: B) Chlorophyll‑a content is a measured response, not a controlled variable. C) Wavelength is the independent variable and is deliberately varied. D) Photosynthetic rate is the dependent variable being measured. Trap: Treating chlorophyll‑a concentration as something to hold constant when it is a measured outcome.

qs.q: What is the percent increase in photosynthetic rate from 550 nm to 650 nm?
qs.x: Correct: (24.9 - 9.2)/9.2 x 100 = 15.7/9.2 x 100 = 170.7%. Why the others are wrong: A) 63.1% divides the 15.7 increase by the final value (24.9). C) 270.7% is the ratio 24.9/9.2 expressed as a percent, not the increase. D) 90.0% does not follow from the table values. Trap: Dividing the increase by the final value instead of the starting value.

qs.q: Which of the following statements incorrectly interprets the data presented in Table 1?
o: The highest chlorophyll‑a concentration occurs at 650 nm.
The photosynthetic rate at 700 nm is lower than at 450 nm.
The rate of photosynthesis increases monotonically with wavelength.
The 550‑nm treatment shows a lower rate than the 450‑nm treatment.
qs.x: Correct: C incorrectly interprets the data; the rate does not rise steadily with wavelength (21.6, 9.2, 24.9, 12.4). Why the others are wrong: A) 12.5 µg mL⁻¹ at 650 nm is the highest chlorophyll‑a value. B) 12.4 is lower than 21.6. D) 9.2 is lower than 21.6. Trap: Seeing the rise from 550 to 650 nm and generalizing it to a steady increase across all wavelengths.

qs.q: The data in Table 1 best illustrate which fundamental concept in plant physiology?
qs.x: The table shows how different wavelengths (light quality) affect photosynthetic rate, directly addressing the concept that photosynthesis depends on light quality. Trap: Choosing photoperiodism because the treatments involve light, although photoperiodism concerns day length, not the wavelength-dependent rates shown in the table.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel antioxidant compound, Antiox-1, on oxidative stress markers in cultured human hepatocytes. Cells were treated with 0, 5, 10, and 20 μM Antiox-1 for 24 hours. After treatment, intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were measured using the DCFH‑DA fluorescence assay, and the expression of the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) was quantified by qRT‑PCR and expressed as fold change relative to a pooled hepatocyte reference RNA sample. The results are summarized in Table 1. The data indicate a dose‑dependent reduction in ROS and a corresponding increase in SOD2 mRNA levels. The authors suggest that Antiox-1 may upregulate endogenous antioxidant defenses, thereby protecting hepatocytes from oxidative damage.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the trend observed in ROS levels across increasing concentrations of Antiox-1?
o: ROS levels increase with higher Antiox-1 concentrations
ROS levels decrease with higher Antiox-1 concentrations
ROS levels remain unchanged across all concentrations
ROS levels first increase then decrease with higher concentrations
qs.x: The mean ROS values decline from 1000 to 400 as Antiox-1 concentration rises, indicating a dose‑dependent reduction. Trap: Confusing the rising SOD2 trend with the falling ROS trend.

qs.q: Which control is needed to attribute the lower ROS values to Antiox-1 rather than to the 24-hour culture conditions?
o: Hepatocytes carried through the same 24-hour incubation without Antiox-1 (0 μM)
Hepatocytes treated with 20 μM Antiox-1 only
ROS measured only once at the end of the 24-hour treatment in treated cells
SOD2 mRNA measured in treated cells without a reference sample
qs.x: Correct: A. Untreated cells handled identically (1000 RFU in the table) give the baseline ROS level, so any decrease can be attributed to the compound. Why the others are wrong: B) A single treated condition has no reference for comparison. C) A single measurement in treated cells cannot show change without a baseline. D) Without a reference sample, SOD2 fold change is undefined and ROS is not addressed. Trap: Selecting a measurement or treated condition that lacks an untreated comparison.

qs.q: Using linear interpolation between the 10 μM and 20 μM measurements, estimate the percent reduction in ROS at 15 μM relative to the 0 μM value.
qs.x: Correct: B. Interpolating between 600 RFU (10 μM) and 400 RFU (20 μM) gives 500 RFU at 15 μM, a reduction of (1000 - 500)/1000 = 50%. Why the others are wrong: A) 30% is below the 40% reduction already seen at 10 μM. C) 70% exceeds the 60% reduction at 20 μM, which is not possible at a lower concentration. D) 90% is far beyond the observed 60% maximum. Trap: Using the 10 μM value (40% reduction) or the 20 μM value (60%) instead of their midpoint.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data in Table 1?
o: ROS levels decrease with higher Antiox-1
qs.x: Correct: C. The table shows lower ROS and higher SOD2 mRNA but includes no measurement of chemical scavenging, so direct scavenging is not demonstrated. Why the others are wrong: A) SOD2 fold change rises from 1.2 to 3.0, so A is supported. B) ROS falls from 1000 to 400 RFU, so B is supported. D) SOD2 is an antioxidant enzyme and its mRNA increases, so D is supported. Trap: Equating a fall in ROS with proof that the compound itself neutralizes ROS.

qs.q: The authors propose that Antiox-1 upregulates endogenous antioxidant defenses. Which observation in Table 1 is consistent with this proposal?
o: SOD2 mRNA rose from 1.2 to 3.0 fold as Antiox-1 increased, while ROS fell
ROS rose as Antiox-1 concentration increased
SOD2 mRNA fell as Antiox-1 concentration increased
SOD2 mRNA was the same at all concentrations
qs.x: Correct: A. A dose-dependent rise in the antioxidant enzyme SOD2 mRNA alongside lower ROS is what the proposal predicts, although this correlation alone does not prove the mechanism. Why the others are wrong: B) ROS fell, not rose, from 1000 to 400 RFU. C) SOD2 increased, not decreased. D) SOD2 values differ across concentrations (1.2, 1.8, 2.4, 3.0). Trap: Reading a correlation as proof of mechanism, or picking an option that contradicts the table.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Effect of Antiox-1 on ROS and SOD2 expression in hepatocytes

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Tanaka group compared two receptor proteins, A and B, that bind a steroid ligand with different affinities. Purified protein was held at 1 nM, a concentration far below either dissociation constant, so that the free ligand concentration was approximately equal to the total added. Ligand was titrated over a wide range, and the fraction of protein with bound ligand was measured by fluorescence anisotropy after each addition reached equilibrium. Each binding curve was hyperbolic and showed no evidence of cooperativity. The researchers intend to use the receptor with the tighter binding as a biosensor, and they want to know what ligand concentration would be required to saturate it at 80% occupancy. All measurements were made at 25 °C in identical buffer. Protein stocks were centrifuged before use to remove aggregates, and ligand stocks were verified by absorbance. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: At [ligand] = 100 nM, what is the fraction of protein A bound?
qs.x: Fraction bound = [L]/(Kd + [L]) = 100/(20+100) = 0.83. The B column gives 0.33. Trap: Reading 0.91 (protein A at 200 nM) or 0.33 (protein B at 100 nM) instead of protein A at 100 nM.

qs.q: Why was protein held far below the Kd?
o: So that cooperativity can be detected
So that the protein is certain to be fully saturated
So that ligand depletion by binding is negligible and free ligand ≈ total ligand
So that Kd equals the protein concentration
qs.x: If protein were comparable to Kd, binding would deplete free ligand and distort the fit to the simple hyperbola. Trap: Thinking the low protein concentration is meant to detect cooperativity or saturate the protein; its purpose is to keep free ligand equal to total ligand.

qs.q: What ligand concentration is needed for 80% occupancy of the higher-affinity protein (Kd = 20 nM)?
qs.x: θ = L/(Kd+L) = 0.8 ⇒ L = 4Kd = 80 nM. Trap: Using 2 x Kd (40 nM) or mixing up 80% with 50% occupancy; at 80% occupancy [L] = 4 x Kd.

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: A hyperbolic curve is consistent with noncooperative binding
Protein A binds the ligand with higher affinity than protein B
A lower Kd means lower affinity
Kd equals the ligand concentration at half-saturation
qs.x: Kd is inversely related to affinity: a smaller Kd means tighter binding. Trap: Equating a lower Kd with weaker binding; a smaller Kd means tighter binding (higher affinity).

qs.q: Which protein behavior differs from these hyperbolic curves?
o: Hemoglobin's sigmoidal oxygen binding due to cooperativity
Binding of a single ligand to one site on a monomeric protein
qs.x: Hemoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively (Hill coefficient > 1), giving a sigmoidal curve, while myoglobin is hyperbolic like proteins A and B. Trap: Picking myoglobin or Michaelis-Menten saturation as different from proteins A and B; both are hyperbolic, and only cooperative hemoglobin is sigmoidal.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers at the University of Midvale investigated the impact of caffeine on reaction time among 120 adolescents aged 13–17. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: a placebo, a low dose (50 mg), a medium dose (100 mg), or a high dose (200 mg) of caffeine. After a 30‑minute absorption period, each subject completed a computerized Go/No‑Go task, and mean reaction times (RT) were recorded. The study aimed to determine whether increasing caffeine dosage linearly reduced RT and to assess potential dose‑related side effects. The researchers also measured heart rate and reported subjective alertness to explore physiological correlates. Data were analyzed using ANOVA and post‑hoc Tukey tests, with significance set at p < .05. The findings suggested that higher caffeine doses were associated with faster RTs, but the high dose group also reported increased jitteriness. The study contributes to understanding how stimulants affect adolescent cognition and informs guidelines for caffeine consumption in youth. Future research should examine long‑term effects and interactions with sleep patterns.

qs.q: Which caffeine condition produced the fastest mean reaction time?
qs.x: The table shows the lowest mean RT (280 ms) for the high dose group, indicating the fastest reaction time among all conditions. Trap: Choosing Medium Dose (290 ms) because its mean is close to the high-dose value, without noticing that 280 ms is lower.

qs.q: Which experimental design best controls for individual differences in baseline reaction time?
qs.x: Correct: B) In a within-subjects design each participant serves as their own control, so stable individual differences in baseline reaction time cancel out. Why the others are wrong: A) A between-subjects design with random assignment balances individuals only on average and leaves individual differences in the data. C) A cross-sectional design compares groups at one time without controlling individual differences. D) A case-control design is observational and does not control baseline differences. Trap: Option A is tempting because the study itself used between‑subjects, but it does not control for individual baseline differences as effectively as within‑subjects.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in mean reaction time from placebo to high dose?
qs.x: Percent reduction = (350 – 280) / 350 × 100 = 20%. The correct answer is 20%. Trap: Dividing the 70 ms drop by the high-dose mean (280 ms) gives 25%; the placebo mean (350 ms) is the correct reference.

qs.q: Which statement is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: High dose caffeine reduces reaction time.
Low dose caffeine reduces reaction time.
Medium dose caffeine reduces reaction time.
High dose caffeine increases reaction time.
qs.x: All dose conditions show a reduction in reaction time compared to placebo; none show an increase. Thus, statement D is incorrect. Trap: Option D is a plausible distractor because students might think higher doses could have a negative effect, but the data show the opposite.

qs.q: Which statement about the dose-response pattern is supported by Table 1?
o: Each higher dose lowered mean RT further, but by a smaller amount at each step (40, 20, then 10 ms).
Each doubling of dose produced the same additional reduction in mean RT.
The high dose produced a larger additional reduction than the medium dose.
The medium dose was slower than the low dose.
qs.x: Correct: A) Means fall 350 to 310 to 290 to 280 ms, so the successive reductions are 40, 20 and 10 ms. Why the others are wrong: B) The reductions per dose step (20 then 10 ms for 50 to 100 to 200 mg) are not equal. C) Medium to high lowered RT by 10 ms, less than the 20 ms from low to medium. D) Medium (290 ms) was faster than low (310 ms). Trap: Assuming more caffeine always gives a proportionally larger benefit, when the table shows diminishing gains (40, 20, 10 ms).

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Tanaka group investigated turnover of IκBα, a regulatory protein that is rapidly degraded in proliferating cells. To measure stability without confounding new synthesis, cells were treated with cycloheximide, an inhibitor of translation elongation, and harvested at the times shown. Lysates were resolved by SDS-PAGE, transferred to a membrane, and probed with an antibody against IκBα; band intensities were quantified and normalized to a loading control. Degradation of IκBα was assumed to follow first-order kinetics. The researchers hoped to compare half-lives under normal and stressed conditions and to learn whether proteasome inhibition would stabilize the protein. Results from unstressed cells are shown; each value is the mean of three biological replicates, with errors below 5% of the mean. Equal total protein was loaded in every lane, as confirmed by the loading control. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What fraction of IκBα remains 90 minutes after cycloheximide treatment?
qs.x: At 90 min, two half-lives have elapsed (100 → 50 → 25%). Trap: Reading the percent remaining as the percent degraded, or using the wrong time point on the table.

qs.q: Why is cycloheximide used in this experiment?
o: It increases transcription of the gene
It blocks new synthesis so that the loss of existing protein can be followed
It accelerates proteasomal degradation of all proteins
It labels the protein for detection by antibody
qs.x: Without blocking translation, newly synthesized protein would obscure the decay of the pre-existing pool. Trap: Leaving out cycloheximide, so newly synthesized protein masks the decay of the existing pool.

qs.q: If the decay continues to be first-order, what percentage of IκBα remains after 180 minutes?
qs.x: 180 min = 4 half-lives of 45 min, so 100 × (1/2)^4 = 6.25%. Trap: Treating the decay as linear, or dividing by n instead of using 100 × (1/2)^n.

qs.q: Which statement about first-order decay is INCORRECT?
o: The half-life is independent of starting concentration
The rate of decay is proportional to the amount remaining
The half-life increases as the starting amount of protein increases
The half-life equals ln 2 divided by the rate constant
qs.x: In first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2/k and does not depend on starting concentration. Trap: Believing a larger starting amount lengthens a first-order half-life; half-life depends only on the rate constant (ln 2 / k).

qs.q: IκBα turnover is typically controlled by which system?
o: Ubiquitination and degradation by the proteasome
Glycosylation in the Golgi apparatus that prevents degradation
Phosphorylation by glycolytic kinases that leads to secretion
qs.x: Polyubiquitin chains (K48-linked) mark proteins for proteasomal degradation; proteasome inhibitors such as MG132 stabilize short-lived regulatory proteins. Trap: Citing lysosomal or secretory pathways for a short-lived regulatory protein instead of ubiquitin tagging and proteasomal degradation.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers studied the impact of a new cognitive training program on working memory performance in adults aged 30–50. A randomized controlled trial was conducted with 120 participants, evenly divided into a training group and a wait‑list control group. Participants completed a standardized working memory task (digit span) before and after a 4‑week intervention. Table 1 summarizes the mean digit‑span scores and standard deviations for each group at baseline and post‑intervention. The training group showed a modest improvement in mean scores, whereas the control group’s scores remained relatively unchanged. The researchers also collected self‑reported measures of perceived cognitive benefit and mood, but these were not included in the primary analysis. The study aimed to determine whether the training program could produce measurable gains in working memory beyond what would be expected from repeated testing alone.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, which of the following statements accurately reflects the change in working memory performance for the training group?
o: The training group’s mean digit‑span score increased by 1.2 points.
The training group’s mean digit‑span score increased by 1.0 point.
The training group’s mean digit‑span score increased by 0.8 points.
The training group’s mean digit‑span score increased by 1.4 points.
qs.x: The training group's mean increased from 7.2 to 8.4, a difference of 1.2 points. Trap: Option C (0.8) confuses the difference with a standard deviation value; option B (1.0) is the post-intervention SD.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes an appropriate experimental design to test whether the observed improvement in the training group is due to the cognitive training program rather than placebo effects?
o: Use a single‑blind design where participants are unaware of their group assignment.
Add an active control group that receives a sham training program of equal duration.
Increase the sample size to 200 participants without changing the control condition.
Measure participants’ mood before and after the intervention to control for affective changes.
qs.x: An active control group that receives a sham training program controls for placebo effects and participant expectations, allowing attribution of differences to the specific content of the training. Trap: Option A incorrectly assumes that blinding participants alone is sufficient; blinding is not feasible in behavioral interventions.

qs.q: Calculate the effect size (Cohen’s d) for the change in digit‑span scores in the training group, using the post‑intervention standard deviation.
qs.x: Cohen's d = (8.4 - 7.2)/1.0 = 1.20, using the post-intervention SD as stated. Trap: Option D (1.00) takes the SD as the effect size.

qs.q: A reader concludes the program works because the training group's mean digit span rose from 7.2 to 8.4. What is the main flaw in relying on that change alone?
o: The control group also rose (7.1 to 7.3), so part of the gain may reflect repeated testing and must be compared with the control change
Baseline scores of 7.2 and 7.1 differ too much to compare the groups
The wait-list control did not take the digit-span task at baseline
Self-reported mood was the primary outcome and was ignored
qs.x: Correct: The training gain is 1.2 versus 0.2 in controls, so practice effects explain a small part; the comparison with control is what supports efficacy. Why the others are wrong: B) Baselines of 7.2 and 7.1 are nearly identical, so there is no large baseline imbalance. C) Table 1 shows control baseline 7.1 ± 1.2, so controls were tested at baseline. D) The passage says mood and perceived benefit were not in the primary analysis. Trap: Attributing the whole pre-post gain to training without subtracting the control group's change.

qs.q: Which comparison best estimates the effect of training beyond what repeated testing alone produces?
o: The training group's change (+1.2) minus the control group's change (+0.2), or 1.0 point
The training group's post-intervention mean minus the control group's baseline mean, or 1.3 points
The training group's change alone, or 1.2 points
The difference between the two baseline means, or 0.1 points
qs.x: Correct: The control group also rose by 0.2 points (7.1 to 7.3) from repeated testing, so the training effect is the difference in changes: 1.2 − 0.2 = 1.0 point. Why the others are wrong: B) subtracting the control baseline from the training post-test mixes different time points and groups. C) 1.2 points includes the practice effect that the control group also showed. D) the baseline difference (7.2 − 7.1) shows the groups started alike and says nothing about the effect of training. Trap: Reporting the training group's raw gain (1.2) as the effect, without subtracting the practice effect seen in the control group.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: A screening group in the Duarte laboratory identified a compound that suppresses aldose reductase activity in cell lysates. To learn how it acts, the group measured initial velocities of the purified enzyme at several glucose concentrations, with and without 40 µM compound. Assays were buffered at pH 7.4 and kept at 30 °C, and the enzyme concentration was held constant. The compound has no structural resemblance to glucose, and a preliminary docking study placed it in a hydrophobic pocket far from the catalytic residues. The researchers recorded velocities as µmol of product per minute and fit each data set to the Michaelis–Menten equation. They then compared the fitted constants with and without compound, expecting the pattern to reveal whether the compound binds the free enzyme, the enzyme–substrate complex, or both with equal affinity. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and solvent carrier alone had no effect on activity. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which pattern does Table 1 show?
o: The ratio of inhibited to control velocity is about the same at every [S]
The inhibited velocity exceeds the control velocity at the lowest [S]
The ratio falls steadily as [S] increases
The ratio of inhibited to control velocity rises steadily as [S] increases
qs.x: At each [S], v(inhibited)/v(control) = 1/2, so the compound lowers velocity by a constant factor. Trap: Assuming inhibition weakens at high [S], as for a competitive inhibitor (options C or D); the ratio stays at 0.50 at every [S].

qs.q: Which experiment would best confirm that the compound does not compete with substrate for the active site?
o: Show that the compound's potency decreases as [S] increases
Show that raising [S] to very high levels does not restore the control Vmax
Show that Km increases linearly with compound concentration
Show that the compound's structure matches the substrate
qs.x: Failure of high [S] to overcome inhibition indicates the inhibitor does not simply compete for the substrate-binding site. Trap: Choosing option A, potency falling as [S] rises, which is the signature of a competitive inhibitor and the opposite of what is asked.

qs.q: If the uninhibited Vmax is 200 µmol/min, what is the apparent Vmax with the compound?
qs.x: Vmax,app = Vmax/α = 200/2 = 100 µmol/min, as seen in the saturating-substrate rows. Trap: Choosing 198 µmol/min (option A) as if Vmax were unaffected, as with a competitive inhibitor; here saturating velocities are halved, so apparent Vmax is 100.

qs.q: Which statement about pure noncompetitive inhibition is INCORRECT?
o: The apparent Km increases because the inhibitor competes with substrate
The inhibitor can bind both free enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex
Lineweaver–Burk lines intersect on the x-axis
qs.x: Pure noncompetitive inhibitors leave Km unchanged. Because binding occurs at a distinct site, the lines in a double-reciprocal plot share an x-intercept (−1/Km). Trap: Assuming a noncompetitive inhibitor raises apparent Km (option A), which is the competitive pattern; pure noncompetitive inhibition leaves Km unchanged.

qs.q: Which cellular regulatory phenomenon most closely resembles this inhibition pattern?
o: Irreversible inhibition by transition-state mimicry at the active site
Allosteric inhibition at a site distinct from the active site
Substrate-level competition by a structural analog
Product activation of the same enzyme by direct covalent change
qs.x: Binding at a distinct regulatory (allosteric) site that lowers catalytic capacity reproduces the noncompetitive pattern, as with feedback inhibition in metabolic pathways. Trap: Choosing competition by a structural analog (option C), the competitive pattern; this compound resembles no substrate and leaves Km unchanged.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Velocity of aldose reductase with and without compound

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel anti‑inflammatory compound on joint pain in a randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial. One hundred and twenty patients with osteoarthritis were assigned to one of four groups: a placebo control, a low‑dose group (10 mg), a medium‑dose group (20 mg), and a high‑dose group (40 mg). Pain was measured using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) at baseline and after 12 weeks of treatment. The mean VAS scores (0–100 mm) and standard deviations (SD) at week 12 are presented in Table 1. The study aimed to determine whether a dose‑dependent reduction in pain could be observed and to assess the safety profile of the compound.

qs.q: Which group had the lowest mean VAS score at week 12?
qs.x: The high‑dose group (40 mg) had the lowest mean VAS score at week 12 (31.1 mm), lower than the control (68.4), low‑dose (55.2) and medium‑dose (42.7) groups. Trap: Students may mistakenly choose the medium‑dose group because it appears to have a lower mean than the low‑dose group, but the high‑dose group is actually lower.

qs.q: Which experimental design best tests for a dose‑response relationship in this study?
o: Crossover design with each patient receiving all doses sequentially
Parallel‑group randomized controlled trial with four dose levels
Case‑control study comparing responders and non‑responders
Observational cohort study following patients over 12 months
qs.x: A parallel‑group randomized controlled trial with multiple dose levels allows direct comparison of each dose against placebo and among doses to assess a dose‑response curve. Trap: Students might choose a crossover design, but the risk of carry‑over effects and the need for washout periods make it less suitable for this dose‑response question.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in mean VAS score from the control group to the high‑dose group?
qs.x: Percent reduction = (68.4 − 31.1) / 68.4 × 100 = 37.3 / 68.4 × 100 ≈ 54.5%. Trap: Reporting the remaining pain (31.1/68.4, about 45%) rather than the reduction, or dividing by the high‑dose mean instead of the control mean.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding the study results?
o: The high‑dose group had the lowest mean VAS at week 12.
The mean VAS score decreased by more than 50% from control to high dose.
The low‑dose group had a lower mean VAS than the medium‑dose group.
Standard deviations were smallest in the high‑dose group.
qs.x: Correct: The low‑dose mean VAS (55.2) is higher than the medium‑dose mean (42.7), so statement C is false. Why the others are wrong: A) 31.1 is the lowest week‑12 mean. B) (68.4 − 31.1)/68.4 = 54.5%, more than 50%. D) 8.9 is the smallest SD in the table. Trap: Students may think the low‑dose group had a lower mean because they misread the numbers; careful comparison is needed.

qs.q: Between the 10 mg and 40 mg groups, by about how much did mean VAS fall per additional 10 mg of drug, on average?
qs.x: Correct: VAS fell from 55.2 to 31.1, a 24.1 mm drop over 30 mg, or 24.1/3 = 8.0 mm per 10 mg. Why the others are wrong: B) 12.5 mm is the fall from 10 mg to 20 mg only (55.2 − 42.7). C) 11.6 mm is the fall from 20 mg to 40 mg (42.7 − 31.1) over a 20 mg interval, not per 10 mg. D) 24.1 mm is the total fall over 30 mg, not per 10 mg. Trap: Reporting the total fall (24.1 mm) or a single interval's change instead of dividing by the number of 10 mg steps (3).

tbl.cap: Table 1. Mean VAS Scores at Week 12

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers studied the effects of four different dietary supplements on the endurance performance of trained cyclists. The study was conducted over a 12‑week period with 80 participants randomly assigned to one of four groups: placebo (Group A), carbohydrate supplement (Group B), protein supplement (Group C), and a combined carbohydrate‑protein supplement (Group D). Endurance performance was measured by time to complete a 40‑km time trial at baseline and after 12 weeks. Table 1 summarizes the mean time (in minutes) and standard deviation for each group at the end of the study. The researchers hypothesized that the combined supplement would yield the greatest improvement, followed by carbohydrate, protein, and placebo. Statistical analysis revealed an interaction between supplement type and time, with Group D showing a 12.5% reduction in completion time compared to baseline, whereas Group A increased by 2.1%. The authors concluded that a combined carbohydrate‑protein supplement enhances endurance performance more effectively than either macronutrient alone or placebo.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the pattern of end-of-study mean times in Table 1?
o: All four groups had nearly identical mean times.
The carbohydrate group had a longer mean time than the placebo group.
Every supplement group had a lower mean time than placebo, and the combined supplement group had the lowest.
The protein group had the longest mean time.
qs.x: Correct: C) End-of-study means were 45.2 (placebo), 42.8 (carbohydrate), 43.5 (protein) and 39.7 (combined), so all supplements are below placebo and combined is lowest. Why the others are wrong: A) Means range from 39.7 to 45.2 min, a spread of 5.5 min. B) Carbohydrate (42.8) is lower than placebo (45.2). D) Placebo, not protein, had the longest mean time. Trap: Reading a lower time as worse performance and concluding that the carbohydrate group performed worse than placebo; shorter completion times mean better performance.

qs.q: Which experimental design feature best supports the validity of the study’s conclusions?
o: Random assignment of participants to supplement groups.
Measurement of time to complete a 40‑km time trial.
Reporting of mean times and standard deviations.
qs.x: Random assignment controls for confounding variables and ensures that differences in outcomes can be attributed to the supplements rather than pre‑existing differences among participants, thereby strengthening internal validity. Trap: Option A focuses on duration, which is important but does not directly address validity; Option C describes the outcome measure, and Option D relates to data reporting.

qs.q: What is the approximate percent reduction in completion time for Group D relative to baseline?
qs.x: The passage states that Group D showed a 12.5% reduction in completion time compared to baseline. Trap: Choosing 8.3% or 5.0% by comparing end-of-study group means; the question asks for Group D's change from its own baseline, which the passage gives as 12.5%.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: The combined supplement group had the lowest mean completion time at 12 weeks.
The placebo group's completion time increased by 2.1% from baseline.
Both single-macronutrient groups had lower mean times than placebo at 12 weeks.
Protein alone produced a lower mean completion time than the combined supplement.
qs.x: A is supported (39.7 min is the lowest mean). B is stated in the passage (+2.1%). C is supported (carbohydrate 42.8 and protein 43.5 are both below placebo 45.2). D is not supported: protein (43.5 min) was slower than the combined supplement (39.7 min). Trap: Option D reverses the ranking in Table 1; the combined supplement had the lowest time, so protein alone cannot have beaten it.

qs.q: What is the difference in mean end-of-study time between the placebo group and the combined carbohydrate-protein group?
qs.x: Correct: C) 45.2 - 39.7 = 5.5 min. Why the others are wrong: A) 1.7 min is the difference between placebo and protein (45.2 - 43.5). B) 3.1 min is the difference between carbohydrate and combined (42.8 - 39.7). D) 6.5 min does not follow from the table values. Trap: Subtracting the wrong pair of groups, such as carbohydrate versus combined (3.1 min) or placebo versus protein (1.7 min).

passages.title: Transmission of genetic information from the gene to the protein · passage
text: Cell biologists in the Mensah laboratory asked whether a metabolic stressor alters transcription of SOD2 in cultured hepatocytes. RNA was extracted from untreated and treated cells, treated with DNase, and reverse transcribed. Quantitative PCR was then performed with primers for SOD2 and for a reference gene whose expression is assumed to be stable. Each reaction contained a fluorescent DNA-binding dye and was run in triplicate. Amplification efficiency was verified to be close to 100% for both primer pairs, meaning the amount of product doubles each cycle. The cycle threshold, Ct, is the cycle at which fluorescence crosses a fixed threshold; mean values are shown. The group planned to calculate relative expression using the comparative Ct method before deciding whether to examine the promoter region for regulatory elements. RNA integrity numbers exceeded 8.5 for every sample. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which condition shows greater starting amounts of SOD2 transcript, based on Table 1?
o: The data cannot be compared without a standard curve
qs.x: A lower Ct means the threshold is reached earlier, indicating more starting template. With equal reference Ct, the condition with the lower target Ct has higher expression. Trap: Concluding that the condition with the higher target Ct has more transcript, or that equal reference Ct means equal expression; a lower target Ct marks the condition with more starting template.

qs.q: Which control best rules out amplification of contaminating genomic DNA?
o: A reaction run at a higher annealing temperature only
A reaction with double the template
qs.x: If product appears without reverse transcriptase, it must come from DNA rather than from RNA-derived cDNA. Trap: Choosing a higher annealing temperature or extra template, which cannot show where the product came from; only a no-reverse-transcriptase reaction that still amplifies reveals genomic DNA.

qs.q: Using the ΔΔCt method with 100% efficiency, what is the fold change in SOD2 in treated versus untreated cells?
qs.x: ΔCt(untreated) = 7; ΔCt(treated) = 4; ΔΔCt = -3. Fold change = 2^−(-3) = 8. Trap: Reporting the Ct difference (3) as the fold change, or inverting the direction; with 100% efficiency fold change = 2^(-ΔΔCt) = 2^(3) = 8.

qs.q: Which statement about Ct values is INCORRECT?
o: A difference of one Ct corresponds to a two-fold difference at 100% efficiency
A higher Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
The reference gene corrects for differences in input RNA
A lower Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
qs.x: Ct and abundance are inversely related; more template reaches threshold sooner. Trap: Reading a higher Ct as more starting template; Ct is the cycle at which signal crosses threshold, so a higher Ct means less target, not more.

qs.q: If expression changes, which feature of the gene would most directly be examined for a transcription-factor response?
o: The number of introns within the coding region only
The poly-A tail of the mature mRNA only
Promoter and enhancer sequences upstream of the transcription start site
The anticodon of the matching tRNA
qs.x: Transcription-factor binding sites (promoter/enhancer elements) govern transcriptional initiation, linking the Ct data to the regulatory mechanism. Trap: Choosing intron number, the poly-A tail or the tRNA anticodon, which concern splicing, mRNA processing or translation rather than transcription-factor control of initiation.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers conducted a randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial to evaluate the antihypertensive effects of a novel compound, Hypertensol, at three different daily doses (10 mg, 20 mg, and 30 mg). A total of 180 adults with stage 1 hypertension were enrolled and randomly assigned to one of the four groups: placebo (n = 30), 10 mg (n = 60), 20 mg (n = 50), or 30 mg (n = 40). Systolic blood pressure (SBP) was measured at baseline and after 12 weeks of treatment. The mean SBP reductions, standard deviations, and sample sizes are summarized in Table 1. The investigators hypothesized a dose‑dependent response, with the 30 mg group expected to show the greatest reduction. Adverse events were mild and comparable across groups. The study’s primary endpoint was the mean change in SBP from baseline to week 12.

qs.q: What is the mean systolic blood pressure (SBP) reduction for the 20 mg dose?
qs.x: Table 1 lists the mean SBP reduction for the 20 mg group as 10.2 mmHg. The other options correspond to the 10 mg dose (7.8 mmHg), the 30 mg dose (12.4 mmHg), or an implausible value. Trap: Choosing 12.4 mmHg, which is the 30 mg result, because the highest dose is assumed to be the answer rather than reading the 20 mg row.

qs.q: Which statement best describes the control group used in this study?
o: Participants received an inert placebo instead of Hypertensol.
Participants received the 10 mg dose of Hypertensol.
Participants received the 30 mg dose of Hypertensol.
qs.x: Correct: The trial was placebo-controlled, so the control group (n = 30) received an inert placebo. Why the others are wrong: B) the 10 mg dose is an active treatment group, not the control. C) the design was placebo-controlled, so controls received a placebo rather than nothing. D) the 30 mg dose is an active treatment group, not the control. Trap: Choosing 'no treatment' because a control is usually thought of as untreated, although the passage describes a placebo-controlled design.

qs.q: What is the overall mean SBP reduction across all dose groups, weighted by sample size?
qs.x: Weighted mean = (10.2×50 + 7.8×60 + 12.4×40) / (50+60+40) = 1474 / 150 ≈ 9.83 mmHg, rounded to 9.8 mmHg. Trap: Taking the simple unweighted mean of the dose means (about 10.1) or the 20 mg value (10.2) instead of weighting each mean by its group size.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a potential confounding variable in this study?
qs.x: Sample size is a design parameter, not a confounder. Age, measurement device, and placebo effect can bias results if unevenly distributed. Trap: Dismissing the measurement device or the placebo effect as non-confounders, when these can bias results and only sample size affects precision rather than distorting the association.

qs.q: Which statement best summarizes the study’s conclusion?
o: Higher doses of Hypertensol produce greater SBP reductions.
The 20 mg dose is the optimal balance of efficacy and safety.
The 30 mg dose was associated with increased adverse events.
qs.x: The data show a clear dose‑dependent trend: 10 mg → 7.8 mmHg, 20 mg → 10.2 mmHg, 30 mg → 12.4 mmHg, supporting a dose‑response relationship. Trap: Reading an optimal 20 mg dose into the data (option C), although the passage reports no dose-by-dose safety comparison from which an optimum could be claimed.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of a novel antihypertensive agent, CardioX, on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in adults with stage‑1 hypertension. In a double‑blind, randomized controlled trial, 200 participants were assigned to either CardioX (n = 100) or placebo (n = 100). Baseline mean SBP was 145 mmHg (SD = 8) for both groups. After 12 weeks of therapy, the CardioX group exhibited a mean SBP reduction of 12 mmHg (SD = 4), whereas the placebo group showed a mean reduction of 3 mmHg (SD = 5). The study reported a statistically significant difference (p < 0.001) favoring CardioX. Secondary outcomes included heart rate, lipid profile, and adverse events, all of which were comparable between groups. The investigators concluded that CardioX effectively lowers SBP with a favorable safety profile.

qs.q: Which of the following best represents the mean systolic blood pressure reduction observed in the CardioX group?
qs.x: The table and passage state that the CardioX group had a mean SBP reduction of 12 mmHg. Trap: Option A reflects the placebo reduction, which may mislead readers into thinking the drug effect is minimal.

qs.q: Which methodological feature best supports attributing the observed blood‑pressure reduction to CardioX?
o: Random assignment to CardioX or placebo
qs.x: Correct: Random assignment balances known and unknown confounders between groups, so differences can be attributed to CardioX. Why the others are wrong: A) A follow-up period sets duration and does not address confounding. C) The baseline SBP was the same in both groups but does not by itself rule out confounding. D) Adverse-event reporting concerns safety, not attribution of the BP effect. Trap: Choosing the follow-up duration or baseline value, which describe the study but do not control confounding.

qs.q: If a patient’s baseline SBP is 150 mmHg, what is the expected SBP after 12 weeks of CardioX therapy?
qs.x: 150 mmHg – 12 mmHg = 138 mmHg. Trap: Option D uses the baseline mean from the study, which could mislead readers into thinking the reduction is smaller.

qs.q: Which statement most accurately reflects a potential limitation of this study?
o: The placebo group had a higher baseline SBP.
The study duration was too short to assess long‑term safety.
The sample size was too large for a pilot study.
The study used a crossover design.
qs.x: A 12‑week trial may not capture long‑term efficacy or rare adverse events. Trap: Option A is incorrect because baseline SBP was equal; readers might incorrectly assume imbalance.

qs.q: Which conclusion about clinical use is best supported by this trial?
o: CardioX should be recommended as first‑line monotherapy for all patients.

In adults with stage‑1 hypertension, 12 weeks of CardioX lowered SBP about 9 mmHg more than placebo with comparable adverse events, but long‑term outcomes and comparison with existing drugs were not tested.
CardioX is ineffective because the placebo group’s SBP also fell by 3 mmHg.
CardioX should be prescribed only for patients with baseline SBP above 160 mmHg.
qs.x: Correct: 12 − 3 = 9 mmHg difference vs placebo in stage‑1 hypertension over 12 weeks; adverse events were comparable between groups. Why the others are wrong: A) No comparison with existing first-line drugs was made and follow-up was short. C) The CardioX fall (12 mmHg) exceeded the placebo fall (3 mmHg), p < 0.001. D) Participants had stage‑1 hypertension with mean baseline SBP of 145 mmHg; no >160 subgroup was studied. Trap: Turning a short placebo-controlled efficacy result into a first-line or add-on recommendation that the trial never tested.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers investigated how varying light intensity influences the rate of photosynthesis in the model plant *Arabidopsis thaliana*. Leaf discs were exposed to five different light intensities (200, 400, 600, 800, and 1000 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹) for 30 minutes while maintaining constant temperature (25 °C) and CO₂ concentration (400 ppm). Oxygen evolution was measured using a Clark-type electrode and expressed as µmol O₂ g⁻¹ FW h⁻¹. The results, summarized in Table 1, indicate a nonlinear response: photosynthetic rate increases sharply up to 600 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ and then plateaus, suggesting a saturation point beyond which additional light does not enhance O₂ production. These findings align with the light‑dependent phase of the photosynthetic light reactions, where electron transport capacity limits further increases in rate.

qs.q: Which light intensity produced the highest rate of oxygen evolution in the experiment?
qs.x: The highest O₂ evolution rate in the table is 36.5 µmol O₂ g⁻¹ FW h⁻¹ at 1000 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹, only slightly above the values at 600 (35.2) and 800 (36.0), consistent with a plateau. Trap: Assuming the rate peaks at the saturation point (600); small further increases continue in the plateau.

qs.q: Design a follow‑up experiment to determine how temperature affects the same photosynthetic rate. Which of the following best outlines the experimental approach?
o: Expose leaf discs to a single temperature (25 °C) while varying light intensity.
Keep light intensity constant at 600 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ and measure O₂ evolution at temperatures ranging from 10 °C to 40 °C.
Vary CO₂ concentration while maintaining constant temperature and light.
Measure chlorophyll fluorescence across different light intensities.
qs.x: To isolate temperature effects, light intensity and CO₂ must be held constant. Option B keeps light at the saturation point (600 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹) and varies temperature, directly testing the temperature dependence of photosynthesis. Trap: Choosing option A, which varies light instead of temperature.

qs.q: Calculate the percent increase in O₂ production when light intensity increases from 200 to 400 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹.
qs.x: Percent increase = (24.8 − 12.5)/12.5 × 100 = 98.4%. Trap: Option A divides by the 400 value (12.3/24.8 = 49.6%); the starting value (200) is the correct denominator.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is a common misconception about photosynthetic light saturation?
o: O₂ production plateaus at high light intensities.
Higher light always increases photosynthetic rate.
Light saturation occurs when electron transport is limited.
The light‑dependent phase produces the ATP and NADPH used by the Calvin cycle.
qs.x: Correct: B) Beyond saturation (about 600 in Table 1), more light does not raise the rate, so 'always' is a misconception. Why the others are wrong: A) The data show a plateau at high light. C) Saturation occurs when downstream capacity, including electron transport, is limiting. D) The light-dependent reactions do make ATP and NADPH for the Calvin cycle. Trap: Accepting 'higher light always increases the rate' because rates rise at low light, ignoring that the plateau above 600 shows saturation.

qs.q: At 600 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹, what percent of the maximum observed O₂ production rate had been reached?
qs.x: Correct: A) The maximum observed rate is 36.5 (at 1000); 35.2 / 36.5 x 100 = 96.4%, consistent with a plateau beginning near 600. Why the others are wrong: B) 97.8% uses the 800 value (36.0) as the maximum, but 36.5 at 1000 is higher. C) 67.9% is the 400 value (24.8) divided by 36.5. D) 34.2% is the 200 value (12.5) divided by 36.5. Trap: Using the 800 value (36.0) as the maximum gives 97.8% (B); the maximum observed rate is 36.5 at 1000 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Biochemists in the Haddad laboratory characterized malate dehydrogenase purified from a bacterial expression system, focusing on its response to a candidate small-molecule inhibitor designed to resemble oxaloacetate. Reactions contained a fixed enzyme concentration in buffered solution at 25 °C, and initial velocities were measured at six oxaloacetate concentrations with and without 120 µM inhibitor. Product formation was followed spectrophotometrically for the first 60 seconds, a window in which less than 5% of substrate was consumed. Each velocity represents the mean of three independent reactions, and the standard error was below 4% of every mean. The team wished to determine whether the compound binds the free enzyme at the active site or instead binds elsewhere, and to estimate its dissociation constant for the enzyme–inhibitor complex before testing it in cultured cells. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and the buffer contained no metal chelators or reducing agents that could interfere with the assay. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, what is the initial velocity in the presence of inhibitor when [S] = 200 µM?
qs.x: Reading the inhibitor column at [S] = 200 µM gives 11.4 µmol/min; the control column value (26.7) is the uninhibited rate. Trap: Reading the uninhibited column (26.7) instead of the inhibitor column at 200 µM, or taking a value from a different substrate row (17.8 or 6.7).

qs.q: Which additional experiment would best distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition by this compound?
o: Measure product formation after 60 minutes rather than 60 seconds
Measure whether very high substrate concentrations restore the uninhibited maximal velocity
Measure velocity at a single substrate concentration with several enzyme concentrations
Repeat the assay at a lower temperature to see whether inhibition disappears
qs.x: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so sufficiently high [S] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax regardless of [S]. Trap: Choosing a time-course or temperature experiment, which changes extent of reaction or enzyme stability but cannot show whether high substrate outcompetes the inhibitor.

qs.q: Assuming simple competitive inhibition, what is the approximate Ki of the inhibitor?
qs.x: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). Here Km,app/Km = 5, so [I]/Ki = 4 and Ki = 120/4 = 30 µM. Trap: Using Km,app/Km = 5 directly as the ratio, giving Ki = 120/5 = 24 µM (option C), which forgets that Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki).

qs.q: Which statement about the data is NOT consistent with competitive inhibition?
o: Vmax is lower in the presence of the inhibitor at saturating [S]
The inhibitor binds the free enzyme in preference to the enzyme–substrate complex
The apparent Km is larger in the presence of the inhibitor
The inhibition is weaker at higher substrate concentrations
qs.x: Competitive inhibitors leave Vmax unchanged; the velocities converge as [S] rises. A reduced Vmax would indicate noncompetitive or uncompetitive behavior. Trap: Treating a lower Vmax as consistent with competition; a competitive inhibitor leaves Vmax unchanged and only raises the apparent Km.

qs.q: Many drugs, such as statins and methotrexate, act as competitive inhibitors. Which property of such drugs most directly explains why they are often structural analogs of the substrate?
o: They must bind the enzyme–substrate complex only
They must occupy the same active site as the substrate
They must lower the enzyme's turnover number at saturating substrate
They must bind covalently to the enzyme
qs.x: Competition requires binding to the same site; structural similarity to the substrate (or transition state) lets the drug fit the active site and compete reversibly. Trap: Assuming drugs must bind covalently or only the enzyme-substrate complex; competitive inhibitors reversibly compete for the same active site as the substrate.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: A screening group in the Fitzgerald laboratory identified a compound that suppresses malate dehydrogenase activity in cell lysates. To learn how it acts, the group measured initial velocities of the purified enzyme at several oxaloacetate concentrations, with and without 20 µM compound. Assays were buffered at pH 7.4 and kept at 30 °C, and the enzyme concentration was held constant. The compound has no structural resemblance to oxaloacetate, and a preliminary docking study placed it in a hydrophobic pocket far from the catalytic residues. The researchers recorded velocities as µmol of product per minute and fit each data set to the Michaelis–Menten equation. They then compared the fitted constants with and without compound, expecting the pattern to reveal whether the compound binds the free enzyme, the enzyme–substrate complex, or both with equal affinity. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and solvent carrier alone had no effect on activity. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which pattern does Table 1 show?
o: The ratio of inhibited to control velocity rises steadily as [S] increases
The ratio falls steadily as [S] increases
The inhibited velocity exceeds the control velocity at the lowest [S]
The ratio of inhibited to control velocity is about the same at every [S]
qs.x: At each [S], v(inhibited)/v(control) = 1/4, so the compound lowers velocity by a constant factor. Trap: Expecting inhibition to shrink at high substrate; the inhibited velocity is one quarter of control at every [S], so substrate does not overcome it.

qs.q: Which experiment would best confirm that the compound does not compete with substrate for the active site?
o: Show that the compound's potency decreases as [S] increases
Show that Km increases linearly with compound concentration
Show that raising [S] to very high levels does not restore the control Vmax
Show that the compound's structure matches the substrate
qs.x: Failure of high [S] to overcome inhibition indicates the inhibitor does not simply compete for the substrate-binding site. Trap: Choosing the option where potency falls as [S] rises, which is the signature of competitive inhibition, the opposite of what is being confirmed.

qs.q: If the uninhibited Vmax is 120 µmol/min, what is the apparent Vmax with the compound?
qs.x: Vmax,app = Vmax/α = 120/4 = 30 µmol/min, as seen in the saturating-substrate rows. Trap: Choosing 24 µmol/min, the inhibited velocity at 200 µM substrate, instead of dividing the uninhibited Vmax of 120 by 4.

qs.q: Which statement about pure noncompetitive inhibition is INCORRECT?
o: The inhibitor can bind both free enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex
The apparent Km increases because the inhibitor competes with substrate
Lineweaver–Burk lines intersect on the x-axis
qs.x: Pure noncompetitive inhibitors leave Km unchanged. Because binding occurs at a distinct site, the lines in a double-reciprocal plot share an x-intercept (−1/Km). Trap: Believing noncompetitive inhibitors raise Km because they lower velocity, when Km is unchanged and only Vmax falls.

qs.q: Which cellular regulatory phenomenon most closely resembles this inhibition pattern?
o: Product activation of the same enzyme by direct covalent change
Allosteric inhibition at a site distinct from the active site
Substrate-level competition by a structural analog
Irreversible inhibition by transition-state mimicry at the active site
qs.x: Binding at a distinct regulatory (allosteric) site that lowers catalytic capacity reproduces the noncompetitive pattern, as with feedback inhibition in metabolic pathways. Trap: Choosing substrate-analog competition, which the passage rules out by noting the compound has no structural resemblance to oxaloacetate.
