passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers in the Reyes laboratory studied three reversible reactions of early carbohydrate metabolism in extracts of rat liver. Each reaction was allowed to reach equilibrium in a sealed reaction vessel at 37 °C and pH 7.0, after which reactants and products were quantified by HPLC to give the equilibrium constant. In a second set of experiments, intact hepatocytes were rapidly freeze-clamped and the steady-state ratio of products to reactants, known as the mass-action ratio Q, was measured for the same reactions. Comparing Q with Keq indicates how far each reaction sits from equilibrium under physiological conditions, and therefore which steps are likely to be regulated. The investigators used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and expected values of ΔG°′ to be consistent with literature compilations. All reagents were of analytical grade, and each reaction vessel was degassed to avoid oxidation of sulfhydryl groups. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which reaction operates closest to equilibrium in hepatocytes?
o: None; all three are far from equilibrium
Reaction A: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP
qs.x: Q/Keq near 1 indicates near-equilibrium operation. Reaction A has Q closest to Keq, so it is the least likely to be a regulatory step. Trap: Comparing Q with Keq by absolute size rather than by the ratio Q/Keq; the reaction nearest equilibrium has Q/Keq closest to 1.

qs.q: Which control best confirms that the measured Keq reflects true equilibrium rather than a slow approach?
o: Measure only product concentration at a single time point
Lower the temperature to slow the reaction before quantifying
Approach equilibrium from both the reactant side and the product side and obtain the same ratio
Double the enzyme concentration and observe a faster rate
qs.x: A true equilibrium ratio is independent of the direction of approach; a path-dependent ratio signals the system has not equilibrated. Trap: Accepting a single time-point ratio as Keq without approaching equilibrium from both directions.

qs.q: For reaction B (Keq = 1.93), what is ΔG°′ at 310 K, in kJ/mol?
qs.x: ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq = −(0.008314 × 310) × ln(1.93) = -1.7 kJ/mol (literature value -1.7 kJ/mol). Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign, gives the wrong values. Trap: Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign in ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq.

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: A reaction with positive ΔG°′ can proceed forward if Q is sufficiently small
ΔG°′ is related to the equilibrium constant but not to the reaction rate
Actual ΔG depends on Q as well as ΔG°′
A reaction with a negative ΔG°′ always proceeds rapidly in the cell
qs.x: Thermodynamics specifies direction, not speed. Rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis. Trap: Assuming a negative standard free energy change means a reaction is fast in the cell, confusing thermodynamic favorability with reaction rate.

qs.q: Which mechanism allows cells to drive reactions with large positive ΔG°′ forward?
o: Removing the catalyst so the reaction is not rate-limited
Coupling them to a strongly exergonic step such as ATP hydrolysis
Raising the temperature enough to make Keq equal 1
Increasing the enzyme concentration to lower ΔG°′
qs.x: Enzymes do not change ΔG°′. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol) or keeping Q very low makes the overall ΔG negative. Trap: Thinking an enzyme or a higher temperature can change ΔG°′; only coupling to an exergonic step or a low Q makes the overall ΔG negative.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of a novel antihypertensive agent, CardioX, in adults with stage 1 hypertension. A total of 120 participants were enrolled and randomly assigned to one of three groups: CardioX 10 mg daily (n=40), CardioX 20 mg daily (n=40), or placebo (n=40). The study duration was 12 weeks, with systolic blood pressure (SBP) measured at baseline and at the end of the study. Table 1 summarizes the mean change in SBP and standard deviation for each group. The investigators hypothesized that the higher dose of CardioX would produce a greater reduction in SBP compared to the lower dose and placebo. In addition to SBP, diastolic blood pressure and adverse events were recorded, but the primary outcome remained the change in SBP. The results indicated a dose‑dependent effect, with the 20 mg group showing the largest mean reduction. The safety profile was comparable across all groups, with no serious adverse events reported. These findings suggest that CardioX may be an effective option for managing mild hypertension, pending further studies on long‑term outcomes.

qs.q: Which group had the greatest reduction in systolic blood pressure (SBP) after 12 weeks?
qs.x: The mean SBP change for the CardioX 20 mg group was -12 mmHg, which is the largest reduction among the groups. Trap: Choosing placebo by ignoring that all changes are negative and treating the smallest change (-2 mmHg) as the largest reduction.

qs.q: What type of study design was used in this research?
qs.x: The passage explicitly states that the study was a randomized controlled trial, with participants randomly assigned to treatment groups. Trap: Choosing observational cohort because participants were followed over 12 weeks, although random assignment makes this a randomized trial.

qs.q: What is the mean difference in SBP reduction between the CardioX 20 mg group and the placebo group?
qs.x: The mean SBP change for CardioX 20 mg is -12 mmHg and for placebo is -2 mmHg; the difference is 10 mmHg. Trap: Reporting 12 mmHg (the 20 mg change alone) or 8 mmHg (the 10 mg change) instead of subtracting the placebo change (-2) from -12.

qs.q: Which statement about the safety profile is incorrect?
o: No serious adverse events were reported
The safety profile was comparable across all groups
Adverse events were recorded but not reported in the table
The study reported a higher incidence of headaches in the CardioX 20 mg group
qs.x: The passage states that the safety profile was comparable and no serious adverse events were reported; it does not mention headaches, so option D is incorrect. Trap: Picking the statement that adverse events were not shown in the table (C); the passage says they were recorded but not tabulated, so it is true.

qs.q: Using the pooled SD of the CardioX 20 mg and placebo groups, what is Cohen's d for the difference in mean SBP change?
qs.x: Correct: C) Pooled SD = sqrt[(4^2 + 6^2)/2] = sqrt(26) = 5.10 mmHg; the difference is 10 mmHg, so d = 10/5.10 = 1.96, about 2.0. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.8 is closer to the standardized difference between the two active doses (4 mmHg, d about 0.9). B) 1.7 divides by the placebo SD (6) alone. D) 2.5 divides by the 20 mg SD (4) alone. Trap: Dividing the 10 mmHg difference by a single group's SD (4 or 6) instead of the pooled SD of about 5.1 mmHg.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of caffeine on cognitive performance in a controlled laboratory setting. A total of 120 healthy adults (age 20–35) were randomly assigned to one of four groups: placebo, low-dose caffeine (100 mg), moderate-dose caffeine (200 mg), and high-dose caffeine (300 mg). Each participant completed a 30‑minute psychomotor vigilance task (PVT) after ingestion. Reaction times were recorded in milliseconds, and the number of lapses (reaction time > 500 ms) was counted. The study aimed to determine whether increasing caffeine dosage correlates with improved vigilance and whether there is a threshold beyond which performance declines. Participants were instructed to abstain from caffeine for 12 hours prior to the experiment. The data were analyzed using a one‑way ANOVA followed by post‑hoc Tukey tests. The researchers hypothesized a dose‑dependent improvement up to 200 mg, with possible plateau or decline at 300 mg due to overstimulation.

qs.q: Based on the data presented, which statement best describes the relationship between caffeine dosage and mean reaction time?
o: Mean reaction time decreases linearly with increasing dosage.
Mean reaction time decreases up to 200 mg and then slightly increases at 300 mg.
Mean reaction time is unaffected by caffeine dosage.
Mean reaction time increases with higher caffeine dosage.
qs.x: The table shows a progressive decrease in mean reaction time from placebo to 200 mg, followed by a small increase at 300 mg, indicating a dose‑dependent improvement that plateaus or slightly worsens at the highest dose. Trap: Option A incorrectly assumes a continuous linear trend, ignoring the slight increase at 300 mg.

qs.q: Which analysis is most appropriate for testing whether the 200 mg group differs from the placebo group while controlling the overall error rate across all pairwise group comparisons?
o: Separate t‑tests for every pair, each at p < 0.05, with no correction
A paired t‑test between the 200 mg and placebo groups
A Tukey post‑hoc test following a significant one‑way ANOVA
qs.x: Correct: A post‑hoc Tukey test after a significant ANOVA compares group pairs while controlling the family‑wise error rate, as the passage describes. Why the others are wrong: A) uncorrected multiple t‑tests inflate the Type I error rate. B) chi‑square tests compare categorical frequencies, but reaction time is continuous. C) a paired test applies to repeated measures on the same participants, but these groups are independent. Trap: Running multiple uncorrected t-tests, which seems simpler but inflates false positives.

qs.q: Assuming the standard deviations reported are accurate and the 120 participants were divided equally among the four groups, calculate the approximate 95% confidence interval for the mean reaction time of the moderate‑dose group.
qs.x: Correct: With 120 participants in 4 equal groups, n = 30 per group. SE = 35/√30 = 6.39 ms, so the 95% CI = 310 ± 1.96 × 6.39 = 310 ± 12.5, about 298 to 323 ms. Why the others are wrong: A) 305–315 ms is only about ±0.8 SE, far too narrow. B) 310–320 ms starts at the mean instead of being centered on it. D) 300–310 ms ends at the mean and is also not centered on it. Trap: Using n = 120 (SE = 3.2) ignores that each group has only 30 participants.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT supported by Table 1?
o: The 200 mg group's mean reaction time was 40 ms lower than the placebo group's.
The 300 mg group had the largest standard deviation.
The 300 mg group's mean reaction time was slightly higher than the 200 mg group's.
The 300 mg group's mean reaction time was worse than the placebo group's.
qs.x: Correct: The 300 mg mean (315 ms) is faster than the placebo mean (350 ms), so performance was not worse than placebo. Why the others are wrong: A) 350 - 310 = 40 ms. B) the 300 mg SD of 50 ms is the largest of the four SDs. C) 315 ms is greater than 310 ms. Trap: Reading the slight rise at 300 mg as a decline below placebo performance.

qs.q: Caffeine improves vigilance primarily through which molecular mechanism?
qs.x: Caffeine is a competitive antagonist of adenosine receptors, blocking adenosine-mediated drowsiness and increasing arousal. Trap: Choosing acetylcholinesterase inhibition because raising acetylcholine also promotes alertness, although caffeine acts by blocking adenosine receptors.

passages.title: Processes of cell division, differentiation, and specialization · passage
text: Researchers investigated the inhibitory effects of two novel kinase inhibitors, KIN-A and KIN-B, on the proliferation of cultured human melanoma cells. The study employed a time‑course design, measuring drug concentrations and cellular response over a 7‑day period. Cells were treated with varying concentrations of each inhibitor, and the percent inhibition of proliferation was assessed using an MTT assay. The data revealed a dose‑dependent decrease in cell viability for both drugs, with KIN-A achieving 80% inhibition at 10 µM after 5 days, whereas KIN-B required 20 µM to reach the same level of inhibition. The researchers noted that the combination of sub‑IC50 concentrations of KIN-A and KIN-B produced a synergistic effect, reducing proliferation by 90% at 5 µM each after 7 days. These findings suggest potential therapeutic benefits of combination therapy in melanoma treatment, warranting further in‑vivo studies.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?
o: At 5 µM on day 7, KIN-B alone inhibited proliferation more than KIN-A alone.
KIN-B reached 80% inhibition at a lower concentration than KIN-A.
The combination at 5 µM each produced greater inhibition than either agent alone at 5 µM.
The combination at 5 µM each produced less inhibition than KIN-A alone at 10 µM.
qs.x: Correct: the combination gave 90% inhibition versus 45% (KIN-A) and 25% (KIN-B) alone at 5 µM on day 7. Why the others are wrong: A) KIN-B gave 25%, less than KIN-A at 45%. B) KIN-A needed 10 µM and KIN-B 20 µM. D) 90% is greater than 80%. Trap: Reading KIN-B's 80% inhibition at 20 µM as greater potency, reversing which drug reached 80% at the lower concentration (KIN-A at 10 µM).

qs.q: Which comparison best isolates the effect of KIN-A on melanoma cell proliferation?
o: Cells treated with 10 µM KIN-A compared with cells given vehicle only
Cells treated with 10 µM KIN-A compared with cells treated with 10 µM KIN-B
Cells treated with 10 µM KIN-A compared with cells treated with 5 µM of each drug
Cells treated with 10 µM KIN-A for 5 days compared with cells treated with 5 µM KIN-A for 7 days
qs.x: Correct: a vehicle-only group differs from the KIN-A group only in the presence of KIN-A. Why the others are wrong: B) This compares two different drugs and does not show the effect of KIN-A against no drug. C) The comparator contains KIN-B and a different dose. D) This changes both concentration and time. Trap: Comparing against another drug instead of an untreated control.

qs.q: At day 7, by how many percentage points did the combination of 5 µM KIN-A plus 5 µM KIN-B exceed 5 µM KIN-A alone?
qs.x: Correct: 90 - 45 = 45 percentage points. Why the others are wrong: A) 20 is the gap between the two single agents (45 - 25), not the combination minus KIN-A. C) 65 uses KIN-B alone (90 - 25). D) 90 is the combination value, not the difference. Trap: Subtracting KIN-B's 25% instead of KIN-A's 45% (giving 65), or taking the gap between the two single agents (20).

qs.q: Which of the following statements is a common misconception about the data presented?
o: The inhibition values for KIN-A are higher than for KIN-B at the same concentration.
The combination of 5 µM KIN-A and 5 µM KIN-B achieves 90% inhibition after 7 days.
KIN-B is more potent than KIN-A because it reaches 80% inhibition at a lower concentration.
KIN-B requires a higher concentration to achieve 80% inhibition than KIN-A.
qs.x: KIN-A reached 80% inhibition at 10 µM, whereas KIN-B needed 20 µM, so KIN-A is the more potent agent. Saying KIN-B is more potent reverses this. Trap: Reversing potency: a lower concentration needed for the same effect means higher potency.

qs.q: The authors propose in vivo studies next. Why can the results of an MTT assay in cultured melanoma cells not alone establish therapeutic benefit?
o: Cultured cells do not capture drug absorption, distribution, metabolism or toxicity to normal tissue in a whole organism.
The MTT assay measures cell migration rather than viability.
Percent inhibition cannot be calculated in cultured cells.
Melanoma cells do not respond to kinase inhibitors in culture.
qs.x: Correct: in vitro assays omit pharmacokinetics and effects on normal tissues that determine in vivo efficacy and safety. Why the others are wrong: B) MTT reflects metabolic activity of viable cells, not migration. C) Percent inhibition is routinely calculated in culture. D) The data show inhibition in cultured melanoma cells. Trap: Treating an in vitro result as proof of clinical benefit.

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: In the Petrov laboratory, researchers measured dehydrogenase activity in a liver homogenate by following production of NADH, which absorbs light at 340 nm with a molar extinction coefficient of 6,220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, whereas NAD⁺ does not absorb appreciably at this wavelength. The homogenate was diluted 50-fold in assay buffer before use, and 1 mL reactions in a 1 cm cuvette contained saturating substrate and NAD⁺ at 25 °C. Absorbance at 340 nm was recorded every minute. A blank containing all components except substrate was run in parallel to correct for non-enzymatic changes. The initial linear region of the progress curve was used to calculate velocity. The researchers wished to report the activity of the undiluted homogenate and to compare it with a published value from a different laboratory. The spectrophotometer was zeroed against buffer, and all readings fell within the instrument's linear range. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What is the change in A340 of the sample between 0 and 2 minutes, according to Table 1?
qs.x: A(2 min) − A(0 min) = 0.423 − 0.05 = 0.373. Trap: Reporting 0.187, the change per minute, or the 2-minute absorbance of 0.423 without subtracting the 0.05 starting value.

qs.q: Why is a blank lacking substrate included?
o: To increase the extinction coefficient of NADH
To detect absorbance changes that occur without the enzyme-catalyzed reaction
To ensure the enzyme is saturated
qs.x: The blank accounts for background drift (e.g., contaminating reductants, instrument drift) independent of the reaction under study. Trap: Thinking the blank supplies the NADH or sets saturation, rather than showing the signal drift occurring without the enzyme reaction.

qs.q: Using Beer–Lambert, what is the initial rate of NADH formation in the cuvette (µM/min), and what activity does the undiluted homogenate have (µM/min)?
o: 30 µM/min in the cuvette; 30 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
0.03 µM/min in the cuvette; 1.5 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
1500 µM/min in the cuvette; 75000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
30 µM/min in the cuvette; 1500 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
qs.x: Rate = (ΔA/min)/(ε·l) = 0.1866/6220 = 30 µM/min in the cuvette. Multiply by the 50-fold dilution to get 1500 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate. Trap: Forgetting to multiply by the 50-fold dilution, giving 30 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate, or misplacing the decimal in the unit conversion.

qs.q: Which statement about this assay is INCORRECT?
o: NADH absorbs at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not
Both NAD⁺ and NADH absorb strongly at 340 nm, so the signal reflects total coenzyme
The initial linear portion of the curve gives the most reliable velocity
Substrate must be saturating for the rate to approximate Vmax
qs.x: Only the reduced coenzyme absorbs at 340 nm; that selective absorbance makes the assay possible. Trap: Choosing the statement that NADH absorbs but NAD⁺ does not, which is true, rather than the false claim that both coenzymes absorb at 340 nm.

qs.q: Which type of assay couples an enzyme of interest to NADH oxidation so that its activity can be monitored at 340 nm?
o: A radioactive assay using ³²P-labeled ATP
An immunoassay using antibodies against the enzyme
A gel assay using SDS-PAGE mobility
A coupled assay using lactate dehydrogenase to reduce pyruvate formed by pyruvate kinase
qs.x: Pyruvate kinase produces pyruvate; LDH then oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, causing a decrease in A340 proportional to pyruvate kinase activity. Trap: Choosing a radioactive, antibody or gel method, none of which monitors NADH absorbance at 340 nm continuously.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of varying concentrations of a novel antimicrobial peptide on the growth of Escherichia coli in vitro. In a controlled experiment, cultures were inoculated with a standardized bacterial load and then exposed to peptide concentrations of 0 µM (control), 5 µM, 10 µM, and 20 µM. After 24 hours of incubation at 37°C, optical density at 600 nm (OD600) was measured to assess bacterial growth. The results, summarized in Table 1, indicate a dose-dependent reduction in OD600, with the highest concentration yielding the greatest inhibition. Additionally, the researchers performed a time-course analysis at the 10 µM concentration, measuring OD600 at 0, 6, 12, and 24 hours to evaluate the kinetics of inhibition. The data suggest that the peptide inhibits growth most rapidly within the first 6 hours, after which the degree of inhibition changed little. These findings support further investigation into the peptide’s potential as a therapeutic agent.

qs.q: Which peptide concentration shows the greatest reduction in OD600 compared to the control?
qs.x: The OD600 at 20 µM (0.25) is the lowest, indicating the greatest reduction relative to the control (1.00). Trap: Choosing 0 µM because it has the highest OD600; the question asks for the greatest reduction, which is the lowest OD600 (0.25 at 20 µM).

qs.q: According to the passage, which culture served as the control for the peptide treatments?
o: A culture inoculated with the standardized bacterial load and exposed to 0 µM peptide
Sterile medium with no bacteria added
A culture exposed to 20 µM peptide
A culture of a different bacterial species at 10 µM
qs.x: Correct: The passage identifies 0 µM as the control: inoculated cells with no peptide, so growth without treatment is the reference. Why the others are wrong: B) sterile medium contains no bacteria and would be a blank for the spectrophotometer, not the growth control. C) 20 µM is a treatment group. D) a different species at 10 µM changes the organism and is a treatment. Trap: Treating a sterile blank as the control, although a control must contain the bacteria without the treatment.

qs.q: What is the percent inhibition of bacterial growth at 10 µM compared to the control?
qs.x: Percent inhibition = ((1.00 – 0.50)/1.00) × 100 = 50%. Trap: Choosing 25% or 75% by reading the 20 µM or 5 µM rows instead of the 10 µM row, or reporting the OD value itself rather than the fall from the control of 1.00.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage and Table 1?
o: The peptide inhibits growth most rapidly within the first 6 hours (at 10 µM).
The peptide completely eradicated E. coli at 20 µM.
There is a dose-dependent reduction in OD600.
The highest concentration yielded the greatest inhibition.
qs.x: Correct: B) At 20 µM the OD600 is still 0.25 (versus 1.00 for the control), so substantial turbidity remains, and OD600 cannot show whether all cells were killed; 'completely eradicated' is not supported. Why the others are wrong: A) the passage states that at 10 µM inhibition was fastest in the first 6 hours. C) OD600 falls from 1.00 to 0.75, 0.50 and 0.25 as concentration rises from 0 to 5, 10 and 20 µM. D) the 20 µM culture has the lowest OD600 (0.25), so it shows the greatest inhibition. Trap: The wording “completely eradicated” may mislead students to think 0.25 OD600 equals eradication.

qs.q: OD600 measures turbidity, which includes dead cells. Which additional measurement would best distinguish bacteriostatic from bactericidal action of the peptide?
o: Plating peptide-treated samples on peptide-free agar and counting colony-forming units
Repeating the OD600 reading at 20 µM at 24 hours
Measuring optical density at 450 nm instead of 600 nm
Testing a 40 µM concentration by OD600
qs.x: Correct: Viable counts (CFU) on peptide-free plates show whether cells were killed or merely stopped dividing. Why the others are wrong: B) repeating OD600 gives the same turbidity information and cannot distinguish viable from dead cells. C) changing wavelength still measures turbidity. D) a higher dose read by OD600 still cannot separate dead from non-growing cells. Trap: Assuming that a low OD600 proves the cells are dead, when it only shows reduced turbidity.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Biochemists in the Duarte laboratory characterized lactate dehydrogenase purified from a bacterial expression system, focusing on its response to a candidate small-molecule inhibitor designed to resemble pyruvate. Reactions contained a fixed enzyme concentration in buffered solution at 25 °C, and initial velocities were measured at six pyruvate concentrations with and without 60 µM inhibitor. Product formation was followed spectrophotometrically for the first 60 seconds, a window in which less than 5% of substrate was consumed. Each velocity represents the mean of three independent reactions, and the standard error was below 4% of every mean. The team wished to determine whether the compound binds the free enzyme at the active site or instead binds elsewhere, and to estimate its dissociation constant for the enzyme–inhibitor complex before testing it in cultured cells. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and the buffer contained no metal chelators or reducing agents that could interfere with the assay. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, what is the initial velocity in the presence of inhibitor when [S] = 200 µM?
qs.x: Reading the inhibitor column at [S] = 200 µM gives 34.3 µmol/min; the control column value (80) is the uninhibited rate. Trap: Reading the no-inhibitor column (80 µmol/min at 200 µM) instead of the 60 µM inhibitor column.

qs.q: Which additional experiment would best distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition by this compound?
o: Measure product formation after 60 minutes rather than 60 seconds
Repeat the assay at a lower temperature to see whether inhibition disappears
Measure whether very high substrate concentrations restore the uninhibited maximal velocity
Measure velocity at a single substrate concentration with several enzyme concentrations
qs.x: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so sufficiently high [S] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax regardless of [S]. Trap: Choosing a longer time course or a single-substrate experiment, which cannot show whether high [S] restores Vmax.

qs.q: Assuming simple competitive inhibition, what is the approximate Ki of the inhibitor?
qs.x: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). Here Km,app/Km = 5, so [I]/Ki = 4 and Ki = 60/4 = 15 µM. Trap: Dividing the inhibitor concentration by the Km ratio of 5 (60/5 = 12 µM) instead of by (ratio - 1) = 4.

qs.q: Which statement about the data is NOT consistent with competitive inhibition?
o: The inhibition is weaker at higher substrate concentrations
The inhibitor binds the free enzyme in preference to the enzyme–substrate complex
The apparent Km is larger in the presence of the inhibitor
Vmax is lower in the presence of the inhibitor at saturating [S]
qs.x: Competitive inhibitors leave Vmax unchanged; the velocities converge as [S] rises. A reduced Vmax would indicate noncompetitive or uncompetitive behavior. Trap: Thinking a competitive inhibitor lowers Vmax; it only raises apparent Km, and velocities converge at high [S].

qs.q: Many drugs, such as statins and methotrexate, act as competitive inhibitors. Which property of such drugs most directly explains why they are often structural analogs of the substrate?
o: They must bind covalently to the enzyme
They must lower the enzyme's turnover number at saturating substrate
They must occupy the same active site as the substrate
They must bind the enzyme–substrate complex only
qs.x: Competition requires binding to the same site; structural similarity to the substrate (or transition state) lets the drug fit the active site and compete reversibly. Trap: Assuming such drugs must bind covalently or only the enzyme–substrate complex, rather than competing reversibly for the active site.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of the novel antihypertensive agent, Hypotensol, in adults with stage 1 hypertension. A total of 120 participants were enrolled and randomly assigned to either the Hypotensol group (n=60) or the placebo group (n=60). Baseline systolic blood pressure (SBP) was measured after a 5-minute seated rest. Follow-up measurements were taken at 4 weeks and 8 weeks. The study aimed to assess both the magnitude and durability of SBP reduction. Table 1 summarizes the mean SBP values (± SD) for each group at the specified time points. The researchers also recorded adverse events, which were mild and comparable between groups. Statistical analysis involved paired t-tests within groups and independent t-tests between groups, with a significance threshold of p<0.05. The results indicated that Hypotensol produced a statistically significant reduction in SBP compared to placebo at both 4-week and 8-week intervals. The mean baseline SBP was 148 mmHg in the Hypotensol group and 147 mmHg in the placebo group. At 4 weeks, the Hypotensol group showed a mean SBP of 132 mmHg, whereas the placebo group was 145 mmHg. At 8 weeks, the Hypotensol group further decreased to 125 mmHg, while the placebo group remained at 144 mmHg. The standard deviations ranged from 8 to 10 mmHg across all measurements. The study concluded that Hypotensol offers a clinically meaningful reduction in SBP over an 8-week period, with a safety profile comparable to placebo.

qs.q: What was the mean systolic blood pressure (SBP) in the Hypotensol group at 8 weeks?
qs.x: The table shows the Hypotensol group’s mean SBP at 8 weeks as 125 mmHg. Trap: Reading the 4-week column (132 mmHg) instead of the 8-week column for the Hypotensol row.

qs.q: Which design feature best limits the influence of participants' and investigators' expectations on the measured SBP?
o: Use of paired t‑tests within groups
Measuring SBP after a 5‑minute seated rest
qs.x: Correct: Masking participants and investigators to treatment prevents expectations from influencing responses or measurements. Why the others are wrong: A) randomization balances groups but does not hide the assignment. C) a statistical test does not affect expectations. D) a rest period standardizes measurement but does not conceal treatment. Trap: Option A tempts readers to credit randomization with preventing expectation bias.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in mean SBP from baseline to 8 weeks in the Hypotensol group?
qs.x: Reduction = 148 - 125 = 23 mmHg. Percent = (23/148) × 100 ≈ 15.5%. Trap: C (20%) is a common miscalculation if the reduction is mistakenly taken as 30 mmHg.

qs.q: According to the passage, which test was used to compare Hypotensol with placebo at a given time point?
qs.x: Correct: The passage states that independent t‑tests were used between groups. Why the others are wrong: A) paired t‑tests were used within groups, not between groups. C) the outcome was a continuous mean SBP, not counts of categories. D) no correlation analysis is described. Trap: Option A tempts readers to confuse the within‑group test with the between‑group test.

qs.q: Which statement about the placebo group is supported by Table 1?
o: Its mean SBP rose over the 8 weeks.
Its mean SBP fell by 3 mmHg, far less than the 23 mmHg fall in the Hypotensol group.
Its mean SBP fell by more than the Hypotensol group's at 4 weeks.
Its 8‑week mean SBP was lower than the Hypotensol group's.
qs.x: Correct: Placebo mean SBP went from 147 to 144 (3 mmHg) while Hypotensol went from 148 to 125 (23 mmHg). Why the others are wrong: A) it decreased from 147 to 144. C) placebo fell 2 mmHg versus 16 mmHg at 4 weeks. D) 144 is higher than 125. Trap: Taking the passage's phrase that placebo SBP 'remained at 144 mmHg' to mean no change or a rise, when the table shows a 3 mmHg fall from 147.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers in the Svensson laboratory studied three reversible reactions of early carbohydrate metabolism in extracts of rat liver. Each reaction was allowed to reach equilibrium in a sealed reaction vessel at 37 °C and pH 7.0, after which reactants and products were quantified by HPLC to give the equilibrium constant. In a second set of experiments, intact hepatocytes were rapidly freeze-clamped and the steady-state ratio of products to reactants, known as the mass-action ratio Q, was measured for the same reactions. Comparing Q with Keq indicates how far each reaction sits from equilibrium under physiological conditions, and therefore which steps are likely to be regulated. The investigators used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and expected values of ΔG°′ to be consistent with literature compilations. All reagents were of analytical grade, and each reaction vessel was degassed to avoid oxidation of sulfhydryl groups. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which reaction operates closest to equilibrium in hepatocytes?
o: Reaction A: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP
None; all three are far from equilibrium
qs.x: Q/Keq near 1 indicates near-equilibrium operation. Reaction B has Q closest to Keq, so it is the least likely to be a regulatory step. Trap: Comparing Q with Keq by absolute size rather than by the ratio Q/Keq; the reaction nearest equilibrium has Q/Keq closest to 1.

qs.q: Which control best confirms that the measured Keq reflects true equilibrium rather than a slow approach?
o: Double the enzyme concentration and observe a faster rate
Approach equilibrium from both the reactant side and the product side and obtain the same ratio
Measure only product concentration at a single time point
Lower the temperature to slow the reaction before quantifying
qs.x: A true equilibrium ratio is independent of the direction of approach; a path-dependent ratio signals the system has not equilibrated. Trap: Accepting a single time-point ratio as Keq without approaching equilibrium from both directions.

qs.q: For reaction A (Keq = 652), what is ΔG°′ at 310 K, in kJ/mol?
qs.x: ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq = −(0.008314 × 310) × ln(652) = -16.7 kJ/mol (literature value -16.7 kJ/mol). Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign, gives the wrong values. Trap: Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign in ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq.

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: ΔG°′ is related to the equilibrium constant but not to the reaction rate
A reaction with a negative ΔG°′ always proceeds rapidly in the cell
A reaction with positive ΔG°′ can proceed forward if Q is sufficiently small
Actual ΔG depends on Q as well as ΔG°′
qs.x: Thermodynamics specifies direction, not speed. Rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis. Trap: Assuming a negative ΔG°′ guarantees a fast reaction; ΔG°′ gives direction and extent only, while rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis.

qs.q: Which mechanism allows cells to drive reactions with large positive ΔG°′ forward?
o: Coupling them to a strongly exergonic step such as ATP hydrolysis
Removing the catalyst so the reaction is not rate-limited
Increasing the enzyme concentration to lower ΔG°′
Raising the temperature enough to make Keq equal 1
qs.x: Enzymes do not change ΔG°′. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol) or keeping Q very low makes the overall ΔG negative. Trap: Thinking an enzyme or a higher temperature can change ΔG°′; only coupling to an exergonic step or a low Q makes the overall ΔG negative.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of varying doses of a novel cognitive enhancer on reaction time in healthy adults. A double‑blind, placebo‑controlled study enrolled 120 participants who were randomly assigned to one of four groups: placebo (n = 30), low dose (5 mg, n = 30), medium dose (10 mg, n = 30), and high dose (20 mg, n = 30). After a single oral administration, participants performed a computerized choice‑reaction task. Mean reaction times (RT) and standard deviations (SD) were recorded. The investigators hypothesized that higher doses would produce faster RTs, but also monitored for potential adverse effects. The study was conducted over a 12‑month period, with interim safety analyses. The results are summarized in Table 3‑4 below. The data provide a basis for dose‑response modeling and future phase‑III trials.

qs.q: Which of the following best represents the observed trend in mean reaction time across the dose groups?
o: Reaction time increases with higher doses.
Reaction time decreases with higher doses.
Reaction time remains unchanged across doses.
Reaction time first decreases then increases with dose.
qs.x: The mean reaction time decreases from 350 ms in the placebo group to 310 ms in the high‑dose group, indicating faster responses with higher doses. Trap: Option A incorrectly states the opposite trend, confusing the direction of the dose‑response relationship.

qs.q: Which experimental design element best supports the validity of the study’s conclusions about dose‑response?
qs.x: Random assignment minimizes selection bias and ensures comparable groups, which is essential for attributing differences in reaction time to the dose of the enhancer. Trap: Option A is incorrect because the study was double‑blind; blinding alone does not establish dose‑response validity.

qs.q: Calculate the absolute difference in mean reaction time between the high‑dose group and the placebo group.
qs.x: Placebo mean = 350 ms; high-dose mean = 310 ms. Absolute difference = 350 - 310 = 40 ms. Trap: Subtracting the wrong rows (for example, medium dose 320 from placebo) gives 30 ms; the question asks about the high-dose group.

qs.q: Which statement is NOT supported by the passage and table?
o: The high-dose group had the fastest mean reaction time.
Adverse effects were monitored during the study.
The sample of 120 was shown to be adequately powered to detect a dose-response.
Mean reaction time fell at each higher dose.
qs.x: Correct: C) The passage reports no power calculation or test result, so adequacy of the sample for detecting a dose-response is not shown. Why the others are wrong: A) The high-dose mean (310 ms) is the lowest. B) The passage says adverse effects were monitored. D) Means were 350, 335, 320 and 310 ms across increasing doses. Trap: Assuming that 120 participants is automatically enough to detect a dose-response, although no power calculation or test result is reported.

qs.q: What is the approximate Cohen's d for the difference in mean reaction time between the placebo group (SD 25) and the high-dose group (SD 30), with equal n?
qs.x: Pooled SD = sqrt[(25^2 + 30^2)/2] = 27.6 ms. d = 40/27.6 = 1.45, a large effect. Trap: Dividing the 40 ms difference by one group's SD only (25 ms gives 1.6; 30 ms gives 1.3) or not dividing at all misstates d.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers investigated the antihypertensive effects of a novel compound, Hypertensol, in a randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial. Eighty adults with stage‑1 hypertension were enrolled and randomly assigned to one of four groups: placebo (n = 20), low dose (10 mg/day, n = 20), medium dose (20 mg/day, n = 20), or high dose (40 mg/day, n = 20). Baseline systolic blood pressure (SBP) was measured after a 5‑minute seated rest. Patients received their assigned treatment for 12 weeks, after which SBP was reassessed. The study aimed to determine dose‑response relationships and identify the optimal dose that maximizes SBP reduction while minimizing adverse events. The investigators also collected data on diastolic BP, heart rate, and serum creatinine to evaluate safety. The trial was conducted at three tertiary care centers, and all participants provided informed consent. The primary outcome was the mean change in SBP from baseline to week 12.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the dose‑response relationship observed in the study?
o: SBP reduction was greatest at the low dose and plateaued thereafter.
SBP reduction increased with dose, with the high dose producing the largest change but a smaller incremental gain per mg at the top dose.
SBP reduction was significant only at the high dose.
SBP reduction was similar across all active doses.
qs.x: Correct: B) Mean change grew from -7 (low) to -12 (medium) to -15 mmHg (high), but the gain per mg fell from 0.5 mmHg/mg (10 to 20 mg) to 0.15 mmHg/mg (20 to 40 mg). Why the others are wrong: A) the reduction kept growing beyond the low dose. C) no significance tests are reported, and every active dose lowered SBP more than placebo (-2). D) the active-dose reductions differ (7, 12 and 15 mmHg). Trap: Assuming a plateau after the low dose ignores continued improvement; assuming strict linearity ignores the smaller gain from 20 to 40 mg.

qs.q: Which study design feature best ensures that the observed SBP changes are attributable to Hypertensol rather than confounding variables?
o: Randomization of participants to treatment groups
Measurement of baseline SBP after a 5‑minute rest
Inclusion of three tertiary care centers
qs.x: Randomization balances known and unknown confounders across groups, attributing differences in SBP change to the intervention. Trap: Focusing on the 12‑week duration (Option B) ignores that duration alone does not control for confounding.

qs.q: What is the absolute reduction in mean SBP for the high‑dose group compared to placebo?
qs.x: Correct: A) High-dose change (-15 mmHg) minus placebo change (-2 mmHg) gives a 13 mmHg greater reduction. Why the others are wrong: B) 15 mmHg is the high-dose change alone, ignoring the placebo decline. C) 17 mmHg adds the placebo decline instead of subtracting it. D) 12 mmHg is the medium-dose change, not the high dose. Trap: Reporting the high-dose change alone (15 mmHg) without subtracting the 2 mmHg decline that also occurred with placebo.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage and Table 1?
o: The high-dose group achieved the greatest SBP reduction.
Placebo recipients experienced a small SBP decline.
Diastolic BP fell in all three active-dose groups.
qs.x: Correct: C) The passage says diastolic BP was collected but reports no diastolic results, so a fall in diastolic BP is not supported. Why the others are wrong: A) The high-dose change was -15 mmHg, the largest. B) The placebo group fell from 148 to 146 mmHg. D) The passage states treatment lasted 12 weeks. Trap: Assuming diastolic BP data were reported and mirror the SBP changes, when the passage says only that they were collected.

qs.q: What is the average incremental SBP reduction per mg of Hypertensol between the medium (20 mg) and high (40 mg) doses?
qs.x: Correct: A) Medium to high: 15 - 12 = 3 mmHg extra over 20 mg = 0.15 mmHg per mg. Why the others are wrong: B) 0.5 mmHg per mg is the low-to-medium interval (5 mmHg over 10 mg). C) 0.3 divides the 3 mmHg by 10 mg instead of the actual 20 mg interval. D) 0.38 divides the total high-dose change (15 mmHg) by 40 mg instead of using the increment between doses. Trap: Using the low-to-medium interval (0.5 mmHg per mg) or dividing the 3 mmHg increment by 10 mg instead of by the 20 mg interval.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers conducted a randomized, double‑blind, dose‑ranging trial to evaluate the antihypertensive efficacy of a novel drug, Hypertensol, in adults with mild to moderate hypertension. The study enrolled 200 participants who were randomized to receive either 10 mg, 20 mg, 30 mg, or 40 mg of Hypertensol once daily for 4 weeks. Blood pressure was measured at baseline and at the end of the study. Table 1 summarizes the mean systolic blood pressure (SBP) change (mmHg) and standard deviation (SD) for each dosage group. The investigators hypothesized a dose‑dependent reduction in SBP, with the greatest effect at the highest dose. The data showed a clear trend: the 30 mg group achieved the largest mean reduction, while the 40 mg group had a slightly smaller mean change but greater variability. These findings suggest an optimal dose range and highlight the importance of balancing efficacy with safety in dose‑finding studies.

qs.q: Which dosage group showed the greatest average reduction in systolic blood pressure?
qs.x: The table indicates that the 30‑mg group had the largest mean SBP reduction of 12.0 mmHg, surpassing all other groups. Trap: Assuming the highest dose (40 mg) gives the largest reduction, as the investigators hypothesized, although its mean of 10.5 mmHg is below the 30 mg group's 12.0 mmHg.

qs.q: Which feature of the design described in the passage best reduces observer bias in measuring blood pressure?
o: Double‑blinding, so investigators do not know which dose each participant received.
qs.x: Correct: A) If investigators do not know each participant’s dose, their expectations cannot bias the measurement. Why the others are wrong: B) A baseline measurement allows calculation of change and does not conceal assignment. C) Several doses allow a dose comparison but do not conceal assignment. D) Duration does not affect observer bias. Trap: Choosing a feature that provides a reference or comparison (baseline, multiple doses) rather than one that conceals assignment.

qs.q: Assuming the 30‑mg group had a mean reduction of 12 mmHg with SD 4 and a sample size of 50 (200 participants in four equal groups), what is the 95% confidence interval for the mean reduction?
qs.x: Correct: A) SE = 4/√50 = 0.566; 95% CI = 12 ± 1.96 × 0.566 = 12 ± 1.11, or 10.9 to 13.1 mmHg. Why the others are wrong: B) 11.4-12.6 corresponds to about ±1 SE, too narrow for 95%. C) 10-14 is ±2 mmHg, wider than 1.96 SE. D) 9-15 is ±3 mmHg, far wider than 1.96 SE. Trap: Choosing 11.4-12.6 (option B), which is only about 1 SE wide, or a round interval not equal to 1.96 standard errors (options C or D).

qs.q: Which statement is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: The 30-mg group had the highest reduction in SBP.
The 10-mg group had the lowest reduction in SBP.
The 40-mg group had the highest variability.
The 10‑mg group had no reduction in SBP.
qs.x: The table shows a 5.0 mmHg reduction for the 10-mg group, so it did have a measurable effect; statement D is false. Statements A, B and C match the table. Trap: Reading the smallest reduction (5.0 mmHg at 10 mg) as 'no reduction'; the 10-mg group still lowered SBP by 5.0 mmHg.

qs.q: Which concept is most closely related to the observed dose‑response relationship?
qs.x: The dose‑response curve reflects pharmacodynamic principles—how the drug’s concentration at the target site influences its therapeutic effect. Trap: Choosing pharmacokinetics because doses are involved, although how effect changes with dose is pharmacodynamics; pharmacokinetics covers absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of three different cognitive training protocols on reaction time in adults aged 20–35. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group that received no training, Treatment A that used a visual-spatial memory task, Treatment B that used a verbal working memory task, and a Combined group that received both tasks. Each training session lasted 30 minutes and was conducted twice a week for six weeks. Reaction times were measured using a computerized Stroop task at baseline, mid-intervention, and post-intervention; Table 1 gives the post-intervention means. The data collected showed that the Combined group had the greatest reduction in reaction time, followed by Treatment A, Treatment B, and the Control group. Researchers concluded that multimodal training may produce the most robust improvements in cognitive processing speed.

qs.q: Which group had the lowest mean reaction time at post-intervention?
qs.x: The table shows the Combined group’s mean response time of 460 ms, which is lower than all other groups (Control 520 ms, Treatment A 485 ms, Treatment B 500 ms). Trap: Choosing Treatment A because it is the first active group listed, instead of comparing all four post‑intervention means.

qs.q: Which experimental design would best isolate the effect of multimodal training on reaction time?
o: A within-subject crossover design where each participant receives all treatments in random order
A between-subjects randomized controlled trial with four parallel groups
A case-control study comparing participants with and without training
A longitudinal cohort study following participants over two years without randomization
qs.x: Correct: B) Randomly assigning participants to four parallel groups lets the Combined group be compared with each single-task group and with untrained controls, while randomization balances individual differences across groups. Why the others are wrong: A) Training produces lasting learning, so in a crossover the effect of an earlier protocol would carry over into later periods. C) A case-control study is observational and starts from outcomes rather than assigning training. D) Without randomization, groups may differ in confounders such as motivation or baseline speed. Trap: Assuming a crossover design is superior because participants serve as their own controls, ignoring that learned skills carry over between periods.

qs.q: Calculate the absolute difference in mean reaction time between Treatment A and the Control group.
qs.x: Treatment A mean = 485 ms; Control mean = 520 ms. Difference = 520 – 485 = 35 ms. Trap: Confusing a standard deviation with a difference: 45 ms is the Control SD, not the gap between the two means (520 − 485).

qs.q: If it differed systematically between the four groups, which of the following would be a confounding variable?
o: Mean response time on the Stroop task
Time of day at which each group completed the Stroop task
The number of groups in the study
qs.x: Correct: Time of day affects reaction time and, if it differed by group, would be mixed with the training effect, so it would be a confounder. Why the others are wrong: A) group assignment is the independent variable. B) response time is the dependent variable. D) the number of groups is a feature of the design that cannot differ between groups. Trap: Calling the independent or dependent variable a confounder instead of a third variable linked to both.

qs.q: Which statement is best supported by Table 1?
o: The Combined group's mean response time was 60 ms lower than the Control group's.
Treatment B had a lower mean response time than Treatment A.
The Control group had the smallest standard deviation.
The Combined group had the largest standard deviation.
qs.x: Correct: 520 − 460 = 60 ms. Why the others are wrong: B) Treatment B (500 ms) was slower than Treatment A (485 ms). C) Control had the largest SD (45 ms). D) Combined had the smallest SD (35 ms). Trap: Assuming the group with the lowest mean must also be the most variable, or confusing the ordering of Treatments A and B.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Abara group investigated turnover of IκBα, a regulatory protein that is rapidly degraded in proliferating cells. To measure stability without confounding new synthesis, cells were treated with cycloheximide, an inhibitor of translation elongation, and harvested at the times shown. Lysates were resolved by SDS-PAGE, transferred to a membrane, and probed with an antibody against IκBα; band intensities were quantified and normalized to a loading control. Degradation of IκBα was assumed to follow first-order kinetics. The researchers hoped to compare half-lives under normal and stressed conditions and to learn whether proteasome inhibition would stabilize the protein. Results from unstressed cells are shown; each value is the mean of three biological replicates, with errors below 5% of the mean. Equal total protein was loaded in every lane, as confirmed by the loading control. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What fraction of IκBα remains 60 minutes after cycloheximide treatment?
qs.x: At 60 min, two half-lives have elapsed (100 → 50 → 25%). Trap: Taking 75% by assuming a linear loss of 25% per 30 minutes, or 50% by stopping at the first half-life; at 60 min two half-lives have passed, giving 25%.

qs.q: Why is cycloheximide used in this experiment?
o: It increases transcription of the gene
It blocks new synthesis so that the loss of existing protein can be followed
It accelerates proteasomal degradation of all proteins
It labels the protein for detection by antibody
qs.x: Without blocking translation, newly synthesized protein would obscure the decay of the pre-existing pool. Trap: Thinking cycloheximide acts on transcription or on degradation; it blocks translation elongation, so no new protein is made and any decline reflects decay of the existing pool.

qs.q: If the decay continues to be first-order, what percentage of IκBα remains after 150 minutes?
qs.x: 150 min = 5 half-lives of 30 min, so 100 × (1/2)^5 = 3.125%. Trap: Miscounting half-lives and choosing 6.25% (4 half-lives) or 1.562% (6 half-lives); 150 min / 30 min = 5 half-lives, giving 3.125%.

qs.q: Which statement about first-order decay is INCORRECT?
o: The half-life equals ln 2 divided by the rate constant
The half-life increases as the starting amount of protein increases
The half-life is independent of starting concentration
The rate of decay is proportional to the amount remaining
qs.x: In first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2/k and does not depend on starting concentration. Trap: Believing a larger starting amount takes longer to halve; in first-order decay the half-life is ln 2/k and does not depend on starting amount.

qs.q: IκBα turnover is typically controlled by which system?
o: Phosphorylation by glycolytic kinases that leads to secretion
Ubiquitination and degradation by the proteasome
Glycosylation in the Golgi apparatus that prevents degradation
qs.x: Polyubiquitin chains (K48-linked) mark proteins for proteasomal degradation; proteasome inhibitors such as MG132 stabilize short-lived regulatory proteins. Trap: Picking glycosylation or glycolytic-kinase phosphorylation because they sound regulatory; short-lived regulators are tagged with polyubiquitin and degraded by the proteasome.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel dietary supplement on cognitive performance in adults aged 30–50. In a randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial, 120 participants were assigned to either the supplement group (n = 60) or the placebo group (n = 60). Cognitive performance was assessed at baseline and after 12 weeks using a standardized battery of tests measuring working memory, processing speed, and executive function. Table 1 summarizes the mean scores and standard deviations for each test at baseline and after the intervention. The supplement group showed a modest improvement in working memory (mean increase of 1.2 points) and processing speed (mean increase of 0.8 points), whereas the placebo group had negligible changes. Executive function scores improved slightly in both groups. The researchers concluded that the supplement may have a small effect on certain cognitive domains, though the clinical relevance remains uncertain.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, which statement best describes the change in working memory scores for the supplement group?
o: The mean score decreased by 1.2 points.
The mean score increased by 1.2 points.
The mean score increased by 0.8 points.
There was no change in the mean score.
qs.x: The supplement group’s working memory mean increased from 28.4 to 29.6, an increase of 1.2 points. Trap: Option C confuses the working memory improvement with the processing speed improvement.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes an appropriate experimental design to test whether the observed cognitive improvements are due to the supplement itself?
o: Use a crossover design where participants receive both supplement and placebo in random order.
Use a single‑blind design with only participants unaware of group assignment.
Use a quasi‑experimental design with no control group.
Use a longitudinal observational study following participants for 5 years.
qs.x: A crossover design controls for inter‑subject variability by having each participant serve as their own control, enhancing the ability to attribute changes to the supplement. Trap: Option B incorrectly assumes single‑blind suffices; double‑blind is required to avoid bias.

qs.q: Calculate the percent change in the supplement group’s mean working memory score from baseline to 12 weeks.
qs.x: Percent change = ((29.6‑28.4)/28.4)×100 ≈ 4.2%. Trap: Dividing the 1.2-point gain by the wrong value (for example the 12-week mean or an SD) or mixing in the processing-speed gain; the denominator must be the baseline mean of 28.4.

qs.q: Which conclusion would be an overinterpretation of this study's findings?
o: The improvement in working memory is clinically meaningful.
The supplement group showed a small increase in working memory score.
Randomization and blinding reduce, but do not eliminate, bias.
A sample of 120 adults aged 30–50 limits generalization to other age groups.
qs.x: The passage says the clinical relevance remains uncertain, so claiming a clinically meaningful improvement overstates the findings. The other statements are accurate. Trap: Option C may look like a hedge, but it is an accurate statement about trial methodology.

qs.q: Suppose the working memory difference between the supplement and placebo groups had p = 0.03. What does this p-value mean?
o: If the supplement had no true effect, a difference at least this large would occur about 3% of the time
There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
The supplement improves memory in 97% of people
The effect size of the supplement is 0.03 standard deviations
qs.x: A p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null is true, a response rate, or an effect size. Trap: Option B is the classic misinterpretation: p-values are conditional on the null hypothesis being true.

r: Values shown are for the supplement group (n = 60); the placebo group (n = 60) is not tabulated.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: A screening group in the Marchetti laboratory identified a compound that suppresses glutamate dehydrogenase activity in cell lysates. To learn how it acts, the group measured initial velocities of the purified enzyme at several α-ketoglutarate concentrations, with and without 40 µM compound. Assays were buffered at pH 7.4 and kept at 30 °C, and the enzyme concentration was held constant. The compound has no structural resemblance to α-ketoglutarate, and a preliminary docking study placed it in a hydrophobic pocket far from the catalytic residues. The researchers recorded velocities as µmol of product per minute and fit each data set to the Michaelis–Menten equation. They then compared the fitted constants with and without compound, expecting the pattern to reveal whether the compound binds the free enzyme, the enzyme–substrate complex, or both with equal affinity. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and solvent carrier alone had no effect on activity. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which pattern does Table 1 show?
o: The ratio of inhibited to control velocity is about the same at every [S]
The ratio falls steadily as [S] increases
The ratio of inhibited to control velocity rises steadily as [S] increases
The inhibited velocity exceeds the control velocity at the lowest [S]
qs.x: At each [S], v(inhibited)/v(control) = 1/2, so the compound lowers velocity by a constant factor. Trap: Expecting inhibition to weaken at high substrate, as with a competitor, rather than checking that the inhibited-to-control ratio stays at 0.5 in every row.

qs.q: Which experiment would best confirm that the compound does not compete with substrate for the active site?
o: Show that the compound's potency decreases as [S] increases
Show that raising [S] to very high levels does not restore the control Vmax
Show that Km increases linearly with compound concentration
Show that the compound's structure matches the substrate
qs.x: Failure of high [S] to overcome inhibition indicates the inhibitor does not simply compete for the substrate-binding site. Trap: Choosing the option that describes competitive behavior (potency falling as [S] rises), which is the opposite of the evidence that the compound does not compete.

qs.q: If the uninhibited Vmax is 200 µmol/min, what is the apparent Vmax with the compound?
qs.x: Vmax,app = Vmax/α = 200/2 = 100 µmol/min, as seen in the saturating-substrate rows. Trap: Choosing 198 µmol/min, as if the compound barely changed Vmax, or confusing Vmax with the 66.7 µmol/min velocity measured at a single substrate level.

qs.q: Which statement about pure noncompetitive inhibition is INCORRECT?
o: The apparent Km increases because the inhibitor competes with substrate
Lineweaver–Burk lines intersect on the x-axis
The inhibitor can bind both free enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex
qs.x: Pure noncompetitive inhibitors leave Km unchanged. Because binding occurs at a distinct site, the lines in a double-reciprocal plot share an x-intercept (−1/Km). Trap: Assuming every inhibitor raises Km because it 'competes' with substrate, which is true only for competitive inhibitors and not for pure noncompetitive ones.

qs.q: Which cellular regulatory phenomenon most closely resembles this inhibition pattern?
o: Product activation of the same enzyme by direct covalent change
Substrate-level competition by a structural analog
Irreversible inhibition by transition-state mimicry at the active site
Allosteric inhibition at a site distinct from the active site
qs.x: Binding at a distinct regulatory (allosteric) site that lowers catalytic capacity reproduces the noncompetitive pattern, as with feedback inhibition in metabolic pathways. Trap: Choosing competition by a structural analog because inhibition is involved, although this compound resembles no substrate and binds far from the active site.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers investigated the antimicrobial efficacy of a novel peptide, Peptidex, against *Escherichia coli* in vitro. The study employed a randomized, controlled design with four experimental groups: a negative control (no peptide), and three treatment groups receiving Peptidex at concentrations of 10 µM, 20 µM, and 40 µM. Bacterial growth was quantified after 24 hours by measuring optical density at 600 nm (OD600). The results, summarized in Table 1, show a dose‑dependent decrease in OD600 values. The 10 µM group exhibited a mean OD600 of 0.45 (SD 0.05), 20 µM yielded 0.30 (SD 0.04), and 40 µM produced 0.15 (SD 0.03). The negative control maintained a mean OD600 of 0.80 (SD 0.06). Statistical analysis revealed significant differences (p < 0.01) between each treatment group and the control; comparisons among the treatment groups were not reported. The authors concluded that Peptidex effectively inhibits bacterial growth in a concentration‑dependent manner and suggested further studies to assess its mechanism of action and potential synergy with existing antibiotics.

qs.q: Which sample had the lowest mean OD600 after 24 hours of exposure?
qs.x: Correct: Mean OD600 was 0.80 (control), 0.45 (10 µM), 0.30 (20 µM) and 0.15 (40 µM), so the 40 µM group had the lowest value. Why the others are wrong: A) the negative control had the highest OD600 (0.80). B) 10 µM gave 0.45, higher than 0.15. C) 20 µM gave 0.30, higher than 0.15. Trap: Option C (20 µM) is a distractor because it also shows a reduced OD600 but not the lowest.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the control condition used in the study?
o: A group receiving the highest peptide concentration
A group receiving a known antibiotic as a positive control
A group receiving no peptide (negative control)
A group receiving a sub‑inhibitory peptide concentration
qs.x: The study’s control group received no peptide, serving as a negative control to compare baseline bacterial growth. Trap: Option B is a distractor; the study did not use a known antibiotic as a positive control.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in bacterial growth (OD600) for the 20 µM Peptidex group relative to the negative control?
qs.x: Correct: Percent reduction = (0.80 − 0.30)/0.80 × 100 = 62.5%. Why the others are wrong: A) 25% matches no calculation from the table. B) 37.5% is the OD600 remaining (0.30/0.80), not the percent reduction. C) 50% would correspond to a fall from 0.80 to 0.40, not 0.30. Trap: Reporting the percent of OD600 remaining (37.5%) rather than the percent reduction.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage?
o: Peptidex reduces bacterial growth in a dose‑dependent manner.
The 40 µM group showed the greatest reduction in OD600.
Statistical analysis showed significant differences among the three Peptidex treatment groups.
The negative control maintained the highest OD600 value.
qs.x: Correct: C) The passage reports significance only between each treatment group and the control; comparisons among treatment groups are not reported. Why the others are wrong: A) OD600 falls from 0.45 to 0.30 to 0.15 as concentration rises; supported. B) 40 µM has the lowest OD600, 0.15; supported. D) The control OD600 of 0.80 is the highest; supported. Trap: Assuming significance against the control also means each dose differs significantly from the other doses; that comparison is not reported.

qs.q: Which of the following future research directions is most directly linked to the study’s conclusions?
o: Evaluating Peptidex’s effect on viral replication in cell culture.
Testing Peptidex’s synergistic activity with conventional antibiotics against resistant *E. coli* strains.
Assessing the environmental impact of Peptidex disposal in wastewater.
Determining the pharmacokinetics of Peptidex in a rodent model.
qs.x: The authors suggested further studies to assess Peptidex’s mechanism of action and potential synergy with existing antibiotics, making option B the most directly linked future direction. Trap: Option D is a distractor; while pharmacokinetics is important, it is not the immediate next step implied by the authors.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: A structural biology group at the Haddad institute is purifying a recombinant enzyme that contains a single surface-exposed histidine near its active site. To locate the residue's ionization constant, the group titrated the protein in a series of buffers while following the histidine imidazole ring by NMR, which reports the fraction of side chains in the protonated, positively charged form. Protein concentration, ionic strength, and temperature were kept constant across buffers, and each measurement was repeated twice. The group later planned to bind the protein to a cation-exchange column and needed to understand how pH controls the protein's net charge. The protonation data also guided a decision about which buffering species to use for storage, since a buffer is most effective within about one pH unit of its own pKa. The protein was greater than 98% pure and monomeric by size-exclusion chromatography. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: At which pH is the histidine approximately half-protonated?
qs.x: Half-protonation (about 50%) occurs at pH = pKa, which in Table 1 is pH 7. Trap: Picking a neighboring pH such as 6 or 8, where 90.9% or 9.1% is protonated, instead of the pH at which exactly half is protonated (pH = pKa = 7).

qs.q: Which design would best verify that the NMR signal reports histidine ionization and not a pH-dependent conformational change?
o: Repeat the titration with a different counterion only
Repeat the titration without the protein
Repeat the titration at twice the protein concentration
Repeat the titration with a variant in which the histidine is mutated to alanine
qs.x: Removing the titratable group should abolish the signal's pH dependence if it truly reports that residue. Trap: Choosing a control that only changes counterion, protein amount or removes protein (A, B, C), none of which can separate histidine ionization from a conformational change the way removing the histidine can.

qs.q: What is the ratio [protonated]:[deprotonated] at pH 6?
qs.x: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), so log([A⁻]/[HA]) = −1 and [HA]/[A⁻] = 10^1 = 10. Trap: Choosing 100:1 by treating the one-unit pH offset as a hundredfold ratio, or 1:1, which holds at pH = pKa (7) rather than at pH 6.

qs.q: Which statement about buffers and this titration is INCORRECT?
o: The histidine side chain is mostly neutral at pH well above its pKa
A buffer's pH is independent of its conjugate base to acid ratio
Protonated histidine carries a positive charge
Buffering capacity is greatest near the pKa
qs.x: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation shows pH depends directly on the base-to-acid ratio. Trap: Believing buffer pH is fixed by the buffer's identity alone and accepting that it is independent of the base-to-acid ratio, which Henderson-Hasselbalch contradicts.

qs.q: At physiological pH, why do histidine residues frequently serve as general acid–base catalysts in enzymes?
o: Its side chain is always fully protonated at pH 7.4
Its side chain forms disulfide bonds with other residues
Its side chain pKa is near physiological pH, so it can readily donate or accept a proton
Its side chain carries no ionizable group
qs.x: A side chain pKa near 6–7 means both protonated and deprotonated forms are populated near pH 7.4, ideal for proton transfer in catalysis (e.g., serine proteases). Trap: Assuming histidine is always fully protonated at pH 7.4 (A) because it is basic, which ignores that its side-chain pKa lies near neutral pH.
