passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers studied the effects of a novel cognitive training program on working memory performance in adults aged 25 to 45. The study recruited 120 participants who were randomly assigned to either a control group (n=60) that received no intervention or an experimental group (n=60) that completed a 12-week training regimen consisting of computer-based working memory tasks. Baseline assessments measured working memory capacity using a standardized digit span test. After the intervention period, post‑intervention assessments were conducted. The results, summarized in Table 1, indicate that the experimental group showed a larger improvement in mean digit span scores than the control group. Specifically, the control group’s mean score increased from 7.2 to 7.5, whereas the experimental group’s mean score rose from 7.3 to 9.1. The study also reported secondary outcomes such as reaction time and self‑reported stress levels, but these were not the primary focus. The authors concluded that the cognitive training program effectively enhances working memory capacity in the studied population. Future research should examine long‑term retention and potential transfer effects to daily functioning.

qs.q: Which group had the highest mean digit span after the intervention period?
o: Both groups had the same mean
qs.x: The experimental group’s mean digit span increased to 9.1, which is higher than the control group’s 7.5. Trap: Choosing 'Not enough information' because baselines are not in the table, although the post-intervention means for both groups are given.

qs.q: Which experimental design best controls for confounding variables in this study?
qs.x: Randomization of participants into control and experimental groups minimizes confounding variables. Trap: Choosing cohort study because participants were followed over time; only random assignment to groups balances unmeasured confounders.

qs.q: What is the percent improvement in mean digit span from the control to the experimental group?
qs.x: Percent improvement = (9.1‑7.5)/7.5 ≈ 21.3%. Rounded to the nearest whole number is 21%. Trap: Dividing the 1.6 difference by the experimental mean (9.1) gives about 18%, not 21%; the reference is the control mean of 7.5.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: The experimental group improved more than the control group.
The control group showed a modest improvement.
The experimental group’s mean increased from 7.3 to 9.1.
The experimental group showed no improvement.
qs.x: The data show a clear improvement in the experimental group; therefore, stating no improvement is incorrect. Trap: Selecting B because the control's rise is small, although a modest improvement (7.2 to 7.5) is supported; the unsupported claim is that the experimental group did not improve.

qs.q: What is the difference between the two groups in mean change in digit span (experimental change minus control change)?
qs.x: Correct: B) Experimental change = 9.1 - 7.3 = 1.8; control change = 7.5 - 7.2 = 0.3; difference = 1.8 - 0.3 = 1.5. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.3 is the control group's change alone. C) 1.6 compares post-intervention means (9.1 - 7.5) and ignores the slightly different baselines. D) 1.8 is the experimental group's change alone. Trap: Computing 9.1 - 7.5 = 1.6 compares post-intervention means only and ignores that the groups started at different baselines (7.3 versus 7.2).

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel cognitive enhancer on reaction time in healthy adults. In a double‑blind, randomized controlled trial, 120 participants were assigned to one of four groups: placebo, low dose (10 mg), medium dose (20 mg), or high dose (30 mg). Each participant completed a computerized simple reaction time task at baseline and after a 4‑week intervention. The mean reaction times (in seconds) and standard deviations for each group are presented in Table 1. The study aimed to determine whether increasing doses would produce a dose‑response improvement in reaction speed. Secondary outcomes included subjective alertness and adverse events. The researchers hypothesized that higher doses would yield faster reaction times without increasing side effects. Data were analyzed using ANOVA followed by post‑hoc comparisons. The results suggested a statistically significant linear trend across doses, with the high dose group showing the fastest reaction times and the fewest reported adverse events.

qs.q: What is the mean reaction time for participants receiving the medium dose of the cognitive enhancer?
qs.x: The table lists the mean reaction time for the medium dose group as 9.4 seconds. Trap: The placebo mean (12.5 s) is often mistaken for the medium dose.

qs.q: Which experimental design was employed in this study?
qs.x: The passage explicitly states the study was a double‑blind, randomized controlled trial. Trap: The mention of a 4‑week intervention may lead some to think it was a cohort study.

qs.q: What percent decrease in mean reaction time does the high dose group show relative to the placebo group?
qs.x: Percent decrease = (12.5 - 8.1) / 12.5 x 100 = 4.4 / 12.5 x 100 = 35.2%. Trap: Using the wrong baseline or subtracting from the wrong value yields lower percentages; the placebo mean is the reference.

qs.q: Which statement is false regarding the study’s findings?
o: Higher doses produced faster reaction times.
The high dose group had the lowest standard deviation.
The placebo group had the fastest reaction times.
The medium dose group had a lower mean reaction time than the low dose group.
qs.x: Correct: C) The placebo group had the slowest mean reaction time (12.5 s), not the fastest. Why the others are wrong: A) means fell from 12.5 to 10.8, 9.4 and 8.1 s as dose rose, so this is true. B) the high dose SD (0.8) is the lowest, so this is true. D) 9.4 s for medium is lower than 10.8 s for low, so this is true. Trap: Reading the placebo group as fastest because its mean (12.5) is the largest number, when a larger reaction time means slower responses.

qs.q: How do the study’s results illustrate the principle of a dose‑response relationship?
o: Higher doses produced larger side‑effect profiles.
Reaction time decreased linearly with increasing dose.
The placebo group showed the greatest improvement.
Standard deviations increased with higher doses.
qs.x: The data show a linear decrease in mean reaction time as dose increases, a classic dose‑response pattern. Trap: Some may focus on adverse events and assume side effects drive the relationship.

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: In the Nakamura laboratory, researchers measured dehydrogenase activity in a liver homogenate by following production of NADH, which absorbs light at 340 nm with a molar extinction coefficient of 6,220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, whereas NAD⁺ does not absorb appreciably at this wavelength. The homogenate was diluted 10-fold in assay buffer before use, and 1 mL reactions in a 1 cm cuvette contained saturating substrate and NAD⁺ at 25 °C. Absorbance at 340 nm was recorded every minute. A blank containing all components except substrate was run in parallel to correct for non-enzymatic changes. The initial linear region of the progress curve was used to calculate velocity. The researchers wished to report the activity of the undiluted homogenate and to compare it with a published value from a different laboratory. The spectrophotometer was zeroed against buffer, and all readings fell within the instrument's linear range. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What is the change in A340 of the sample between 0 and 2 minutes, according to Table 1?
qs.x: A(2 min) − A(0 min) = 0.299 − 0.05 = 0.249. Trap: Reporting the raw 2-minute reading (0.299, option A) without subtracting the 0.05 starting absorbance.

qs.q: Why is a blank lacking substrate included?
o: To detect absorbance changes that occur without the enzyme-catalyzed reaction
To ensure the enzyme is saturated
To increase the extinction coefficient of NADH
qs.x: The blank accounts for background drift (e.g., contaminating reductants, instrument drift) independent of the reaction under study. Trap: Thinking the blank ensures enzyme saturation; it only reports background absorbance drift in the absence of the substrate-dependent reaction.

qs.q: Using Beer–Lambert, what is the initial rate of NADH formation in the cuvette (µM/min), and what activity does the undiluted homogenate have (µM/min)?
o: 200 µM/min in the cuvette; 2000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
20 µM/min in the cuvette; 20 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
0.02 µM/min in the cuvette; 0.2 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
20 µM/min in the cuvette; 200 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
qs.x: Rate = (ΔA/min)/(ε·l) = 0.1244/6220 = 20 µM/min in the cuvette. Multiply by the 10-fold dilution to get 200 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate. Trap: Forgetting to multiply by the 10-fold dilution (option B gives 20 µM/min for both) or mis-scaling the values by a factor of 10 (option A).

qs.q: Which statement about this assay is INCORRECT?
o: Substrate must be saturating for the rate to approximate Vmax
The initial linear portion of the curve gives the most reliable velocity
Both NAD⁺ and NADH absorb strongly at 340 nm, so the signal reflects total coenzyme
NADH absorbs at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not
qs.x: Only the reduced coenzyme absorbs at 340 nm; that selective absorbance makes the assay possible. Trap: Believing NAD+ also absorbs strongly at 340 nm so the signal reflects total coenzyme; only NADH absorbs, which is what makes the assay possible.

qs.q: Which type of assay couples an enzyme of interest to NADH oxidation so that its activity can be monitored at 340 nm?
o: A gel assay using SDS-PAGE mobility
A coupled assay using lactate dehydrogenase to reduce pyruvate formed by pyruvate kinase
A radioactive assay using ³²P-labeled ATP
An immunoassay using antibodies against the enzyme
qs.x: Pyruvate kinase produces pyruvate; LDH then oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, causing a decrease in A340 proportional to pyruvate kinase activity. Trap: Choosing a gel, radioactive or antibody assay: none of these links the enzyme to NADH oxidation, so none gives a change in A340.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers investigated the influence of different monochromatic light wavelengths on the growth of the freshwater alga *Chlorella vulgaris*. Cultures were grown in identical photobioreactors under controlled temperature (25 °C) and CO₂ concentration (2 %). Five wavelengths (400 nm, 450 nm, 500 nm, 550 nm, 600 nm) were applied for 14 days, with a dark control. Growth was measured as the daily increase in cell density (×10⁶ cells/mL per day), photosynthetic efficiency (PE) via chlorophyll fluorescence, and final biomass concentration (g/L). The results suggested a peak in growth and PE at 450 nm, while 550 nm produced the lowest values. The study aimed to identify optimal illumination for maximizing algal productivity in biofuel production.

qs.q: Which wavelength produced the highest growth rate in the study?
qs.x: The table shows a growth rate of 1.9 × 10⁶ cells/mL per day at 450 nm, higher than all other wavelengths. Trap: Choosing 600 nm because orange-red light is often described as most effective for photosynthesis, although its growth rate (1.6) was below that at 450 nm (1.9).

qs.q: Which of the following would be the most appropriate control for this experiment?
o: A culture illuminated with 500 nm light for 7 days
A culture kept in complete darkness for 14 days
A culture illuminated with 550 nm light for 14 days
A culture illuminated with 400 nm light for 14 days
qs.x: A dark control establishes the baseline growth without light, allowing comparison of light-induced effects. Trap: Students may choose a light wavelength as control, but the study already tests multiple wavelengths; the only true baseline is darkness.

qs.q: What is the average growth rate across all five wavelengths?
qs.x: Correct: B) (1.5 + 1.9 + 1.2 + 0.9 + 1.6)/5 = 7.1/5 = 1.42 × 10⁶ cells/mL per day. Why the others are wrong: A) 1.32 is not the mean of the five rates. C) 1.48 is not the mean of the five rates. D) 1.56 is close to the 600 nm value (1.6) rather than the mean of all five. Trap: Estimating near the middle value (about 1.5) instead of summing all five rates (7.1) and dividing by 5.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding the study?
o: The experiment controlled for temperature and CO₂ concentration.
The highest photosynthetic efficiency was observed at 600 nm.
A dark control was included to assess baseline growth.
Growth rates were expressed as increases in cell density per day.
qs.x: Correct: B) The highest photosynthetic efficiency was 68% at 450 nm; 600 nm gave 60%, so the statement is false. Why the others are wrong: A) the passage states that temperature (25 °C) and CO₂ (2%) were controlled. C) the passage states that a dark control was included. D) the passage states that growth was measured as the daily increase in cell density. Trap: Assuming 600 nm had the highest efficiency because its growth (1.6) is the second highest; the table shows the highest PE (68%) at 450 nm.

qs.q: Which concept is most directly related to the study’s focus on maximizing algal productivity?
qs.x: The study manipulates light wavelength to optimize photosynthetic efficiency, which is a key component of the light-dependent reactions. Trap: Photoperiodism refers to day length, not wavelength; students may confuse the two.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Biochemists in the Petrov laboratory characterized lactate dehydrogenase purified from a bacterial expression system, focusing on its response to a candidate small-molecule inhibitor designed to resemble pyruvate. Reactions contained a fixed enzyme concentration in buffered solution at 25 °C, and initial velocities were measured at six pyruvate concentrations with and without 60 µM inhibitor. Product formation was followed spectrophotometrically for the first 60 seconds, a window in which less than 5% of substrate was consumed. Each velocity represents the mean of three independent reactions, and the standard error was below 4% of every mean. The team wished to determine whether the compound binds the free enzyme at the active site or instead binds elsewhere, and to estimate its dissociation constant for the enzyme–inhibitor complex before testing it in cultured cells. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and the buffer contained no metal chelators or reducing agents that could interfere with the assay. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, what is the initial velocity in the presence of inhibitor when [S] = 400 µM?
qs.x: Reading the inhibitor column at [S] = 400 µM gives 30 µmol/min; the control column value (40) is the uninhibited rate. Trap: Reading the no-inhibitor column (40 µmol/min) instead of the inhibitor column, which gives 30 µmol/min at 400 µM.

qs.q: Which additional experiment would best distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition by this compound?
o: Measure velocity at a single substrate concentration with several enzyme concentrations
Measure whether very high substrate concentrations restore the uninhibited maximal velocity
Repeat the assay at a lower temperature to see whether inhibition disappears
Measure product formation after 60 minutes rather than 60 seconds
qs.x: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so sufficiently high [S] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax regardless of [S]. Trap: Choosing several enzyme concentrations at one substrate level; this changes the rate but cannot show whether high [S] restores Vmax.

qs.q: Assuming simple competitive inhibition, what is the approximate Ki of the inhibitor?
qs.x: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). Here Km,app/Km = 2, so [I]/Ki = 1 and Ki = 60/1 = 60 µM. Trap: Multiplying [I] by the 2-fold Km shift (60 × 2 = 120 µM) instead of solving 2 = 1 + [I]/Ki, which gives Ki = 60 µM.

qs.q: Which statement about the data is NOT consistent with competitive inhibition?
o: The inhibition is weaker at higher substrate concentrations
The apparent Km is larger in the presence of the inhibitor
The inhibitor binds the free enzyme in preference to the enzyme–substrate complex
The maximal velocity extrapolated to infinite [S] is lower with the inhibitor
qs.x: Correct: D. In competitive inhibition Vmax is unchanged (60 µmol/min in both data sets); only the apparent Km rises (200 to 400 µM). Why the others are wrong: A) velocities converge as [S] rises (6.7/12 at 50 versus 48/53.3 at 1600). B) the apparent Km doubles. C) a competitive inhibitor binds free enzyme, not the enzyme–substrate complex. Trap: Expecting inhibition to be equally strong at all [S]; for a competitive inhibitor, substrate overcomes it and velocities converge at high [S].

qs.q: Many drugs, such as statins and methotrexate, act as competitive inhibitors. Which property of such drugs most directly explains why they are often structural analogs of the substrate?
o: They must bind covalently to the enzyme
They must occupy the same active site as the substrate
They must bind the enzyme–substrate complex only
They must lower the enzyme's turnover number at saturating substrate
qs.x: Competition requires binding to the same site; structural similarity to the substrate (or transition state) lets the drug fit the active site and compete reversibly. Trap: Assuming drugs must bind covalently; reversible competitive inhibitors bind the same active site noncovalently.

text: Researchers at Green Valley University investigated how varying light intensity influences the rate of photosynthesis in the common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris). The experiment employed a controlled growth chamber where plants were grown under identical temperature (25 °C), humidity (60 %), and CO₂ concentration (400 ppm). Light intensity was adjusted using calibrated LED panels and measured with a quantum sensor as photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD, µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹). After a 48‑hour acclimation period, oxygen evolution was recorded over a 10‑minute interval using a Clark-type electrode. The resulting data are summarized in Table 1. The researchers observed that photosynthetic rate increased with light intensity, with smaller gains at higher light, approaching an asymptote at the highest intensities. These findings suggest that light is a limiting factor for photosynthesis up to a threshold, beyond which other factors (e.g., enzyme activity) constrain the process. The study’s implications extend to optimizing greenhouse lighting and understanding plant responses to changing solar irradiance.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between light intensity and photosynthetic rate observed in the study?
o: A linear increase in photosynthetic rate across the whole range
Rate increased with light at a decreasing rate, approaching a plateau at the highest intensities
An exponential increase in photosynthetic rate with light intensity
An inverse relationship between light intensity and photosynthetic rate
qs.x: Correct: Increments per 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ are 17.5, 15.3, 12.5, and 5.4 nmol/min, so the rate keeps rising but each gain is smaller, flattening toward 63 nmol/min at 1000 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. Why the others are wrong: A) Equal steps in light did not give equal steps in rate (the last step was only 5.4). C) An exponential increase would show growing increments, but they shrink. D) The rate rose, not fell, with light. Trap: Calling the curve linear or exponential from the early rise while ignoring the flattening between 800 and 1000 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.

qs.q: If the researchers wanted to test whether increasing CO₂ concentration would further enhance photosynthetic rate at high light intensity, which of the following experimental designs would be most appropriate?
o: Keep CO₂ concentration constant and vary light intensity
Keep light intensity constant and vary CO₂ concentration
Vary both light intensity and CO₂ concentration simultaneously
Measure photosynthetic rate at only one CO₂ level
qs.x: To isolate the effect of CO₂, light intensity must be held constant while CO₂ is varied. Trap: Varying light and CO₂ together would confound their effects, so the CO₂ effect could not be isolated.

qs.q: What is the percent increase in photosynthetic rate when light intensity increases from 200 to 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹?
qs.x: Correct: C) (57.8 − 12.5)/12.5 × 100 = 362%. Why the others are wrong: A) 200% would require a rate of 37.5 at 800. B) 250% would require a rate of 43.8 at 800. D) 400% would require a rate of 62.5 at 800. Trap: Dividing the increase by the final rate (57.8) or reporting the ratio instead of the percent increase over the starting rate.

qs.q: Which variable was held constant to isolate the effect of light intensity?
qs.x: All environmental factors were held constant so that changes in photosynthetic rate could be attributed solely to light intensity. Trap: Choosing a single factor (such as CO₂ only) when the passage states temperature, humidity and CO₂ were all held constant.

qs.q: At high light the O2 evolution rate plateaus (57.8 to 63.2 nmol/min from 800 to 1000 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹) even though temperature and CO₂ are constant. Which process most plausibly limits the rate at saturation?
o: The capacity of the Calvin cycle (e.g., Rubisco activity and RuBP regeneration) to use ATP and NADPH
The number of photons reaching photosystem II
The absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a
qs.x: Correct: A) At saturating light the light reactions supply more ATP and NADPH than the Calvin cycle (Rubisco activity, RuBP regeneration, CO₂ diffusion) can use, so carbon-fixation capacity limits the rate. Why the others are wrong: B) more photons were delivered at higher light, so photon supply is not what limits the rate. C) water for photolysis is not limiting in a well-watered plant, and it would not explain a plateau at high light. D) the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a does not change with light intensity. Trap: Picking photon supply as the limit even though more photons are delivered at higher light; at saturation the bottleneck is the Calvin cycle's capacity to use ATP and NADPH, not light capture or water for photolysis.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers in the Nakamura laboratory studied three reversible reactions of early carbohydrate metabolism in extracts of rat liver. Each reaction was allowed to reach equilibrium in a sealed reaction vessel at 37 °C and pH 7.0, after which reactants and products were quantified by HPLC to give the equilibrium constant. In a second set of experiments, intact hepatocytes were rapidly freeze-clamped and the steady-state ratio of products to reactants, known as the mass-action ratio Q, was measured for the same reactions. Comparing Q with Keq indicates how far each reaction sits from equilibrium under physiological conditions, and therefore which steps are likely to be regulated. The investigators used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and expected values of ΔG°′ to be consistent with literature compilations. All reagents were of analytical grade, and each reaction vessel was degassed to avoid oxidation of sulfhydryl groups. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which reaction operates closest to equilibrium in hepatocytes?
o: Reaction A: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP
None; all three are far from equilibrium
qs.x: Q/Keq near 1 indicates near-equilibrium operation. Reaction C has Q closest to Keq, so it is the least likely to be a regulatory step. Trap: Picking the reaction with the largest Keq or the largest Q instead of the one where Q equals Keq.

qs.q: Which control best confirms that the measured Keq reflects true equilibrium rather than a slow approach?
o: Lower the temperature to slow the reaction before quantifying
Measure only product concentration at a single time point
Approach equilibrium from both the reactant side and the product side and obtain the same ratio
Double the enzyme concentration and observe a faster rate
qs.x: A true equilibrium ratio is independent of the direction of approach; a path-dependent ratio signals the system has not equilibrated. Trap: Believing a faster rate or a single measurement proves equilibrium, when only reaching the same ratio from both directions shows it.

qs.q: For reaction B (Keq = 1.93), what is ΔG°′ at 310 K, in kJ/mol?
qs.x: ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq = −(0.008314 × 310) × ln(1.93) = -1.7 kJ/mol (literature value -1.7 kJ/mol). Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign, gives the wrong values. Trap: Using log10 instead of the natural log, or dropping the minus sign, which gives -0.7 or +1.7 kJ/mol instead of -1.7.

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: Actual ΔG depends on Q as well as ΔG°′
A reaction with a negative ΔG°′ always proceeds rapidly in the cell
ΔG°′ is related to the equilibrium constant but not to the reaction rate
A reaction with positive ΔG°′ can proceed forward if Q is sufficiently small
qs.x: Thermodynamics specifies direction, not speed. Rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis. Trap: Assuming a negative standard free energy means a reaction is fast in the cell, confusing thermodynamics with kinetics.

qs.q: Which mechanism allows cells to drive reactions with large positive ΔG°′ forward?
o: Coupling them to a strongly exergonic step such as ATP hydrolysis
Removing the catalyst so the reaction is not rate-limited
Increasing the enzyme concentration to lower ΔG°′
Raising the temperature enough to make Keq equal 1
qs.x: Enzymes do not change ΔG°′. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol) or keeping Q very low makes the overall ΔG negative. Trap: Thinking an enzyme or higher temperature changes the standard free energy, when cells actually couple the reaction to a strongly exergonic step.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers studied the effects of a novel dietary supplement on resting metabolic rate (RMR) in healthy adults. The study recruited 90 participants, randomly assigned to three groups: Group A received the supplement, Group B received a placebo, and Group C received no intervention. After a 4‑week intervention period, RMR was measured using indirect calorimetry. The data are summarized in Table 1. The researchers reported that Group A had a mean RMR of 6.1 kcal/min (SD = 0.8, N = 30), Group B had a mean RMR of 5.2 kcal/min (SD = 0.9, N = 30), and Group C had a mean RMR of 4.9 kcal/min (SD = 0.7, N = 30). The authors concluded that the supplement increased RMR compared to placebo and no‑intervention controls.

qs.q: Which sample shows the greatest variability?
qs.x: Correct: B) Sample B has the largest SD (0.9) and also the largest coefficient of variation (0.9/5.2 = 17%, versus 13% for A and 14% for C). Why the others are wrong: A) Sample A has SD 0.8, less than B, though it has the highest mean. C) Sample C has the smallest SD (0.7). D) The SDs of 0.7 to 0.9 are not identical, and B is highest. Trap: Students often assume that the sample with the largest mean has the greatest variability.

qs.q: Which statistical test would best test whether the difference between Sample A and Sample B is significant?
qs.x: Correct: Groups A and B are different, independent groups of 30 participants, so their means are compared with an independent-samples t-test. Why the others are wrong: A) a one-sample t-test compares one mean with a fixed value. C) a paired t-test needs the same participants measured twice. D) chi-square tests compare categorical counts, not means. Trap: Choosing a paired t‑test assumes the same participants were measured twice, which is not the case.

qs.q: Calculate the Cohen’s d effect size for the difference between Sample A and Sample B.
qs.x: Pooled SD = √[(0.8² + 0.9²)/2] ≈ 0.851; mean difference = 0.9; Cohen’s d = 0.9/0.851 ≈ 1.06. Trap: Students often use the larger SD instead of the pooled SD, yielding an underestimate of the effect size.

qs.q: Which of the following is a common mistake when interpreting the results of this study?
o: Concluding the effect is clinically important from statistical significance alone, without considering effect size and variability
qs.x: A p-value does not indicate the practical size or importance of an effect; effect size, variability and clinical relevance must also be considered. Using a large sample, reporting means and calculating SDs are standard good practice. Trap: Treating a significant p-value as proof of a large, clinically meaningful effect.

qs.q: Which comparison best isolates the effect of the supplement itself from the effect of receiving a pill-like treatment?
o: Group C versus its own baseline
qs.x: Correct: A) Groups A and B differ only in receiving the supplement or the placebo, so A versus B isolates the supplement (6.1 versus 5.2 kcal/min). Why the others are wrong: B) Group C received nothing, so A versus C mixes the supplement with the effect of receiving any treatment. C) B versus C estimates the placebo effect only. D) No baseline values were reported for Group C. Trap: Comparing the supplement group with the no-intervention group, which mixes the supplement effect with any effect of simply receiving a treatment.

passages.title: Transmission of genetic information from the gene to the protein · passage
text: Cell biologists in the Kowalski laboratory asked whether a metabolic stressor alters transcription of IL6 in cultured hepatocytes. RNA was extracted from untreated and treated cells, treated with DNase, and reverse transcribed. Quantitative PCR was then performed with primers for IL6 and for a reference gene whose expression is assumed to be stable. Each reaction contained a fluorescent DNA-binding dye and was run in triplicate. Amplification efficiency was verified to be close to 100% for both primer pairs, meaning the amount of product doubles each cycle. The cycle threshold, Ct, is the cycle at which fluorescence crosses a fixed threshold; mean values are shown. The group planned to calculate relative expression using the comparative Ct method before deciding whether to examine the promoter region for regulatory elements. RNA integrity numbers exceeded 8.5 for every sample. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which condition shows greater starting amounts of IL6 transcript, based on Table 1?
o: The data cannot be compared without a standard curve
qs.x: A lower Ct means the threshold is reached earlier, indicating more starting template. With equal reference Ct, the condition with the lower target Ct has higher expression. Trap: Reading the larger Ct (untreated) as higher expression, or assuming equal reference Ct means equal IL6.

qs.q: Which control best rules out amplification of contaminating genomic DNA?
o: A reaction with double the template
A reaction run at a higher annealing temperature only
qs.x: If product appears without reverse transcriptase, it must come from DNA rather than from RNA-derived cDNA. Trap: Choosing more template or a higher annealing temperature, neither of which shows whether genomic DNA is being amplified.

qs.q: Using the ΔΔCt method with 100% efficiency, what is the fold change in IL6 in treated versus untreated cells?
qs.x: ΔCt(untreated) = 8; ΔCt(treated) = 5; ΔΔCt = -3. Fold change = 2^−(-3) = 8. Trap: Reporting the ΔΔCt of 3 as a 3-fold change instead of converting with 2^3 = 8, or flipping the sign to 0.125.

qs.q: Which statement about Ct values is INCORRECT?
o: The reference gene corrects for differences in input RNA
A higher Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
A lower Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
A difference of one Ct corresponds to a two-fold difference at 100% efficiency
qs.x: Ct and abundance are inversely related; more template reaches threshold sooner. Trap: Thinking a higher Ct means more template; Ct is the cycle needed to reach threshold, so higher Ct means less.

qs.q: If expression changes, which feature of the gene would most directly be examined for a transcription-factor response?
o: The anticodon of the matching tRNA
The poly-A tail of the mature mRNA only
The number of introns within the coding region only
Promoter and enhancer sequences upstream of the transcription start site
qs.x: Transcription-factor binding sites (promoter/enhancer elements) govern transcriptional initiation, linking the Ct data to the regulatory mechanism. Trap: Choosing tRNA anticodon, poly-A tail or intron count, which are not where transcription factors act.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers investigated the acute effect of a novel antihypertensive agent, Hypril, on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in a cohort of 20 adults with stage‑1 hypertension. Twenty participants were randomly assigned to receive either Hypril (n = 10) or a placebo (n = 10). Baseline SBP was recorded after a 5‑minute seated rest. Participants then received a single oral dose of the assigned treatment and SBP was reassessed at 30 minutes post‑dose. The investigators focused on the magnitude of SBP reduction, hypothesizing that Hypril would produce a clinically significant drop (≥ 10 mm Hg) compared with placebo. The study also monitored heart rate and reported no adverse events. The table lists the SBP changes of five Hypril-treated participants (H1-H5), highlighting individual variability.

qs.q: Which patient experienced the greatest percent reduction in systolic blood pressure after receiving Hypril?
qs.x: Percent reductions: H1 14/148 = 9.46%, H2 15/155 = 9.68%, H3 4/142 = 2.82%, H4 15/160 = 9.38%, H5 13/150 = 8.67%. H2 has the greatest percent reduction (H2 and H4 tie in absolute terms at 15 mm Hg). Trap: H4 is tempting because it ties H2 for the largest absolute drop (15 mm Hg), but its higher baseline (160) gives a smaller percent reduction.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes an appropriate control condition for this study?
o: A group receiving a higher dose of Hypril
A group receiving a different antihypertensive drug
qs.x: The study already uses a placebo group to compare against Hypril. A placebo provides a baseline to assess the drug’s effect while controlling for the placebo effect. Options A and B introduce additional variables, and option D lacks a comparison. Trap: Option D (no intervention) may seem plausible but does not control for the placebo effect.

qs.q: What is the mean reduction in SBP among the five Hypril patients listed in Table 1?
qs.x: Correct: The five changes sum to −61 mm Hg, so the mean is −61/5 = −12.2 mm Hg, a reduction of 12.2 mm Hg. Why the others are wrong: B) 13.0 mm Hg does not follow from the five listed changes. C) 13.6 mm Hg does not follow from the five listed changes. D) 14.4 mm Hg is close to the mean of the four larger drops (14.25), which ignores patient H3's 4 mm Hg change. Trap: Leaving out H3's small 4 mm Hg drop inflates the mean (the other four drops average about 14), tempting the larger options.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?
o: Hypril lowered SBP by at least 10 mm Hg in every listed patient
The average SBP reduction among the listed patients was greater than 10 mm Hg
Patient H3 had the smallest SBP reduction
At least one listed patient had a reduction of 15 mm Hg
qs.x: Correct: Patient H3 had a reduction of only 4 mm Hg, so not every listed patient dropped by at least 10 mm Hg. Why the others are wrong: B) the mean of the five listed reductions is 12.2 mm Hg, which exceeds 10. C) H3's 4 mm Hg drop is the smallest. D) H2 and H4 each dropped 15 mm Hg. Trap: Assuming that because the mean reduction exceeds 10 mm Hg, every listed patient must have dropped by at least 10 mm Hg.

qs.q: What is the range of the SBP reductions among the five listed Hypril patients?
qs.x: Correct: The reductions run from 4 mm Hg (H3) to 15 mm Hg (H2 and H4), so the range is 15 - 4 = 11 mm Hg. Why the others are wrong: A) 4 mm Hg is the smallest reduction, not the range. C) 15 mm Hg is the largest reduction, not the range. D) 18 mm Hg is the spread of the baseline SBP values (142 to 160), not of the reductions. Trap: Reporting the largest reduction (15 mm Hg) or the baseline spread (18 mm Hg) instead of the largest minus the smallest reduction.

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: In the Haddad laboratory, researchers measured dehydrogenase activity in a liver homogenate by following production of NADH, which absorbs light at 340 nm with a molar extinction coefficient of 6,220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, whereas NAD⁺ does not absorb appreciably at this wavelength. The homogenate was diluted 20-fold in assay buffer before use, and 1 mL reactions in a 1 cm cuvette contained saturating substrate and NAD⁺ at 25 °C. Absorbance at 340 nm was recorded every minute. A blank containing all components except substrate was run in parallel to correct for non-enzymatic changes. The initial linear region of the progress curve was used to calculate velocity. The researchers wished to report the activity of the undiluted homogenate and to compare it with a published value from a different laboratory. The spectrophotometer was zeroed against buffer, and all readings fell within the instrument's linear range. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What is the change in A340 of the sample between 0 and 2 minutes, according to Table 1?
qs.x: A(2 min) − A(0 min) = 0.299 − 0.05 = 0.249. Trap: Using the raw 2-minute reading (0.299), the 3-minute change (0.373) or the per-minute change (0.124) instead of A(2 min) minus A(0 min) = 0.249.

qs.q: Why is a blank lacking substrate included?
o: To ensure the enzyme is saturated
To increase the extinction coefficient of NADH
To detect absorbance changes that occur without the enzyme-catalyzed reaction
qs.x: The blank accounts for background drift (e.g., contaminating reductants, instrument drift) independent of the reaction under study. Trap: Thinking the blank saturates the enzyme, converts NAD⁺ to NADH or changes the extinction coefficient; its role is to reveal absorbance change without the reaction.

qs.q: Using Beer–Lambert, what is the initial rate of NADH formation in the cuvette (µM/min), and what activity does the undiluted homogenate have (µM/min)?
o: 0.02 µM/min in the cuvette; 0.4 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
20 µM/min in the cuvette; 20 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
400 µM/min in the cuvette; 8000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
20 µM/min in the cuvette; 400 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
qs.x: Rate = (ΔA/min)/(ε·l) = 0.1244/6220 = 20 µM/min in the cuvette. Multiply by the 20-fold dilution to get 400 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate. Trap: Skipping the 20-fold dilution factor (same value for cuvette and homogenate), or slipping by a power of ten when converting M to µM.

qs.q: Which statement about this assay is INCORRECT?
o: NADH absorbs at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not
Both NAD⁺ and NADH absorb strongly at 340 nm, so the signal reflects total coenzyme
The initial linear portion of the curve gives the most reliable velocity
Substrate must be saturating for the rate to approximate Vmax
qs.x: Only the reduced coenzyme absorbs at 340 nm; that selective absorbance makes the assay possible. Trap: Believing NAD⁺ also absorbs at 340 nm so the signal reflects total coenzyme; only NADH absorbs, so absorbance tracks NADH production.

qs.q: Which type of assay couples an enzyme of interest to NADH oxidation so that its activity can be monitored at 340 nm?
o: An immunoassay using antibodies against the enzyme
A radioactive assay using ³²P-labeled ATP
A gel assay using SDS-PAGE mobility
A coupled assay using lactate dehydrogenase to reduce pyruvate formed by pyruvate kinase
qs.x: Pyruvate kinase produces pyruvate; LDH then oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, causing a decrease in A340 proportional to pyruvate kinase activity. Trap: Choosing assays that do not link activity to NADH absorbance (immunoassay, gel mobility, radiolabel); only the coupled LDH assay changes A340.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel dietary supplement on resting metabolic rate (RMR) in healthy adults. Eighty participants were randomly assigned to either the supplement group (n = 40) or a placebo group (n = 40). RMR was measured using indirect calorimetry after an overnight fast. The supplement group received 500 mg of the active ingredient daily for 12 weeks, while the placebo group received an inert capsule. Table 1 summarizes the mean RMR (kcal/day) and standard deviation for each group at baseline and after the intervention. The researchers hypothesized that the supplement would increase RMR by at least 10% compared to placebo.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, what is the absolute increase in mean RMR for the supplement group after 12 weeks?
qs.x: Absolute increase = 1650 - 1500 = 150 kcal/day. Trap: Subtracting the placebo group's baseline (1650 − 1490 = 160 kcal/day, option B) instead of the supplement group's own baseline of 1500.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the study’s design?
qs.x: Participants were randomly assigned to supplement or placebo groups, and the outcome (RMR) was measured after a defined intervention period, which is the hallmark of a randomized controlled trial. Trap: Option D incorrectly labels the study as a cohort study, which would follow participants over time without random assignment.

qs.q: What is the percent increase in mean RMR for the supplement group after 12 weeks?
qs.x: Correct: B) (1650 − 1500)/1500 × 100 = 10.0% within the supplement group (net of the placebo change, 130/1500 ≈ 8.7%, short of the hypothesized 10%). Why the others are wrong: A) 9.1% divides the 150 kcal/day rise by the 12-week value (1650) instead of the baseline. C) 12.5% would require a rise of about 188 kcal/day. D) 15.0% would require a rise of 225 kcal/day. Trap: Dividing by the 12-week value (150/1650 = 9.1%) instead of the baseline is a common error; the baseline 1500 is the correct denominator.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: The supplement group's mean RMR increased by 150 kcal/day.
The placebo group’s mean RMR increased by 20 kcal/day.
The supplement group's SD increased from 200 to 210 kcal/day.
The study used a double‑blind design.
qs.x: Correct: D) The passage never mentions blinding, so a double-blind design cannot be inferred. Why the others are wrong: A) 1650 − 1500 = 150 kcal/day in Table 1. B) 1510 − 1490 = 20 kcal/day. C) Table 1 lists SDs of 200 at baseline and 210 at 12 weeks for the supplement group. Trap: Assuming a placebo-controlled trial must also be double-blind, although the passage never states who was blinded.

qs.q: What is the difference between the supplement group and the placebo group in mean change in RMR over 12 weeks?
qs.x: Correct: A. The supplement group changed by 1650 - 1500 = +150 kcal/day and the placebo group by 1510 - 1490 = +20 kcal/day, so the net difference is 150 - 20 = 130 kcal/day. Why the others are wrong: B) 150 is the supplement change alone and ignores the placebo change. C) 20 is the placebo change alone. D) 140 does not follow from the table (it would result from comparing 12-week values, 1650 - 1510). Trap: Reporting the supplement group change without subtracting the change seen with placebo.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Biochemists in the Kowalski laboratory characterized lactate dehydrogenase purified from a bacterial expression system, focusing on its response to a candidate small-molecule inhibitor designed to resemble pyruvate. Reactions contained a fixed enzyme concentration in buffered solution at 25 °C, and initial velocities were measured at six pyruvate concentrations with and without 60 µM inhibitor. Product formation was followed spectrophotometrically for the first 60 seconds, a window in which less than 5% of substrate was consumed. Each velocity represents the mean of three independent reactions, and the standard error was below 4% of every mean. The team wished to determine whether the compound binds the free enzyme at the active site or instead binds elsewhere, and to estimate its dissociation constant for the enzyme–inhibitor complex before testing it in cultured cells. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and the buffer contained no metal chelators or reducing agents that could interfere with the assay. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, what is the initial velocity in the presence of inhibitor when [S] = 100 µM?
qs.x: Reading the inhibitor column at [S] = 100 µM gives 60 µmol/min; the control column value (100) is the uninhibited rate. Trap: Reading the velocity from the wrong column (control versus inhibitor) or from a neighboring [S] row of Table 1.

qs.q: Which additional experiment would best distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition by this compound?
o: Measure whether very high substrate concentrations restore the uninhibited maximal velocity
Repeat the assay at a lower temperature to see whether inhibition disappears
Measure velocity at a single substrate concentration with several enzyme concentrations
Measure product formation after 60 minutes rather than 60 seconds
qs.x: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so sufficiently high [S] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax regardless of [S]. Trap: Choosing an experiment that does not vary substrate concentration, which is what distinguishes competitive from noncompetitive inhibition.

qs.q: Assuming simple competitive inhibition, what is the approximate Ki of the inhibitor?
qs.x: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). Here Km,app/Km = 3, so [I]/Ki = 2 and Ki = 60/2 = 30 µM. Trap: Using [I]/α or [I]·α instead of Ki = [I]/(α − 1), where α = Km,app/Km.

qs.q: Which statement about the data is NOT consistent with competitive inhibition?
o: The apparent Km is larger in the presence of the inhibitor
The inhibition is weaker at higher substrate concentrations
The inhibitor binds the free enzyme in preference to the enzyme–substrate complex
Vmax is lower in the presence of the inhibitor at saturating [S]
qs.x: Competitive inhibitors leave Vmax unchanged; the velocities converge as [S] rises. A reduced Vmax would indicate noncompetitive or uncompetitive behavior. Trap: Believing any inhibitor that slows the reaction must lower Vmax; a competitive inhibitor only raises apparent Km, so velocities converge toward the same Vmax at high substrate.

qs.q: Many drugs, such as statins and methotrexate, act as competitive inhibitors. Which property of such drugs most directly explains why they are often structural analogs of the substrate?
o: They must occupy the same active site as the substrate
They must bind the enzyme–substrate complex only
They must lower the enzyme's turnover number at saturating substrate
They must bind covalently to the enzyme
qs.x: Competition requires binding to the same site; structural similarity to the substrate (or transition state) lets the drug fit the active site and compete reversibly. Trap: Assuming a competitive inhibitor must bind covalently or only the enzyme–substrate complex; it competes with substrate for the active site.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers studied the impact of a novel dietary supplement on blood pressure among adults aged 40–60. Sixty participants were randomly assigned to either the supplement group (n = 30) or a placebo group (n = 30). After 12 weeks, systolic and diastolic blood pressure readings were recorded. The data showed that the supplement group had an average systolic pressure of 122 mm Hg (SD = 8) and a diastolic pressure of 78 mm Hg (SD = 6), whereas the placebo group averaged 128 mm Hg systolic (SD = 9) and 82 mm Hg diastolic (SD = 7). The researchers concluded that the supplement led to a modest but statistically significant reduction in both systolic and diastolic pressures. The study also collected data on heart rate, cholesterol, and adherence rates, but the primary outcome was blood pressure. The authors suggested that further research should examine long‑term effects and potential interactions with antihypertensive medications.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, which of the following best describes the mean systolic blood pressure difference between the supplement and placebo groups?
o: The supplement group had a higher mean systolic pressure.
The placebo group had a higher mean systolic pressure.
Both groups had identical mean systolic pressures.
The data are insufficient to determine the mean systolic pressure.
qs.x: The supplement group’s mean systolic pressure is 122 mm Hg, which is lower than the placebo group’s 128 mm Hg. Therefore, the placebo group had the higher mean. Trap: Choosing the supplement group as higher (option A) by reversing the direction; 122 mm Hg is lower than the placebo's 128 mm Hg.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the experimental design used in this study?
o: Observational cohort study with matched controls.
Randomized controlled trial with a placebo control.
Case‑control study comparing hypertensive and normotensive participants.
qs.x: Correct: B) The passage states random assignment to supplement or placebo, which defines a randomized controlled trial with a placebo control. Why the others are wrong: A) Participants were assigned by the researchers, not merely observed. C) The study measured blood pressure after 12 weeks of treatment, not dietary habits at one time. D) Groups were created by random assignment, not selected by hypertension status. Trap: Choosing the observational cohort design (option A) because participants were followed for 12 weeks; random assignment to supplement or placebo makes this a trial.

qs.q: Calculate the absolute mean difference in systolic blood pressure between the supplement and placebo groups.
qs.x: Absolute mean difference = 128 mm Hg (placebo) – 122 mm Hg (supplement) = 6 mm Hg. Trap: Choosing 8 mm Hg (option B), which is the supplement group's SD, not the difference in means; 128 - 122 = 6.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by Table 1 and the passage?
o: The supplement group’s diastolic pressure was lower than the placebo group’s.
The study demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in systolic pressure.
Heart rate was higher in the supplement group.
The authors recommend further research on long‑term effects.
qs.x: Correct: C) Heart rate was 72 bpm with the supplement and 74 bpm with placebo, so it was lower, not higher. Why the others are wrong: A) Diastolic pressure was 78 versus 82 mm Hg, so it was lower. B) The passage reports the authors concluded the systolic reduction was statistically significant. D) The authors suggested further research on long-term effects. Trap: Assuming heart rate rose with the supplement; the table shows 72 versus 74 bpm, so it was slightly lower.

qs.q: Using the systolic means and SDs (equal group sizes), what is the approximate standardized effect size (Cohen's d) of the supplement versus placebo?
qs.x: Correct: A) Pooled SD = sqrt((8² + 9²)/2) = sqrt(72.5) ≈ 8.5, so d = 6/8.5 ≈ 0.70. Why the others are wrong: B) 0.35 would result from dividing 6 by about 17, such as the sum of SDs. C) 1.40 would require a pooled SD of about 4.3. D) 0.07 would require a pooled SD of about 85. Trap: Dividing the 6 mm Hg difference by the sum of the SDs (17) rather than the pooled SD, which halves the effect size to about 0.35.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers in the Marchetti laboratory studied three reversible reactions of early carbohydrate metabolism in extracts of rat liver. Each reaction was allowed to reach equilibrium in a sealed reaction vessel at 37 °C and pH 7.0, after which reactants and products were quantified by HPLC to give the equilibrium constant. In a second set of experiments, intact hepatocytes were rapidly freeze-clamped and the steady-state ratio of products to reactants, known as the mass-action ratio Q, was measured for the same reactions. Comparing Q with Keq indicates how far each reaction sits from equilibrium under physiological conditions, and therefore which steps are likely to be regulated. The investigators used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and expected values of ΔG°′ to be consistent with literature compilations. All reagents were of analytical grade, and each reaction vessel was degassed to avoid oxidation of sulfhydryl groups. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which reaction operates closest to equilibrium in hepatocytes?
o: Reaction A: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP
None; all three are far from equilibrium
qs.x: Q/Keq near 1 indicates near-equilibrium operation. Reaction C has Q closest to Keq, so it is the least likely to be a regulatory step. Trap: Treating a large Q or large Keq as nearness to equilibrium; closeness depends on Q/Keq (0.5 for reaction C versus 100 for each of the others).

qs.q: Which control best confirms that the measured Keq reflects true equilibrium rather than a slow approach?
o: Measure only product concentration at a single time point
Approach equilibrium from both the reactant side and the product side and obtain the same ratio
Lower the temperature to slow the reaction before quantifying
Double the enzyme concentration and observe a faster rate
qs.x: A true equilibrium ratio is independent of the direction of approach; a path-dependent ratio signals the system has not equilibrated. Trap: Choosing the enzyme‑doubling control, which only shows faster catalysis; enzymes do not change Keq and a faster rate does not prove equilibrium was reached.

qs.q: For reaction A (Keq = 652), what is ΔG°′ at 310 K, in kJ/mol?
qs.x: ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq = −(0.008314 × 310) × ln(652) = -16.7 kJ/mol (literature value -16.7 kJ/mol). Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign, gives the wrong values. Trap: Using log10 instead of the natural log (giving −7.3 kJ/mol) or dropping the negative sign (giving +16.7 kJ/mol).

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: A reaction with positive ΔG°′ can proceed forward if Q is sufficiently small
ΔG°′ is related to the equilibrium constant but not to the reaction rate
A reaction with a negative ΔG°′ always proceeds rapidly in the cell
Actual ΔG depends on Q as well as ΔG°′
qs.x: Thermodynamics specifies direction, not speed. Rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis. Trap: Believing that a negative ΔG°′ means a fast reaction; ΔG°′ gives direction and extent, not rate.

qs.q: Which mechanism allows cells to drive reactions with large positive ΔG°′ forward?
o: Raising the temperature enough to make Keq equal 1
Increasing the enzyme concentration to lower ΔG°′
Coupling them to a strongly exergonic step such as ATP hydrolysis
Removing the catalyst so the reaction is not rate-limited
qs.x: Enzymes do not change ΔG°′. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol) or keeping Q very low makes the overall ΔG negative. Trap: Thinking an enzyme or a higher temperature can change ΔG°′ to make a reaction go; catalysts speed approach to equilibrium but do not alter ΔG°′.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of four different dietary supplements on exercise performance in healthy adults. One hundred twenty volunteers were randomly assigned to one of four groups (A-D) and received the supplement daily for eight weeks. Performance was measured by a 5‑kilometer time trial at baseline and after the intervention. The mean improvement in time (in minutes), standard deviation (SD) and n for each group are presented in Table 1. The study used a double‑blind, randomized controlled design to minimize bias. Compliance was monitored through weekly pill counts, and adverse events were recorded. The investigators hypothesized that Supplement B would produce the greatest improvement in performance due to its higher concentration of creatine monohydrate. Statistical analysis involved comparing mean changes between groups using one‑way ANOVA followed by post‑hoc Tukey tests. The authors reported a significant difference (p < 0.05) between groups B and C, but not between A and D. They concluded that Supplement B was most effective, though they acknowledged that the clinical relevance of a 1.6‑minute difference remains uncertain.

qs.q: Which supplement group showed the greatest improvement in the 5‑kilometer time trial performance?
qs.x: Table 1 now lists mean improvement in 5-km time; Supplement B had the largest mean improvement (2.8 min) versus A 1.5, C 1.2 and D 0.9. Trap: Option A is tempting as the first listed group, but its improvement (1.5 min) is smaller than B's.

qs.q: Which aspect of the study design best controls for placebo effect?
qs.x: A double‑blind design ensures neither participants nor investigators know who receives which supplement, thereby minimizing placebo and observer bias. Trap: Option A is a common distractor but randomization alone does not control for placebo effect.

qs.q: What is the approximate mean difference in time improvement between groups B and C?
qs.x: The text states a significant difference of 1.6 minutes between B and C, which matches option C. Trap: Choosing 1.2 minutes, which is Supplement C's own mean improvement, instead of the difference between B and C (2.8 - 1.2 = 1.6).

qs.q: Which of the following statements is supported by the reported p‑value?
o: The difference between B and C is clinically significant
The difference between B and C is statistically significant
There is no difference between any groups
qs.x: A p‑value < 0.05 indicates a statistically significant difference between B and C, but it does not imply clinical significance or causation. Trap: Option A incorrectly equates statistical significance with clinical relevance.

qs.q: Using the table, what is Cohen's d for the difference in mean improvement between groups B and C (pooled SD)?
qs.x: Correct: A) Pooled SD = sqrt((2.1^2 + 2.5^2)/2) = 2.31; d = (2.8 - 1.2)/2.31 = 0.69. Why the others are wrong: B) 0.76 divides by only Supplement B's SD (2.1). C) 0.64 divides by only Supplement C's SD (2.5). D) 1.60 is the raw difference in minutes, not a standardized effect size. Trap: Dividing the 1.6 minute difference by a single group's SD, or reporting the raw difference as the effect size, instead of dividing by the pooled SD.

passages.title: Transmission of genetic information from the gene to the protein · passage
text: Cell biologists in the Haddad laboratory asked whether a metabolic stressor alters transcription of SOD2 in cultured hepatocytes. RNA was extracted from untreated and treated cells, treated with DNase, and reverse transcribed. Quantitative PCR was then performed with primers for SOD2 and for a reference gene whose expression is assumed to be stable. Each reaction contained a fluorescent DNA-binding dye and was run in triplicate. Amplification efficiency was verified to be close to 100% for both primer pairs, meaning the amount of product doubles each cycle. The cycle threshold, Ct, is the cycle at which fluorescence crosses a fixed threshold; mean values are shown. The group planned to calculate relative expression using the comparative Ct method before deciding whether to examine the promoter region for regulatory elements. RNA integrity numbers exceeded 8.5 for every sample. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which condition shows greater starting amounts of SOD2 transcript, based on Table 1?
o: The data cannot be compared without a standard curve
qs.x: A lower Ct means the threshold is reached earlier, indicating more starting template. With equal reference Ct, the condition with the lower target Ct has higher expression. Trap: Concluding that the condition with the higher target Ct has more transcript, or that equal reference Ct means equal expression; a lower target Ct marks the condition with more starting template.

qs.q: Which control best rules out amplification of contaminating genomic DNA?
o: A reaction run at a higher annealing temperature only
A reaction with double the template
qs.x: If product appears without reverse transcriptase, it must come from DNA rather than from RNA-derived cDNA. Trap: Choosing a higher annealing temperature or extra template, which cannot show where the product came from; only a no-reverse-transcriptase reaction that still amplifies reveals genomic DNA.

qs.q: Using the ΔΔCt method with 100% efficiency, what is the fold change in SOD2 in treated versus untreated cells?
qs.x: ΔCt(untreated) = 8; ΔCt(treated) = 7; ΔΔCt = -1. Fold change = 2^−(-1) = 2. Trap: Reporting the Ct difference (1) as the fold change, or inverting the direction; with 100% efficiency fold change = 2^(-ΔΔCt) = 2^(1) = 2.

qs.q: Which statement about Ct values is INCORRECT?
o: A higher Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
A lower Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
A difference of one Ct corresponds to a two-fold difference at 100% efficiency
The reference gene corrects for differences in input RNA
qs.x: Ct and abundance are inversely related; more template reaches threshold sooner. Trap: Reading a higher Ct as more starting template; Ct is the cycle at which signal crosses threshold, so a higher Ct means less target, not more.

qs.q: If expression changes, which feature of the gene would most directly be examined for a transcription-factor response?
o: The number of introns within the coding region only
The poly-A tail of the mature mRNA only
Promoter and enhancer sequences upstream of the transcription start site
The anticodon of the matching tRNA
qs.x: Transcription-factor binding sites (promoter/enhancer elements) govern transcriptional initiation, linking the Ct data to the regulatory mechanism. Trap: Choosing intron number, the poly-A tail or the tRNA anticodon, which concern splicing, mRNA processing or translation rather than transcription-factor control of initiation.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers investigated how varying doses of caffeine influence reaction time in healthy adults. A randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled study was conducted with 120 participants aged 18–35. Participants were assigned to one of four groups: placebo, 50 mg caffeine, 100 mg caffeine, or 200 mg caffeine. After ingestion, a computerized simple reaction time task was administered, and mean response times were recorded. The study aimed to determine whether higher caffeine doses correlate with faster reaction times and to assess the dose‑response relationship. The findings are summarized in Table 1 below. The researchers noted that while all caffeine groups performed better than placebo, the improvement plateaued at 100 mg, suggesting a threshold effect. These results have implications for optimizing alertness in high‑stakes environments such as aviation and shift work.

qs.q: Which group exhibited the fastest mean reaction time?
qs.x: The table shows the mean reaction time for each group. The 200 mg caffeine group has the lowest mean (0.478 s), indicating the fastest reaction time among all groups. Trap: Reading the plateau at 100 mg as meaning 100 mg is fastest, although 200 mg is still marginally faster (0.478 versus 0.480 s).

qs.q: What type of experimental design was used in this study?
qs.x: The passage describes a randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled study, which is a randomized controlled trial (RCT). Trap: The mention of a placebo group might suggest a case‑control design, but the random assignment indicates an RCT.

qs.q: What percent improvement in mean reaction time does the 200 mg group have over placebo?
qs.x: Percent improvement = (0.520 − 0.478) / 0.520 × 100 = 0.042 / 0.520 × 100 ≈ 8.1%. Trap: Dividing by 0.478 gives 8.8%; the placebo mean is the reference value.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?
o: Caffeine reduces reaction time compared to placebo.
The 200 mg group shows a slightly faster mean than the 100 mg group.
The improvement from 100 mg to 200 mg was larger than the improvement from placebo to 50 mg.
The 50 mg group has the highest standard deviation among caffeine groups.
qs.x: From 100 mg to 200 mg the mean RT fell only 0.002 s (0.480 to 0.478), while placebo to 50 mg fell 0.025 s (0.520 to 0.495), so the statement is not supported; the effect plateaus. Trap: Assuming a linear dose-response when the data show a plateau beyond 100 mg.

qs.q: Which concept is most directly linked to the observed plateau in reaction time improvement?
qs.x: The plateau at 100 mg indicates that increasing the dose beyond this point does not produce further improvement, a classic feature of a dose‑response curve where the response levels off at higher concentrations. Trap: Option D might be tempting because the study uses a placebo, but the plateau is due to pharmacodynamics, not placebo.

NADH absorbs at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not
qs.x: Only the reduced coenzyme absorbs at 340 nm; that selective absorbance makes the assay possible. Trap: Missing the INCORRECT wording or assuming NAD⁺ also absorbs at 340 nm; only NADH absorbs, so the signal tracks NADH formation, not total coenzyme.

qs.q: Which type of assay couples an enzyme of interest to NADH oxidation so that its activity can be monitored at 340 nm?
o: An immunoassay using antibodies against the enzyme
A radioactive assay using ³²P-labeled ATP
A gel assay using SDS-PAGE mobility
A coupled assay using lactate dehydrogenase to reduce pyruvate formed by pyruvate kinase
qs.x: Pyruvate kinase produces pyruvate; LDH then oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, causing a decrease in A340 proportional to pyruvate kinase activity. Trap: Choosing an immunoassay or radioactive assay; these do not report on NADH oxidation by A340, which is the basis of coupled assays.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel dietary supplement on the recovery of muscle strength after resistance training in healthy adults. Twenty-eight participants were randomly assigned to either the supplement group (n=14) or a placebo group (n=14). Over a 6‑week period, all subjects performed a standardized resistance‑training regimen three times per week. Muscle strength was assessed by measuring one‑repetition maximum (1RM) for the bench press and leg press at baseline, week 3, and week 6. In addition, serum creatine kinase (CK) levels were measured at the same time points to evaluate muscle damage. In the supplement group, bench‑press 1RM rose 12% from baseline to week 6 (Table 1), a gain significantly greater than that of the placebo group (p = 0.02). CK levels rose modestly in both groups but were significantly lower in the supplement group at week 6 (p = 0.04). These findings suggest that the supplement may enhance strength gains and reduce exercise‑induced muscle damage.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the change in bench‑press 1RM for the supplement group from baseline to week 6?
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows bench‑press 1RM rising from 100 to 112 kg in the supplement group, a 12% increase at week 6. Why the others are wrong: A) 10% is the week 3 value. C) 15% does not appear in the data. D) 8% does not appear in the data. Trap: Option A reflects the 10% increase reported at week 3, not week 6.

qs.q: Which of the following is a strength of the study’s design?
qs.x: Randomized assignment reduces selection bias and is a key strength of the study. Trap: Option B is wrong because n = 28 is small; D is a weakness here since outcomes were measured objectively.

qs.q: What is the percent change in the supplement group's mean CK from baseline to week 6?
qs.x: Correct: A) (210 - 200) / 200 x 100 = +5%, a small rise. Why the others are wrong: B) 4.8% divides the 10 U/L change by the week 6 value (210) instead of baseline. C) 10% is the week 3 percent change in bench 1RM, not CK. D) The sign is wrong; CK rose, it did not fall. Trap: Dividing the 10 U/L change by the week 6 value (210) gives 4.8% (B), and reading CK as falling (D) confuses it with the group comparison at week 6.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage and Table 1?
o: Bench‑press 1RM in the supplement group was higher at week 6 than at baseline.
At week 6, CK was significantly lower in the supplement group than in the placebo group.
In the supplement group, CK at week 6 was lower than at baseline.
Participants were randomly assigned to supplement or placebo.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows supplement group CK of 200 U/L at baseline and 210 U/L at week 6, a slight rise, not a fall. Why the others are wrong: A) 1RM rose from 100 to 112 kg. B) the passage reports lower CK in the supplement group at week 6 (p = 0.04). D) the passage states random assignment to groups of 14. Trap: Reading "lower than placebo" as "lower than its own baseline".

qs.q: Elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) after resistance exercise is a standard indicator of which process?
o: Leakage of muscle cell contents into the blood due to muscle fiber damage
Increased glucose uptake by adipose tissue
Reduced bile flow from the liver
qs.x: Correct: CK is an intracellular muscle enzyme; when fibers are damaged it leaks into the blood, which is why the passage uses it to evaluate muscle damage. Why the others are wrong: B) adipose glucose uptake is not reflected by serum CK. C) reduced bile flow is assessed by liver markers such as bilirubin, not CK. D) thyroid hormone synthesis is assessed by TSH and thyroid hormones, not CK. Trap: Picking a metabolic or endocrine process because CK is "a blood enzyme", rather than recalling its muscle origin.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Biochemists in the Fitzgerald laboratory characterized dihydrofolate reductase purified from a bacterial expression system, focusing on its response to a candidate small-molecule inhibitor designed to resemble dihydrofolate. Reactions contained a fixed enzyme concentration in buffered solution at 25 °C, and initial velocities were measured at six dihydrofolate concentrations with and without 120 µM inhibitor. Product formation was followed spectrophotometrically for the first 60 seconds, a window in which less than 5% of substrate was consumed. Each velocity represents the mean of three independent reactions, and the standard error was below 4% of every mean. The team wished to determine whether the compound binds the free enzyme at the active site or instead binds elsewhere, and to estimate its dissociation constant for the enzyme–inhibitor complex before testing it in cultured cells. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and the buffer contained no metal chelators or reducing agents that could interfere with the assay. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, what is the initial velocity in the presence of inhibitor when [S] = 200 µM?
qs.x: Reading the inhibitor column at [S] = 200 µM gives 26.7 µmol/min; the control column value (53.3) is the uninhibited rate. Trap: Reading the uninhibited column (53.3) instead of the inhibitor column at 200 µM, or taking a value from another substrate row (16 or 40).

qs.q: Which additional experiment would best distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition by this compound?
o: Repeat the assay at a lower temperature to see whether inhibition disappears
Measure product formation after 60 minutes rather than 60 seconds
Measure velocity at a single substrate concentration with several enzyme concentrations
Measure whether very high substrate concentrations restore the uninhibited maximal velocity
qs.x: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so sufficiently high [S] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax regardless of [S]. Trap: Choosing a temperature or time-course experiment, which changes enzyme stability or extent of reaction but cannot show whether high substrate outcompetes the inhibitor.

qs.q: Assuming simple competitive inhibition, what is the approximate Ki of the inhibitor?
qs.x: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). Here Km,app/Km = 4, so [I]/Ki = 3 and Ki = 120/3 = 40 µM. Trap: Using Km,app/Km = 4 directly as [I]/Ki gives 120/4 = 30 µM (option A); since Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki), [I]/Ki is 3, not 4.

qs.q: Which statement about the data is NOT consistent with competitive inhibition?
o: The inhibition is weaker at higher substrate concentrations
The inhibitor binds the free enzyme in preference to the enzyme–substrate complex
Vmax is lower in the presence of the inhibitor at saturating [S]
The apparent Km is larger in the presence of the inhibitor
qs.x: Competitive inhibitors leave Vmax unchanged; the velocities converge as [S] rises. A reduced Vmax would indicate noncompetitive or uncompetitive behavior. Trap: Treating a lower Vmax as consistent with competition; a competitive inhibitor leaves Vmax unchanged and only raises the apparent Km.

qs.q: Many drugs, such as statins and methotrexate, act as competitive inhibitors. Which property of such drugs most directly explains why they are often structural analogs of the substrate?
o: They must occupy the same active site as the substrate
They must bind covalently to the enzyme
They must bind the enzyme–substrate complex only
They must lower the enzyme's turnover number at saturating substrate
qs.x: Competition requires binding to the same site; structural similarity to the substrate (or transition state) lets the drug fit the active site and compete reversibly. Trap: Assuming drugs must bind covalently or only the enzyme-substrate complex; competitive inhibitors reversibly compete for the same active site as the substrate.
