passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of a novel cognitive training program on working memory performance in adults aged 25–35. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) the training group received 30 minutes of adaptive working‑memory tasks daily for four weeks; (2) an active control group completed 30 minutes of non‑adaptive memory tasks; and (3) a passive control group received no intervention. Pre‑ and post‑tests measured reaction times (RT) on a digit‑span task. The study aimed to determine whether the adaptive training would produce measurable improvements in RT compared to controls and to assess the magnitude of any effect. Table 1 reports post‑test values. The researchers hypothesized that the training group would show a statistically significant reduction in mean RT relative to both control groups, with the active control exhibiting a modest improvement due to general task engagement. The study’s implications could inform educational and clinical interventions targeting working‑memory deficits.

qs.q: Which group exhibited the lowest mean reaction time after the intervention?
o: All groups had identical mean RTs
qs.x: The table shows the Training group’s mean RT (420 ms) is lower than both control groups (460 ms and 470 ms), indicating faster responses. Trap: Treating a higher reaction time as better performance; a lower RT means faster responses, and Training's 420 ms is the lowest mean.

qs.q: Which experimental design feature best controls for potential confounding variables in this study?
o: Using a passive control group only
Collecting data at a single time point
Blinding participants to the study purpose
qs.x: Random assignment distributes individual differences evenly across groups, reducing confounding. The passive control alone would not control for placebo or engagement effects, and single‑time‑point data would not allow pre‑post comparisons. Trap: Choosing participant blinding, which the passage never describes and which addresses only expectancy, not the pre-existing differences that random assignment balances.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in mean RT for the Training group relative to the Passive Control group?
qs.x: Correct: A) (470 − 420)/470 × 100 = 50/470 × 100 ≈ 10.6%. Why the others are wrong: B) 4.3% (20/470) does not match the 50 ms difference. C) 11.9% divides the 50 ms difference by the Training mean (420) instead of the Passive Control reference. D) 2.1% (10/470) is the Active versus Passive Control difference. Trap: Dividing the 50 ms difference by the Training mean (420 ms), which gives 11.9%, instead of by the Passive Control reference (470 ms).

qs.q: Which group has the highest standard deviation in reaction time?
o: Both Active Control and Passive Control equally
qs.x: The table lists SDs of 35 ms (Training), 40 ms (Active Control), and 45 ms (Passive Control). The Passive Control group has the highest SD. Trap: Confusing variability with the mean or assuming the two control groups tie; the SDs are 35, 40 and 45 ms, so only the Passive Control has the highest.

qs.q: Which comparison in Table 1 best isolates the benefit of the adaptive nature of the training from the effect of simply doing 30 minutes of memory tasks daily?
o: Training group versus Active Control group
Training group versus Passive Control group
Active Control group versus Passive Control group
Passive Control group's SD versus Training group's SD
qs.x: Correct: Both groups do 30 minutes of memory tasks daily, differing mainly in whether the tasks are adaptive, so their difference (420 versus 460 ms) reflects adaptiveness. Why the others are wrong: B) The passive group did no tasks, so the difference mixes adaptiveness with task engagement. C) Neither group received adaptive training, so this comparison says nothing about adaptiveness. D) SDs describe spread, not the effect of the program. Trap: Using the passive control as the comparison, which cannot separate adaptive training from general task engagement.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a new dietary supplement on blood glucose levels in adults with prediabetes. In a randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial, 120 participants were assigned to either the supplement group (n = 60) or placebo group (n = 60) for 12 weeks. Baseline fasting glucose levels were recorded, followed by weekly measurements. Table 1 shows the mean fasting glucose (mg/dL) and standard deviation at baseline, week 6, and week 12 for both groups. The supplement group showed a mean reduction of 12 mg/dL at week 12, whereas the placebo group had a mean reduction of 3 mg/dL. Secondary outcomes included HbA1c, weight, and adherence rates. Adherence was high (>90 %) in both groups. The authors concluded that the supplement improved glycemic control compared to placebo. The study’s strengths include randomization, blinding, and high adherence, but limitations such as short duration and the use of a single supplement dose were noted.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the change in mean fasting glucose for the supplement group from baseline to week 12?
qs.x: The supplement group’s mean fasting glucose decreased from 140 mg/dL at baseline to 128 mg/dL at week 12, a reduction of 12 mg/dL. Trap: Option B might be confused with the placebo group’s reduction, but the question specifically asks for the supplement group.

qs.q: Which statement best describes the study design?
qs.x: The passage explicitly states that participants were randomized to supplement or placebo, the study was double‑blind, and placebo‑controlled, indicating a randomized controlled trial. Trap: Option B might be tempting because the study followed participants over time, but it was not observational.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in mean fasting glucose for the supplement group from baseline to week 12?
qs.x: Percent reduction = (12 mg/dL ÷ 140 mg/dL) × 100 % ≈ 8.57 %, which rounds to 8.6 %. Trap: Option D might be chosen by mistakenly dividing 12 by 100 instead of 140.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage?
o: The supplement was tested at several different doses.
qs.x: Correct: D) The passage lists the use of a single supplement dose as a limitation. Why the others are wrong: A) Adherence was reported as above 90% in both groups. B) The trial is described as randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled. C) The intervention lasted 12 weeks. Trap: Assuming that a trial with a dose-free description tested several doses; the passage explicitly names the single dose as a limitation.

qs.q: What is the standard error of the mean fasting glucose in the supplement group at week 12 (SD 10 mg/dL, n = 60)?
qs.x: Correct: C) SE = SD/sqrt(n) = 10/sqrt(60) = 1.29 mg/dL. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.17 divides the SD by n (60) instead of sqrt(n). B) 0.91 uses n = 120, both groups combined. D) 10.0 is the SD itself, not the SE. Trap: Dividing the SD by n instead of the square root of n, or reporting the SD itself as the standard error.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis in spinach leaves. Using a controlled growth chamber, they exposed leaf discs to five different light intensities: 100, 200, 400, 600, and 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. After a 30‑minute acclimation period, the rate of CO₂ uptake was measured using a gas exchange system. The experiment was repeated three times for each intensity to account for biological variability. The results indicated a saturating relationship, with photosynthetic rates increasing rapidly at lower intensities, plateauing around 600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, and showing a slight decline at 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, likely due to photoinhibition. The researchers concluded that optimal light intensity for maximum CO₂ uptake in spinach occurs near 600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ under the conditions tested.

qs.q: Which light intensity resulted in the highest mean photosynthetic rate?
qs.x: The table shows the mean CO₂ uptake peaks at 52.7 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹ at 600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, which is higher than the values at 100, 200, 400, or 800 µmol photons. Trap: The answer might be misread as 800 µmol photons because the rate declines after 600 µmol photons, but the peak is still at 600 µmol photons.

qs.q: Which of the following would best serve as a control in this experiment?
o: Leaf discs exposed to 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹
Leaf discs exposed to 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹
Leaf discs kept in complete darkness
Leaf discs exposed to 600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹
qs.x: A control should represent the baseline condition; complete darkness provides a baseline where photosynthesis does not occur, allowing comparison with light‑treated samples. Trap: Some might choose 200 µmol photons because it is the lowest intensity tested, but it still induces photosynthesis, not a true baseline.

qs.q: What is the percent increase in mean CO₂ uptake from 200 to 400 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹?
qs.x: Percent increase = (45.9 − 28.4) / 28.4 × 100 = 17.5 / 28.4 × 100 ≈ 61.6%. Trap: Reporting the absolute difference (17.5) as a percent, or dividing by 45.9 (38.1%), gives the wrong answer.

qs.q: Which statement is FALSE regarding the experimental results?
o: Photosynthetic rate increases with light intensity up to a point.
The rate at 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ is higher than at 600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
Standard deviation values are relatively small, indicating low variability.
The gain in CO₂ uptake per unit of added light was smaller between 400 and 600 than between 200 and 400.
qs.x: Correct: B) The mean rate at 800 (49.3) is lower than at 600 (52.7), so B is false. Why the others are wrong: A) Uptake rises from 12.5 to 52.7 up to 600. C) SDs of 0.8 to 1.3 are small relative to the means. D) The gain was 6.8 between 400 and 600 versus 17.5 between 200 and 400. Trap: Reading the slight dip at 800 as noise and assuming the highest light gives the highest rate; the mean at 800 is lower than at 600.

qs.q: Which concept is most directly related to the observed plateau in photosynthetic rate at high light intensities?
qs.x: The plateau reflects the light saturation point where photosynthetic machinery is operating at maximum capacity and cannot increase further despite higher light. Trap: Stomatal conductance (B) affects CO₂ diffusion but does not explain the plateau in light‑dependent rate.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel antioxidant compound, Antiox-7, on oxidative stress markers in adult mice. In a randomized controlled trial, 120 mice were divided into three groups: a control group receiving a standard diet (n=40), a low-dose group receiving 10 mg/kg Antiox-7 (n=40), and a high-dose group receiving 30 mg/kg Antiox-7 (n=40). After 12 weeks, plasma malondialdehyde (MDA) levels were measured as an index of lipid peroxidation. The control group had a mean MDA of 12.5 µmol/L (SD 1.2). The low-dose group had a mean of 9.8 µmol/L (SD 1.0), and the high-dose group had a mean of 7.6 µmol/L (SD 0.9). The investigators reported a dose-dependent reduction in MDA, with a statistically significant difference between the control and high-dose groups (p<0.001). The study suggests Antiox-7 may mitigate oxidative damage in vivo.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the pattern of MDA levels observed in the study?
o: MDA levels increased with higher Antiox-7 doses.
MDA levels were unchanged across all groups.
MDA levels decreased in a dose-dependent manner.
Only the low-dose group showed a significant reduction in MDA.
qs.x: The data show a progressive decline in mean MDA from control (12.5) to low-dose (9.8) to high-dose (7.6), indicating a dose-dependent reduction. Trap: Assuming that because significance was reported only for control versus high dose, only one dose lowered MDA, instead of reading the stepwise fall in means (12.5, 9.8, 7.6).

qs.q: Which follow-up experiment would give the strongest evidence that upregulation of endogenous superoxide dismutase (SOD) is required for the reduction in MDA produced by Antiox-7?
o: Randomize mice to Antiox-7 or placebo and measure MDA only.
Repeat the three-group design and measure SOD activity alongside MDA, without any other manipulation.
Give each mouse Antiox-7 and then placebo in sequence and measure MDA only.
Add a group given Antiox-7 plus an SOD inhibitor and compare its MDA with the Antiox-7-only group.
qs.x: Correct: D. Blocking SOD while giving Antiox-7 tests necessity: if the MDA reduction disappears when SOD is inhibited, SOD is required. Why the others are wrong: A) Measuring MDA only cannot address any mechanism. B) Measuring SOD alongside MDA shows correlation, which does not show that SOD is required. C) A sequential design measuring MDA only has no mechanistic measurement and adds carryover problems. Trap: Choosing a correlational measurement when the question asks for evidence that a mechanism is required.

qs.q: Calculate the absolute difference in mean MDA between the control and high-dose groups.
qs.x: Correct: C) 12.5 - 7.6 = 4.9 µmol/L. Why the others are wrong: A) 2.2 is low dose minus high dose (9.8 - 7.6). B) 2.7 is control minus low dose (12.5 - 9.8). D) 12.5 is the control mean alone, not a difference. Trap: Subtracting the wrong pair of groups, such as control minus low dose (2.7) or low dose minus high dose (2.2), instead of control minus high dose.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: Mean MDA in the high-dose group was 4.9 µmol/L lower than in the control group.
Mean MDA fell at each step from control to low dose to high dose.
The SDs (0.9 to 1.2 µmol/L) were similar across the three groups.
Antiox-7 increased SOD enzyme activity in the treated mice.
qs.x: Correct: D. Only plasma MDA was measured; SOD activity was not reported, so no effect on SOD can be concluded. Why the others are wrong: A) 12.5 - 7.6 = 4.9, so A is supported. B) 12.5, 9.8, 7.6 fall at each step, so B is supported. C) SDs of 1.2, 1.0 and 0.9 are similar, so C is supported. Trap: Assuming that a proposed mechanism was measured because the passage discusses oxidative stress.

qs.q: Plasma MDA was measured as an index of lipid peroxidation. What does the lower MDA in the Antiox-7 groups most directly indicate?
o: Less oxidative damage to membrane lipids
More oxidative damage to membrane lipids
Higher production of reactive oxygen species
qs.x: Correct: A. MDA is a breakdown product of lipid peroxidation caused by reactive oxygen species, so lower MDA indicates less lipid oxidative damage. Why the others are wrong: B) Lower MDA means less, not more, peroxidation. C) More ROS would raise lipid peroxidation and MDA. D) Diet was not manipulated and MDA is not a measure of fat intake. Trap: Reading a lower marker value as a higher level of the process it measures.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel dietary supplement on blood pressure in adults aged 40–60. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 120 participants who were randomly assigned to either the supplement group (n = 60) or the placebo group (n = 60). Baseline systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were recorded for all participants. After 12 weeks of daily supplementation, SBP and DBP were measured again. The study also collected data on heart rate (HR) and body mass index (BMI) to assess potential confounding variables. The researchers reported the following summary statistics in Table 1.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, which statement most accurately reflects the effect of the supplement on systolic blood pressure after 12 weeks?
o: The supplement group had a larger mean reduction in SBP than the placebo group.
Both groups showed similar reductions in SBP, indicating no effect of the supplement.
The placebo group had a greater reduction in SBP than the supplement group.
The supplement group’s SBP increased relative to baseline.
qs.x: Correct: Supplement SBP fell 132.4 − 125.1 = 7.3 mmHg; placebo fell 131.8 − 129.3 = 2.5 mmHg, a 4.8 mmHg difference. Why the others are wrong: B) 7.3 versus 2.5 mmHg are not similar. C) The placebo reduction (2.5) was smaller than the supplement reduction (7.3). D) SBP fell from 132.4 to 125.1 mmHg in the supplement group. Trap: Assuming the placebo group’s smaller fall means no effect, or the reductions are similar; the difference is 4.8 mmHg.

qs.q: Which of the following design elements best supports attributing the observed SBP changes to the supplement?
o: Using a crossover design where participants receive both supplement and placebo.
Matching participants on baseline SBP before randomization.
Randomly assigning participants to supplement or placebo, balancing known and unknown confounders between groups.
Increasing the sample size to 200 participants.
qs.x: Correct: Random assignment balances known and unknown confounders between groups, so differences can be attributed to the supplement. Why the others are wrong: A) A crossover design was not used and would add carry-over concerns. B) Matching on one variable does not balance other confounders and is not what makes the comparison causal. D) A larger sample improves precision but not confounding control. Trap: Choosing sample size or matching because they sound rigorous; neither balances unknown confounders the way random assignment does.

qs.q: Calculate the mean difference in SBP change between the supplement and placebo groups.
qs.x: Change in supplement group = 132.4 – 125.1 = 7.3 mmHg. Change in placebo group = 131.8 – 129.3 = 2.5 mmHg. Mean difference = 7.3 – 2.5 = 4.8 mmHg. Trap: Option D uses the supplement group’s absolute change rather than the difference between groups.

qs.q: Which statement is NOT supported by Table 1?
o: The supplement lowers SBP by 7.3 mmHg in every patient.
Mean week 12 DBP was lower in the supplement group than in the placebo group.
The two groups had similar mean baseline SBP.
Mean SBP in the placebo group fell by about 2.5 mmHg.
qs.x: Correct: A) The 7.3 mmHg figure is a group mean; the table gives no individual responses. Why the others are wrong: B) 80.2 versus 83.7 mmHg; supported. C) 132.4 versus 131.8 mmHg; supported. D) 131.8 − 129.3 = 2.5 mmHg; supported. Trap: Reading the group mean change of 7.3 mmHg as the effect in every individual patient.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by this trial?
o: The supplement should be prescribed to all hypertensive patients regardless of baseline BP.
Over 12 weeks in adults aged 40–60, the supplement lowered mean SBP about 4.8 mmHg more than placebo, but long‑term outcomes and other populations were not tested.
The supplement should be avoided because it raises heart rate.
The supplement should be used only for patients with BMI above 30 kg/m^2.
qs.x: Correct: The SBP fall was 7.3 versus 2.5 mmHg (4.8 mmHg difference) in a 12-week trial of adults aged 40–60. Why the others are wrong: A) The trial did not enroll or analyze all hypertensive patients. C) Heart rate was similar (72.3 versus 71.9 bpm). D) Mean BMI was about 27.5 and no BMI subgroup was analyzed. Trap: Extending a short placebo-controlled result to all patients or to subgroups that were never analyzed.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of three different dietary supplements on the reduction of systolic blood pressure in adults with prehypertension. A randomized controlled trial enrolled 120 participants who were assigned to one of four groups: a control group receiving a placebo, and three treatment groups receiving either supplement A, supplement B, or supplement C. Baseline systolic blood pressure (SBP) was measured for all participants, and SBP was reassessed after four weeks of supplementation. The study found that supplement A lowered SBP by an average of 8.5 mmHg, supplement B by 5.2 mmHg, and supplement C by 3.1 mmHg. The placebo group showed a negligible change of 0.4 mmHg. The authors concluded that supplement A was the most effective in reducing SBP over the short term. The data are summarized in Table 1 below.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, which group experienced the greatest absolute reduction in systolic blood pressure after four weeks?
qs.x: Supplement A shows the largest absolute decrease of 8.5 mmHg, which is greater than the reductions seen in the other treatment groups and the negligible change in the control group. Trap: Many students may incorrectly choose the group with the highest baseline SBP, but the question asks for the greatest absolute reduction, not the highest starting value.

qs.q: Which element of the design best supports attributing SBP differences to the supplements rather than to participant characteristics?
o: Random assignment of participants to the four groups
The authors' conclusion that supplement A was most effective
qs.x: Correct: Random assignment tends to balance participant characteristics across groups, so differences in change are more plausibly caused by the supplements. Why the others are wrong: B) Percent change is a way of expressing the results; it does not control for group differences. C) The authors' conclusion is an interpretation of the data, not a design feature that controls bias. D) The study measured SBP at baseline and at 4 weeks; a single follow-up value would remove the within-person comparison. Trap: Treating the authors' conclusion or summary statistics as evidence of design quality.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in SBP for participants in the supplement B group?
qs.x: Percent reduction = (Change / Baseline) × 100 = (5.2 / 137) × 100 ≈ 3.8%. Trap: Students may confuse the percent reduction with the absolute change in mmHg.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: Supplement A produced the largest absolute reduction in SBP.
The placebo group experienced a clinically significant reduction in SBP.
Supplement B reduced SBP by approximately 3.8%.
Supplement C had the smallest effect on SBP among the treatments.
qs.x: The placebo group's change was only -0.4 mmHg, which is not clinically significant. The other statements accurately reflect the data. Trap: Students may incorrectly think any reduction is clinically significant, ignoring the magnitude.

qs.q: What was the placebo-adjusted reduction in SBP for supplement A (supplement A's change minus the placebo group's change)?
qs.x: Correct: Supplement A lowered SBP by 8.5 mmHg and the placebo group by 0.4 mmHg, so the placebo-adjusted reduction is 8.5 − 0.4 = 8.1 mmHg. Why the others are wrong: B) 8.5 mmHg is the unadjusted change in the supplement A group. C) 8.9 mmHg adds the placebo change instead of subtracting it. D) 6.3 is supplement A's percent change, not a change in mmHg. Trap: Reporting the raw change in the supplement group as the supplement effect without subtracting the placebo response.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis in spinach leaves. In a controlled laboratory setting, fresh leaf discs were exposed to four different photon flux densities: 200, 400, 600, and 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. The oxygen production rate was measured in nanomoles per minute (nmol/min) over a 10‑minute interval. The experiment was repeated three times for each intensity to ensure reproducibility. Results indicated a positive correlation between light intensity and oxygen production, with the highest rate observed at 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. The study aimed to quantify this relationship and assess whether the increase in light intensity led to a linear or plateaued response in photosynthetic output. The data were recorded in a table for subsequent analysis and graphing.

qs.q: Which light intensity produced the highest rate of oxygen production?
qs.x: Correct: D) The 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ row gives the highest rate, 45.2 nmol/min. Why the others are wrong: A) 200 gave the lowest rate (12.5 nmol/min). B) 400 gave 25.3 nmol/min, lower than 45.2. C) 600 gave 36.7 nmol/min, lower than 45.2. Trap: Assuming the highest rate is at 600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ because it appears in the middle of the range.

qs.q: In this experiment, which variable is the dependent variable?
qs.x: Correct: Oxygen production rate is the outcome measured in response to the manipulated light intensity. Why the others are wrong: A) light intensity is the independent variable that the researchers set. B) leaf species (spinach) is held constant. D) the 10‑minute interval is a fixed measurement condition. Trap: Naming the manipulated variable (light intensity) rather than the measured outcome.

qs.q: What is the percent increase in oxygen production from 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ to 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹?
qs.x: Correct: A) (45.2 - 12.5) / 12.5 x 100 = 261.6%. Why the others are wrong: B) 72.3% divides the 32.7 increase by the final value (45.2) instead of the starting value. C) 200.8% does not follow from the table values. D) 240.8% does not follow from the table values. Trap: Dividing the 32.7 increase by the final rate (45.2) gives 72.3% (B); the starting rate at 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ is the baseline for percent increase.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the table?
o: Oxygen production increased at every step from 200 to 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
The increase from 600 to 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ was smaller than the increase from 200 to 400 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
Oxygen production at 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ was more than 3.5 times that at 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
Oxygen production did not increase between 600 and 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
qs.x: Correct: Oxygen production rose from 36.7 to 45.2 nmol/min between 600 and 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, so there was no plateau. Why the others are wrong: A) values rise 12.5, 25.3, 36.7, 45.2. B) 8.5 is smaller than 12.8 nmol/min. C) 45.2/12.5 = 3.6. Trap: Taking the smaller increment from 600 to 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ as evidence of no increase.

qs.q: Which statement best links the observed data to the underlying biochemical process of photosynthesis?
o: Oxygen is released when CO₂ is reduced in the Calvin cycle.
Oxygen production is independent of photosynthetic electron transport.
The increase in oxygen production reflects enhanced electron transport in the light reactions, where water is split at photosystem II.
Oxygen is produced by Rubisco-catalyzed carboxylation of RuBP.
qs.x: O₂ comes from photolysis of water at photosystem II in the light-dependent reactions. Greater light intensity drives more electron transport, producing more O₂. The Calvin cycle fixes CO₂ and does not release O₂. Trap: Choosing A or D because the Calvin cycle is the better-known part of photosynthesis, although the O₂ released comes from water splitting in the light reactions.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Biochemists in the Nakamura laboratory characterized lactate dehydrogenase purified from a bacterial expression system, focusing on its response to a candidate small-molecule inhibitor designed to resemble pyruvate. Reactions contained a fixed enzyme concentration in buffered solution at 25 °C, and initial velocities were measured at six pyruvate concentrations with and without 120 µM inhibitor. Product formation was followed spectrophotometrically for the first 60 seconds, a window in which less than 5% of substrate was consumed. Each velocity represents the mean of three independent reactions, and the standard error was below 4% of every mean. The team wished to determine whether the compound binds the free enzyme at the active site or instead binds elsewhere, and to estimate its dissociation constant for the enzyme–inhibitor complex before testing it in cultured cells. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and the buffer contained no metal chelators or reducing agents that could interfere with the assay. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, what is the initial velocity in the presence of inhibitor when [S] = 100 µM?
qs.x: Reading the inhibitor column at [S] = 100 µM gives 22.9 µmol/min; the control column value (53.3) is the uninhibited rate. Trap: Reading the uninhibited column (53.3) instead of the inhibitor column at 100 µM, or taking an inhibitor value from another row (35.6 or 13.3).

qs.q: Which additional experiment would best distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition by this compound?
o: Measure whether very high substrate concentrations restore the uninhibited maximal velocity
Measure velocity at a single substrate concentration with several enzyme concentrations
Repeat the assay at a lower temperature to see whether inhibition disappears
Measure product formation after 60 minutes rather than 60 seconds
qs.x: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so sufficiently high [S] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax regardless of [S]. Trap: Choosing a time-course, temperature or enzyme-concentration experiment, which cannot show whether high substrate outcompetes the inhibitor.

qs.q: Assuming simple competitive inhibition, what is the approximate Ki of the inhibitor?
qs.x: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). Here Km,app/Km = 5, so [I]/Ki = 4 and Ki = 120/4 = 30 µM. Trap: Using Km,app/Km = 5 directly as the ratio, giving Ki = 120/5 = 24 µM (option B), which forgets that Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki).

qs.q: Which statement about the data is NOT consistent with competitive inhibition?
o: The inhibition is weaker at higher substrate concentrations
The inhibitor binds the free enzyme in preference to the enzyme–substrate complex
The apparent Km is larger in the presence of the inhibitor
Vmax is lower in the presence of the inhibitor at saturating [S]
qs.x: Competitive inhibitors leave Vmax unchanged; the velocities converge as [S] rises. A reduced Vmax would indicate noncompetitive or uncompetitive behavior. Trap: Treating a lower Vmax as consistent with competition; a competitive inhibitor leaves Vmax unchanged and only raises the apparent Km.

qs.q: Many drugs, such as statins and methotrexate, act as competitive inhibitors. Which property of such drugs most directly explains why they are often structural analogs of the substrate?
o: They must occupy the same active site as the substrate
They must lower the enzyme's turnover number at saturating substrate
They must bind covalently to the enzyme
They must bind the enzyme–substrate complex only
qs.x: Competition requires binding to the same site; structural similarity to the substrate (or transition state) lets the drug fit the active site and compete reversibly. Trap: Assuming drugs must bind covalently or only the enzyme-substrate complex; competitive inhibitors reversibly compete for the same active site as the substrate.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a brief mindfulness exercise on cognitive performance in 120 adults. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: (1) a 5‑minute guided meditation, (2) a 5‑minute breathing exercise, (3) a 5‑minute reading task, and (4) a no‑intervention control. After the intervention, all participants completed a computerized reaction‑time task measuring response latency to visual stimuli. The study aimed to determine whether brief mindfulness practices could improve attentional focus and reduce reaction times compared to control and other active conditions. The sample was balanced for age (mean 35.2 ± 9.8 years) and gender (58% female). The researchers hypothesized that the meditation group would show the greatest reduction in mean reaction time, followed by breathing, reading, and control. Data were analyzed using ANOVA and post‑hoc Tukey tests. The findings suggested a statistically significant difference between groups, with the meditation group exhibiting the fastest responses. These results support the notion that even short mindfulness interventions can enhance cognitive efficiency in everyday settings.

qs.q: Based on the table, which group exhibited the fastest mean reaction time?
qs.x: The table shows the lowest mean response time (0.412 s) for Group 1, the guided meditation group, indicating the fastest reactions. Trap: Students may mistakenly choose the control group because it has the highest mean, but the question asks for the fastest (lowest) time.

qs.q: Which experimental design best isolates the effect of the mindfulness intervention?
o: Randomized controlled trial with four parallel groups
Crossover design where each participant receives all interventions
Observational cohort study following participants over time
Case‑control study comparing meditators to non‑meditators
qs.x: A randomized controlled trial with parallel groups ensures each participant experiences only one intervention, controlling for confounding variables and allowing causal inference. Trap: Students may choose the crossover design (B) because it seems efficient, but it introduces carry‑over effects that could confound the results.

qs.q: Calculate the mean difference in reaction time between the meditation group and the control group.
qs.x: Mean difference = 0.498 s (control) – 0.412 s (meditation) = 0.086 s. Trap: Misreading a table value or using the wrong pair of groups, which gives 0.084 or 0.098 instead of 0.498 − 0.412 = 0.086.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the study’s findings?
o: The meditation group had the lowest mean reaction time.
All groups showed statistically significant differences from each other.
The breathing exercise group performed better than the reading task group.
The control group had the highest mean reaction time.
qs.x: The passage reports a significant overall difference between groups (ANOVA with Tukey tests), but it does not state that every pairwise comparison was significant; neighboring groups (e.g., 0.438 s vs 0.465 s with SDs of about 0.05-0.06) may not differ. Claiming all pairs differ is therefore unsupported. Trap: Students often assume that a significant ANOVA implies all pairwise differences are significant, which is a common misconception.

qs.q: Why is the 5-minute reading task a useful comparison group for the meditation group?
o: It matches the time and engagement of an activity without mindfulness, so a faster response after meditation is less likely due to simply doing any task
It ensures every participant receives all four interventions
It replaces the need for random assignment
It raises the standard deviation of reaction times in the meditation group
qs.x: Correct: A) An active comparison with similar duration but no mindfulness helps separate the effect of mindfulness from the effect of doing any short activity. Why the others are wrong: B) participants were assigned to one group each, not to all four. C) random assignment is separate and was still used. D) a comparison group does not change another group's variability. Trap: Assuming that the no-intervention control alone is enough, which cannot separate the effect of mindfulness from the effect of doing any task.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers in the Petrov laboratory studied three reversible reactions of early carbohydrate metabolism in extracts of rat liver. Each reaction was allowed to reach equilibrium in a sealed reaction vessel at 37 °C and pH 7.0, after which reactants and products were quantified by HPLC to give the equilibrium constant. In a second set of experiments, intact hepatocytes were rapidly freeze-clamped and the steady-state ratio of products to reactants, known as the mass-action ratio Q, was measured for the same reactions. Comparing Q with Keq indicates how far each reaction sits from equilibrium under physiological conditions, and therefore which steps are likely to be regulated. The investigators used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and expected values of ΔG°′ to be consistent with literature compilations. All reagents were of analytical grade, and each reaction vessel was degassed to avoid oxidation of sulfhydryl groups. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which reaction operates closest to equilibrium in hepatocytes?
o: Reaction A: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP
None; all three are far from equilibrium
qs.x: Q/Keq near 1 indicates near-equilibrium operation. Reaction C has Q closest to Keq, so it is the least likely to be a regulatory step. Trap: Comparing Q with Keq by absolute size rather than by the ratio Q/Keq; the reaction nearest equilibrium has Q/Keq closest to 1.

qs.q: Which control best confirms that the measured Keq reflects true equilibrium rather than a slow approach?
o: Approach equilibrium from both the reactant side and the product side and obtain the same ratio
Double the enzyme concentration and observe a faster rate
Lower the temperature to slow the reaction before quantifying
Measure only product concentration at a single time point
qs.x: A true equilibrium ratio is independent of the direction of approach; a path-dependent ratio signals the system has not equilibrated. Trap: Accepting a single time-point ratio as Keq without approaching equilibrium from both directions.

qs.q: For reaction B (Keq = 1.93), what is ΔG°′ at 310 K, in kJ/mol?
qs.x: ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq = −(0.008314 × 310) × ln(1.93) = -1.7 kJ/mol (literature value -1.7 kJ/mol). Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign, gives the wrong values. Trap: Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign in ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq.

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: A reaction with a negative ΔG°′ always proceeds rapidly in the cell
ΔG°′ is related to the equilibrium constant but not to the reaction rate
Actual ΔG depends on Q as well as ΔG°′
A reaction with positive ΔG°′ can proceed forward if Q is sufficiently small
qs.x: Thermodynamics specifies direction, not speed. Rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis. Trap: Assuming a negative standard free energy change means a reaction is fast in the cell, confusing thermodynamic favorability with reaction rate.

qs.q: Which mechanism allows cells to drive reactions with large positive ΔG°′ forward?
o: Raising the temperature enough to make Keq equal 1
Coupling them to a strongly exergonic step such as ATP hydrolysis
Removing the catalyst so the reaction is not rate-limited
Increasing the enzyme concentration to lower ΔG°′
qs.x: Enzymes do not change ΔG°′. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol) or keeping Q very low makes the overall ΔG negative. Trap: Thinking an enzyme or a higher temperature can change ΔG°′; only coupling to an exergonic step or a low Q makes the overall ΔG negative.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers at the Coastal Marine Institute investigated how different light wavelengths affect the growth and photosynthetic efficiency of the marine alga *Ulva lactuca*. Cultures were grown in identical nutrient media under controlled temperature and light intensity conditions, with only the wavelength of the light source varied. Four monochromatic LED lights (400 nm, 470 nm, 530 nm, and 600 nm) were used, each maintained at 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. Over a 14‑day period, daily samples were taken to measure chlorophyll‑a concentration (µg mL⁻¹), cell density (cells mL⁻¹), and photosynthetic efficiency (ΦPSII). The results indicated a peak in chlorophyll‑a and growth rate at 470 nm, while 530 nm produced the highest photosynthetic efficiency. The 600 nm light yielded the lowest values across all measured parameters, suggesting limited utilization by *U. lactuca* at orange (600 nm) wavelengths. These findings provide insight into optimizing light conditions for large‑scale algal cultivation and bio‑fuel production.

qs.q: Which wavelength produced the highest chlorophyll‑a concentration in *Ulva lactuca* cultures?
qs.x: The table shows chlorophyll‑a concentrations of 1.8, 3.4, 2.9, and 0.9 µg/mL for 400, 470, 530, and 600 nm respectively; 470 nm is highest. Trap: Assuming the highest photosynthetic efficiency automatically indicates the highest chlorophyll‑a.

qs.q: Which of the following experimental controls would best isolate the effect of light wavelength on *Ulva lactuca* growth?
o: Varying the nutrient concentration while keeping light constant
Using a single light wavelength but varying temperature
Maintaining constant temperature and nutrient levels while changing only the wavelength
Changing the light intensity while keeping wavelength constant
qs.x: To attribute differences in growth to wavelength alone, all other variables (temperature, nutrients, light intensity) must be held constant; only wavelength is varied. Trap: Assuming that varying temperature is sufficient to control for wavelength effects.

qs.q: Calculate the average growth rate (cells/day) for the 470‑nm and 530‑nm light conditions.
qs.x: Average = (25,000 + 21,000) / 2 = 23,000 cells/day. Trap: Using only the 530 nm value (21,000) or only the 470 nm value (25,000) instead of averaging the two.

qs.q: Which statement is NOT supported by the data presented in the passage?
o: 470 nm light leads to the highest growth rate among the tested wavelengths.
600 nm light results in the lowest photosynthetic efficiency.
Chlorophyll‑a concentration is highest at 530 nm.
All wavelengths tested were delivered at the same light intensity.
qs.x: The table shows chlorophyll‑a is highest at 470 nm (3.4 µg/mL), not 530 nm (2.9 µg/mL). Trap: Assuming the highest photosynthetic efficiency correlates with highest chlorophyll‑a.

qs.q: Which of the following best links the study’s findings to a real‑world application?
o: Using 400 nm LEDs to grow *U. lactuca* for ornamental aquariums.
Optimizing blue‑green LED spectra to maximize bio‑fuel production from *U. lactuca*.
Developing 600 nm light sources for indoor vertical farms.
Implementing 470 nm lighting in freshwater algae bioreactors.
qs.x: 470 nm gave the highest growth rate (25,000 cells/day) and chlorophyll-a (3.4 µg/mL), so optimizing blue-green spectra centred near 470-530 nm is the best link to bio-fuel cultivation; 600 nm gave the poorest results. Trap: Choosing a wavelength that performed poorly (600 nm) for commercial use.

passages.title: Transmission of genetic information from the gene to the protein · passage
text: Cell biologists in the Kowalski laboratory asked whether a metabolic stressor alters transcription of HSP70 in cultured hepatocytes. RNA was extracted from untreated and treated cells, treated with DNase, and reverse transcribed. Quantitative PCR was then performed with primers for HSP70 and for a reference gene whose expression is assumed to be stable. Each reaction contained a fluorescent DNA-binding dye and was run in triplicate. Amplification efficiency was verified to be close to 100% for both primer pairs, meaning the amount of product doubles each cycle. The cycle threshold, Ct, is the cycle at which fluorescence crosses a fixed threshold; mean values are shown. The group planned to calculate relative expression using the comparative Ct method before deciding whether to examine the promoter region for regulatory elements. RNA integrity numbers exceeded 8.5 for every sample. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which condition shows greater starting amounts of HSP70 transcript, based on Table 1?
o: The data cannot be compared without a standard curve
qs.x: A lower Ct means the threshold is reached earlier, indicating more starting template. With equal reference Ct, the condition with the lower target Ct has higher expression. Trap: Choosing untreated cells because their Ct (25) is the larger number; a lower Ct (23) means more starting HSP70 transcript.

qs.q: Which control best rules out amplification of contaminating genomic DNA?
o: A reaction run at a higher annealing temperature only
A reaction with double the template
qs.x: If product appears without reverse transcriptase, it must come from DNA rather than from RNA-derived cDNA. Trap: Choosing a higher annealing temperature, which alters primer stringency but cannot show whether the signal came from genomic DNA.

qs.q: Using the ΔΔCt method with 100% efficiency, what is the fold change in HSP70 in treated versus untreated cells?
qs.x: ΔCt(untreated) = 8; ΔCt(treated) = 6; ΔΔCt = -2. Fold change = 2^−(-2) = 4. Trap: Choosing 0.25-fold by inverting the ratio; treated cells cross threshold two cycles earlier, so expression is 2² = 4-fold higher.

qs.q: Which statement about Ct values is INCORRECT?
o: A lower Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
A difference of one Ct corresponds to a two-fold difference at 100% efficiency
A higher Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
The reference gene corrects for differences in input RNA
qs.x: Ct and abundance are inversely related; more template reaches threshold sooner. Trap: Believing a higher Ct means more starting target because a larger number seems like a larger amount; Ct and abundance are inversely related.

qs.q: If expression changes, which feature of the gene would most directly be examined for a transcription-factor response?
o: The anticodon of the matching tRNA
The poly-A tail of the mature mRNA only
Promoter and enhancer sequences upstream of the transcription start site
The number of introns within the coding region only
qs.x: Transcription-factor binding sites (promoter/enhancer elements) govern transcriptional initiation, linking the Ct data to the regulatory mechanism. Trap: Choosing tRNA anticodons, introns or poly-A tails, which do not set transcription initiation by transcription factors.

passages.title: Structure and integrative functions of the main organ systems · passage
text: Researchers conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of a novel antihypertensive agent, Hypertenso, in reducing systolic blood pressure among adults with stage 1 hypertension. Two hundred and forty participants were enrolled and randomly assigned to either the Hypertenso group (n=120) or a placebo group (n=120). Baseline mean systolic blood pressure (SBP) was 145.2 mmHg (SD 10.5) in the Hypertenso group and 144.8 mmHg (SD 10.3) in the placebo group. After a 4‑week treatment period, the Hypertenso group’s mean SBP decreased to 130.4 mmHg (SD 9.8), while the placebo group’s mean SBP fell to 141.6 mmHg (SD 10.1). The mean change in SBP was −14.8 mmHg (SD 3.2) for Hypertenso and −3.2 mmHg (SD 3.5) for placebo. The study also recorded adverse events, with 5% of participants in the Hypertenso group reporting dizziness compared to 2% in placebo. These findings suggest Hypertenso produces a clinically meaningful reduction in systolic blood pressure over a short period, with a tolerable safety profile.

qs.q: Which group experienced a greater average reduction in systolic blood pressure after 4 weeks?
o: Both groups had the same reduction
qs.x: The mean change in systolic blood pressure was −14.8 mmHg for the Hypertenso group and −3.2 mmHg for placebo, indicating a greater reduction in the Hypertenso group. Trap: Students pick the placebo group by overlooking the sign, but placebo SBP fell only 3.2 mmHg versus 14.8 mmHg with Hypertenso.

qs.q: What best describes the study design used in this trial?
qs.x: Participants were randomly assigned to Hypertenso or placebo, which is the hallmark of a randomized controlled trial. Trap: Students may pick an observational cohort design because participants were followed over time, but random assignment to Hypertenso or placebo defines an RCT.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in mean systolic blood pressure for the Hypertenso group over the 4‑week period?
qs.x: Percent reduction = (145.2 − 130.4) / 145.2 × 100 ≈ 10.2%. Trap: Students report 14.8% by treating the absolute change in mmHg as a percentage, instead of dividing by the baseline of 145.2 mmHg.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the safety profile of Hypertenso?
o: 5% reported dizziness, which is higher than placebo
5% reported dizziness, which is lower than placebo
qs.x: The study reported dizziness in 5% of the Hypertenso group versus 2% in placebo, indicating a higher incidence in the treatment group. Trap: Students reverse the comparison, reading 5% versus 2% as lower for Hypertenso, when the treatment group had the higher dizziness rate.

qs.q: Dizziness occurred in 5% of the Hypertenso group and 2% of the placebo group. What is the approximate number needed to harm (NNH) for dizziness?
qs.x: Absolute risk increase = 5% − 2% = 3% (0.03). NNH = 1 / 0.03 ≈ 33. Trap: Using the raw 3% difference or the relative risk as the answer; NNH is the reciprocal of the absolute risk difference.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of caffeine on reaction time in a controlled laboratory setting. One hundred healthy adults were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a placebo (control) group, a low-dose caffeine group (50 mg), a medium-dose caffeine group (100 mg), and a high-dose caffeine group (200 mg). Each participant completed a computerized simple reaction time task 30 minutes after ingestion. The task required pressing a button as quickly as possible when a visual stimulus appeared on the screen. Mean reaction times (RT) and standard deviations (SD) were recorded for each group. The researchers hypothesized that moderate caffeine intake would improve reaction speed, whereas excessive intake might produce a plateau or even a decline due to overstimulation. The study also monitored heart rate and subjective alertness to assess potential side effects. Results indicated a dose-dependent improvement in RT up to 100 mg, after which the benefit plateaued. No significant differences were observed in heart rate or alertness scores between groups. These findings suggest that moderate caffeine consumption can enhance cognitive performance without adverse cardiovascular effects.

qs.q: Based on the data presented, which statement best describes the relationship between caffeine dose and reaction time?
o: Reaction time improves linearly with increasing caffeine dose.
Reaction time improves up to 100 mg, then plateaus.
Reaction time worsens at the highest caffeine dose.
There is no significant difference in reaction time across doses.
qs.x: The table shows mean RT decreasing from 350 ms (control) to 310 ms at both 100 mg and 200 mg, indicating improvement up to 100 mg and a plateau thereafter. Trap: Option A suggests a continuous linear improvement, which is contradicted by the plateau at 200 mg.

qs.q: If the researchers wanted to determine whether caffeine’s effect on reaction time is dose-dependent, which experimental design modification would be most appropriate?
o: Add a group receiving 150 mg of caffeine to create a finer dose gradient.
Replace the reaction time task with a memory recall task.
Increase the sample size to 200 participants per group.
Administer caffeine orally instead of intravenously.
qs.x: Adding a 150 mg group provides an intermediate dose, allowing the researchers to better characterize the dose-response curve and confirm the plateau hypothesis. Trap: Option C focuses on sample size but does not address dose-dependency directly.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in mean reaction time when comparing the control group to the medium-dose caffeine group?
qs.x: Percent reduction = (350 - 310)/350 × 100 = 40/350 × 100 ≈ 11.4%. Trap: Option C (10.3%) appears close but is not the exact percent reduction.

qs.q: Which of the following is a potential confounding variable that could bias the study’s findings?
o: Time of day when the test was administered.
The color of the laboratory walls.
The brand of the computer used for the task.
qs.x: Circadian rhythms influence alertness and reaction time; if not controlled, time of day could confound caffeine effects. Trap: Option B is irrelevant and distracts from the actual confounder.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the data in the table?
o: Increasing the dose from 100 mg to 200 mg gave no further reduction in mean reaction time.
The 200 mg dose slowed reaction time relative to 100 mg.
Caffeine reduced heart rate compared with placebo.
qs.x: Correct: Mean RT was 310 ms at both 100 mg and 200 mg, so the higher dose added no further speed benefit. Why the others are wrong: B) Both doses had the same mean RT. C) The passage says heart rate did not differ between groups. D) Memory was not measured. Trap: Assuming a higher dose must give a bigger effect, or generalizing a simple reaction-time result to memory, which was not measured.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Hartwell group investigated turnover of cyclin B, a regulatory protein that is rapidly degraded in proliferating cells. To measure stability without confounding new synthesis, cells were treated with cycloheximide, an inhibitor of translation elongation, and harvested at the times shown. Lysates were resolved by SDS-PAGE, transferred to a membrane, and probed with an antibody against cyclin B; band intensities were quantified and normalized to a loading control. Degradation of cyclin B was assumed to follow first-order kinetics. The researchers hoped to compare half-lives under normal and stressed conditions and to learn whether proteasome inhibition would stabilize the protein. Results from unstressed cells are shown; each value is the mean of three biological replicates, with errors below 5% of the mean. Equal total protein was loaded in every lane, as confirmed by the loading control. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What fraction of cyclin B remains 40 minutes after cycloheximide treatment?
qs.x: At 40 min, two half-lives have elapsed (100 → 50 → 25%). Trap: Choosing 50% by stopping after the first half-life; 40 min is two half-lives of 20 min, so 100% falls to 50% then 25%.

qs.q: Why is cycloheximide used in this experiment?
o: It accelerates proteasomal degradation of all proteins
It increases transcription of the gene
It labels the protein for detection by antibody
It blocks new synthesis so that the loss of existing protein can be followed
qs.x: Without blocking translation, newly synthesized protein would obscure the decay of the pre-existing pool. Trap: Thinking cycloheximide speeds degradation; it blocks translation so no new cyclin B is made, letting the decay of the existing pool be measured.

qs.q: If the decay continues to be first-order, what percentage of cyclin B remains after 100 minutes?
qs.x: 100 min = 5 half-lives of 20 min, so 100 × (1/2)^5 = 3.125%. Trap: Using the wrong number of half-lives: 4 half-lives gives 6.25% and 6 gives 1.562%, but 100 min / 20 min = 5 half-lives, giving 3.125%.

qs.q: Which statement about first-order decay is INCORRECT?
o: The half-life is independent of starting concentration
The rate of decay is proportional to the amount remaining
The half-life equals ln 2 divided by the rate constant
The half-life increases as the starting amount of protein increases
qs.x: In first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2/k and does not depend on starting concentration. Trap: Choosing a true statement about first-order decay; the half-life is constant (ln 2/k) and does not rise with starting protein amount, so D is the incorrect one.

qs.q: cyclin B turnover is typically controlled by which system?
o: Phosphorylation by glycolytic kinases that leads to secretion
Ubiquitination and degradation by the proteasome
Glycosylation in the Golgi apparatus that prevents degradation
qs.x: Polyubiquitin chains (K48-linked) mark proteins for proteasomal degradation; proteasome inhibitors such as MG132 stabilize short-lived regulatory proteins. Trap: Choosing lysosomal, Golgi or secretion mechanisms because they sound like protein fates; short-lived regulatory proteins such as cyclin B are ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of three novel cognitive enhancers on working memory performance in healthy adults. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group receiving a placebo, or one of three treatment groups receiving Enhancer A, Enhancer B, or Enhancer C. Each participant completed a 30‑minute working memory task, and the time (in milliseconds) taken to correctly retrieve each item was recorded. The mean response times and standard deviations for each group are presented in Table 1. The study aimed to determine whether any of the enhancers produced a statistically significant improvement over the placebo. The researchers also collected secondary measures such as subjective alertness and heart rate variability to assess potential side effects. All participants provided informed consent, and the protocol was approved by the institutional review board. The data were analyzed using ANOVA followed by post‑hoc Tukey tests to compare group means. The results suggested that Enhancer A reduced response times relative to placebo, whereas Enhancer B and C did not differ significantly from the control. The authors concluded that Enhancer A may have a modest cognitive benefit, but further research is needed to confirm these findings and explore long‑term effects.

qs.q: Which group had the lowest mean response time according to Table 1?
qs.x: The table shows that Enhancer A had a mean response time of 780 ms, which is lower than the other groups. Trap: Picking Enhancer C because 860 ms is the largest number, forgetting that a lower response time means faster performance.

qs.q: Which design element described in the passage best ensures that differences in response time between groups are not due to pre-existing differences among participants?
o: Collecting heart rate variability as a secondary measure
Use of ANOVA followed by post-hoc tests
qs.x: Correct: random assignment balances participant characteristics across groups. Why the others are wrong: B) Secondary measures describe side effects but do not equate groups. C) Statistical tests compare groups after the fact. D) Consent is ethical, not a control for differences. Trap: Choosing the post-hoc Tukey tests, which compare groups after the fact and cannot remove pre-existing differences.

qs.q: What is the absolute difference in mean response time between Enhancer A and the Control group?
qs.x: Control mean is 850 ms; Enhancer A mean is 780 ms. 850 – 780 = 70 ms. Trap: Choosing 80 ms, the gap between Enhancer C (860 ms) and Enhancer A (780 ms), instead of using the control as the reference.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: Enhancer A produced a faster mean response time than placebo.
Enhancer B produced a slower mean response time than placebo.
Enhancer C’s mean response time was higher than that of the control group.
The standard deviation for Enhancer A was lower than that for the control group.
qs.x: Enhancer B’s mean (840 ms) is actually slightly faster than the control (850 ms), so it did not produce a slower response time. Trap: Students often assume any non‑significant difference means the treatment was slower, but the raw mean shows the opposite.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Enhancer A reduced mean response time relative to placebo, whereas Enhancers B and C did not differ significantly from control.
All three enhancers significantly improved response time.
Enhancer A's benefit was shown to persist over the long term.
Enhancer C produced the fastest mean response time.
qs.x: Correct: the passage reports exactly this pattern and Table 1 gives 780 ms for Enhancer A versus 850 ms for control. Why the others are wrong: B) B and C did not differ significantly from control. C) Long-term effects were not studied. D) Enhancer C had the slowest mean (860 ms). Trap: Choosing the option that says all three enhancers significantly improved response time, when only Enhancer A was reported to.
