passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers in the Haddad laboratory studied three reversible reactions of early carbohydrate metabolism in extracts of rat liver. Each reaction was allowed to reach equilibrium in a sealed reaction vessel at 37 °C and pH 7.0, after which reactants and products were quantified by HPLC to give the equilibrium constant. In a second set of experiments, intact hepatocytes were rapidly freeze-clamped and the steady-state ratio of products to reactants, known as the mass-action ratio Q, was measured for the same reactions. Comparing Q with Keq indicates how far each reaction sits from equilibrium under physiological conditions, and therefore which steps are likely to be regulated. The investigators used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and expected values of ΔG°′ to be consistent with literature compilations. All reagents were of analytical grade, and each reaction vessel was degassed to avoid oxidation of sulfhydryl groups. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which reaction operates closest to equilibrium in hepatocytes?
o: None; all three are far from equilibrium
Reaction A: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP
qs.x: Q/Keq near 1 indicates near-equilibrium operation. Reaction B has Q closest to Keq, so it is the least likely to be a regulatory step. Trap: Picking the reaction with the largest Q or Keq instead of comparing Q with Keq for each reaction and choosing the ratio nearest 1.

qs.q: Which control best confirms that the measured Keq reflects true equilibrium rather than a slow approach?
o: Measure only product concentration at a single time point
Double the enzyme concentration and observe a faster rate
Lower the temperature to slow the reaction before quantifying
Approach equilibrium from both the reactant side and the product side and obtain the same ratio
qs.x: A true equilibrium ratio is independent of the direction of approach; a path-dependent ratio signals the system has not equilibrated. Trap: Believing a faster rate or a single measurement proves equilibrium, when only reaching the same ratio from both directions shows it.

qs.q: For reaction A (Keq = 652), what is ΔG°′ at 310 K, in kJ/mol?
qs.x: ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq = −(0.008314 × 310) × ln(652) = -16.7 kJ/mol (literature value -16.7 kJ/mol). Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign, gives the wrong values. Trap: Using log10 instead of the natural log, or dropping the minus sign, which gives -7.3 or +16.7 kJ/mol instead of -16.7.

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: A reaction with positive ΔG°′ can proceed forward if Q is sufficiently small
Actual ΔG depends on Q as well as ΔG°′
A reaction with a negative ΔG°′ always proceeds rapidly in the cell
ΔG°′ is related to the equilibrium constant but not to the reaction rate
qs.x: Thermodynamics specifies direction, not speed. Rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis. Trap: Assuming a negative standard free energy means a reaction is fast in the cell, confusing thermodynamics with kinetics.

qs.q: Which mechanism allows cells to drive reactions with large positive ΔG°′ forward?
o: Removing the catalyst so the reaction is not rate-limited
Increasing the enzyme concentration to lower ΔG°′
Raising the temperature enough to make Keq equal 1
Coupling them to a strongly exergonic step such as ATP hydrolysis
qs.x: Enzymes do not change ΔG°′. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol) or keeping Q very low makes the overall ΔG negative. Trap: Thinking an enzyme or higher temperature changes the standard free energy, when cells actually couple the reaction to a strongly exergonic step.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: A structural biology group at the Haddad institute is purifying a recombinant enzyme that contains a single surface-exposed histidine near its active site. To locate the residue's ionization constant, the group titrated the protein in a series of buffers while following the histidine imidazole ring by NMR, which reports the fraction of side chains in the protonated, positively charged form. Protein concentration, ionic strength, and temperature were kept constant across buffers, and each measurement was repeated twice. The group later planned to bind the protein to a cation-exchange column and needed to understand how pH controls the protein's net charge. The protonation data also guided a decision about which buffering species to use for storage, since a buffer is most effective within about one pH unit of its own pKa. The protein was greater than 98% pure and monomeric by size-exclusion chromatography. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: At which pH is the histidine approximately half-protonated?
qs.x: Half-protonation (about 50%) occurs at pH = pKa, which in Table 1 is pH 7. Trap: Choosing a pH where the histidine is nearly all protonated or nearly all deprotonated (99% or 1%) instead of the pH at 50% protonation, which equals the pKa of 7.

qs.q: Which design would best verify that the NMR signal reports histidine ionization and not a pH-dependent conformational change?
o: Repeat the titration with a variant in which the histidine is mutated to alanine
Repeat the titration without the protein
Repeat the titration at twice the protein concentration
Repeat the titration with a different counterion only
qs.x: Removing the titratable group should abolish the signal's pH dependence if it truly reports that residue. Trap: Choosing a repeat that leaves the histidine in place (different counterion, no protein, or double the concentration); only removing the titratable residue tests whether the signal reports its ionization.

qs.q: What is the ratio [protonated]:[deprotonated] at pH 6?
qs.x: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), so log([A⁻]/[HA]) = −1 and [HA]/[A⁻] = 10^1 = 10. Trap: Inverting the ratio; at pH 6, below the pKa of 7, the protonated form predominates, so the ratio is 10:1 and not 1:10.

qs.q: Which statement about buffers and this titration is INCORRECT?
o: The histidine side chain is mostly neutral at pH well above its pKa
A buffer's pH is independent of its conjugate base to acid ratio
Buffering capacity is greatest near the pKa
Protonated histidine carries a positive charge
qs.x: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation shows pH depends directly on the base-to-acid ratio. Trap: Believing a buffer's pH is fixed regardless of composition; the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation shows pH = pKa + log(base/acid), so the statement that pH is independent of the ratio is the incorrect one.

qs.q: At physiological pH, why do histidine residues frequently serve as general acid–base catalysts in enzymes?
o: Its side chain is always fully protonated at pH 7.4
Its side chain pKa is near physiological pH, so it can readily donate or accept a proton
Its side chain carries no ionizable group
Its side chain forms disulfide bonds with other residues
qs.x: A side chain pKa near 6–7 means both protonated and deprotonated forms are populated near pH 7.4, ideal for proton transfer in catalysis (e.g., serine proteases). Trap: Thinking histidine is always charged or forms disulfides; its imidazole pKa is near physiological pH, so both protonation states are populated and it can shuttle protons.

passages.title: Transmission of genetic information from the gene to the protein · passage
text: Cell biologists in the Svensson laboratory asked whether a metabolic stressor alters transcription of HSP70 in cultured hepatocytes. RNA was extracted from untreated and treated cells, treated with DNase, and reverse transcribed. Quantitative PCR was then performed with primers for HSP70 and for a reference gene whose expression is assumed to be stable. Each reaction contained a fluorescent DNA-binding dye and was run in triplicate. Amplification efficiency was verified to be close to 100% for both primer pairs, meaning the amount of product doubles each cycle. The cycle threshold, Ct, is the cycle at which fluorescence crosses a fixed threshold; mean values are shown. The group planned to calculate relative expression using the comparative Ct method before deciding whether to examine the promoter region for regulatory elements. RNA integrity numbers exceeded 8.5 for every sample. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which condition shows greater starting amounts of HSP70 transcript, based on Table 1?
o: The data cannot be compared without a standard curve
qs.x: A lower Ct means the threshold is reached earlier, indicating more starting template. With equal reference Ct, the condition with the lower target Ct has higher expression. Trap: Reading the higher Ct (untreated) as higher expression, or assuming equal reference Ct means equal HSP70.

qs.q: Which control best rules out amplification of contaminating genomic DNA?
o: A reaction run at a higher annealing temperature only
A reaction with double the template
qs.x: If product appears without reverse transcriptase, it must come from DNA rather than from RNA-derived cDNA. Trap: Choosing a no-primer control or a higher annealing temperature, neither of which shows whether genomic DNA is amplified.

qs.q: Using the ΔΔCt method with 100% efficiency, what is the fold change in HSP70 in treated versus untreated cells?
qs.x: ΔCt(untreated) = 7; ΔCt(treated) = 5; ΔΔCt = -2. Fold change = 2^−(-2) = 4. Trap: Reporting the ΔΔCt of 2 as a 2-fold change or flipping the sign to get 0.25-fold, instead of 2^2 = 4.

qs.q: Which statement about Ct values is INCORRECT?
o: A higher Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
A difference of one Ct corresponds to a two-fold difference at 100% efficiency
A lower Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
The reference gene corrects for differences in input RNA
qs.x: Ct and abundance are inversely related; more template reaches threshold sooner. Trap: Thinking a higher Ct means more template; Ct is the cycle needed to reach threshold, so higher Ct means less.

qs.q: If expression changes, which feature of the gene would most directly be examined for a transcription-factor response?
o: The number of introns within the coding region only
The poly-A tail of the mature mRNA only
The anticodon of the matching tRNA
Promoter and enhancer sequences upstream of the transcription start site
qs.x: Transcription-factor binding sites (promoter/enhancer elements) govern transcriptional initiation, linking the Ct data to the regulatory mechanism. Trap: Choosing intron count, poly-A tail or tRNA anticodon, which are not where transcription factors act.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Nakamura group compared two receptor proteins, A and B, that bind oxygen analog with different affinities. Purified protein was held at 1 nM, a concentration far below either dissociation constant, so that the free ligand concentration was approximately equal to the total added. Ligand was titrated over a wide range, and the fraction of protein with bound ligand was measured by fluorescence anisotropy after each addition reached equilibrium. Each binding curve was hyperbolic and showed no evidence of cooperativity. The researchers intend to use the receptor with the tighter binding as a biosensor, and they want to know what ligand concentration would be required to saturate it at 80% occupancy. All measurements were made at 25 °C in identical buffer. Protein stocks were centrifuged before use to remove aggregates, and ligand stocks were verified by absorbance. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: At [ligand] = 100 nM, what is the fraction of protein A bound?
qs.x: Fraction bound = [L]/(Kd + [L]) = 100/(20+100) = 0.83. The B column gives 0.5. Trap: Reading the protein B column (0.50 at 100 nM) or a different ligand row instead of protein A at 100 nM.

qs.q: Why was protein held far below the Kd?
o: So that ligand depletion by binding is negligible and free ligand ≈ total ligand
So that Kd equals the protein concentration
So that the protein is certain to be fully saturated
So that cooperativity can be detected
qs.x: If protein were comparable to Kd, binding would deplete free ligand and distort the fit to the simple hyperbola. Trap: Thinking the protein is kept low so that Kd equals the protein concentration, to guarantee saturation, or to detect cooperativity, rather than to avoid depleting free ligand.

qs.q: What ligand concentration is needed for 80% occupancy of the higher-affinity protein (Kd = 20 nM)?
qs.x: θ = L/(Kd+L) = 0.8 ⇒ L = 4Kd = 80 nM. Trap: Using Kd itself (20 nM, only 50% occupancy) or 2 × Kd (40 nM) instead of L = 4 × Kd for 80% occupancy.

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: Kd equals the ligand concentration at half-saturation
Protein A binds the ligand with higher affinity than protein B
A hyperbolic curve is consistent with noncooperative binding
A lower Kd means lower affinity
qs.x: Kd is inversely related to affinity: a smaller Kd means tighter binding. Trap: Reversing the relationship between Kd and affinity by thinking a smaller dissociation constant means weaker binding.

qs.q: Which protein behavior differs from these hyperbolic curves?
o: Binding of a single ligand to one site on a monomeric protein
Hemoglobin's sigmoidal oxygen binding due to cooperativity
qs.x: Hemoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively (Hill coefficient > 1), giving a sigmoidal curve, while myoglobin is hyperbolic like proteins A and B. Trap: Choosing myoglobin's hyperbolic curve, a single-site binding or a simple saturation curve, all of which match proteins A and B; only cooperative binding gives a sigmoidal curve.

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: In the Lindqvist laboratory, researchers measured dehydrogenase activity in a liver homogenate by following production of NADH, which absorbs light at 340 nm with a molar extinction coefficient of 6,220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, whereas NAD⁺ does not absorb appreciably at this wavelength. The homogenate was diluted 20-fold in assay buffer before use, and 1 mL reactions in a 1 cm cuvette contained saturating substrate and NAD⁺ at 25 °C. Absorbance at 340 nm was recorded every minute. A blank containing all components except substrate was run in parallel to correct for non-enzymatic changes. The initial linear region of the progress curve was used to calculate velocity. The researchers wished to report the activity of the undiluted homogenate and to compare it with a published value from a different laboratory. The spectrophotometer was zeroed against buffer, and all readings fell within the instrument's linear range. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What is the change in A340 of the sample between 0 and 2 minutes, according to Table 1?
qs.x: A(2 min) − A(0 min) = 0.174 − 0.05 = 0.124. Trap: Using the raw 2-minute reading (0.174), the 3-minute change (0.187) or the per-minute change (0.062) instead of A(2 min) minus A(0 min) = 0.124.

qs.q: Why is a blank lacking substrate included?
o: To detect absorbance changes that occur without the enzyme-catalyzed reaction
To increase the extinction coefficient of NADH
To ensure the enzyme is saturated
qs.x: The blank accounts for background drift (e.g., contaminating reductants, instrument drift) independent of the reaction under study. Trap: Thinking the blank saturates the enzyme, converts NAD⁺ to NADH or changes the extinction coefficient; its role is to reveal absorbance change without the reaction.

qs.q: Using Beer–Lambert, what is the initial rate of NADH formation in the cuvette (µM/min), and what activity does the undiluted homogenate have (µM/min)?
o: 10 µM/min in the cuvette; 10 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
0.01 µM/min in the cuvette; 0.2 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
10 µM/min in the cuvette; 200 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
200 µM/min in the cuvette; 4000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
qs.x: Rate = (ΔA/min)/(ε·l) = 0.0622/6220 = 10 µM/min in the cuvette. Multiply by the 20-fold dilution to get 200 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate. Trap: Skipping the 20-fold dilution factor (same value for cuvette and homogenate), or slipping by a power of ten when converting M to µM.

qs.q: Which statement about this assay is INCORRECT?
o: Substrate must be saturating for the rate to approximate Vmax
Both NAD⁺ and NADH absorb strongly at 340 nm, so the signal reflects total coenzyme
The initial linear portion of the curve gives the most reliable velocity
NADH absorbs at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not
qs.x: Only the reduced coenzyme absorbs at 340 nm; that selective absorbance makes the assay possible. Trap: Believing NAD⁺ also absorbs at 340 nm so the signal reflects total coenzyme; only NADH absorbs, so absorbance tracks NADH production.

qs.q: Which type of assay couples an enzyme of interest to NADH oxidation so that its activity can be monitored at 340 nm?
o: An immunoassay using antibodies against the enzyme
A gel assay using SDS-PAGE mobility
A radioactive assay using ³²P-labeled ATP
A coupled assay using lactate dehydrogenase to reduce pyruvate formed by pyruvate kinase
qs.x: Pyruvate kinase produces pyruvate; LDH then oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, causing a decrease in A340 proportional to pyruvate kinase activity. Trap: Choosing assays that do not link activity to NADH absorbance (immunoassay, gel mobility, radiolabel); only the coupled LDH assay changes A340.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Nakamura group investigated turnover of c-Myc, a regulatory protein that is rapidly degraded in proliferating cells. To measure stability without confounding new synthesis, cells were treated with cycloheximide, an inhibitor of translation elongation, and harvested at the times shown. Lysates were resolved by SDS-PAGE, transferred to a membrane, and probed with an antibody against c-Myc; band intensities were quantified and normalized to a loading control. Degradation of c-Myc was assumed to follow first-order kinetics. The researchers hoped to compare half-lives under normal and stressed conditions and to learn whether proteasome inhibition would stabilize the protein. Results from unstressed cells are shown; each value is the mean of three biological replicates, with errors below 5% of the mean. Equal total protein was loaded in every lane, as confirmed by the loading control. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What fraction of c-Myc remains 120 minutes after cycloheximide treatment?
qs.x: At 120 min, two half-lives have elapsed (100 → 50 → 25%). Trap: Counting one half-life (50%) or three (12.5%) instead of the two half-lives that have elapsed; with a 60-minute half-life, 75% would be the amount lost.

qs.q: Why is cycloheximide used in this experiment?
o: It accelerates proteasomal degradation of all proteins
It labels the protein for detection by antibody
It blocks new synthesis so that the loss of existing protein can be followed
It increases transcription of the gene
qs.x: Without blocking translation, newly synthesized protein would obscure the decay of the pre-existing pool. Trap: Thinking cycloheximide accelerates degradation or labels the protein, rather than blocking translation so the decline reflects decay of the existing pool only.

qs.q: If the decay continues to be first-order, what percentage of c-Myc remains after 240 minutes?
qs.x: 240 min = 4 half-lives of 60 min, so 100 × (1/2)^4 = 6.25%. Trap: Miscounting the half-lives (3 gives 12.5%, 5 gives 3.125%) or reporting the 93.75% lost instead of the 6.25% remaining.

qs.q: Which statement about first-order decay is INCORRECT?
o: The rate of decay is proportional to the amount remaining
The half-life equals ln 2 divided by the rate constant
The half-life increases as the starting amount of protein increases
The half-life is independent of starting concentration
qs.x: In first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2/k and does not depend on starting concentration. Trap: Believing a larger starting amount means a longer half-life; in first-order decay the half-life (ln 2 / k) is independent of the starting amount.

qs.q: c-Myc turnover is typically controlled by which system?
o: Ubiquitination and degradation by the proteasome
Glycosylation in the Golgi apparatus that prevents degradation
Phosphorylation by glycolytic kinases that leads to secretion
qs.x: Polyubiquitin chains (K48-linked) mark proteins for proteasomal degradation; proteasome inhibitors such as MG132 stabilize short-lived regulatory proteins. Trap: Choosing a glycosylation, phosphorylation or lysosomal option because it sounds like regulation, when short-lived regulators are tagged with ubiquitin for proteasomal degradation.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Biochemists in the Fitzgerald laboratory characterized malate dehydrogenase purified from a bacterial expression system, focusing on its response to a candidate small-molecule inhibitor designed to resemble oxaloacetate. Reactions contained a fixed enzyme concentration in buffered solution at 25 °C, and initial velocities were measured at six oxaloacetate concentrations with and without 60 µM inhibitor. Product formation was followed spectrophotometrically for the first 60 seconds, a window in which less than 5% of substrate was consumed. Each velocity represents the mean of three independent reactions, and the standard error was below 4% of every mean. The team wished to determine whether the compound binds the free enzyme at the active site or instead binds elsewhere, and to estimate its dissociation constant for the enzyme–inhibitor complex before testing it in cultured cells. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and the buffer contained no metal chelators or reducing agents that could interfere with the assay. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, what is the initial velocity in the presence of inhibitor when [S] = 40 µM?
qs.x: Reading the inhibitor column at [S] = 40 µM gives 60 µmol/min; the control column value (80) is the uninhibited rate. Trap: Reading the velocity from the wrong column (control versus inhibitor) or from a neighboring [S] row of Table 1.

qs.q: Which additional experiment would best distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition by this compound?
o: Measure whether very high substrate concentrations restore the uninhibited maximal velocity
Measure product formation after 60 minutes rather than 60 seconds
Measure velocity at a single substrate concentration with several enzyme concentrations
Repeat the assay at a lower temperature to see whether inhibition disappears
qs.x: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so sufficiently high [S] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax regardless of [S]. Trap: Choosing an experiment that does not vary substrate concentration, which is what distinguishes competitive from noncompetitive inhibition.

qs.q: Assuming simple competitive inhibition, what is the approximate Ki of the inhibitor?
qs.x: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). Here Km,app/Km = 2, so [I]/Ki = 1 and Ki = 60/1 = 60 µM. Trap: Using [I]/α or [I]·α instead of Ki = [I]/(α − 1), where α = Km,app/Km.

qs.q: Which statement about the data is NOT consistent with competitive inhibition?
o: The apparent Km is larger in the presence of the inhibitor
The inhibition is weaker at higher substrate concentrations
The inhibitor binds the free enzyme in preference to the enzyme–substrate complex
Vmax is lower in the presence of the inhibitor at saturating [S]
qs.x: Competitive inhibitors leave Vmax unchanged; the velocities converge as [S] rises. A reduced Vmax would indicate noncompetitive or uncompetitive behavior. Trap: Believing any inhibitor that slows the reaction must lower Vmax; a competitive inhibitor only raises apparent Km, so velocities converge toward the same Vmax at high substrate.

qs.q: Many drugs, such as statins and methotrexate, act as competitive inhibitors. Which property of such drugs most directly explains why they are often structural analogs of the substrate?
o: They must lower the enzyme's turnover number at saturating substrate
They must bind the enzyme–substrate complex only
They must occupy the same active site as the substrate
They must bind covalently to the enzyme
qs.x: Competition requires binding to the same site; structural similarity to the substrate (or transition state) lets the drug fit the active site and compete reversibly. Trap: Assuming a competitive inhibitor must bind covalently or only the enzyme–substrate complex; it competes with substrate for the active site.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: A screening group in the Petrov laboratory identified a compound that suppresses aldose reductase activity in cell lysates. To learn how it acts, the group measured initial velocities of the purified enzyme at several glucose concentrations, with and without 20 µM compound. Assays were buffered at pH 7.4 and kept at 30 °C, and the enzyme concentration was held constant. The compound has no structural resemblance to glucose, and a preliminary docking study placed it in a hydrophobic pocket far from the catalytic residues. The researchers recorded velocities as µmol of product per minute and fit each data set to the Michaelis–Menten equation. They then compared the fitted constants with and without compound, expecting the pattern to reveal whether the compound binds the free enzyme, the enzyme–substrate complex, or both with equal affinity. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and solvent carrier alone had no effect on activity. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which pattern does Table 1 show?
o: The ratio falls steadily as [S] increases
The ratio of inhibited to control velocity is about the same at every [S]
The inhibited velocity exceeds the control velocity at the lowest [S]
The ratio of inhibited to control velocity rises steadily as [S] increases
qs.x: At each [S], v(inhibited)/v(control) = 1/4, so the compound lowers velocity by a constant factor. Trap: Assuming inhibition weakens at high [S] (option D), as for a competitive inhibitor; the inhibited-to-control ratio stays at 0.25 at every [S].

qs.q: Which experiment would best confirm that the compound does not compete with substrate for the active site?
o: Show that raising [S] to very high levels does not restore the control Vmax
Show that Km increases linearly with compound concentration
Show that the compound's potency decreases as [S] increases
Show that the compound's structure matches the substrate
qs.x: Failure of high [S] to overcome inhibition indicates the inhibitor does not simply compete for the substrate-binding site. Trap: Choosing option B or C, which are signatures of competitive inhibition; the question asks for evidence against competition.

qs.q: If the uninhibited Vmax is 120 µmol/min, what is the apparent Vmax with the compound?
qs.x: Vmax,app = Vmax/α = 120/4 = 30 µmol/min, as seen in the saturating-substrate rows. Trap: Choosing 116 µmol/min (option C) as if Vmax were barely affected, as with a competitive inhibitor; saturating velocities fall to a fraction of control, so apparent Vmax is 30.

qs.q: Which statement about pure noncompetitive inhibition is INCORRECT?
o: The apparent Km increases because the inhibitor competes with substrate
The inhibitor can bind both free enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex
Lineweaver–Burk lines intersect on the x-axis
qs.x: Pure noncompetitive inhibitors leave Km unchanged. Because binding occurs at a distinct site, the lines in a double-reciprocal plot share an x-intercept (−1/Km). Trap: Assuming a noncompetitive inhibitor raises apparent Km (option A), which is the competitive pattern; pure noncompetitive inhibition leaves Km unchanged.

qs.q: Which cellular regulatory phenomenon most closely resembles this inhibition pattern?
o: Substrate-level competition by a structural analog
Irreversible inhibition by transition-state mimicry at the active site
Product activation of the same enzyme by direct covalent change
Allosteric inhibition at a site distinct from the active site
qs.x: Binding at a distinct regulatory (allosteric) site that lowers catalytic capacity reproduces the noncompetitive pattern, as with feedback inhibition in metabolic pathways. Trap: Choosing competition by a structural analog (option A), which would raise apparent Km; this compound resembles no substrate and leaves Km unchanged.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers in the Lindqvist laboratory studied three reversible reactions of early carbohydrate metabolism in extracts of rat liver. Each reaction was allowed to reach equilibrium in a sealed reaction vessel at 37 °C and pH 7.0, after which reactants and products were quantified by HPLC to give the equilibrium constant. In a second set of experiments, intact hepatocytes were rapidly freeze-clamped and the steady-state ratio of products to reactants, known as the mass-action ratio Q, was measured for the same reactions. Comparing Q with Keq indicates how far each reaction sits from equilibrium under physiological conditions, and therefore which steps are likely to be regulated. The investigators used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and expected values of ΔG°′ to be consistent with literature compilations. All reagents were of analytical grade, and each reaction vessel was degassed to avoid oxidation of sulfhydryl groups. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which reaction operates closest to equilibrium in hepatocytes?
o: Reaction A: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP
None; all three are far from equilibrium
qs.x: Q/Keq near 1 indicates near-equilibrium operation. Reaction A has Q closest to Keq, so it is the least likely to be a regulatory step. Trap: Choosing 'none' because Q and Keq are not identical; reaction A's Q is only 2‑fold from Keq, whereas the other two are 100‑fold below theirs.

qs.q: Which control best confirms that the measured Keq reflects true equilibrium rather than a slow approach?
o: Double the enzyme concentration and observe a faster rate
Measure only product concentration at a single time point
Approach equilibrium from both the reactant side and the product side and obtain the same ratio
Lower the temperature to slow the reaction before quantifying
qs.x: A true equilibrium ratio is independent of the direction of approach; a path-dependent ratio signals the system has not equilibrated. Trap: Choosing the enzyme‑doubling control, which only shows faster catalysis; enzymes do not change Keq and a faster rate does not prove equilibrium was reached.

qs.q: For reaction B (Keq = 1.93), what is ΔG°′ at 310 K, in kJ/mol?
qs.x: ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq = −(0.008314 × 310) × ln(1.93) = -1.7 kJ/mol (literature value -1.7 kJ/mol). Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign, gives the wrong values. Trap: Using log10 instead of the natural log (giving −0.7 kJ/mol) or reversing the sign (giving +1.7 kJ/mol).

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: ΔG°′ is related to the equilibrium constant but not to the reaction rate
A reaction with positive ΔG°′ can proceed forward if Q is sufficiently small
Actual ΔG depends on Q as well as ΔG°′
A reaction with a negative ΔG°′ always proceeds rapidly in the cell
qs.x: Thermodynamics specifies direction, not speed. Rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis. Trap: Believing that a negative ΔG°′ means a fast reaction; ΔG°′ gives direction and extent, not rate.

qs.q: Which mechanism allows cells to drive reactions with large positive ΔG°′ forward?
o: Increasing the enzyme concentration to lower ΔG°′
Coupling them to a strongly exergonic step such as ATP hydrolysis
Raising the temperature enough to make Keq equal 1
Removing the catalyst so the reaction is not rate-limited
qs.x: Enzymes do not change ΔG°′. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol) or keeping Q very low makes the overall ΔG negative. Trap: Thinking an enzyme or a higher temperature can change ΔG°′ to make a reaction go; catalysts speed approach to equilibrium but do not alter ΔG°′.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: A structural biology group at the Okonkwo institute is purifying a recombinant enzyme that contains a single surface-exposed histidine near its active site. To locate the residue's ionization constant, the group titrated the protein in a series of buffers while following the histidine imidazole ring by NMR, which reports the fraction of side chains in the protonated, positively charged form. Protein concentration, ionic strength, and temperature were kept constant across buffers, and each measurement was repeated twice. The group later planned to bind the protein to a cation-exchange column and needed to understand how pH controls the protein's net charge. The protonation data also guided a decision about which buffering species to use for storage, since a buffer is most effective within about one pH unit of its own pKa. The protein was greater than 98% pure and monomeric by size-exclusion chromatography. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: At which pH is the histidine approximately half-protonated?
qs.x: Half-protonation (about 50%) occurs at pH = pKa, which in Table 1 is pH 7. Trap: Choosing a pH at the end of the range, such as pH 9, where ionization is nearly complete; half-protonation occurs at pH = pKa, which is pH 7.

qs.q: Which design would best verify that the NMR signal reports histidine ionization and not a pH-dependent conformational change?
o: Repeat the titration without the protein
Repeat the titration with a variant in which the histidine is mutated to alanine
Repeat the titration with a different counterion only
Repeat the titration at twice the protein concentration
qs.x: Removing the titratable group should abolish the signal's pH dependence if it truly reports that residue. Trap: Doubling protein concentration or changing the counterion would not separate ionization from conformational change; only removing the titratable residue tests that.

qs.q: What is the ratio [protonated]:[deprotonated] at pH 6?
qs.x: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), so log([A⁻]/[HA]) = −1 and [HA]/[A⁻] = 10^1 = 10. Trap: Inverting the ratio to 1:10; one pH unit below the pKa the protonated form predominates, giving protonated:deprotonated = 10:1.

qs.q: Which statement about buffers and this titration is INCORRECT?
o: Buffering capacity is greatest near the pKa
The histidine side chain is mostly neutral at pH well above its pKa
Protonated histidine carries a positive charge
A buffer's pH is independent of its conjugate base to acid ratio
qs.x: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation shows pH depends directly on the base-to-acid ratio. Trap: Believing buffer pH is independent of the base-to-acid ratio; pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), so the ratio sets the pH.

qs.q: At physiological pH, why do histidine residues frequently serve as general acid–base catalysts in enzymes?
o: Its side chain carries no ionizable group
Its side chain forms disulfide bonds with other residues
Its side chain pKa is near physiological pH, so it can readily donate or accept a proton
Its side chain is always fully protonated at pH 7.4
qs.x: A side chain pKa near 6–7 means both protonated and deprotonated forms are populated near pH 7.4, ideal for proton transfer in catalysis (e.g., serine proteases). Trap: Choosing 'always fully protonated at pH 7.4'; with a pKa near 6 to 7 histidine is only partly protonated at pH 7.4, so both forms are present for proton transfer.

passages.title: Transmission of genetic information from the gene to the protein · passage
text: Cell biologists in the Fitzgerald laboratory asked whether a metabolic stressor alters transcription of CYP3A4 in cultured hepatocytes. RNA was extracted from untreated and treated cells, treated with DNase, and reverse transcribed. Quantitative PCR was then performed with primers for CYP3A4 and for a reference gene whose expression is assumed to be stable. Each reaction contained a fluorescent DNA-binding dye and was run in triplicate. Amplification efficiency was verified to be close to 100% for both primer pairs, meaning the amount of product doubles each cycle. The cycle threshold, Ct, is the cycle at which fluorescence crosses a fixed threshold; mean values are shown. The group planned to calculate relative expression using the comparative Ct method before deciding whether to examine the promoter region for regulatory elements. RNA integrity numbers exceeded 8.5 for every sample. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which condition shows greater starting amounts of CYP3A4 transcript, based on Table 1?
o: The data cannot be compared without a standard curve
qs.x: A lower Ct means the threshold is reached earlier, indicating more starting template. With equal reference Ct, the condition with the lower target Ct has higher expression. Trap: Concluding that the condition with the higher target Ct has more transcript, or that equal reference Ct means equal expression; a lower target Ct marks the condition with more starting template.

qs.q: Which control best rules out amplification of contaminating genomic DNA?
o: A reaction run at a higher annealing temperature only
A reaction with double the template
qs.x: If product appears without reverse transcriptase, it must come from DNA rather than from RNA-derived cDNA. Trap: Choosing a higher annealing temperature or extra template, which cannot show where the product came from; only a no-reverse-transcriptase reaction that still amplifies reveals genomic DNA.

qs.q: Using the ΔΔCt method with 100% efficiency, what is the fold change in CYP3A4 in treated versus untreated cells?
qs.x: ΔCt(untreated) = 6; ΔCt(treated) = 7; ΔΔCt = 1. Fold change = 2^−(1) = 0.5. Trap: Reporting the Ct difference (1) as the fold change, or inverting the direction; with 100% efficiency fold change = 2^(-ΔΔCt) = 2^(-1) = 0.5.

qs.q: Which statement about Ct values is INCORRECT?
o: A difference of one Ct corresponds to a two-fold difference at 100% efficiency
A higher Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
A lower Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
The reference gene corrects for differences in input RNA
qs.x: Ct and abundance are inversely related; more template reaches threshold sooner. Trap: Reading a higher Ct as more starting template; Ct is the cycle at which signal crosses threshold, so a higher Ct means less target, not more.

qs.q: If expression changes, which feature of the gene would most directly be examined for a transcription-factor response?
o: The anticodon of the matching tRNA
Promoter and enhancer sequences upstream of the transcription start site
The poly-A tail of the mature mRNA only
The number of introns within the coding region only
qs.x: Transcription-factor binding sites (promoter/enhancer elements) govern transcriptional initiation, linking the Ct data to the regulatory mechanism. Trap: Choosing intron number, the poly-A tail or the tRNA anticodon, which concern splicing, mRNA processing or translation rather than transcription-factor control of initiation.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Okonkwo group compared two receptor proteins, A and B, that bind oxygen analog with different affinities. Purified protein was held at 1 nM, a concentration far below either dissociation constant, so that the free ligand concentration was approximately equal to the total added. Ligand was titrated over a wide range, and the fraction of protein with bound ligand was measured by fluorescence anisotropy after each addition reached equilibrium. Each binding curve was hyperbolic and showed no evidence of cooperativity. The researchers intend to use the receptor with the tighter binding as a biosensor, and they want to know what ligand concentration would be required to saturate it at 80% occupancy. All measurements were made at 25 °C in identical buffer. Protein stocks were centrifuged before use to remove aggregates, and ligand stocks were verified by absorbance. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: At [ligand] = 100 nM, what is the fraction of protein A bound?
qs.x: Fraction bound = [L]/(Kd + [L]) = 100/(20+100) = 0.83. The B column gives 0.33. Trap: Reading the 200 nM row (0.91) or the protein B column (0.33) instead of the 100 nM row of the protein A column.

qs.q: Why was protein held far below the Kd?
o: So that Kd equals the protein concentration
So that cooperativity can be detected
So that ligand depletion by binding is negligible and free ligand ≈ total ligand
So that the protein is certain to be fully saturated
qs.x: If protein were comparable to Kd, binding would deplete free ligand and distort the fit to the simple hyperbola. Trap: Thinking the very low protein concentration is meant to saturate the protein or to make Kd equal the protein concentration, rather than to keep ligand depletion negligible.

qs.q: What ligand concentration is needed for 80% occupancy of the higher-affinity protein (Kd = 20 nM)?
qs.x: θ = L/(Kd+L) = 0.8 ⇒ L = 4Kd = 80 nM. Trap: Taking [L] equal to Kd (20 nM) or twice Kd as 80% occupancy, when 80% needs four times Kd (80 nM).

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: A lower Kd means lower affinity
Protein A binds the ligand with higher affinity than protein B
A hyperbolic curve is consistent with noncooperative binding
Kd equals the ligand concentration at half-saturation
qs.x: Kd is inversely related to affinity: a smaller Kd means tighter binding. Trap: Confusing Kd with an association constant and treating a lower Kd as weaker binding, when a lower Kd means tighter binding.

qs.q: Which protein behavior differs from these hyperbolic curves?
o: Hemoglobin's sigmoidal oxygen binding due to cooperativity
Binding of a single ligand to one site on a monomeric protein
qs.x: Hemoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively (Hill coefficient > 1), giving a sigmoidal curve, while myoglobin is hyperbolic like proteins A and B. Trap: Choosing a one-site monomer or a Michaelis–Menten curve because they sound unusual, when both are hyperbolic and only cooperative hemoglobin binding is sigmoidal.

qs.q: What is the change in A340 of the sample between 0 and 2 minutes, according to Table 1?

qs.q: Why is a blank lacking substrate included?

To ensure the enzyme is saturated
To increase the extinction coefficient of NADH

o: 50 µM/min in the cuvette; 50 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
0.05 µM/min in the cuvette; 2.5 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
50 µM/min in the cuvette; 2500 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
2500 µM/min in the cuvette; 125000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
qs.x: Rate = (ΔA/min)/(ε·l) = 0.311/6220 = 50 µM/min in the cuvette. Multiply by the 50-fold dilution to get 2500 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate. Trap: Forgetting the 50-fold dilution (option A) or slipping by a factor of 1,000 in units (options B and D).

qs.q: Which statement about this assay is INCORRECT?
o: The initial linear portion of the curve gives the most reliable velocity
Both NAD⁺ and NADH absorb strongly at 340 nm, so the signal reflects total coenzyme
NADH absorbs at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not
Substrate must be saturating for the rate to approximate Vmax
qs.x: Only the reduced coenzyme absorbs at 340 nm; that selective absorbance makes the assay possible. Trap: Missing the INCORRECT wording or assuming NAD⁺ also absorbs at 340 nm; only NADH absorbs, so the signal tracks NADH formation, not total coenzyme.

qs.q: Which type of assay couples an enzyme of interest to NADH oxidation so that its activity can be monitored at 340 nm?
o: A coupled assay using lactate dehydrogenase to reduce pyruvate formed by pyruvate kinase
A gel assay using SDS-PAGE mobility
An immunoassay using antibodies against the enzyme
A radioactive assay using ³²P-labeled ATP
qs.x: Pyruvate kinase produces pyruvate; LDH then oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, causing a decrease in A340 proportional to pyruvate kinase activity. Trap: Choosing a gel, immunoassay or radioactive assay; these do not report on NADH oxidation by A340, which is the basis of coupled assays.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Nakamura group investigated turnover of HIF-1α, a regulatory protein that is rapidly degraded in proliferating cells. To measure stability without confounding new synthesis, cells were treated with cycloheximide, an inhibitor of translation elongation, and harvested at the times shown. Lysates were resolved by SDS-PAGE, transferred to a membrane, and probed with an antibody against HIF-1α; band intensities were quantified and normalized to a loading control. Degradation of HIF-1α was assumed to follow first-order kinetics. The researchers hoped to compare half-lives under normal and stressed conditions and to learn whether proteasome inhibition would stabilize the protein. Results from unstressed cells are shown; each value is the mean of three biological replicates, with errors below 5% of the mean. Equal total protein was loaded in every lane, as confirmed by the loading control. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What fraction of HIF-1α remains 90 minutes after cycloheximide treatment?
qs.x: At 90 min, two half-lives have elapsed (100 → 50 → 25%). Trap: Choosing 12.5% (three half-lives) or 50% (one half-life) rather than the value at 90 min; two half-lives have elapsed there.

qs.q: Why is cycloheximide used in this experiment?
o: It increases transcription of the gene
It labels the protein for detection by antibody
It blocks new synthesis so that the loss of existing protein can be followed
It accelerates proteasomal degradation of all proteins
qs.x: Without blocking translation, newly synthesized protein would obscure the decay of the pre-existing pool. Trap: Thinking cycloheximide accelerates degradation or raises transcription rather than stopping new synthesis so only the decay of the pre-existing pool is observed.

qs.q: If the decay continues to be first-order, what percentage of HIF-1α remains after 225 minutes?
qs.x: 225 min = 5 half-lives of 45 min, so 100 × (1/2)^5 = 3.125%. Trap: Miscounting half-lives: 4 half-lives gives 6.25% and 6 gives 1.562%, while 225 / 45 = 5 half-lives gives 3.125%; 96.875% is the amount lost, not remaining.

qs.q: Which statement about first-order decay is INCORRECT?
o: The half-life is independent of starting concentration
The rate of decay is proportional to the amount remaining
The half-life increases as the starting amount of protein increases
The half-life equals ln 2 divided by the rate constant
qs.x: In first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2/k and does not depend on starting concentration. Trap: Accepting that the half-life increases with starting amount as true, confusing first-order decay with kinetics where half-life depends on concentration.

qs.q: HIF-1α turnover is typically controlled by which system?
o: Phosphorylation by glycolytic kinases that leads to secretion
Glycosylation in the Golgi apparatus that prevents degradation
Ubiquitination and degradation by the proteasome
qs.x: Polyubiquitin chains (K48-linked) mark proteins for proteasomal degradation; proteasome inhibitors such as MG132 stabilize short-lived regulatory proteins. Trap: Choosing lysosomal, Golgi glycosylation or secretion routes, none of which explains the short half-life of HIF-1α; the ubiquitin-proteasome system does.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Biochemists in the Mensah laboratory characterized malate dehydrogenase purified from a bacterial expression system, focusing on its response to a candidate small-molecule inhibitor designed to resemble oxaloacetate. Reactions contained a fixed enzyme concentration in buffered solution at 25 °C, and initial velocities were measured at six oxaloacetate concentrations with and without 60 µM inhibitor. Product formation was followed spectrophotometrically for the first 60 seconds, a window in which less than 5% of substrate was consumed. Each velocity represents the mean of three independent reactions, and the standard error was below 4% of every mean. The team wished to determine whether the compound binds the free enzyme at the active site or instead binds elsewhere, and to estimate its dissociation constant for the enzyme–inhibitor complex before testing it in cultured cells. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and the buffer contained no metal chelators or reducing agents that could interfere with the assay. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, what is the initial velocity in the presence of inhibitor when [S] = 40 µM?
qs.x: Reading the inhibitor column at [S] = 40 µM gives 16 µmol/min; the control column value (26.7) is the uninhibited rate. Trap: Reading the uninhibited column (26.7) instead of the inhibitor column at 40 µM, or taking an inhibitor value from another row (10 or 22.9).

qs.q: Which additional experiment would best distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition by this compound?
o: Measure velocity at a single substrate concentration with several enzyme concentrations
Repeat the assay at a lower temperature to see whether inhibition disappears
Measure whether very high substrate concentrations restore the uninhibited maximal velocity
Measure product formation after 60 minutes rather than 60 seconds
qs.x: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so sufficiently high [S] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax regardless of [S]. Trap: Choosing a time-course, temperature or enzyme-concentration experiment, which cannot show whether high substrate outcompetes the inhibitor.

qs.q: Assuming simple competitive inhibition, what is the approximate Ki of the inhibitor?
qs.x: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). Here Km,app/Km = 3, so [I]/Ki = 2 and Ki = 60/2 = 30 µM. Trap: Using Km,app/Km = 3 directly as [I]/Ki gives Ki = 60/3 = 20 µM (option A); since Km,app/Km = 1 + [I]/Ki, [I]/Ki = 2.

qs.q: Which statement about the data is NOT consistent with competitive inhibition?
o: The inhibitor binds the free enzyme in preference to the enzyme–substrate complex
Vmax is lower in the presence of the inhibitor at saturating [S]
The inhibition is weaker at higher substrate concentrations
The apparent Km is larger in the presence of the inhibitor
qs.x: Competitive inhibitors leave Vmax unchanged; the velocities converge as [S] rises. A reduced Vmax would indicate noncompetitive or uncompetitive behavior. Trap: Treating a lower Vmax as consistent with competition; a competitive inhibitor leaves Vmax unchanged and only raises the apparent Km.

qs.q: Many drugs, such as statins and methotrexate, act as competitive inhibitors. Which property of such drugs most directly explains why they are often structural analogs of the substrate?
o: They must bind the enzyme–substrate complex only
They must occupy the same active site as the substrate
They must lower the enzyme's turnover number at saturating substrate
They must bind covalently to the enzyme
qs.x: Competition requires binding to the same site; structural similarity to the substrate (or transition state) lets the drug fit the active site and compete reversibly. Trap: Assuming drugs must bind covalently or only the enzyme-substrate complex; competitive inhibitors reversibly compete for the same active site as the substrate.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: A screening group in the Marchetti laboratory identified a compound that suppresses malate dehydrogenase activity in cell lysates. To learn how it acts, the group measured initial velocities of the purified enzyme at several oxaloacetate concentrations, with and without 40 µM compound. Assays were buffered at pH 7.4 and kept at 30 °C, and the enzyme concentration was held constant. The compound has no structural resemblance to oxaloacetate, and a preliminary docking study placed it in a hydrophobic pocket far from the catalytic residues. The researchers recorded velocities as µmol of product per minute and fit each data set to the Michaelis–Menten equation. They then compared the fitted constants with and without compound, expecting the pattern to reveal whether the compound binds the free enzyme, the enzyme–substrate complex, or both with equal affinity. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and solvent carrier alone had no effect on activity. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which pattern does Table 1 show?
o: The ratio falls steadily as [S] increases
The inhibited velocity exceeds the control velocity at the lowest [S]
The ratio of inhibited to control velocity rises steadily as [S] increases
The ratio of inhibited to control velocity is about the same at every [S]
qs.x: At each [S], v(inhibited)/v(control) = 1/5, so the compound lowers velocity by a constant factor. Trap: Expecting inhibition to shrink at high substrate; the inhibited velocity is one fifth of control at every [S], so substrate does not overcome it.

qs.q: Which experiment would best confirm that the compound does not compete with substrate for the active site?
o: Show that raising [S] to very high levels does not restore the control Vmax
Show that Km increases linearly with compound concentration
Show that the compound's structure matches the substrate
Show that the compound's potency decreases as [S] increases
qs.x: Failure of high [S] to overcome inhibition indicates the inhibitor does not simply compete for the substrate-binding site. Trap: Choosing the option in which Km rises with inhibitor, the signature of competitive inhibition, the opposite of what is being confirmed.

qs.q: If the uninhibited Vmax is 100 µmol/min, what is the apparent Vmax with the compound?
qs.x: Vmax,app = Vmax/α = 100/5 = 20 µmol/min, as seen in the saturating-substrate rows. Trap: Choosing 16.7 µmol/min, which is 100/6, by adding 1 to the factor of 5 instead of dividing Vmax by 5.

qs.q: Which statement about pure noncompetitive inhibition is INCORRECT?
o: The inhibitor can bind both free enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex
Lineweaver–Burk lines intersect on the x-axis
The apparent Km increases because the inhibitor competes with substrate
qs.x: Pure noncompetitive inhibitors leave Km unchanged. Because binding occurs at a distinct site, the lines in a double-reciprocal plot share an x-intercept (−1/Km). Trap: Believing noncompetitive inhibitors raise Km because they lower velocity, when Km is unchanged and only Vmax falls.

qs.q: Which cellular regulatory phenomenon most closely resembles this inhibition pattern?
o: Allosteric inhibition at a site distinct from the active site
Substrate-level competition by a structural analog
Irreversible inhibition by transition-state mimicry at the active site
Product activation of the same enzyme by direct covalent change
qs.x: Binding at a distinct regulatory (allosteric) site that lowers catalytic capacity reproduces the noncompetitive pattern, as with feedback inhibition in metabolic pathways. Trap: Choosing substrate-analog competition, which the passage rules out by noting the compound has no structural resemblance to oxaloacetate.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers in the Fitzgerald laboratory studied three reversible reactions of early carbohydrate metabolism in extracts of rat liver. Each reaction was allowed to reach equilibrium in a sealed reaction vessel at 37 °C and pH 7.0, after which reactants and products were quantified by HPLC to give the equilibrium constant. In a second set of experiments, intact hepatocytes were rapidly freeze-clamped and the steady-state ratio of products to reactants, known as the mass-action ratio Q, was measured for the same reactions. Comparing Q with Keq indicates how far each reaction sits from equilibrium under physiological conditions, and therefore which steps are likely to be regulated. The investigators used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and expected values of ΔG°′ to be consistent with literature compilations. All reagents were of analytical grade, and each reaction vessel was degassed to avoid oxidation of sulfhydryl groups. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which reaction operates closest to equilibrium in hepatocytes?
o: None; all three are far from equilibrium
Reaction A: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP
qs.x: Q/Keq near 1 indicates near-equilibrium operation. Reaction B has Q closest to Keq, so it is the least likely to be a regulatory step. Trap: Comparing Q with Keq by absolute size rather than by the ratio Q/Keq; the reaction nearest equilibrium has Q/Keq closest to 1.

qs.q: Which control best confirms that the measured Keq reflects true equilibrium rather than a slow approach?
o: Double the enzyme concentration and observe a faster rate
Approach equilibrium from both the reactant side and the product side and obtain the same ratio
Lower the temperature to slow the reaction before quantifying
Measure only product concentration at a single time point
qs.x: A true equilibrium ratio is independent of the direction of approach; a path-dependent ratio signals the system has not equilibrated. Trap: Accepting a single time-point ratio as Keq without approaching equilibrium from both directions.

qs.q: For reaction C (Keq = 0.0545), what is ΔG°′ at 310 K, in kJ/mol?
qs.x: ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq = −(0.008314 × 310) × ln(0.0545) = 7.5 kJ/mol (literature value 7.5 kJ/mol). Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign, gives the wrong values. Trap: Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign in ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq.

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: Actual ΔG depends on Q as well as ΔG°′
A reaction with a negative ΔG°′ always proceeds rapidly in the cell
ΔG°′ is related to the equilibrium constant but not to the reaction rate
A reaction with positive ΔG°′ can proceed forward if Q is sufficiently small
qs.x: Thermodynamics specifies direction, not speed. Rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis. Trap: Assuming a negative standard free energy change means a reaction is fast in the cell, confusing thermodynamic favorability with reaction rate.

qs.q: Which mechanism allows cells to drive reactions with large positive ΔG°′ forward?
o: Increasing the enzyme concentration to lower ΔG°′
Raising the temperature enough to make Keq equal 1
Removing the catalyst so the reaction is not rate-limited
Coupling them to a strongly exergonic step such as ATP hydrolysis
qs.x: Enzymes do not change ΔG°′. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol) or keeping Q very low makes the overall ΔG negative. Trap: Thinking an enzyme or a higher temperature can change ΔG°′; only coupling to an exergonic step or a low Q makes the overall ΔG negative.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: A structural biology group at the Hartwell institute is purifying a recombinant enzyme that contains a single surface-exposed histidine near its active site. To locate the residue's ionization constant, the group titrated the protein in a series of buffers while following the histidine imidazole ring by NMR, which reports the fraction of side chains in the protonated, positively charged form. Protein concentration, ionic strength, and temperature were kept constant across buffers, and each measurement was repeated twice. The group later planned to bind the protein to a cation-exchange column and needed to understand how pH controls the protein's net charge. The protonation data also guided a decision about which buffering species to use for storage, since a buffer is most effective within about one pH unit of its own pKa. The protein was greater than 98% pure and monomeric by size-exclusion chromatography. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: At which pH is the histidine approximately half-protonated?
qs.x: Half-protonation (about 50%) occurs at pH = pKa, which in Table 1 is pH 6.5. Trap: Choosing pH 7.5 or pH 5.5, where about 9% or 91% is protonated, rather than pH 6.5, where exactly half is protonated.

qs.q: Which design would best verify that the NMR signal reports histidine ionization and not a pH-dependent conformational change?
o: Repeat the titration without the protein
Repeat the titration at twice the protein concentration
Repeat the titration with a variant in which the histidine is mutated to alanine
Repeat the titration with a different counterion only
qs.x: Removing the titratable group should abolish the signal's pH dependence if it truly reports that residue. Trap: Choosing a no-protein blank, which shows buffer background but cannot show that the signal comes from this histidine rather than a conformational change.

qs.q: What is the ratio [protonated]:[deprotonated] at pH 5.5?
qs.x: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), so log([A⁻]/[HA]) = −1 and [HA]/[A⁻] = 10^1 = 10. Trap: Inverting the ratio to 1:10; at pH 5.5, one unit below the pKa of 6.5, the protonated form predominates 10:1.

qs.q: Which statement about buffers and this titration is INCORRECT?
o: Buffering capacity is greatest near the pKa
Protonated histidine carries a positive charge
The histidine side chain is mostly neutral at pH well above its pKa
A buffer's pH is independent of its conjugate base to acid ratio
qs.x: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation shows pH depends directly on the base-to-acid ratio. Trap: Thinking pH is independent of the base-to-acid ratio; the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]).

qs.q: At physiological pH, why do histidine residues frequently serve as general acid–base catalysts in enzymes?
o: Its side chain is always fully protonated at pH 7.4
Its side chain pKa is near physiological pH, so it can readily donate or accept a proton
Its side chain carries no ionizable group
Its side chain forms disulfide bonds with other residues
qs.x: A side chain pKa near 6–7 means both protonated and deprotonated forms are populated near pH 7.4, ideal for proton transfer in catalysis (e.g., serine proteases). Trap: Assuming histidine is fully protonated at pH 7.4; with a pKa near the physiological range both forms are populated, which is what allows proton transfer.

passages.title: Transmission of genetic information from the gene to the protein · passage
text: Cell biologists in the Nakamura laboratory asked whether a metabolic stressor alters transcription of SOD2 in cultured hepatocytes. RNA was extracted from untreated and treated cells, treated with DNase, and reverse transcribed. Quantitative PCR was then performed with primers for SOD2 and for a reference gene whose expression is assumed to be stable. Each reaction contained a fluorescent DNA-binding dye and was run in triplicate. Amplification efficiency was verified to be close to 100% for both primer pairs, meaning the amount of product doubles each cycle. The cycle threshold, Ct, is the cycle at which fluorescence crosses a fixed threshold; mean values are shown. The group planned to calculate relative expression using the comparative Ct method before deciding whether to examine the promoter region for regulatory elements. RNA integrity numbers exceeded 8.5 for every sample. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which condition shows greater starting amounts of SOD2 transcript, based on Table 1?
o: The data cannot be compared without a standard curve
qs.x: A lower Ct means the threshold is reached earlier, indicating more starting template. With equal reference Ct, the condition with the lower target Ct has higher expression. Trap: Choosing untreated cells because their Ct (26) is the larger number; a lower Ct means more starting SOD2 transcript.

qs.q: Which control best rules out amplification of contaminating genomic DNA?
o: A reaction with double the template
A reaction run at a higher annealing temperature only
qs.x: If product appears without reverse transcriptase, it must come from DNA rather than from RNA-derived cDNA. Trap: Choosing a higher annealing temperature, which alters primer stringency but cannot show whether the signal came from genomic DNA.

qs.q: Using the ΔΔCt method with 100% efficiency, what is the fold change in SOD2 in treated versus untreated cells?
qs.x: ΔCt(untreated) = 7; ΔCt(treated) = 5; ΔΔCt = -2. Fold change = 2^−(-2) = 4. Trap: Choosing 0.25-fold by inverting the ratio; treated cells cross threshold 2 cycles earlier, so expression is 2² = 4-fold higher.

qs.q: Which statement about Ct values is INCORRECT?
o: The reference gene corrects for differences in input RNA
A higher Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
A lower Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
A difference of one Ct corresponds to a two-fold difference at 100% efficiency
qs.x: Ct and abundance are inversely related; more template reaches threshold sooner. Trap: Believing a higher Ct means more starting target because a larger number seems like a larger amount; Ct and abundance are inversely related.

qs.q: If expression changes, which feature of the gene would most directly be examined for a transcription-factor response?
o: The number of introns within the coding region only
The poly-A tail of the mature mRNA only
The anticodon of the matching tRNA
Promoter and enhancer sequences upstream of the transcription start site
qs.x: Transcription-factor binding sites (promoter/enhancer elements) govern transcriptional initiation, linking the Ct data to the regulatory mechanism. Trap: Choosing tRNA anticodons, introns or poly-A tails, which do not set transcription initiation by transcription factors.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Svensson group compared two receptor proteins, A and B, that bind oxygen analog with different affinities. Purified protein was held at 1 nM, a concentration far below either dissociation constant, so that the free ligand concentration was approximately equal to the total added. Ligand was titrated over a wide range, and the fraction of protein with bound ligand was measured by fluorescence anisotropy after each addition reached equilibrium. Each binding curve was hyperbolic and showed no evidence of cooperativity. The researchers intend to use the receptor with the tighter binding as a biosensor, and they want to know what ligand concentration would be required to saturate it at 80% occupancy. All measurements were made at 25 °C in identical buffer. Protein stocks were centrifuged before use to remove aggregates, and ligand stocks were verified by absorbance. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: At [ligand] = 100 nM, what is the fraction of protein A bound?
qs.x: Fraction bound = [L]/(Kd + [L]) = 100/(20+100) = 0.83. The B column gives 0.33. Trap: Students read the B column (0.33) or the protein A value at a different ligand concentration (0.71 at 50 nM, 0.91 at 200 nM) instead of 0.83 at 100 nM.

qs.q: Why was protein held far below the Kd?
o: So that the protein is certain to be fully saturated
So that ligand depletion by binding is negligible and free ligand ≈ total ligand
So that cooperativity can be detected
So that Kd equals the protein concentration
qs.x: If protein were comparable to Kd, binding would deplete free ligand and distort the fit to the simple hyperbola. Trap: Students think a very low protein concentration saturates the protein or reveals cooperativity, but it only keeps free ligand approximately equal to total ligand.

qs.q: What ligand concentration is needed for 80% occupancy of the higher-affinity protein (Kd = 20 nM)?
qs.x: θ = L/(Kd+L) = 0.8 ⇒ L = 4Kd = 80 nM. Trap: Students pick 20 nM (half-saturation) or mis-scale Kd to 40 or 160 nM; 80% occupancy requires [L] = 4 x Kd = 80 nM.

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: A lower Kd means lower affinity
Kd equals the ligand concentration at half-saturation
A hyperbolic curve is consistent with noncooperative binding
Protein A binds the ligand with higher affinity than protein B
qs.x: Kd is inversely related to affinity: a smaller Kd means tighter binding. Trap: Students assume a lower Kd means lower affinity because 'lower' sounds weaker, but Kd is a dissociation constant, so a smaller Kd means tighter binding.

qs.q: Which protein behavior differs from these hyperbolic curves?
o: Hemoglobin's sigmoidal oxygen binding due to cooperativity
Binding of a single ligand to one site on a monomeric protein
qs.x: Hemoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively (Hill coefficient > 1), giving a sigmoidal curve, while myoglobin is hyperbolic like proteins A and B. Trap: Students pick monomeric single-site binding, Michaelis–Menten saturation or myoglobin because they sound like binding curves, but those are hyperbolic like A and B; only cooperative hemoglobin is sigmoidal.

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: In the Petrov laboratory, researchers measured dehydrogenase activity in a liver homogenate by following production of NADH, which absorbs light at 340 nm with a molar extinction coefficient of 6,220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, whereas NAD⁺ does not absorb appreciably at this wavelength. The homogenate was diluted 20-fold in assay buffer before use, and 1 mL reactions in a 1 cm cuvette contained saturating substrate and NAD⁺ at 25 °C. Absorbance at 340 nm was recorded every minute. A blank containing all components except substrate was run in parallel to correct for non-enzymatic changes. The initial linear region of the progress curve was used to calculate velocity. The researchers wished to report the activity of the undiluted homogenate and to compare it with a published value from a different laboratory. The spectrophotometer was zeroed against buffer, and all readings fell within the instrument's linear range. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What is the change in A340 of the sample between 0 and 2 minutes, according to Table 1?
qs.x: A(2 min) − A(0 min) = 0.672 − 0.05 = 0.622. Trap: Reporting 0.672, the 2-minute absorbance, or 0.933 without subtracting the 0.05 starting value.

qs.q: Why is a blank lacking substrate included?
o: To ensure the enzyme is saturated
To increase the extinction coefficient of NADH
To detect absorbance changes that occur without the enzyme-catalyzed reaction
qs.x: The blank accounts for background drift (e.g., contaminating reductants, instrument drift) independent of the reaction under study. Trap: Thinking the blank supplies NADH or sets saturation, rather than showing signal drift that occurs without the enzyme reaction.

qs.q: Using Beer–Lambert, what is the initial rate of NADH formation in the cuvette (µM/min), and what activity does the undiluted homogenate have (µM/min)?
o: 50 µM/min in the cuvette; 1000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
0.05 µM/min in the cuvette; 1 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
50 µM/min in the cuvette; 50 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
1000 µM/min in the cuvette; 20000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
qs.x: Rate = (ΔA/min)/(ε·l) = 0.311/6220 = 50 µM/min in the cuvette. Multiply by the 20-fold dilution to get 1000 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate. Trap: Forgetting to multiply by the 20-fold dilution, giving 50 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate, or misplacing the decimal point in the unit conversion.

qs.q: Which statement about this assay is INCORRECT?
o: Both NAD⁺ and NADH absorb strongly at 340 nm, so the signal reflects total coenzyme
NADH absorbs at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not
The initial linear portion of the curve gives the most reliable velocity
Substrate must be saturating for the rate to approximate Vmax
qs.x: Only the reduced coenzyme absorbs at 340 nm; that selective absorbance makes the assay possible. Trap: Choosing the true statement that NADH absorbs at 340 nm and NAD⁺ does not, rather than the false claim that both coenzymes absorb.

qs.q: Which type of assay couples an enzyme of interest to NADH oxidation so that its activity can be monitored at 340 nm?
o: A gel assay using SDS-PAGE mobility
A coupled assay using lactate dehydrogenase to reduce pyruvate formed by pyruvate kinase
A radioactive assay using ³²P-labeled ATP
An immunoassay using antibodies against the enzyme
qs.x: Pyruvate kinase produces pyruvate; LDH then oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, causing a decrease in A340 proportional to pyruvate kinase activity. Trap: Choosing a radioactive, antibody or gel method, none of which monitors NADH absorbance at 340 nm continuously.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Mensah group investigated turnover of cyclin B, a regulatory protein that is rapidly degraded in proliferating cells. To measure stability without confounding new synthesis, cells were treated with cycloheximide, an inhibitor of translation elongation, and harvested at the times shown. Lysates were resolved by SDS-PAGE, transferred to a membrane, and probed with an antibody against cyclin B; band intensities were quantified and normalized to a loading control. Degradation of cyclin B was assumed to follow first-order kinetics. The researchers hoped to compare half-lives under normal and stressed conditions and to learn whether proteasome inhibition would stabilize the protein. Results from unstressed cells are shown; each value is the mean of three biological replicates, with errors below 5% of the mean. Equal total protein was loaded in every lane, as confirmed by the loading control. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What fraction of cyclin B remains 120 minutes after cycloheximide treatment?
qs.x: At 120 min, two half-lives have elapsed (100 → 50 → 25%). Trap: Stopping at one half-life (50%) or counting three (12.5%); 120 min is two half-lives of 60 min, so 100% falls to 50% and then 25%.

qs.q: Why is cycloheximide used in this experiment?
o: It blocks new synthesis so that the loss of existing protein can be followed
It accelerates proteasomal degradation of all proteins
It labels the protein for detection by antibody
It increases transcription of the gene

qs.q: If the decay continues to be first-order, what percentage of cyclin B remains after 300 minutes?
