qs.q: Which statement about first-order decay is INCORRECT?
o: The rate of decay is proportional to the amount remaining
The half-life equals ln 2 divided by the rate constant
The half-life increases as the starting amount of protein increases
The half-life is independent of starting concentration
qs.x: In first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2/k and does not depend on starting concentration. Trap: Choosing a true statement about first-order decay; the half-life is constant (ln 2/k) and does not rise with starting amount, so the claim that it increases is the incorrect one.

qs.q: cyclin B turnover is typically controlled by which system?
o: Glycosylation in the Golgi apparatus that prevents degradation
Phosphorylation by glycolytic kinases that leads to secretion
Ubiquitination and degradation by the proteasome
qs.x: Polyubiquitin chains (K48-linked) mark proteins for proteasomal degradation; proteasome inhibitors such as MG132 stabilize short-lived regulatory proteins. Trap: Choosing lysosomal, Golgi or secretion mechanisms because they sound like protein fates; short-lived regulatory proteins such as cyclin B are ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Biochemists in the Svensson laboratory characterized lactate dehydrogenase purified from a bacterial expression system, focusing on its response to a candidate small-molecule inhibitor designed to resemble pyruvate. Reactions contained a fixed enzyme concentration in buffered solution at 25 °C, and initial velocities were measured at six pyruvate concentrations with and without 120 µM inhibitor. Product formation was followed spectrophotometrically for the first 60 seconds, a window in which less than 5% of substrate was consumed. Each velocity represents the mean of three independent reactions, and the standard error was below 4% of every mean. The team wished to determine whether the compound binds the free enzyme at the active site or instead binds elsewhere, and to estimate its dissociation constant for the enzyme–inhibitor complex before testing it in cultured cells. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and the buffer contained no metal chelators or reducing agents that could interfere with the assay. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, what is the initial velocity in the presence of inhibitor when [S] = 200 µM?
qs.x: Reading the inhibitor column at [S] = 200 µM gives 75 µmol/min; the control column value (100) is the uninhibited rate. Trap: Reading the no-inhibitor value (100 µmol/min at 200 µM) instead of the 120 µM inhibitor column.

qs.q: Which additional experiment would best distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition by this compound?
o: Measure whether very high substrate concentrations restore the uninhibited maximal velocity
Repeat the assay at a lower temperature to see whether inhibition disappears
Measure product formation after 60 minutes rather than 60 seconds
Measure velocity at a single substrate concentration with several enzyme concentrations
qs.x: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so sufficiently high [S] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax regardless of [S]. Trap: Choosing a temperature or time-course change, which does not test whether high [S] restores Vmax.

qs.q: Assuming simple competitive inhibition, what is the approximate Ki of the inhibitor?
qs.x: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). Here Km,app/Km = 2, so [I]/Ki = 1 and Ki = 120/1 = 120 µM. Trap: Multiplying the inhibitor concentration by the Km ratio of 2 (240 µM) instead of using [I]/(ratio − 1) = 120 µM.

qs.q: Which statement about the data is NOT consistent with competitive inhibition?
o: Vmax is lower in the presence of the inhibitor at saturating [S]
The apparent Km is larger in the presence of the inhibitor
The inhibitor binds the free enzyme in preference to the enzyme–substrate complex
The inhibition is weaker at higher substrate concentrations
qs.x: Competitive inhibitors leave Vmax unchanged; the velocities converge as [S] rises. A reduced Vmax would indicate noncompetitive or uncompetitive behavior. Trap: Thinking a competitive inhibitor lowers Vmax; it only raises apparent Km, and velocities converge at high [S].

qs.q: Many drugs, such as statins and methotrexate, act as competitive inhibitors. Which property of such drugs most directly explains why they are often structural analogs of the substrate?
o: They must bind covalently to the enzyme
They must bind the enzyme–substrate complex only
They must lower the enzyme's turnover number at saturating substrate
They must occupy the same active site as the substrate
qs.x: Competition requires binding to the same site; structural similarity to the substrate (or transition state) lets the drug fit the active site and compete reversibly. Trap: Assuming such drugs bind covalently or only the enzyme–substrate complex rather than competing for the active site.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: A screening group in the Fitzgerald laboratory identified a compound that suppresses aldose reductase activity in cell lysates. To learn how it acts, the group measured initial velocities of the purified enzyme at several glucose concentrations, with and without 20 µM compound. Assays were buffered at pH 7.4 and kept at 30 °C, and the enzyme concentration was held constant. The compound has no structural resemblance to glucose, and a preliminary docking study placed it in a hydrophobic pocket far from the catalytic residues. The researchers recorded velocities as µmol of product per minute and fit each data set to the Michaelis–Menten equation. They then compared the fitted constants with and without compound, expecting the pattern to reveal whether the compound binds the free enzyme, the enzyme–substrate complex, or both with equal affinity. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and solvent carrier alone had no effect on activity. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which pattern does Table 1 show?
o: The inhibited velocity exceeds the control velocity at the lowest [S]
The ratio falls steadily as [S] increases
The ratio of inhibited to control velocity is about the same at every [S]
The ratio of inhibited to control velocity rises steadily as [S] increases
qs.x: At each [S], v(inhibited)/v(control) = 1/5, so the compound lowers velocity by a constant factor. Trap: Expecting inhibition to be strongest at low [S] or to change with [S] (as in competitive inhibition), when the inhibited/control ratio stays constant at every [S].

qs.q: Which experiment would best confirm that the compound does not compete with substrate for the active site?
o: Show that the compound's structure matches the substrate
Show that Km increases linearly with compound concentration
Show that the compound's potency decreases as [S] increases
Show that raising [S] to very high levels does not restore the control Vmax
qs.x: Failure of high [S] to overcome inhibition indicates the inhibitor does not simply compete for the substrate-binding site. Trap: Choosing a signature of competitive inhibition (potency falling as [S] rises, Km rising with inhibitor) or substrate resemblance, which is the opposite of what is asked.

qs.q: If the uninhibited Vmax is 200 µmol/min, what is the apparent Vmax with the compound?
qs.x: Vmax,app = Vmax/α = 200/5 = 40 µmol/min, as seen in the saturating-substrate rows. Trap: Multiplying Vmax by 5 (1000) or subtracting a small amount (195) instead of dividing 200 by the factor of 5 seen in the table.

qs.q: Which statement about pure noncompetitive inhibition is INCORRECT?
o: The apparent Km increases because the inhibitor competes with substrate
The inhibitor can bind both free enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex
Lineweaver–Burk lines intersect on the x-axis
qs.x: Pure noncompetitive inhibitors leave Km unchanged. Because binding occurs at a distinct site, the lines in a double-reciprocal plot share an x-intercept (−1/Km). Trap: Assuming every inhibitor raises apparent Km, which is true only for competitive inhibition; pure noncompetitive inhibition leaves Km unchanged.

qs.q: Which cellular regulatory phenomenon most closely resembles this inhibition pattern?
o: Allosteric inhibition at a site distinct from the active site
Substrate-level competition by a structural analog
Product activation of the same enzyme by direct covalent change
Irreversible inhibition by transition-state mimicry at the active site
qs.x: Binding at a distinct regulatory (allosteric) site that lowers catalytic capacity reproduces the noncompetitive pattern, as with feedback inhibition in metabolic pathways. Trap: Choosing substrate competition by a structural analog, which would raise Km, although the compound lacks substrate resemblance and Km is unchanged.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers in the Hartwell laboratory studied three reversible reactions of early carbohydrate metabolism in extracts of rat liver. Each reaction was allowed to reach equilibrium in a sealed reaction vessel at 37 °C and pH 7.0, after which reactants and products were quantified by HPLC to give the equilibrium constant. In a second set of experiments, intact hepatocytes were rapidly freeze-clamped and the steady-state ratio of products to reactants, known as the mass-action ratio Q, was measured for the same reactions. Comparing Q with Keq indicates how far each reaction sits from equilibrium under physiological conditions, and therefore which steps are likely to be regulated. The investigators used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and expected values of ΔG°′ to be consistent with literature compilations. All reagents were of analytical grade, and each reaction vessel was degassed to avoid oxidation of sulfhydryl groups. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which reaction operates closest to equilibrium in hepatocytes?
o: Reaction A: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP
None; all three are far from equilibrium
qs.x: Q/Keq near 1 indicates near-equilibrium operation. Reaction B has Q closest to Keq, so it is the least likely to be a regulatory step. Trap: Comparing Q with Keq by absolute size rather than by the ratio Q/Keq; the reaction nearest equilibrium has Q/Keq closest to 1.

qs.q: Which control best confirms that the measured Keq reflects true equilibrium rather than a slow approach?
o: Measure only product concentration at a single time point
Lower the temperature to slow the reaction before quantifying
Double the enzyme concentration and observe a faster rate
Approach equilibrium from both the reactant side and the product side and obtain the same ratio
qs.x: A true equilibrium ratio is independent of the direction of approach; a path-dependent ratio signals the system has not equilibrated. Trap: Accepting a single time-point ratio as Keq without approaching equilibrium from both directions.

qs.q: For reaction C (Keq = 0.0545), what is ΔG°′ at 310 K, in kJ/mol?
qs.x: ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq = −(0.008314 × 310) × ln(0.0545) = 7.5 kJ/mol (literature value 7.5 kJ/mol). Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign, gives the wrong values. Trap: Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign in ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq.

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: Actual ΔG depends on Q as well as ΔG°′
ΔG°′ is related to the equilibrium constant but not to the reaction rate
A reaction with positive ΔG°′ can proceed forward if Q is sufficiently small
A reaction with a negative ΔG°′ always proceeds rapidly in the cell
qs.x: Thermodynamics specifies direction, not speed. Rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis. Trap: Assuming a negative ΔG°′ guarantees a fast reaction; ΔG°′ gives direction and extent only, while rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis.

qs.q: Which mechanism allows cells to drive reactions with large positive ΔG°′ forward?
o: Coupling them to a strongly exergonic step such as ATP hydrolysis
Removing the catalyst so the reaction is not rate-limited
Increasing the enzyme concentration to lower ΔG°′
Raising the temperature enough to make Keq equal 1
qs.x: Enzymes do not change ΔG°′. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol) or keeping Q very low makes the overall ΔG negative. Trap: Thinking an enzyme or a higher temperature can change ΔG°′; only coupling to an exergonic step or a low Q makes the overall ΔG negative.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: A structural biology group at the Kowalski institute is purifying a recombinant enzyme that contains a single surface-exposed histidine near its active site. To locate the residue's ionization constant, the group titrated the protein in a series of buffers while following the histidine imidazole ring by NMR, which reports the fraction of side chains in the protonated, positively charged form. Protein concentration, ionic strength, and temperature were kept constant across buffers, and each measurement was repeated twice. The group later planned to bind the protein to a cation-exchange column and needed to understand how pH controls the protein's net charge. The protonation data also guided a decision about which buffering species to use for storage, since a buffer is most effective within about one pH unit of its own pKa. The protein was greater than 98% pure and monomeric by size-exclusion chromatography. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: At which pH is the histidine approximately half-protonated?
qs.x: Half-protonation (about 50%) occurs at pH = pKa, which in Table 1 is pH 7. Trap: Picking pH 6 or 8, where the histidine is still about 91% or 9% protonated, or an extreme pH, instead of the pH at which exactly half is protonated.

qs.q: Which design would best verify that the NMR signal reports histidine ionization and not a pH-dependent conformational change?
o: Repeat the titration with a different counterion only
Repeat the titration at twice the protein concentration
Repeat the titration with a variant in which the histidine is mutated to alanine
Repeat the titration without the protein
qs.x: Removing the titratable group should abolish the signal's pH dependence if it truly reports that residue. Trap: Doubling the protein concentration, changing the counterion or omitting the protein does not test the residue; only removing the histidine shows the signal depends on it.

qs.q: What is the ratio [protonated]:[deprotonated] at pH 6?
qs.x: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), so log([A⁻]/[HA]) = −1 and [HA]/[A⁻] = 10^1 = 10. Trap: Inverting the ratio (1:10) or treating one unit below the pKa as two units (100:1) instead of 10:1.

qs.q: Which statement about buffers and this titration is INCORRECT?
o: A buffer's pH is independent of its conjugate base to acid ratio
Protonated histidine carries a positive charge
The histidine side chain is mostly neutral at pH well above its pKa
Buffering capacity is greatest near the pKa
qs.x: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation shows pH depends directly on the base-to-acid ratio. Trap: Believing a buffer's pH does not depend on its base-to-acid ratio; the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]).

qs.q: At physiological pH, why do histidine residues frequently serve as general acid–base catalysts in enzymes?
o: Its side chain carries no ionizable group
Its side chain pKa is near physiological pH, so it can readily donate or accept a proton
Its side chain is always fully protonated at pH 7.4
Its side chain forms disulfide bonds with other residues
qs.x: A side chain pKa near 6–7 means both protonated and deprotonated forms are populated near pH 7.4, ideal for proton transfer in catalysis (e.g., serine proteases). Trap: Assuming histidine is always fully protonated at pH 7.4 or has no ionizable group, when its pKa near neutrality leaves both forms populated.

passages.title: Transmission of genetic information from the gene to the protein · passage
text: Cell biologists in the Haddad laboratory asked whether a metabolic stressor alters transcription of SOD2 in cultured hepatocytes. RNA was extracted from untreated and treated cells, treated with DNase, and reverse transcribed. Quantitative PCR was then performed with primers for SOD2 and for a reference gene whose expression is assumed to be stable. Each reaction contained a fluorescent DNA-binding dye and was run in triplicate. Amplification efficiency was verified to be close to 100% for both primer pairs, meaning the amount of product doubles each cycle. The cycle threshold, Ct, is the cycle at which fluorescence crosses a fixed threshold; mean values are shown. The group planned to calculate relative expression using the comparative Ct method before deciding whether to examine the promoter region for regulatory elements. RNA integrity numbers exceeded 8.5 for every sample. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which condition shows greater starting amounts of SOD2 transcript, based on Table 1?
o: The data cannot be compared without a standard curve
qs.x: A lower Ct means the threshold is reached earlier, indicating more starting template. With equal reference Ct, the condition with the lower target Ct has higher expression. Trap: Reading a higher Ct as higher expression; a lower Ct means the threshold was reached sooner, so more starting template.

qs.q: Which control best rules out amplification of contaminating genomic DNA?
o: A reaction with double the template
A reaction run at a higher annealing temperature only
qs.x: If product appears without reverse transcriptase, it must come from DNA rather than from RNA-derived cDNA. Trap: Omitting the no-reverse-transcriptase control, so amplification of genomic DNA could be mistaken for cDNA signal.

qs.q: Using the ΔΔCt method with 100% efficiency, what is the fold change in SOD2 in treated versus untreated cells?
qs.x: ΔCt(untreated) = 9; ΔCt(treated) = 6; ΔΔCt = -3. Fold change = 2^−(-3) = 8. Trap: Using 2^(+ΔΔCt) instead of 2^(−ΔΔCt), or forgetting to normalize the target Ct to the reference gene.

qs.q: Which statement about Ct values is INCORRECT?
o: A higher Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
A lower Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
A difference of one Ct corresponds to a two-fold difference at 100% efficiency
The reference gene corrects for differences in input RNA
qs.x: Ct and abundance are inversely related; more template reaches threshold sooner. Trap: Equating a higher Ct with more starting transcript; Ct is the cycle at which signal crosses threshold, so a lower Ct means more template.

qs.q: If expression changes, which feature of the gene would most directly be examined for a transcription-factor response?
o: The number of introns within the coding region only
The poly-A tail of the mature mRNA only
Promoter and enhancer sequences upstream of the transcription start site
The anticodon of the matching tRNA
qs.x: Transcription-factor binding sites (promoter/enhancer elements) govern transcriptional initiation, linking the Ct data to the regulatory mechanism. Trap: Looking for the regulatory effect in the poly-A tail, introns or tRNA instead of the promoter and enhancer sequences that control initiation.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Tanaka group compared two receptor proteins, A and B, that bind a peptide hormone with different affinities. Purified protein was held at 1 nM, a concentration far below either dissociation constant, so that the free ligand concentration was approximately equal to the total added. Ligand was titrated over a wide range, and the fraction of protein with bound ligand was measured by fluorescence anisotropy after each addition reached equilibrium. Each binding curve was hyperbolic and showed no evidence of cooperativity. The researchers intend to use the receptor with the tighter binding as a biosensor, and they want to know what ligand concentration would be required to saturate it at 80% occupancy. All measurements were made at 25 °C in identical buffer. Protein stocks were centrifuged before use to remove aggregates, and ligand stocks were verified by absorbance. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: At [ligand] = 100 nM, what is the fraction of protein A bound?
qs.x: Fraction bound = [L]/(Kd + [L]) = 100/(20+100) = 0.83. The B column gives 0.33. Trap: Choosing 0.33 (option B), protein B's fraction bound at 100 nM, instead of reading the protein A column.

qs.q: Why was protein held far below the Kd?
o: So that cooperativity can be detected
So that Kd equals the protein concentration
So that the protein is certain to be fully saturated
So that ligand depletion by binding is negligible and free ligand ≈ total ligand
qs.x: If protein were comparable to Kd, binding would deplete free ligand and distort the fit to the simple hyperbola. Trap: Choosing cooperativity detection (option A); a low protein concentration prevents ligand depletion and has nothing to do with detecting cooperativity.

qs.q: What ligand concentration is needed for 80% occupancy of the higher-affinity protein (Kd = 20 nM)?
qs.x: θ = L/(Kd+L) = 0.8 ⇒ L = 4Kd = 80 nM. Trap: Choosing 20 nM (option C), the Kd itself, which gives only 50% occupancy; 80% needs [L] = 4 x Kd = 80 nM.

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: A hyperbolic curve is consistent with noncooperative binding
Protein A binds the ligand with higher affinity than protein B
A lower Kd means lower affinity
Kd equals the ligand concentration at half-saturation
qs.x: Kd is inversely related to affinity: a smaller Kd means tighter binding. Trap: Accepting 'lower Kd means lower affinity' (option C) because lower often means weaker; a smaller Kd means tighter binding.

qs.q: Which protein behavior differs from these hyperbolic curves?
o: Binding of a single ligand to one site on a monomeric protein
Hemoglobin's sigmoidal oxygen binding due to cooperativity
qs.x: Hemoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively (Hill coefficient > 1), giving a sigmoidal curve, while myoglobin is hyperbolic like proteins A and B. Trap: Choosing myoglobin or a single-site monomer (options D or B); both give hyperbolic curves like A and B, and only cooperative hemoglobin is sigmoidal.

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: In the Duarte laboratory, researchers measured dehydrogenase activity in a liver homogenate by following production of NADH, which absorbs light at 340 nm with a molar extinction coefficient of 6,220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, whereas NAD⁺ does not absorb appreciably at this wavelength. The homogenate was diluted 10-fold in assay buffer before use, and 1 mL reactions in a 1 cm cuvette contained saturating substrate and NAD⁺ at 25 °C. Absorbance at 340 nm was recorded every minute. A blank containing all components except substrate was run in parallel to correct for non-enzymatic changes. The initial linear region of the progress curve was used to calculate velocity. The researchers wished to report the activity of the undiluted homogenate and to compare it with a published value from a different laboratory. The spectrophotometer was zeroed against buffer, and all readings fell within the instrument's linear range. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What is the change in A340 of the sample between 0 and 2 minutes, according to Table 1?
qs.x: A(2 min) − A(0 min) = 0.174 − 0.05 = 0.124. Trap: Reporting 0.062 (the change per minute) or 0.174 (the raw 2‑minute absorbance) instead of the 0 to 2 minute change.

qs.q: Why is a blank lacking substrate included?
o: To increase the extinction coefficient of NADH
To detect absorbance changes that occur without the enzyme-catalyzed reaction
To ensure the enzyme is saturated
qs.x: The blank accounts for background drift (e.g., contaminating reductants, instrument drift) independent of the reaction under study. Trap: Choosing 'to ensure the enzyme is saturated'; the blank omits substrate and only checks for background absorbance change.

qs.q: Using Beer–Lambert, what is the initial rate of NADH formation in the cuvette (µM/min), and what activity does the undiluted homogenate have (µM/min)?
o: 10 µM/min in the cuvette; 10 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
10 µM/min in the cuvette; 100 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
0.01 µM/min in the cuvette; 0.1 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
100 µM/min in the cuvette; 1000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
qs.x: Rate = (ΔA/min)/(ε·l) = 0.0622/6220 = 10 µM/min in the cuvette. Multiply by the 10-fold dilution to get 100 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate. Trap: Forgetting the 10‑fold dilution (giving 10 µM/min for the homogenate) or mis‑scaling units (0.01 µM/min); the undiluted rate is the cuvette rate times 10.

qs.q: Which statement about this assay is INCORRECT?
o: Both NAD⁺ and NADH absorb strongly at 340 nm, so the signal reflects total coenzyme
NADH absorbs at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not
The initial linear portion of the curve gives the most reliable velocity
Substrate must be saturating for the rate to approximate Vmax
qs.x: Only the reduced coenzyme absorbs at 340 nm; that selective absorbance makes the assay possible. Trap: Believing both coenzyme forms absorb at 340 nm; only NADH does, and that selectivity is what makes the assay work.

qs.q: Which type of assay couples an enzyme of interest to NADH oxidation so that its activity can be monitored at 340 nm?
o: An immunoassay using antibodies against the enzyme
A gel assay using SDS-PAGE mobility
A radioactive assay using ³²P-labeled ATP
A coupled assay using lactate dehydrogenase to reduce pyruvate formed by pyruvate kinase
qs.x: Pyruvate kinase produces pyruvate; LDH then oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, causing a decrease in A340 proportional to pyruvate kinase activity. Trap: Choosing a gel, radioactive or antibody method; none links the enzyme to a continuous NADH absorbance change at 340 nm.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Fitzgerald group investigated turnover of c-Myc, a regulatory protein that is rapidly degraded in proliferating cells. To measure stability without confounding new synthesis, cells were treated with cycloheximide, an inhibitor of translation elongation, and harvested at the times shown. Lysates were resolved by SDS-PAGE, transferred to a membrane, and probed with an antibody against c-Myc; band intensities were quantified and normalized to a loading control. Degradation of c-Myc was assumed to follow first-order kinetics. The researchers hoped to compare half-lives under normal and stressed conditions and to learn whether proteasome inhibition would stabilize the protein. Results from unstressed cells are shown; each value is the mean of three biological replicates, with errors below 5% of the mean. Equal total protein was loaded in every lane, as confirmed by the loading control. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What fraction of c-Myc remains 120 minutes after cycloheximide treatment?
qs.x: At 120 min, two half-lives have elapsed (100 → 50 → 25%). Trap: Choosing 50% by stopping at the first half-life or 12.5% by overcounting; 120 min is two 60-minute half-lives, leaving 25%.

qs.q: Why is cycloheximide used in this experiment?

It labels the protein for detection by antibody
It increases transcription of the gene
It accelerates proteasomal degradation of all proteins

qs.q: If the decay continues to be first-order, what percentage of c-Myc remains after 240 minutes?

qs.q: Which statement about first-order decay is INCORRECT?
o: The half-life equals ln 2 divided by the rate constant
The half-life increases as the starting amount of protein increases
The half-life is independent of starting concentration
The rate of decay is proportional to the amount remaining
qs.x: In first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2/k and does not depend on starting concentration. Trap: Believing a larger starting pool lengthens the half-life; for first-order decay t1/2 = ln 2/k is independent of starting amount.

qs.q: c-Myc turnover is typically controlled by which system?

Ubiquitination and degradation by the proteasome
Glycosylation in the Golgi apparatus that prevents degradation

Trap: Picking Golgi glycosylation, glycolytic-kinase phosphorylation or ribosome degradation because they sound regulatory; c-Myc is ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome.

qs.x: Competition requires binding to the same site; structural similarity to the substrate (or transition state) lets the drug fit the active site and compete reversibly. Trap: Choosing covalent binding or a lower turnover number; reversible competitive drugs are substrate analogs because they must fit the same active site as the substrate.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: A screening group in the Mensah laboratory identified a compound that suppresses alcohol dehydrogenase activity in cell lysates. To learn how it acts, the group measured initial velocities of the purified enzyme at several acetaldehyde concentrations, with and without 40 µM compound. Assays were buffered at pH 7.4 and kept at 30 °C, and the enzyme concentration was held constant. The compound has no structural resemblance to acetaldehyde, and a preliminary docking study placed it in a hydrophobic pocket far from the catalytic residues. The researchers recorded velocities as µmol of product per minute and fit each data set to the Michaelis–Menten equation. They then compared the fitted constants with and without compound, expecting the pattern to reveal whether the compound binds the free enzyme, the enzyme–substrate complex, or both with equal affinity. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and solvent carrier alone had no effect on activity. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which pattern does Table 1 show?
o: The inhibited velocity exceeds the control velocity at the lowest [S]
The ratio falls steadily as [S] increases
The ratio of inhibited to control velocity is about the same at every [S]
The ratio of inhibited to control velocity rises steadily as [S] increases
qs.x: At each [S], v(inhibited)/v(control) = 1/5, so the compound lowers velocity by a constant factor. Trap: Expecting inhibition to weaken at high [S], as with a competitive inhibitor, instead of noticing the constant ratio of 1/5 in every row.

qs.q: Which experiment would best confirm that the compound does not compete with substrate for the active site?
o: Show that the compound's structure matches the substrate
Show that raising [S] to very high levels does not restore the control Vmax
Show that Km increases linearly with compound concentration
Show that the compound's potency decreases as [S] increases
qs.x: Failure of high [S] to overcome inhibition indicates the inhibitor does not simply compete for the substrate-binding site. Trap: Choosing the option that describes competitive behavior (potency falling or Km rising), or a structural match, which would support active-site competition rather than refute it.

qs.q: If the uninhibited Vmax is 80 µmol/min, what is the apparent Vmax with the compound?
qs.x: Vmax,app = Vmax/α = 80/5 = 16 µmol/min, as seen in the saturating-substrate rows. Trap: Multiplying Vmax by 5 (400 µmol/min) or choosing a value near the uninhibited Vmax instead of dividing by the fold change of 5.

qs.q: Which statement about pure noncompetitive inhibition is INCORRECT?
o: The apparent Km increases because the inhibitor competes with substrate
Lineweaver–Burk lines intersect on the x-axis
The inhibitor can bind both free enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex
qs.x: Pure noncompetitive inhibitors leave Km unchanged. Because binding occurs at a distinct site, the lines in a double-reciprocal plot share an x-intercept (−1/Km). Trap: Assuming every inhibitor raises Km because it 'competes' with substrate, which is true only for competitive inhibitors and not for pure noncompetitive ones.

qs.q: Which cellular regulatory phenomenon most closely resembles this inhibition pattern?
o: Allosteric inhibition at a site distinct from the active site
Irreversible inhibition by transition-state mimicry at the active site
Substrate-level competition by a structural analog
Product activation of the same enzyme by direct covalent change
qs.x: Binding at a distinct regulatory (allosteric) site that lowers catalytic capacity reproduces the noncompetitive pattern, as with feedback inhibition in metabolic pathways. Trap: Choosing competition by a structural analog or irreversible active-site inhibition, although this compound resembles no substrate and binds far from the active site.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers in the Lindqvist laboratory studied three reversible reactions of early carbohydrate metabolism in extracts of rat liver. Each reaction was allowed to reach equilibrium in a sealed reaction vessel at 37 °C and pH 7.0, after which reactants and products were quantified by HPLC to give the equilibrium constant. In a second set of experiments, intact hepatocytes were rapidly freeze-clamped and the steady-state ratio of products to reactants, known as the mass-action ratio Q, was measured for the same reactions. Comparing Q with Keq indicates how far each reaction sits from equilibrium under physiological conditions, and therefore which steps are likely to be regulated. The investigators used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and expected values of ΔG°′ to be consistent with literature compilations. All reagents were of analytical grade, and each reaction vessel was degassed to avoid oxidation of sulfhydryl groups. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which reaction operates closest to equilibrium in hepatocytes?
o: Reaction A: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP
None; all three are far from equilibrium
qs.x: Q/Keq near 1 indicates near-equilibrium operation. Reaction A has Q closest to Keq, so it is the least likely to be a regulatory step. Trap: Choosing reaction B or C because Q looks small; closeness to equilibrium is Q/Keq, which is 2 for reaction A but 0.01 for B and C.

qs.q: Which control best confirms that the measured Keq reflects true equilibrium rather than a slow approach?
o: Measure only product concentration at a single time point
Lower the temperature to slow the reaction before quantifying
Approach equilibrium from both the reactant side and the product side and obtain the same ratio
Double the enzyme concentration and observe a faster rate
qs.x: A true equilibrium ratio is independent of the direction of approach; a path-dependent ratio signals the system has not equilibrated. Trap: Choosing faster rate with more enzyme; catalysis speeds approach but does not show that the same equilibrium ratio is reached from both sides.

qs.q: For reaction A (Keq = 652), what is ΔG°′ at 310 K, in kJ/mol?
qs.x: ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq = −(0.008314 × 310) × ln(652) = -16.7 kJ/mol (literature value -16.7 kJ/mol). Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign, gives the wrong values. Trap: Using log10 instead of the natural log (option D, −7.3) or reversing the sign (option B, +16.7).

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: ΔG°′ is related to the equilibrium constant but not to the reaction rate
Actual ΔG depends on Q as well as ΔG°′
A reaction with positive ΔG°′ can proceed forward if Q is sufficiently small
A reaction with a negative ΔG°′ always proceeds rapidly in the cell
qs.x: Thermodynamics specifies direction, not speed. Rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis. Trap: Assuming a negative ΔG°′ guarantees a fast reaction; thermodynamics gives direction, not rate, so the statement about always proceeding rapidly is the incorrect one.

qs.q: Which mechanism allows cells to drive reactions with large positive ΔG°′ forward?
o: Increasing the enzyme concentration to lower ΔG°′
Raising the temperature enough to make Keq equal 1
Removing the catalyst so the reaction is not rate-limited
Coupling them to a strongly exergonic step such as ATP hydrolysis
qs.x: Enzymes do not change ΔG°′. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol) or keeping Q very low makes the overall ΔG negative. Trap: Believing enzymes or higher temperature can change ΔG°′ or Keq; only coupling to an exergonic step or keeping Q low drives such reactions forward.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: A structural biology group at the Abara institute is purifying a recombinant enzyme that contains a single surface-exposed histidine near its active site. To locate the residue's ionization constant, the group titrated the protein in a series of buffers while following the histidine imidazole ring by NMR, which reports the fraction of side chains in the protonated, positively charged form. Protein concentration, ionic strength, and temperature were kept constant across buffers, and each measurement was repeated twice. The group later planned to bind the protein to a cation-exchange column and needed to understand how pH controls the protein's net charge. The protonation data also guided a decision about which buffering species to use for storage, since a buffer is most effective within about one pH unit of its own pKa. The protein was greater than 98% pure and monomeric by size-exclusion chromatography. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: At which pH is the histidine approximately half-protonated?
qs.x: Half-protonation (about 50%) occurs at pH = pKa, which in Table 1 is pH 6. Trap: Picking a neighboring pH, where 90.9% or 9.1% is protonated, rather than the pH at which exactly half is protonated (pH = pKa = 6).

qs.q: Which design would best verify that the NMR signal reports histidine ionization and not a pH-dependent conformational change?
o: Repeat the titration at twice the protein concentration
Repeat the titration with a variant in which the histidine is mutated to alanine
Repeat the titration with a different counterion only
Repeat the titration without the protein
qs.x: Removing the titratable group should abolish the signal's pH dependence if it truly reports that residue. Trap: Choosing a control that removes the protein, doubles it or only changes the counterion, none of which can separate histidine ionization from a conformational change the way removing the histidine can.

qs.q: What is the ratio [protonated]:[deprotonated] at pH 4?
qs.x: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), so log([A⁻]/[HA]) = −2 and [HA]/[A⁻] = 10^2 = 100. Trap: Choosing 1:100, which inverts the ratio, or 1000:1, which overcounts; at pH 4, two units below the pKa of 6, protonated:deprotonated is 100:1.

qs.q: Which statement about buffers and this titration is INCORRECT?
o: The histidine side chain is mostly neutral at pH well above its pKa
A buffer's pH is independent of its conjugate base to acid ratio
Protonated histidine carries a positive charge
Buffering capacity is greatest near the pKa
qs.x: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation shows pH depends directly on the base-to-acid ratio. Trap: Believing buffer pH is fixed by the buffer's identity alone and accepting that it is independent of the base-to-acid ratio, which Henderson-Hasselbalch contradicts.

qs.q: At physiological pH, why do histidine residues frequently serve as general acid–base catalysts in enzymes?
o: Its side chain carries no ionizable group
Its side chain is always fully protonated at pH 7.4
Its side chain forms disulfide bonds with other residues
Its side chain pKa is near physiological pH, so it can readily donate or accept a proton
qs.x: A side chain pKa near 6–7 means both protonated and deprotonated forms are populated near pH 7.4, ideal for proton transfer in catalysis (e.g., serine proteases). Trap: Assuming histidine is always fully protonated at pH 7.4 because it is basic, which ignores that its side-chain pKa lies near neutral pH.

passages.title: Transmission of genetic information from the gene to the protein · passage
text: Cell biologists in the Haddad laboratory asked whether a metabolic stressor alters transcription of HSP70 in cultured hepatocytes. RNA was extracted from untreated and treated cells, treated with DNase, and reverse transcribed. Quantitative PCR was then performed with primers for HSP70 and for a reference gene whose expression is assumed to be stable. Each reaction contained a fluorescent DNA-binding dye and was run in triplicate. Amplification efficiency was verified to be close to 100% for both primer pairs, meaning the amount of product doubles each cycle. The cycle threshold, Ct, is the cycle at which fluorescence crosses a fixed threshold; mean values are shown. The group planned to calculate relative expression using the comparative Ct method before deciding whether to examine the promoter region for regulatory elements. RNA integrity numbers exceeded 8.5 for every sample. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which condition shows greater starting amounts of HSP70 transcript, based on Table 1?
o: The data cannot be compared without a standard curve
qs.x: A lower Ct means the threshold is reached earlier, indicating more starting template. With equal reference Ct, the condition with the lower target Ct has higher expression. Trap: Choosing untreated cells because their Ct (26) is the larger number, forgetting that a higher Ct means less starting template.

qs.q: Which control best rules out amplification of contaminating genomic DNA?
o: A reaction run at a higher annealing temperature only
A reaction with double the template
qs.x: If product appears without reverse transcriptase, it must come from DNA rather than from RNA-derived cDNA. Trap: Choosing the no-primer control with cDNA, which tests primer-independent signal rather than contamination by genomic DNA.

qs.q: Using the ΔΔCt method with 100% efficiency, what is the fold change in HSP70 in treated versus untreated cells?
qs.x: ΔCt(untreated) = 8; ΔCt(treated) = 5; ΔΔCt = -3. Fold change = 2^−(-3) = 8. Trap: Choosing 3-fold by using the ΔΔCt value (3 cycles) as the fold change instead of 2^3 = 8.

qs.q: Which statement about Ct values is INCORRECT?
o: A higher Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
The reference gene corrects for differences in input RNA
A lower Ct indicates a higher starting amount of target
A difference of one Ct corresponds to a two-fold difference at 100% efficiency
qs.x: Ct and abundance are inversely related; more template reaches threshold sooner. Trap: Believing a higher Ct means more template; Ct is the cycle at which fluorescence crosses threshold, so a higher Ct means less starting template.

qs.q: If expression changes, which feature of the gene would most directly be examined for a transcription-factor response?
o: The anticodon of the matching tRNA
The number of introns within the coding region only
Promoter and enhancer sequences upstream of the transcription start site
The poly-A tail of the mature mRNA only
qs.x: Transcription-factor binding sites (promoter/enhancer elements) govern transcriptional initiation, linking the Ct data to the regulatory mechanism. Trap: Picking a feature of translation or mRNA processing (anticodon, introns, poly-A tail), which does not govern transcription initiation in response to a factor.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Kowalski group compared two receptor proteins, A and B, that bind oxygen analog with different affinities. Purified protein was held at 1 nM, a concentration far below either dissociation constant, so that the free ligand concentration was approximately equal to the total added. Ligand was titrated over a wide range, and the fraction of protein with bound ligand was measured by fluorescence anisotropy after each addition reached equilibrium. Each binding curve was hyperbolic and showed no evidence of cooperativity. The researchers intend to use the receptor with the tighter binding as a biosensor, and they want to know what ligand concentration would be required to saturate it at 80% occupancy. All measurements were made at 25 °C in identical buffer. Protein stocks were centrifuged before use to remove aggregates, and ligand stocks were verified by absorbance. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: At [ligand] = 100 nM, what is the fraction of protein A bound?
qs.x: Fraction bound = [L]/(Kd + [L]) = 100/(20+100) = 0.83. The B column gives 0.33. Trap: Choosing 0.33, protein B's value at 100 nM, or a neighboring row for protein A (0.71 or 0.91).

qs.q: Why was protein held far below the Kd?
o: So that ligand depletion by binding is negligible and free ligand ≈ total ligand
So that the protein is certain to be fully saturated
So that cooperativity can be detected
So that Kd equals the protein concentration
qs.x: If protein were comparable to Kd, binding would deplete free ligand and distort the fit to the simple hyperbola. Trap: Thinking the low protein concentration is meant to saturate the protein or make Kd equal protein concentration, rather than to avoid ligand depletion.

qs.q: What ligand concentration is needed for 80% occupancy of the higher-affinity protein (Kd = 20 nM)?
qs.x: θ = L/(Kd+L) = 0.8 ⇒ L = 4Kd = 80 nM. Trap: Choosing 20 nM, the Kd, which gives half occupancy rather than 80%; 0.8 requires L = 4 Kd = 80 nM.

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: Protein A binds the ligand with higher affinity than protein B
Kd equals the ligand concentration at half-saturation
A lower Kd means lower affinity
A hyperbolic curve is consistent with noncooperative binding
qs.x: Kd is inversely related to affinity: a smaller Kd means tighter binding. Trap: Believing a lower Kd means weaker binding, when a smaller Kd means less ligand is needed for half-saturation and thus tighter binding.

qs.q: Which protein behavior differs from these hyperbolic curves?
o: Binding of a single ligand to one site on a monomeric protein
Hemoglobin's sigmoidal oxygen binding due to cooperativity
qs.x: Hemoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively (Hill coefficient > 1), giving a sigmoidal curve, while myoglobin is hyperbolic like proteins A and B. Trap: Choosing myoglobin or a simple saturation curve as different, although both are hyperbolic like proteins A and B.

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: In the Reyes laboratory, researchers measured dehydrogenase activity in a liver homogenate by following production of NADH, which absorbs light at 340 nm with a molar extinction coefficient of 6,220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, whereas NAD⁺ does not absorb appreciably at this wavelength. The homogenate was diluted 20-fold in assay buffer before use, and 1 mL reactions in a 1 cm cuvette contained saturating substrate and NAD⁺ at 25 °C. Absorbance at 340 nm was recorded every minute. A blank containing all components except substrate was run in parallel to correct for non-enzymatic changes. The initial linear region of the progress curve was used to calculate velocity. The researchers wished to report the activity of the undiluted homogenate and to compare it with a published value from a different laboratory. The spectrophotometer was zeroed against buffer, and all readings fell within the instrument's linear range. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What is the change in A340 of the sample between 0 and 2 minutes, according to Table 1?
qs.x: A(2 min) − A(0 min) = 0.672 − 0.05 = 0.622. Trap: Reporting the raw 2-minute reading (0.672, option D) without subtracting the 0.05 starting absorbance.

qs.q: Why is a blank lacking substrate included?
o: To detect absorbance changes that occur without the enzyme-catalyzed reaction
To ensure the enzyme is saturated
To increase the extinction coefficient of NADH
qs.x: The blank accounts for background drift (e.g., contaminating reductants, instrument drift) independent of the reaction under study. Trap: Thinking the blank converts NAD+ to NADH or ensures saturation; it only reports background absorbance drift without the substrate-dependent reaction.

qs.q: Using Beer–Lambert, what is the initial rate of NADH formation in the cuvette (µM/min), and what activity does the undiluted homogenate have (µM/min)?
o: 50 µM/min in the cuvette; 50 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
50 µM/min in the cuvette; 1000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
1000 µM/min in the cuvette; 20000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
0.05 µM/min in the cuvette; 1 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
qs.x: Rate = (ΔA/min)/(ε·l) = 0.311/6220 = 50 µM/min in the cuvette. Multiply by the 20-fold dilution to get 1000 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate. Trap: Forgetting to multiply by the 20-fold dilution (option A gives the same value for cuvette and homogenate) or applying the dilution factor to the cuvette rate (option C).

qs.q: Which statement about this assay is INCORRECT?
o: The initial linear portion of the curve gives the most reliable velocity
NADH absorbs at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not
Substrate must be saturating for the rate to approximate Vmax
Both NAD⁺ and NADH absorb strongly at 340 nm, so the signal reflects total coenzyme
qs.x: Only the reduced coenzyme absorbs at 340 nm; that selective absorbance makes the assay possible. Trap: Believing NAD+ also absorbs strongly at 340 nm so the signal reflects total coenzyme; only NADH absorbs, which is what makes the assay possible.

qs.q: Which type of assay couples an enzyme of interest to NADH oxidation so that its activity can be monitored at 340 nm?
o: A gel assay using SDS-PAGE mobility
An immunoassay using antibodies against the enzyme
A coupled assay using lactate dehydrogenase to reduce pyruvate formed by pyruvate kinase
A radioactive assay using ³²P-labeled ATP
qs.x: Pyruvate kinase produces pyruvate; LDH then oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, causing a decrease in A340 proportional to pyruvate kinase activity. Trap: Choosing a gel, radioactive or antibody assay: none of these links the enzyme to NADH oxidation, so none gives a change in A340.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: The Duarte group investigated turnover of IκBα, a regulatory protein that is rapidly degraded in proliferating cells. To measure stability without confounding new synthesis, cells were treated with cycloheximide, an inhibitor of translation elongation, and harvested at the times shown. Lysates were resolved by SDS-PAGE, transferred to a membrane, and probed with an antibody against IκBα; band intensities were quantified and normalized to a loading control. Degradation of IκBα was assumed to follow first-order kinetics. The researchers hoped to compare half-lives under normal and stressed conditions and to learn whether proteasome inhibition would stabilize the protein. Results from unstressed cells are shown; each value is the mean of three biological replicates, with errors below 5% of the mean. Equal total protein was loaded in every lane, as confirmed by the loading control. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What fraction of IκBα remains 90 minutes after cycloheximide treatment?
qs.x: At 90 min, two half-lives have elapsed (100 → 50 → 25%). Trap: Reading 50% (the 45-minute value) or 12.5% (the 135-minute value) instead of the 90-minute value of 25%.

qs.q: Why is cycloheximide used in this experiment?
o: It labels the protein for detection by antibody
It blocks new synthesis so that the loss of existing protein can be followed
It increases transcription of the gene
It accelerates proteasomal degradation of all proteins
qs.x: Without blocking translation, newly synthesized protein would obscure the decay of the pre-existing pool. Trap: Thinking cycloheximide speeds degradation or labels the protein; it blocks translation so only the decay of existing protein is measured.

qs.q: If the decay continues to be first-order, what percentage of IκBα remains after 225 minutes?
qs.x: 225 min = 5 half-lives of 45 min, so 100 × (1/2)^5 = 3.125%. Trap: Choosing 96.875% (the fraction lost) or 1.562% (six half-lives) instead of five half-lives, 3.125% remaining.

qs.q: Which statement about first-order decay is INCORRECT?
o: The half-life increases as the starting amount of protein increases
The rate of decay is proportional to the amount remaining
The half-life is independent of starting concentration
The half-life equals ln 2 divided by the rate constant
qs.x: In first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2/k and does not depend on starting concentration. Trap: Believing a larger starting amount lengthens the half-life; for first-order decay the half-life is constant and independent of concentration.

qs.q: IκBα turnover is typically controlled by which system?
o: Glycosylation in the Golgi apparatus that prevents degradation
Phosphorylation by glycolytic kinases that leads to secretion
Ubiquitination and degradation by the proteasome
qs.x: Polyubiquitin chains (K48-linked) mark proteins for proteasomal degradation; proteasome inhibitors such as MG132 stabilize short-lived regulatory proteins. Trap: Choosing lysosomal, Golgi or secretion mechanisms; short-lived regulatory proteins like IκBα are tagged with ubiquitin and degraded by the proteasome.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: Biochemists in the Svensson laboratory characterized aldose reductase purified from a bacterial expression system, focusing on its response to a candidate small-molecule inhibitor designed to resemble glucose. Reactions contained a fixed enzyme concentration in buffered solution at 25 °C, and initial velocities were measured at six glucose concentrations with and without 120 µM inhibitor. Product formation was followed spectrophotometrically for the first 60 seconds, a window in which less than 5% of substrate was consumed. Each velocity represents the mean of three independent reactions, and the standard error was below 4% of every mean. The team wished to determine whether the compound binds the free enzyme at the active site or instead binds elsewhere, and to estimate its dissociation constant for the enzyme–inhibitor complex before testing it in cultured cells. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and the buffer contained no metal chelators or reducing agents that could interfere with the assay. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, what is the initial velocity in the presence of inhibitor when [S] = 200 µM?
qs.x: Reading the inhibitor column at [S] = 200 µM gives 42.9 µmol/min; the control column value (100) is the uninhibited rate. Trap: Reading the no-inhibitor column (100 µmol/min) instead of the inhibitor column, which gives 42.9 µmol/min at 200 µM.

qs.q: Which additional experiment would best distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition by this compound?
o: Measure velocity at a single substrate concentration with several enzyme concentrations
Measure whether very high substrate concentrations restore the uninhibited maximal velocity
Repeat the assay at a lower temperature to see whether inhibition disappears
Measure product formation after 60 minutes rather than 60 seconds
qs.x: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so sufficiently high [S] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax regardless of [S]. Trap: Choosing a single-concentration enzyme titration; changing enzyme amount changes the rate but cannot show whether high [S] restores Vmax.

qs.q: Assuming simple competitive inhibition, what is the approximate Ki of the inhibitor?
qs.x: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). Here Km,app/Km = 5, so [I]/Ki = 4 and Ki = 120/4 = 30 µM. Trap: Dividing [I] by the 5-fold Km shift (120/5 = 24 µM) instead of by 5 - 1 = 4, which gives Ki = 30 µM.

qs.q: Which statement about the data is NOT consistent with competitive inhibition?
o: The inhibition is weaker at higher substrate concentrations
The inhibitor binds the free enzyme in preference to the enzyme–substrate complex
The maximal velocity extrapolated to infinite [S] is lower with the inhibitor
The apparent Km is larger in the presence of the inhibitor
qs.x: Correct: C. In competitive inhibition Vmax is unchanged (150 µmol/min in both data sets); only the apparent Km rises (100 to 500 µM). Why the others are wrong: D) the apparent Km increases 5-fold. A) the inhibited rate approaches the uninhibited rate as [S] rises (92.3 versus 133.3 at the highest [S]). B) a competitive inhibitor binds free enzyme, not the enzyme–substrate complex. Trap: Expecting inhibition to be equally strong at all [S]; for a competitive inhibitor, substrate overcomes it and velocities converge at high [S].

qs.q: Many drugs, such as statins and methotrexate, act as competitive inhibitors. Which property of such drugs most directly explains why they are often structural analogs of the substrate?
o: They must bind covalently to the enzyme
They must bind the enzyme–substrate complex only
They must lower the enzyme's turnover number at saturating substrate
They must occupy the same active site as the substrate
qs.x: Competition requires binding to the same site; structural similarity to the substrate (or transition state) lets the drug fit the active site and compete reversibly. Trap: Assuming drugs must bind covalently; reversible competitive inhibitors bind the same active site noncovalently.

passages.title: Structure and function of proteins and their constituent amino acids · passage
text: A screening group in the Lindqvist laboratory identified a compound that suppresses dihydrofolate reductase activity in cell lysates. To learn how it acts, the group measured initial velocities of the purified enzyme at several dihydrofolate concentrations, with and without 40 µM compound. Assays were buffered at pH 7.4 and kept at 30 °C, and the enzyme concentration was held constant. The compound has no structural resemblance to dihydrofolate, and a preliminary docking study placed it in a hydrophobic pocket far from the catalytic residues. The researchers recorded velocities as µmol of product per minute and fit each data set to the Michaelis–Menten equation. They then compared the fitted constants with and without compound, expecting the pattern to reveal whether the compound binds the free enzyme, the enzyme–substrate complex, or both with equal affinity. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and solvent carrier alone had no effect on activity. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: Which pattern does Table 1 show?
o: The ratio falls steadily as [S] increases
The inhibited velocity exceeds the control velocity at the lowest [S]
The ratio of inhibited to control velocity is about the same at every [S]
The ratio of inhibited to control velocity rises steadily as [S] increases
qs.x: At each [S], v(inhibited)/v(control) = 1/2, so the compound lowers velocity by a constant factor. Trap: Students expect inhibition to weaken at high [S], as with a competitive inhibitor, and pick the option in which the ratio rises; here the ratio stays at 1/2 at every [S].

qs.q: Which experiment would best confirm that the compound does not compete with substrate for the active site?
o: Show that the compound's structure matches the substrate
Show that Km increases linearly with compound concentration
Show that the compound's potency decreases as [S] increases
Show that raising [S] to very high levels does not restore the control Vmax
qs.x: Failure of high [S] to overcome inhibition indicates the inhibitor does not simply compete for the substrate-binding site. Trap: Students pick the option showing potency falling as [S] rises, which is the hallmark of competitive inhibition, the very mechanism being ruled out.

qs.q: If the uninhibited Vmax is 60 µmol/min, what is the apparent Vmax with the compound?
qs.x: Vmax,app = Vmax/α = 60/2 = 30 µmol/min, as seen in the saturating-substrate rows. Trap: Students multiply by 2 and get 120 µmol/min, or pick 58 µmol/min as if high [S] restored the uninhibited Vmax; the apparent Vmax is 60/2 = 30 µmol/min.

qs.q: Which statement about pure noncompetitive inhibition is INCORRECT?
o: Lineweaver–Burk lines intersect on the x-axis
The apparent Km increases because the inhibitor competes with substrate
The inhibitor can bind both free enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex
qs.x: Pure noncompetitive inhibitors leave Km unchanged. Because binding occurs at a distinct site, the lines in a double-reciprocal plot share an x-intercept (−1/Km). Trap: Students recall that competitive inhibitors raise Km and attribute that to noncompetitive inhibition, but pure noncompetitive inhibitors lower Vmax and leave Km unchanged.

qs.q: Which cellular regulatory phenomenon most closely resembles this inhibition pattern?
o: Allosteric inhibition at a site distinct from the active site
Irreversible inhibition by transition-state mimicry at the active site
Substrate-level competition by a structural analog
Product activation of the same enzyme by direct covalent change
qs.x: Binding at a distinct regulatory (allosteric) site that lowers catalytic capacity reproduces the noncompetitive pattern, as with feedback inhibition in metabolic pathways. Trap: Students pick active-site transition-state mimicry or structural-analog competition because they involve inhibition, but this compound binds away from the active site and does not resemble the substrate.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers in the Lindqvist laboratory studied three reversible reactions of early carbohydrate metabolism in extracts of rat liver. Each reaction was allowed to reach equilibrium in a sealed reaction vessel at 37 °C and pH 7.0, after which reactants and products were quantified by HPLC to give the equilibrium constant. In a second set of experiments, intact hepatocytes were rapidly freeze-clamped and the steady-state ratio of products to reactants, known as the mass-action ratio Q, was measured for the same reactions. Comparing Q with Keq indicates how far each reaction sits from equilibrium under physiological conditions, and therefore which steps are likely to be regulated. The investigators used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and expected values of ΔG°′ to be consistent with literature compilations. All reagents were of analytical grade, and each reaction vessel was degassed to avoid oxidation of sulfhydryl groups. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which reaction operates closest to equilibrium in hepatocytes?
o: Reaction A: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP
None; all three are far from equilibrium
qs.x: Q/Keq near 1 indicates near-equilibrium operation. Reaction B has Q closest to Keq, so it is the least likely to be a regulatory step. Trap: Picking the reaction with the largest Q or Keq instead of comparing Q with Keq for each reaction and choosing the ratio nearest 1.

qs.q: Which control best confirms that the measured Keq reflects true equilibrium rather than a slow approach?
o: Lower the temperature to slow the reaction before quantifying
Approach equilibrium from both the reactant side and the product side and obtain the same ratio
Measure only product concentration at a single time point
Double the enzyme concentration and observe a faster rate
qs.x: A true equilibrium ratio is independent of the direction of approach; a path-dependent ratio signals the system has not equilibrated. Trap: Believing a faster rate or a single measurement proves equilibrium, when only reaching the same ratio from both directions shows it.

qs.q: For reaction C (Keq = 0.0545), what is ΔG°′ at 310 K, in kJ/mol?
qs.x: ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq = −(0.008314 × 310) × ln(0.0545) = 7.5 kJ/mol (literature value 7.5 kJ/mol). Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign, gives the wrong values. Trap: Forgetting that a Keq below 1 gives a positive ΔG°′, so the answer is +7.5 and not −7.5 kJ/mol.

qs.q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
o: A reaction with a negative ΔG°′ always proceeds rapidly in the cell
A reaction with positive ΔG°′ can proceed forward if Q is sufficiently small
ΔG°′ is related to the equilibrium constant but not to the reaction rate
Actual ΔG depends on Q as well as ΔG°′
qs.x: Thermodynamics specifies direction, not speed. Rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis. Trap: Assuming a negative standard free energy means a reaction is fast in the cell, confusing thermodynamics with kinetics.

qs.q: Which mechanism allows cells to drive reactions with large positive ΔG°′ forward?
o: Increasing the enzyme concentration to lower ΔG°′
Removing the catalyst so the reaction is not rate-limited
Coupling them to a strongly exergonic step such as ATP hydrolysis
Raising the temperature enough to make Keq equal 1
qs.x: Enzymes do not change ΔG°′. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol) or keeping Q very low makes the overall ΔG negative. Trap: Thinking an enzyme or higher temperature changes the standard free energy, when cells actually couple the reaction to a strongly exergonic step.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: A structural biology group at the Fitzgerald institute is purifying a recombinant enzyme that contains a single surface-exposed histidine near its active site. To locate the residue's ionization constant, the group titrated the protein in a series of buffers while following the histidine imidazole ring by NMR, which reports the fraction of side chains in the protonated, positively charged form. Protein concentration, ionic strength, and temperature were kept constant across buffers, and each measurement was repeated twice. The group later planned to bind the protein to a cation-exchange column and needed to understand how pH controls the protein's net charge. The protonation data also guided a decision about which buffering species to use for storage, since a buffer is most effective within about one pH unit of its own pKa. The protein was greater than 98% pure and monomeric by size-exclusion chromatography. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: At which pH is the histidine approximately half-protonated?
qs.x: Half-protonation (about 50%) occurs at pH = pKa, which in Table 1 is pH 6.5. Trap: Choosing a pH where the histidine is nearly all protonated or nearly all deprotonated (99% or 1%) instead of the pH at 50% protonation, which equals the pKa of 6.5.

qs.q: Which design would best verify that the NMR signal reports histidine ionization and not a pH-dependent conformational change?
o: Repeat the titration with a different counterion only
Repeat the titration without the protein
Repeat the titration with a variant in which the histidine is mutated to alanine
Repeat the titration at twice the protein concentration
qs.x: Removing the titratable group should abolish the signal's pH dependence if it truly reports that residue. Trap: Choosing a repeat that leaves the histidine in place (different counterion, no protein, or double the concentration); only removing the titratable residue tests whether the signal reports its ionization.

qs.q: What is the ratio [protonated]:[deprotonated] at pH 4.5?
qs.x: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), so log([A⁻]/[HA]) = −2 and [HA]/[A⁻] = 10^2 = 100. Trap: Inverting the ratio; at pH 4.5, below the pKa of 6.5, the protonated form predominates, so the ratio is 100:1 and not 1:100.

qs.q: Which statement about buffers and this titration is INCORRECT?
o: Protonated histidine carries a positive charge
Buffering capacity is greatest near the pKa
The histidine side chain is mostly neutral at pH well above its pKa
A buffer's pH is independent of its conjugate base to acid ratio
qs.x: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation shows pH depends directly on the base-to-acid ratio. Trap: Believing a buffer's pH is fixed regardless of composition; the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation shows pH = pKa + log(base/acid), so the statement that pH is independent of the ratio is the incorrect one.

qs.q: At physiological pH, why do histidine residues frequently serve as general acid–base catalysts in enzymes?
o: Its side chain forms disulfide bonds with other residues
Its side chain is always fully protonated at pH 7.4
Its side chain carries no ionizable group
Its side chain pKa is near physiological pH, so it can readily donate or accept a proton
qs.x: A side chain pKa near 6–7 means both protonated and deprotonated forms are populated near pH 7.4, ideal for proton transfer in catalysis (e.g., serine proteases). Trap: Thinking histidine is always charged or forms disulfides; its imidazole pKa is near physiological pH, so both protonation states are populated and it can shuttle protons.
